keywords: soil-input uncertainty; solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence; vapor pressure deficit; irrigated cropland; spatial support; TROPOSIF; China; reproducibility

title: Data and analysis scripts for "Coupling the Noah-MP Land Surface Model to the Korean Integrated Model (KIM)"
description: This archive contains model outputs, processed data, and analysis and plotting scripts associated with the manuscript “Coupling the Noah-MP Land Surface Model to the Korean Integrated Model (KIM).” The archive is provided to support the reproducibility of the analyses and figures presented in the manuscript. The archive includes output from offline land surface model simulations using the original (MPorg) and revised (MPnew) Noah-MP configurations, together with the analysis and plotting scripts used to generate the corresponding figures. KIM atmospheric model outputs used for the forecast evaluation are also provided. Figures 13–18 were generated using the KAT (KIM Analysis/Evaluation Tools) visualization and verification system. KAT was used for remapping, calculation of verification statistics, and figure generation. KAT is not publicly available due to institutional restrictions and is therefore not included in this archive. The KIM model outputs used as input to KAT and the individual figure panels generated by KAT are provided. For Figure 19, the numerical verification data underlying the figure are also provided. External reference datasets used in the analyses, including IFS analysis, FluxCom, GLEAM, ERA5-Land, and CERES EBAF, are not redistributed in this archive and should be obtained from their respective data providers. Detailed information on the directory structure, datasets, software requirements, and reproduction procedures, and a summary of source-code modifications is provided in the README files included in the archive.
producing_institution: Korea Institute of Atmospheric Prediction Systems
keywords: Noah-MP; Korean Integrated Model; KIM; land surface model; numerical weather prediction

title: UExP-FNN-U full surface ocean carbonate system
description: Product Information Product name UExP-FNN-U SOCOM-style name UExP-FNN-U Product version v2026-1 Changelog at end of repository Coverage January 1980 – December 2025 Global ocean (including under ice regions) at ~0.2 m depth Resolution Monthly 1° x 1° Contact Daniel J. Ford d.ford@exeter.ac.uk Jamie D. Shutler j.d.shutler@exeter.ac.uk Traceable code and inputs Information on the input datasets and code can be found after the changelog How to reference these data? If these data are used please reference Ford et al. (2024a) and this repository with the version (the version is key to tracability) . Note: If you use these data for a new analysis or publication, please contact Daniel J. Ford (d.ford@exeter.ac.uk). This will allow the opportunity to contribute with detailed information on the dataset and depending on the level of involvement be considered for co-authorship. Product Description The UExP-FNN-U approach is described in detail within Ford et al. (2024a) and therefore we provide a summary of the algorithm for interpolating the fugacity of CO 2 in seawater (fCO 2 (sw) ). The UExP-FNN-U is a two step neural network interpolation technique, the self-organising map feed forward neural network (SOM-FNN) (Landschützer et al., 2014, 2016). The first step is a self-organising map (SOM) which was used to divide the global oceans into regions, or provinces, of similar oceanic conditions. The inputs to this step were monthly climatology of sea surface temperature (SST) from the European Space Agency Climate Change Initiative (ESA-CCI) SST, merged sea surface salinity (SSS) from the CCI and the CMEMS reanalysis (GLORYS12V1; merged using a hierarchy approach described in Gregor et al., 2024), CMEMS GLORYS12V1 mixed layer dapth (MLD), and spatailly and temporally complete OC-CCI chlorophyll-a (chl-a) (Ford et al. 2026a; Sathyendranath et al. 2019) and the Takahashi et al. (2009) fCO 2 (sw) climatology updated in Fay et al. (2024). The SOM produces 16 provinces, and two manual provinces are implemented to cover the Arctic Ocean and Mediterranean + Red Sea using Longhurst biogeochemical provinces (Longhurst, 1998). The second step uses a feed forward neural network (FNN) ensemble (10 members) for each province to estimate the relationships between the target variable (i.e in situ fCO 2 (sw) from the recalculated SOCAT dataset; Bakker et al., 2016; Ford et al., 2025; Ford et al. 2026c) and oceanic properties that likely control their variability. For the UExP-FNN-U v2026-pre1 these were SST, SSS, MLD, chl-a and xCO 2 (atm) and anomalies of each. In v2026-pre1, we implemented a probability based SOM approach, which provides a probability that each monthly 1 degree pixel is assigned to each of the 18 provinces. To achieve the probabilities, the SOM training occurs as in Ford et al. (2024a) and then the inputs are perturbed within the limits of their uncertainties and the resulting SOM provinces retrieved for 400 ensembles. The probability that each monhtly 1 degree regions fall within a province are calculated. If a province probability is found to be less than 5%, this is set to 0 % to reduce computation. Locations where the sum of the probability is greater than 1 or less than 1 are scaled linearly to equal 1. In the FNN training stage the provinces are defined for the initial SOM (i.e the hard provinces that the SOM predicts with the data unperturbed). In the mapping stage the fCO 2 (sw) and the uncertainties are predicted for each location and province, and a weighted sum of the resulting fCO 2 (sw) and uncertainties is taken. This approach was shown to reduce large biases at the edge of provinces and reduced the appearance of provinces in the geographical outputs within a model testbed approach within the Surface Ocean CO 2 mapping intercomparison (SOCOMv2 Experiment 2; Roobaret et al. 2026). Additionally, the global ocean CO 2 sink for v2026-pre1 using the standard SOM approach as in Ford et al. (2024a) compared to this updated probability approach showed only minor differences (~2%). We have used this same probability based apporach in v2026-1. Expansion to Total Alkalinity using a consistent SOM-FNN The UExP-FNN-U approach was expanded to estimate Total Alkalinity (TA) on the same monthly 1 degree grid. The first step, the SOM, was trained on a monthly climatology of CCI-SST, CCI+CMEMS SSS and an annual TA climatology (DIVA interpolated in situ TA). Gregor and Gruber (2021) use the gridded GLODAPv2.2016 surface TA field for this step, but these have not been updated in recent years. Therefore, we use a merged in situ TA dataset produced from observations in GLODAPv3 (Lange et al. submitted) , SNAP-O-CO2v2 and Sharkweb datasets to produce a surface TA annual climatology using DIVA interpolation (Schlitzer and Reiner 2025). Data are currently too sparse to produce a monthly climatology of TA (highlighted in Gregor and Gruber; 2021). The SOM produces 16 provinces for the second FNN step, and there were no manual province modifications for TA. For the FNN step, as described in Gregor and Gruber (2021) the available TA observations are much lower than that for fCO 2 (sw) . Gridding the TA observations onto a monthly 1 degree grid before input into the UExP-FNN-U would greatly reduce the available constraints. Consistent to Gregor and Gruber (2021), the individual bottle observations were provided to the neural network (as the target), and the coincident temperature, salinity, and the WOA phosphate and silicate (WOA nutrients extracted from the monthly 1 degree climatology and linear interpolated to the spatial location). This parameter combination was consistent to Gregor and Gruber (2021), and testing indicated from the quality assessment this was the optimal parameter choice. For the mapping to a monthly 1 degree global grid, the CCI-SST, CCI+CMEMS SSS and WOA phosphate and silicate (for the WOA nutrients monthly climatologies) were used. The selection of CCI-SST and CMEMS SSS ensures that the TA fields are produced to the same SST and SSS as the fCO 2 (sw) , and therefore consistency in the carbonate system. In 2026-1 we also use the probability based SOM approach for the TA mapping as descirbed in the fCO 2 (sw) section. Calculation of full surface ocean carbonate system The remaining components of the carbonate system (i.e DIC, pH etc) were calculated from fCO 2 (sw) and TA using pyCO2SYS (v1.8.3.3) (Humphreys et al., 2022, 2024). The calculation also requires SST, SSS, phosphate and silicate, where the same temperature, salinity and nutrient datasets were used (as used in the neural network stages) to consistently calculate the carbonate system. pH was calculated on the total scale. The dissociation constants of Lueker et al. (2000), bisulfate dissociation constants of Dickson (1990) and total boron-salinity relationship of Uppström (1974) were used as recommended in Orr et al. (2015) and Raimondi et al. (2019) (and are the default sets used in pyCO2sys). The surface ocean carbonate system was therefore considered representative of ~0.2 m water depth. Uncertainties due to the fCO 2 (sw) , TA, SST, SSS, phosphate and silicate were propaged through the caluclations providing a uncertainty due to each component and a total uncertainity. In v2026-1, we also add an uncertainty component due to the dissociation constants as provided in Orr et al. (2018). Calculation of air-sea CO 2 fluxes The air-sea CO 2 fluxes (F) were calculated, such that vertical temperature gradients can be accounted for (Dong et al., 2022, 2024; Ford, Shutler, et al., 2024; Shutler et al., 2020; Watson et al., 2020; Woolf et al., 2016, 2019) as described in detail by Woolf et al. (2016), using FluxEngine v4.2.0 (Holding et al., 2019; Shutler et al., 2016). The CO 2 flux takes the form: F = K 600 (Sc / 600) -0.5 (α subskin fCO 2(sw, subskin) – α skin fCO 2(atm) ) (1-ice) where K 600 is the gas transfer coefficient estimated using the Nightingale et al. (2000) parameterisation and wind speeds from the CCMP (v3.1) (Mears et al., 2022; Remote Sensing Systems et al., 2022). Sc is the Schmidt number estimated using the calculation in Wanninkhof et al. (2014) and the ocean’s skin temperature. α is the solubility of CO 2 at the respective subskin or skin temperature and salinities which was estimated as in Weiss (1974). fCO 2 (atm) and fCO 2 (sw,subskin) are the fugacity of CO 2 in the atmosphere and the seawater subskin layer respectively. The CCI-SST and CCI+CMEMS SSS are considered representative of the subskin temperature and salinities and used in the calculation of α subskin . For the atmospheric side, the ocean’s skin temperature was estimated from the CCI-SST with a cool skin deviation calculated with NOAA-COARE3.6 (Edson et al., 2013; Fairall et al., 1996) using CCMP wind speed, CCI-SST and ERA5 fields as inputs. Skin salinity was calculated assuming a +0.1 psu change from the CCI+CMEMS SSS (i.e a salty skin) as in Watson et al. (2020) and Woolf et al. (2019). fCO 2 (atm) was calculated using NOAA-GML atmospheric dry mixing ratio of CO 2 (xCO 2 (atm) ; Lan et al., 2023), the skin temperature and ERA5 atmospheric pressure following Dickson et al. (2009). Sea ice concentrations from the OSISAF dataset (OSI SAF, 2022) were used for the ice component. Variables All variables are provided in a single netCDF file, that has been zipped to reduce file sizes with a filename: Fordetal_UExP-FNN-U_surface-carbonate-system_vXXXX-X.nc. XXXX-X refers to the version number. Variable Units Description alpha mol m -3 uatm -1 Solubility of CO 2 in seawater alpha_skin mol m -3 uatm -1 Skin solubilty of CO 2 in seawater area m 2 Total surface area of each 1 degree region dic μmol kg -1 Dissolved Inorganic Carbon fco2 μatm Fugacity of CO 2 in seawater flux g C m -2 d -1 Air-sea CO 2 flux (+ve indicates outgassing) ice unitless Sea ice concentration kw cm hr -1 Gas transfer velocity mask_sfc unitless Proportion of ocean in each 1 degree region pH unitless pH on the total scale (i.e [H + ] + [HSO 4 - ]) pH_free unitless pH on the free scale (i.e [H + ]) saturation_aragonite unitless Aragonite Saturation State skin_salinity psu Skin Salinity skin_temperature ºC Skin Temperature subskin_salinity psu Subskin Salinity subskin_temperature ºC Subskin Temperature ta μmol kg -1 Total Alkalinity wind_speed m s -1 Wind speed wind_speed_second_moment m 2 s -2 Second moment of wind speed Each variable contains an uncertainty estimate that follows the BIPM (2008) principles, comprising of multiple components and then a total uncertainty. We refer the user to the netCDF file for available uncertainties, but in most cases the total uncertainty is the required component. title: Global Dam Landsat
description: The Global Dam Landsat (GDL) is a publicly available dataset developed for training and evaluating deep learning models for multispectral image generation and dam construction analysis. Since no public dataset previously provided paired multispectral images acquired before dam construction and after the first reservoir impoundment together with corresponding Dam-Reservoir (DR) masks, GDL was created to address this gap. The dataset was generated using information from the Global Dam Watch (GDW) database, Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 imagery (Landsat 4–9), Google Earth Engine (GEE), OpenStreetMap, the GLC_FCS30D and Dynamic World land-cover datasets, and a newly developed Detection of Initial Reservoir Impoundment (DIRI) algorithm. DIRI estimates the first reservoir impoundment year by analyzing long-term surface water dynamics within the reservoir extent. Each sample contains: 1. A six-band multispectral Landsat image acquired before dam construction. 2. A corresponding six-band multispectral image acquired after the first reservoir impoundment. 3. A DR mask indicating the dam crest, reservoir area, and background. All images have a spatial size of 512 × 512 pixels (covering 15.36 × 15.36 km²) and include the Red, Green, Blue, NIR, SWIR1, and SWIR2 bands normalized to the range [0, 1]. The DR masks were generated using NDWI-based water extraction and land-cover information, followed by manual refinement to ensure accurate reservoir and dam crest boundaries. After quality control and manual verification, the final dataset contains 2,734 samples. GDL is intended for research on remote sensing image generation, conditional generative models, dam and reservoir monitoring, environmental monitoring and management, assessment of the potential environmental and socioeconomic impacts of dam construction, analysis of hydrological and land-cover changes, and the evaluation and comparison of alternative dam development scenarios. By providing spatially explicit information on changes associated with dam construction, the dataset can also support evidence-based decision-making, infrastructure planning, and the assessment of alternative project designs and reservoir configurations.

title: Spatial counterfactual geometry shapes coal-mine impact assessments: research data and analysis code
description: Research data and analysis code supporting the manuscript: “Spatial counterfactual geometry shapes coal-mine impact assessments” This repository contains the derived mine-level datasets, matching outputs, satellite extraction outputs, footprint-geometry sensitivity analyses, formal geometry tests, biomass analyses, recovery-chronology analyses, Earth Engine scripts, statistical analysis code, data dictionaries and provenance documentation used to produce the reported results. The study evaluates how spatial counterfactual geometry affects satellite-derived environmental contrasts between matched surface and underground coal mines. The primary outcomes are land-surface temperature (LST), normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) and woody above-ground biomass (AGB). The repository includes the complete reproducibility archive corresponding to version 1.0.0 of the analysis. Source datasets are third-party resources and remain subject to their original provider terms. These include the Global Coal Mine Tracker, Landsat Collection 2, GLC_FCS30D and the ESA Climate Change Initiative Biomass product. This repository is intended to support reproducibility, peer review and subsequent reuse of the derived analysis materials.

title: Uranium comminution ages and denudation rates for quartz-poor Sumatran catchments, with global ¹⁰Be comparison
description: This dataset contains the supporting tables for the manuscript: "Uranium Comminution Ages as a Denudation Chronometer in Tectonically Active Orogens" It contains: 1. Supplementary Note S1 – Methodology Detailed description of the sequential leaching protocol for detrital uranium isolation, total digestion and uranium purification, MC‑ICP‑MS measurement procedures, determination of the α‑recoil loss fraction (fα), and construction of the flux‑weighted effective initial ratio (A0), including piecewise‑linear integration and Excel implementation. 2. Supplementary Note S2 – Supporting tables Contains two tables: Table 1 Sample details, comminution ages, and denudation rates for detrital sediments from the Asahan and Batang Toru rivers (Sumatra). Comminution ages were calculated under the conventional secular-equilibrium assumption ( A ₀ = 1) and with the flux-weighted effective initial ratio ( A ₀ᵉᶠᶠ). Denudation rates were derived via the steady-state relation ε = h / t com using SoilGrids regolith thicknesses. Table 2 Global comparison of uranium-series comminution-age-derived denudation rates with independent in-situ ¹⁰Be denudation rates. For each catchment, the comminution age is calculated first under the conventional A ₀ = 1 assumption, and then with a representative non-equilibrium A ₀ (0.98–0.99), consistent with the bedrock ²³⁴U depletion observed in active orogens. The ¹⁰Be denudation rate serves as the independent reference.

title: CitiesGOER: Globally Observed Environmental Data for 52,602 Cities with a Population ≥ 5000
description: CitiesGOER is a database that provides environmental data for 52,602 cities and 48 environmental variables, including 38 bioclimatic variables, 8 soil variables and 2 topographic variables. Data were extracted from the same 30 arc-seconds global grid layers that were prepared when making the TreeGOER (Tree Globally Observed Environmental Ranges) database that is available from https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7922927 . Details on the preparations of these layers are provided by Kindt, R. (2023). TreeGOER: A database with globally observed environmental ranges for 48,129 tree species . Global Change Biology 29: 6303–6318. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/gcb.16914 . CitiesGOER was designed to be used together with TreeGOER and possibly also with the GlobalUsefulNativeTrees database (Kindt et al. 2023 ) to allow users to filter suitable tree species based on environmental conditions of the planting site. The identities and coordinates of cities were sourced from a data set with information for cities with a population size larger than 1000 that was created by Opendatasoft and made available from https://public.opendatasoft.com/explore/dataset/geonames-all-cities-with-a-population-1000/table/?disjunctive.cou_name_en&sort=name . The data was downloaded on 22-JULY-2023 and afterwards filtered for cities with a population of 5000 or above. Cities where information on the country was missing were removed. The coordinates of cities were used to extract the environmental data via the terra package (Hijmans et al. 2022, version 1.6-47) in the R 4.2.1 environment . Version 2023.08 provided median values from 23 Global Climate Models (GCMs) for Shared Socio-Economic Pathway (SSP) 1-2.6 and from 18 GCMs for SSP 3-7.0, both for the 2050s (2041-2060). Similar methods were used to calculate these median values as in the case studies for the TreeGOER manuscript (calculations were partially done via the BiodiversityR::ensemble.envirem.run function and with downscaled bioclimatic and monthly climate 2.5 arc-minutes future grid layers available from WorldClim 2.1 ). Version 2023.09 used similar methods as for previous versions to provide median values from 13 GCMs for the 2090s (2081-2100) for SSP 5-8.5. The locations of the 52,602 cities are mapped in one of the series available from the TreeGOER Global Zones atlas that can be obtained from https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8252756 . Version 2024.10 includes a new data set that documents the location of the city locations in Holdridge Life Zones . Information is given for historical (1901-1920), contemporary (1979-2013) and future (2061-2080; separately for RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5) climates inferred from global raster layers that are available for download from DRYAD and were created for the following article: Elsen et al. 2022. Accelerated shifts in terrestrial life zones under rapid climate change. Global Change Biology , 28, 918–935. https://doi.org/10.1111/gcb.15962 . Version 2024.10 further includes Holdridge Life Zones for the climates that were available from the previous versions, calculating biotemperatures and life zones with similar methods as used by Holdridge ( 1947 ; 1967 ) and Elsen et al. ( 2022 ) (for future climates, median values were determined first for monthly maximum and minimum temperatures across GCMs ). The distributions of the 48,129 species documented in TreeGOER across the Holdridge Life Zones are given in this Zenodo archive: https://zenodo.org/records/14020914 . Version 2024.11 includes a new data set that documents the location of the city locations in Köppen-Geiger climate zones . Information is given for historical (1901-1930, 1931-1960, 1961-1990) and future (2041-2070 and 2071-2099) climates, with for the future climates seven scenarios each (SSP 1-1.9, SSP 1-2.6, SSP 2-4.5, SSP 3-7.0, SSP 4-3.4, SSP 4-6.0 and SSP 5-8.5). This data set was created from 30 arc-second raster layers available via: Beck, H.E., McVicar, T.R., Vergopolan, N. et al. High-resolution (1 km) Köppen-Geiger maps for 1901–2099 based on constrained CMIP6 projections. Sci Data 10, 724 (2023). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-023-02549-6 Version 2025.03 includes extra columns for the baseline, 2050s and 2090s datasets that partially correspond to climate zones used in the GlobalUsefulNativeTrees database. One of these zones are the Whittaker biome types , available as a polygon from the plotbiomes package (see also here ). Whittaker biome types were extracted with similar R scripts as described by Kindt 2025 (these were also used to calculate environmental ranges of TreeGOER species, as archived here ). Version 2025.03 further includes information for the baseline climate on the steady state water table depth, obtained from a 30 arc-seconds raster layer calculated by the GLOBGM v1.0 model (Verkaik et al. 2024 ). Also included was the elevation, obtained from the same WorldClim 2.1 raster layer used to prepare TreeGOER. Version 2026.04 includes a new Excel workbook that provides the nearest urban centre centroid from the Global Human Settlement Urban Centre Database ( UCDB R2024A, reference epoch 2025 , World Mollweide, EPSG:54009, 1km; https://human-settlement.emergency.copernicus.eu/datasets.php ; Melchiori et al. 2024 ). Different searches were done for the nearest urban centre centroid, searching among all centres, among all centres with a 2025 population size ≥ 100,000, among all centres with a population size ≥ 500,000, among all centres with a population size ≥ 1 million, among all centres with a population size ≥ 5 million and among all centres with a population size ≥ 10 million. Distances between city locations from CitiesGOER and urban centre centroids were calculated in R via geosphere::distGeo (version 1.5-20; Hijmans 2024 ). Version 2026.09 includes a new Excel workbook (CitiesGOER_GAIPED) that provide the locations of cities in Climatic Moisture Index zones ( https://zenodo.org/records/21808912 ) calculated via the Potential Evapotranspiration ( ET 0 ) obtained from the Global Aridity Index and Potential Evapotranspiration Database (GAIPED; Zomer et al. 2022 ). Version 2026.09 also includes a new Excel workbook (CitiesGOER_Global Climate Zones_Audebert) that provides the locations of cities in Global Climate Zones derived via the Mean Annual Biotemperature and the Inverted Aridity Index ( https://zenodo.org/records/21901225 ), using the decision framework developed by Audebert et al. ( 2026 ). As an alternative to CitiesGOER, the ClimateForecasts database ( https://zenodo.org/records/10776414 ) documents the environmental conditions at the locations of 15,504 weather stations. ClimateForecasts was integrated in the GlobalUsefulNativeTrees database (see Kindt et al. 2023 ). When using CitiesGOER in your work, cite this depository and the following: Fick, S. title: Data and code for "Physiological costs of drought resistance shape vegetation recovery"
description: This Zenodo record contains the analysis-ready data and Python scripts supporting the manuscript "Physiological costs of drought resistance shape vegetation recovery". The study examines the relationships between the physiological costs of drought resistance and vegetation recovery using satellite observations, meteorological datasets, and FLUXNET measurements during 2018-2023. The deposited data include event-level and model-ready tables for the main analysis, the alternative-meteorology analysis, and the FLUXNET site-level evaluation. The deposited code contains the Python scripts used for the analyses and figure generation reported in the manuscript. The original TROPOSIF, MODIS LAI, ERA5-Land, GLEAM, MERRA-2, and FLUXNET datasets are not redistributed in this record and should be obtained from the original providers identified in the manuscript’s Data availability statement.

title: ClimateForecasts: Globally Observed Environmental Data for 15,504 Weather Station Locations
description: ClimateForecasts is a database that provides environmental data for 15,504 weather station locations and 49 environmental variables, including 38 bioclimatic variables, 8 soil variables and 3 topographic variables. Data were extracted from the same 30 arc-seconds global grid layers that were prepared when making the TreeGOER (Tree Globally Observed Environmental Ranges) database that is available from https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7922927 . Details on the preparations of these layers are provided by Kindt, R. (2023). TreeGOER: A database with globally observed environmental ranges for 48,129 tree species . Global Change Biology 29: 6303–6318. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/gcb.16914 . A similar extraction process was used for the CitiesGOER database that is also available from Zenodo via https://zenodo.org/doi/10.5281/zenodo.8175429 . ClimateForecasts (as the CitiesGOER) was designed to be used together with TreeGOER and possibly also with the GlobalUsefulNativeTrees database (Kindt et al. 2023 ) or EcoregionsTreeFinder (Kindt & Pedercini 2025 ) to allow users to filter suitable tree species based on environmental conditions of the planting site. One example of combining data from these different sets in the R statistical environment is available from this Rpub: https://rpubs.com/Roeland-KINDT/1114902 . The identities including the geographical coordinates of weather stations were sourced from Meteostat , specifically by downloading (17-FEB-2024) the ‘lite dump’ data set with information for active weather stations only. Two weather stations where the country could not be determined from the ISO 3166-1 code of ‘XA’ were removed. If weather stations had the same name, but occurred in different ISO 3166-2 regions, this region code was added to the name of the weather station between square brackets. Afterwards duplicates (weather stations of the same name and region) were manually removed. Bioclimatic variables for future climates correspond to the median values from 24 Global Climate Models (GCMs) for Shared Socio-Economic Pathway (SSP) 1-2.6 for the 2050s (2041-2060), from 21 GCMs for SSP 3-7.0 for the 2050s and from 13 GCMs for SSP 5-8.5 for the 2090s. Similar methods were used to calculate these median values as in the case studies for the TreeGOER manuscript (calculations were partially done via the BiodiversityR::ensemble.envirem.run function and with downscaled bioclimatic and monthly climate 2.5 arc-minutes future grid layers available from WorldClim 2.1 ). Maps were added in version 2024.03 where locations of weather stations were shown on a map of the Climatic Moisture Index (CMI). These maps were created by a similar process as in the TreeGOER Global Zones Atlas from the environmental raster layers used to create the TreeGOER via the terra package (Hijmans et al. 2022, version 1.7-46) in the R 4.2.1 environment . Added country boundaries were obtained from Natural Earth as Admin 0 – countries vector layers (version 5.1.1). Also added after obtaining them from Natural Earth were Admin 0 – Breakaway, Disputed areas (version 5.1.0, coloured yellow in the atlas) and Roads (version 5.0.0, coloured red in the atlas). For countries where the GlobalUsefulNativeTrees database included subnational levels, boundaries were added and depicted as dot-dash lines. These subnational levels correspond to level 3 boundaries in the World Geographical Scheme for Recording Plant Distributions. These were obtained from https://github.com/tdwg/wgsrpd . Check Brummit 2001 for details such as the maps shown at the end of this document. Maps for version 2024.07 modified the dimensions of the sheets to those used in version 2024.06 of the TreeGOER Global Zones Atlas . Another modification was the inclusion of Natural Earth boundaries for Lakes (version 5.0.0, coloured darkblue in the atlas). Version 2024.10 includes a new data set that documents the location of the city locations in Holdridge Life Zones . Information is given for historical (1901-1920), contemporary (1979-2013) and future (2061-2080; separately for RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5) that are available for download from DRYAD and were created for the following article: Elsen et al. 2022. Accelerated shifts in terrestrial life zones under rapid climate change. Global Change Biology , 28, 918–935. https://doi.org/10.1111/gcb.15962 . Version 2024.10 further includes Holdridge Life Zones for the climates available from the previously included climates, calculating biotemperatures and life zones with similar methods as used by Holdridge ( 1947 ; 1967 ) and Elsen et al. ( 2022 ) (for future climates, median values were determined first for monthly maximum and minimum temperatures across GCMs ). The distributions of the 48,129 species documented in TreeGOER across the Holdridge Life Zones are given in this Zenodo archive: https://zenodo.org/records/14020914 . Version 2024.11 includes a new data set that documents the location of the weather stations in Köppen-Geiger climate zones . Information is given for historical (1901-1930, 1931-1960, 1961-1990) and future (2041-2070 and 2071-2099) climates, with for the future climates seven scenarios each (SSP 1-1.9, SSP 1-2.6, SSP 2-4.5, SSP 3-7.0, SSP 4-3.4, SSP 4-6.0 and SSP 5-8.5). This data set was created from raster layers available via: Beck, H.E., McVicar, T.R., Vergopolan, N. et al. High-resolution (1 km) Köppen-Geiger maps for 1901–2099 based on constrained CMIP6 projections. Sci Data 10, 724 (2023). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-023-02549-6 . Version 2025.03 includes extra columns for the baseline, 2050s and 2090s datasets that partially correspond to climate zones used in the GlobalUsefulNativeTrees database. One of these zones are the Whittaker biome types , available as a polygon from the plotbiomes package (see also here ). Whittaker biome types were extracted with similar R scripts as described by Kindt 2025 (these were also used to calculate environmental ranges of TreeGOER species, as archived here ). Version 2025.03 further includes information for the baseline climate on the steady state water table depth, obtained from a 30 arc-seconds raster layer calculated by the GLOBGM v1.0 model (Verkaik et al. 2024 ). Version 2026.04 includes a new Excel workbook that provides the nearest urban centre centroid from the Global Human Settlement Urban Centre Database ( UCDB R2024A, reference epoch 2025 , World Mollweide, EPSG:54009, 1km; https://human-settlement.emergency.copernicus.eu/datasets.php ; Melchiori et al. 2024 ). Different searches were done for the nearest urban centre centroid, searching among all centres, among all centres with a 2025 population size ≥ 100,000, among all centres with a population size ≥ 500,000, among all centres with a population size ≥ 1 million, among all centres with a population size ≥ 5 million and among all centres with a population size ≥ 10 million. This distance was calculated in R via geosphere::distGeo (version 1.5-20; Hijmans 2024 ). Version 2026.09 includes a new Excel workbook (CitiesGOER_GAIPED) that provide the locations of cities in Climatic Moisture Index zones ( https://zenodo.org/records/21808912 ) calculated via the Potential Evapotranspiration ( ET 0 ) obtained from the Global Aridity Index and Potential Evapotranspiration Database (GAIPED; Zomer et al. 2022 ). Version 2026.09 also includes a new Excel workbook (CitiesGOER_Global Climate Zones_Audebert) that provides the locations of cities in Global Climate Zones derived via the Mean Annual Biotemperature and the Inverted Aridity Index ( https://zenodo.org/records/21901225 ), using the decision framework developed by Audebert et al. title: Global Reservoir Sedimentation Rate (GRSR) dataset
description: The Global Reservoir Sedimentation Rate (GRSR) dataset provides estimates of annual sediment volume and reservoir sedimentation rate (RSR) for 34,372 reservoirs worldwide. The dataset was developed using the Integrated Reservoir Sedimentation Prediction (IRSP) framework, which integrates machine learning with climatic, geomorphic, hydrological, and reservoir-specific predictors. For each reservoir, the dataset provides the predicted annual sediment volume, its prediction variability quantified by the standard deviation (SD) across spatial cross-validation folds, and the RSR, defined as the ratio of annual sediment volume to initial reservoir storage capacity. Each reservoir is linked to the Global Dam Watch (GDW) v1.0 dataset through its corresponding GDW identifier.

title: Analysis-derived datasets for: "Rating Curves Dominate Flood Exposure Uncertainty in Data-Scarce Transboundary Basins"
description: Derived datasets underlying Ismail and Yamashiki, "Rating Curves Dominate Flood Exposure Uncertainty in Data-Scarce Transboundary Basins", submitted to Earth Systems and Environment. The study assesses fluvial flood hazard and population exposure across Pakistan's five major drainage basins (872,782 km², 99% of national territory) from the 50-year to the 500-year return period, combining Height Above Nearest Drainage (HAND) inundation mapping with GloFAS ERA5 reanalysis discharge, Generalised Extreme Value flood frequency analysis, and hydraulic-geometry depth estimation. A first-order sensitivity decomposition attributes total exposure uncertainty to four sources: rating curve parameters, DEM resolution, GEV parameter uncertainty and population data uncertainty. CONTENTS Derived datasets (14 CSV files) AMS_5basins.csv annual maximum series, five basins, 1979-2025 GEV_parameters_47yr.csv fitted GEV location, scale and shape parameters gev_shape_intervals.csv 95% intervals on the shape parameter GEV_return_levels_47yr.csv return levels, T50 to T500 prep_design_discharges.csv design discharges by basin and return period prep_depths.csv design depths from the generalised rating curve prep_depth_agreement.csv depth agreement across rating curve formulations prep_exposure_90m.csv population and built-up exposure, 90 m framework prep_exposure_southern_30m.csv Southern Basin exposure at 30 m prep_exposure_ranges.csv exposure ranges and range factors by basin prep_national_totals.csv national exposure totals prep_uncertainty_decomposition.csv four-source sensitivity decomposition prep_central_bayes.csv Central Basin Bayesian GEV estimates prior_sensitivity_grid.csv prior sensitivity for the Bayesian fit Published tables (22 CSV files) Every table in the paper as a separate file: the five main tables (Table1-Table5) and all seventeen supplementary table parts (TableS1-TableS14, including the a/b splits of S5, S6 and S12), exactly as published. Every number reported in the paper can be checked directly against these files. NOT INCLUDED Input rasters and gauge records are third-party data distributed under their own terms and are not redistributed here. Their sources and versions are listed in the paper's Data Availability statement: GloFAS ERA5 reanalysis discharge v4.0 (Copernicus Climate Change Service); SRTM 30 m and 90 m (NASA Earthdata, USGS EarthExplorer); GHS-POP and GHS-BUILT-S R2023A epoch 2025 (European Commission JRC); HydroBASINS Level 4 (HydroSHEDS); Sentinel-1 GRD (Copernicus, via Google Earth Engine); Global Flood Database 2010 extent. Gauge records are available from the Global Runoff Data Centre, Koblenz, on request under their data-sharing policy and are not redistributable. Analysis code is available from the corresponding author on reasonable request. CHANGES FROM VERSION 1.0 Version 1.0 (April 2026) accompanied the originally submitted manuscript. This version corresponds to the revised manuscript and supersedes it. The sensitivity decomposition has been recomputed: the population uncertainty term now uses the full width of the symmetric ±30% bound on gridded population counts, as set out in Section 3.7 of the revised paper. Shape-parameter confidence intervals, design depths, Southern Basin dual-resolution exposure and the full set of published tables have been added.

title: Soil Organic Carbon Threshold and Historical-baseline Datasets Underlying a Soil Degradation Boundary Assessment for India
description: Overview This record contains the full dataset (data/) supporting the Research Paper titled Integrating functionally-based soil organic carbon threshold models with reconstructed historical baselines to evaluate a soil degradation boundary in India and every raw/reconstructed geospatial input, every pixel- and ecoregion-level analysis-ready table, and every precomputed intermediate result (threshold-fit curves, sensitivity and resilience classifications) used to generate the Research paper results using the code accessible openly as Jupyter-notebook analysis code on https://github.com/sirtiza34/SOC_Functional_Thresholds_India_Analysis and https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22806576 . Together they allow full reproduction of the Research Paper's quantitative results. All the dataset files are distributed only through this Zenodo record and the code repositories document this and points here. Spatial and temporal scope The dataset covers the soilscapes delimited by the territorial extents of India. Contemporary layers are at 250 m pixel resolution (50.48 million pixels) and temporal snapshot of 2019 developed from the SOC concentration data available at https://soilgrids.org/ . The historical baseline is sourced from the Sanderman et al. (2017)’s paleo-SOC reconstructions available at https://github.com/whrc/Soil-Carbon-Debt . The baseline is reconstructed on a coarser (~10 km) grid. All analyses are synthesized to 49 terrestrial ecoregions (World Wildlife Federation) covering the territory of India, and further stratified into 1,156 ecoregion × soil-order × land-use Environmental Context Units (ECUs) for threshold assignment. Contents, by category Pixel-level analysis-ready tables (the three large files) master_analysis_database.parquet — the master contemporary pixel database, 50.48 million rows, carrying assigned functional thresholds and derived metrics for every 250 m pixel in India. step6_functional_state_sample.csv — a spatially block-declustered sample of 395,750 pixels carrying per-pixel probability of being below threshold, P(SOC<T), for each of the four response domains. step4_distance_sample.csv — a pixel sample used to compute distance-to-functional-transition. Geospatial layers (rasters and vectors) ecoregion_id.tif, accel_class_map.tif, step10_feature_stack.tif, step13_soc_stack.tif — raster layers used in mapping and feature construction. step11_map_c_class_raster.npy / step14_boundary_raster.npy (with matching *_meta.pkl files) — precomputed classification and boundary-classification rasters plus their georeferencing metadata. india_boundary.geojson — national boundary vector used for map masking/plotting. Ecoregion-level and threshold tables About 30 CSV files cover, among others, the common analytical framework and state variables per ecoregion, tiered threshold assignment and tier-usage area shares, national and per-ecoregion threshold estimates and their uncertainty, historical-depletion/functional-risk correlation by response domain, degradation-boundary classification per ecoregion, area-weighted vs. unit-weighted synthesis, directional consistency and cross-domain overlap, resilience-opportunity and continued-loss-risk groupings, degradation hotspot lists, and area-weighting tables. Precomputed model curves step12_curves.pkl, step13_curves.pkl — fitted threshold-response curve objects. Data provenance Historical SOC baseline: depth-integrated (0–30 cm) reconstruction following the global SOC-debt method of Sanderman, Hengl & Fiske (2017, PNAS). Contemporary soil properties: SoilGrids v2.0 (Poggio et al., 2021, SOIL). Ecoregion boundaries: WWF terrestrial ecoregions. File formats GeoTIFF (.tif), NumPy array (.npy) with pickled metadata (.pkl), GeoJSON (.geojson), Apache Parquet (.parquet), and CSV — all openly readable with standard open-source GIS/Python tooling (rasterio, pyarrow, pandas, geopandas).

title: A Global Soil Spectral Library and Soil Organic Carbon Estimation Dataset Based on Geographical Stratification
description: This dataset comprises 784 topsoil samples selected from the Open Soil Spectral Library (OSSL), including soil organic carbon content, geographic coordinates, and visible–near-infrared spectral data covering 400–2400 nm at a standardized 10 nm interval. The dataset also integrates ten environmental covariates: clay content, silt content, cation exchange capacity, soil pH, elevation, slope, annual mean temperature, annual precipitation, NDVI, and land-cover type. Based on these covariates, the samples were classified into five geographical environmental zones using a Gaussian mixture model. The dataset supports comparisons between global and geographically stratified models for soil organic carbon estimation and facilitates the regional application of global soil spectral libraries.

title: The Global Carbon Budget (GCB) Allocation Debate in Post-Paris Climate Politics: New Insights for Current Discussions-Database Construction
description: The deposit contains three tables. gcb_panel.csv is a country–year panel with 13,327 rows covering 1990–2050: greenhouse gas emissions in CO₂e with and without LULUCF, population observed to 2019 and projected thereafter, and GDP at current and at constant 2015 prices. gcb_indicators.csv holds one row per country with every allocation indicator, the components of the re-specified ECPC, and the descriptive weights. gcb_national_budgets.csv converts each share into an allocation in GtCO₂e, into years of 2019 emissions, and into the constant annual reduction rate that exhausts it by 2050, for every combination of criterion and budget scenario. codebook.md defines every variable with its unit, time window and source, and is regenerated from the configuration file on every run, so it cannot drift from the calculation. MANIFEST.json records the SHA-256 checksum of each of the 12 source files and of each output, together with the versions of Python and of every library used. A single command, run_all.py, rebuilds everything from the frozen sources and exits with a non-zero status if the replication of the published tables fails.

title: Code and trained model weights for "GRBD: A Global-Scale Multiple-Type River Barrier Annotation Database for Global River Barrier Mapping with Deep Learning"
description: This Zenodo record contains code and analysis data supporting a study on deep-learning-based mapping and evaluation of river barriers. The materials cover annotation-format conversion, dataset preparation, model training and inference, detection-performance evaluation, approximate barrier-size classification, and cross-basin barrier-density analysis. The repository includes scripts for converting LabelMe annotations to YOLO and COCO formats, randomly splitting a COCO dataset into training, validation, and test subsets using an 8:1:1 ratio, training YOLO11 and RT-DETRv2 models, conducting batch inference with RT-DETRv2, and evaluating predictions against manually interpreted ground-truth annotations using intersection over union (IoU). An additional script estimates approximate barrier lengths from annotated coordinates and classifies barriers into three size classes (≤30 m, 30–100 m, and >100 m). The record also includes analysis data for 58 selected sub-basins used to compare barrier counts and densities derived from three sources: manual visual interpretation, deep-learning predictions, and Global Dam Watch (GDW). These data were used for the statistical analyses reported in the associated study. The object-detection workflow includes six river-barrier classes: weir, dam, sluice, tide, earth, and lock. Some scripts retain environment-specific file paths and therefore require users to modify input/output paths before execution. RT-DETRv2 and YOLO scripts also depend on their respective external frameworks, configuration files, and model weights. Further details are provided in the accompanying README. RT-DETRv2-x-bestpt.zip contains the trained weights of the best-performing RT-DETRv2-X model used in this study. The model was selected for subsequent cross-basin generalization testing and river-barrier detection analyses.

title: Global shifts in lake thermal structure under climate change
description: Global shifts in lake thermal structure under climate change 1. Overview This archive contains the processed data, Python scripts, reproduced figure outputs, and per-figure statistics used for the manuscript "Global shifts in lake thermal structure under climate change" . The original daily meteorological forcing data and high-resolution process-based model outputs for 1,427,688 lakes are too large to include here. The archive instead provides processed lake-level, gridded, validation, and figure-source datasets sufficient to reproduce the main quantitative results and figures included in this package. 2. Getting Started and System Requirements 2.1 Zenodo Archives and Extraction The repository is distributed as standard ZIP archives and approximately 1 GB file parts so that large downloads can be transferred reliably: README.md : documentation for archive extraction, software setup, data contents, and reproduction. lake_thermal_scripts_v1.0.zip : script/ and requirements.txt . lake_thermal_data_core_v1.0.zip : demo data, external geospatial data, and processed data (including lake_qc_exclusions.csv ) other than the two largest NPZ files. lake_thermal_data_daily_v1.0.zip.part000 through .part007 : parts of the ZIP archive containing data/processed/daily_nonoverlap_results.npz . lake_thermal_data_background_v1.0.zip.part000 through .part011 : parts of the ZIP archive containing data/processed/background_results.npz . lake_thermal_results_v1.0.zip : 26 reference PDF/JPG files for 13 manuscript figures and 13 per-figure statistics CSV files, regenerated in the latest test run. Demo outputs are generated separately by script/demo.py . The README, scripts, core data archive, and every part of both large data archives are required to rerun every analysis. The results archive is optional and provides reference outputs for comparison. Download all required files into one directory. Individual .partNNN files cannot be extracted directly; they must first be joined in numerical order. On macOS, open Terminal in the download directory and run: cat lake_thermal_data_daily_v1.0.zip.part??? > lake_thermal_data_daily_v1.0.zip cat lake_thermal_data_background_v1.0.zip.part??? > lake_thermal_data_background_v1.0.zip mkdir -p lake_thermal_structure cp README.md lake_thermal_structure/ tar -xf lake_thermal_scripts_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure tar -xf lake_thermal_data_core_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure tar -xf lake_thermal_data_daily_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure tar -xf lake_thermal_data_background_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure tar -xf lake_thermal_results_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure cd lake_thermal_structure On Windows 11, open PowerShell in the download directory. Paste and run the entire function definition below before running the two Join-FileParts commands. Each command reports the part being joined and the completed ZIP path. Joining several gigabytes may take a few minutes. function Join-FileParts($Pattern, $OutputFile, [int]$ExpectedParts) { $directory = (Get-Location).ProviderPath $parts = @(Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath $directory -Filter $Pattern -File | Sort-Object Name) if ($parts.Count -ne $ExpectedParts) { throw "Expected $ExpectedParts parts in $directory; found $($parts.Count)." } for ($i = 0; $i -lt $ExpectedParts; $i++) { $expected = $OutputFile + ('.part{0:D3}' -f $i) if ($parts[$i].Name -ne $expected) { throw "Missing or incorrectly named part: $expected" } } $outputPath = Join-Path $directory $OutputFile $temporaryPath = $outputPath + '.joining' $outputStream = [System.IO.File]::Create($temporaryPath) try { foreach ($part in $parts) { Write-Host "Joining $($part.Name)..." $partStream = [System.IO.File]::OpenRead($part.FullName) try { $partStream.CopyTo($outputStream) } finally { $partStream.Dispose() } } } finally { $outputStream.Dispose() } $expectedSize = ($parts | Measure-Object -Property Length -Sum).Sum if ((Get-Item -LiteralPath $temporaryPath).Length -ne $expectedSize) { throw "Joined file size does not match the total part size." } Move-Item -LiteralPath $temporaryPath -Destination $outputPath -Force Write-Host "Completed: $outputPath" } Join-FileParts "lake_thermal_data_daily_v1.0.zip.part*" "lake_thermal_data_daily_v1.0.zip" 8 Join-FileParts "lake_thermal_data_background_v1.0.zip.part*" "lake_thermal_data_background_v1.0.zip" 12 New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force lake_thermal_structure | Out-Null Copy-Item README.md lake_thermal_structure/ tar -xf lake_thermal_scripts_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure tar -xf lake_thermal_data_core_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure tar -xf lake_thermal_data_daily_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure tar -xf lake_thermal_data_background_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure tar -xf lake_thermal_results_v1.0.zip -C lake_thermal_structure Set-Location lake_thermal_structure The commands use built-in macOS and Windows 11 tools. If the optional results ZIP was not downloaded, omit its tar -xf command. Extracting the archives into the same destination reconstructs this layout: lake_thermal_structure/ ├── README.md ├── requirements.txt ├── script/ ├── data/ └── results/ 2.2 Hardware A standard desktop or laptop computer can run the scripts, but the full data workflow is memory intensive. We recommend: RAM: at least 64 GB for the full datasets included here. Storage: at least 25 GB for the extracted repository and generated outputs. Allow at least 65 GB of free space while joining and extracting all downloaded archive parts; the downloaded parts and reconstructed ZIP files can be deleted after successful extraction. GPU: not required. Non-standard hardware: not required. The lightweight Poyang Lake demo dataset requires substantially less memory than the full figure workflows. 2.3 Software Setup and First Run The scripts were developed and tested with Python 3.13.5 on Windows 11. Required Python packages are listed in requirements.txt . Install them and run the lightweight demo from the reconstructed repository root: python -m pip install -r requirements.txt python script/demo.py The demo writes its outputs to results/demo/ . Full manuscript figures can be regenerated with the commands in Section 6. Generating each figure takes approximately 10 minutes. Figure 4 may take longer time for its large amount of data input. title: Beijing MTHI: Data and Reproducibility Package (2000–2019)
description: This record contains the public reproducibility package supporting the study “Persistent spatial organization and period-dependent associations in Beijing’s surface thermal–moisture environment”. The package includes the model-ready analytical dataset, temporal-screening and provenance records, cross-validation folds, model parameters and random-seed records, formal scripts for pooled and period-specific XGBoost–SHAP analyses, GeoDetector analysis, stored model outputs, quality-control and checksum records, and selected figure-source materials. The study comprises seven quality-controlled summer observation periods: 2000, 2004, 2005, 2009, 2010, 2016, and 2019. The primary reproducibility target of this package is the reported statistical analysis beginning from the archived ModelReady dataset. Production scripts preserve the original execution paths used during the formal analysis; users reproducing the analyses should update input and output paths to their local repository location. Upstream geospatial preprocessing scripts are retained for methodological provenance and may require the original third-party source products and local GIS configuration. Original Landsat, GLC_FCS30D, WorldPop, and Copernicus DEM source archives are not redistributed in this record and should be obtained from their respective providers. Detailed package structure, provenance, execution scope, and reproducibility notes are provided in the included README. title: Global ensemble of land cover indicators at 100 m (2000-2003): Terra firma short vegetation cover (part 1 of 7)
description: This dataset provides a global time series of land cover indicators at 100 m spatial resolution for the period 2000–2024. It is part of a global ensemble of eight land cover indicators derived from two global land cover products, namely GLAD GLCLUC and GLC_FCS30D . The dataset was generated by combining the source land cover products through temporal interpolation, weighted averaging, and class overwriting. The native resolution of the source products is 30 m. The resulting data were resampled to 100 m using average resampling and are provided as COGs. The eight land cover indicators included in the overall dataset are: tfshortveg, tftrees, wtshortveg, wttrees, water, cropland, snowice, builtup Further details on the methodology, source datasets, processing workflow, and data structure are available in the associated GitHub repository . This Zenodo record contains the terra firma short vegetation cover (tfshortveg) indicator. The indicator represents cover of short vegetation on dry ground, from true desert (~3%) to dense short vegetation (100%). Value type: Percentage (0-100%) Years covered: 2000-2003
keywords: land cover; land cover change; remote sensing; GLAD GLCLU; GLC_FCS30D; time series; global

title: Geospatial Dataset of Forest Canopy Height and Structural Regionalization in La Malinche, Mexico: 2019 Random Forest–Derived Canopy-Height and Structural Products and Structural Products Derived from the 2020 Global Canopy Height Map
description: La Malinche Canopy Height and Structural Regionalization (LMCHSR) is a public geospatial dataset of forest canopy height and structural regionalization for an area of interest encompassing the La Montaña Malinche o Matlalcuéyatl Federal Protected Natural Area, Mexico, and the adjacent peripheral area included in the analysis. The 2019 canopy-height raster was produced by integrating three Random Forest models corresponding to Sentinel-2 Level-2A acquisitions on 22 January, 28 March, and 12 April 2019. Each model used the red (B4), red-edge (B5), and shortwave-infrared (B12) bands, together with elevation and slope, as predictors. Canopy heights from CHMv2 (Brandt et al., 2026) served as the response reference after spatial harmonization to the 10 m modeling grid. The date-specific predictions were integrated into a multitemporal canopy-height surface. Structural products were derived from this RF surface on a 20 m analytical grid. They include structural objects, aggregated regions, five canopy-height classes (S01–S05), and connected class patches. An independent set of 20 m structural products was derived from the 2020 Global Canopy Height Map of Lang et al. (2023), with separately determined objects, regions, and five classes (E01–E05). The harmonized source ETH canopy-height raster is not redistributed. The release contains 18 geospatial assets: one area-of-interest boundary, the 2019 RF canopy-height raster (RF 2019), eight RF-derived structural products, and eight ETH2020-derived structural products. Raster and vector files are supplied as GeoTIFF and GeoPackage files, respectively, using the WGS 84 / UTM zone 14N coordinate reference system (CRS; EPSG:32614). The release also includes metadata, dictionaries, a class legend, and Secure Hash Algorithm 256-bit (SHA-256) checksums. The two structural classifications were generated independently; matching class codes do not imply identical class definitions or direct temporal forest change.

title: Global Pasture Watch: Pantropical calibrated Gross Primary Productivity (GPP) for croplands at 30m (2020)
description: This dataset provides calibrated gross primary productivity (GPP) at 30 m spatial resolution for the pantropical belt (48°S-36°N) for the period 2020-2024. It is part of a set of calibrated GPP layers -- annual GPP and its rate of change -- for cropland and grassland, derived by multiplying the Global Pasture Watch uncalibrated GPP (uGPP) product by land cover specific light use efficiency (LUE) factors taken from the Global Harmonized Land Cover (GHLC) map of the same year. Further details on the methodology, source datasets, and LUE factors are available in the umbrella record for this collection. This Zenodo record contains the pantropical calibrated GPP for cropland . Value type: gC m -2 yr -1 (UInt16) Years covered: 2020

title: Pantropical calibrated gross primary productivity (GPP) of cropland and grassland at 30 m (2020-2024)
description: This dataset provides annual calibrated gross primary productivity (GPP) for cropland and grassland at 30 m spatial resolution for the pantropical belt (48°S-36°N) for the years 2020-2024 , and the rate of change of GPP for both land-cover classes. The calibrated GPP is derived from the Global Pasture Watch uncalibrated GPP (uGPP) product (Isik et al., 2025) , which uses a uniform light-use efficiency (LUE) of 1 gC m-2 d-1 MJ-1 across all land cover types. Here, uGPP is multiplied, pixel by pixel and year by year, by a land-cover-specific LUE factor taken from the Global Harmonized Land Cover (Moreno et al., 2026) map of the same year. The result is then masked to the cropland and grassland classes of that year. Layers Layer Value Unit Data type NoData Annual GPP (cropland) calibrated GPP of the year gC m -2 yr -1 UInt16 65535 Annual GPP (grassland) calibrated GPP of the year gC m -2 yr -1 UInt16 65535 Rate of change 2020-2024 (cropland) [mean(GPP2023, GPP2024) - mean(GPP2020, GPP2021)] / 4 gC m -2 yr -1 per year Float32 -9999 Rate of change 2020-2024 (grassland) [mean(GPP2023, GPP2024) - mean(GPP2020, GPP2021)] / 4 gC m -2 yr -1 per year Float32 -9999 Methods Input alignment. The annual uGPP and GHLC land cover maps for 2020-2024 were placed on one common grid (0.00025°, EPSG:4326) using virtual rasters (VRT). Both products share the same pixel grid, so no resampling was applied. Calibration. For every pixel and year: GPP = uGPP × LUE(land-cover class of the same year) , using the LUE factors below. uGPP values ≥ 65000 and land-cover nodata (255) are treated as nodata. Values are rounded to 1 gC m -2 yr -1 . Masking. The annual GPP was retained only where the land cover for that year belongs to the cropland (classes 2-9) or grassland (classes 10-11) group; all other pixels are nodata. Rate of change. Computed from the masked annual GPP as rate = [mean(GPP2023, GPP2024) - mean(GPP2020, GPP2021)] / 4 , i.e. the difference between the late and the early two-year means, divided by the 2020-2024 period length (4 years). A pixel has a rate only if it belongs to the group in all four years used (2020, 2021, 2023, 2024) and has valid, non-capped GPP in all of them. Processing and quality control. Processing was done in 1° × 1° tiles in parallel. Each tile is tagged with the input version and a fingerprint of the LUE table. After processing, all tiles were scanned for block-shaped gaps caused by failed data transfers (areas missing in one year but valid in all other years); affected tiles were recomputed. (2017) 5 Annual crops - other 1.80 Yan et al. (2015) 6 Perennial crops - coffee 1.20 Chen et al. (2025) Land cover: Global Harmonized Land Cover, 30m, v1.2 (2020-2024) - Moreno et al. (2026) Tropical layer: Tropical data used to extract the extent - Pantropical Tree Cover Density Usage notes and limitations Land-cover changes. The rate-of-change layers are restricted to pixels that remain in the same group across 2020, 2021, 2023, and 2024. Rate period. The two 2-year means are centered on 2020.5 and 2023.5; the rate is divided by the 4-year span 2020-2024 as defined above. Extent. Only the pantropical belt (48°S-36°N) is covered; areas outside the land-cover or uGPP extent are nodata.

title: Code and data for: Ignoring plant responses to rising CO₂ overestimates dryland expansion under high emissions in a Brazilian Cerrado agricultural frontier (MATOPIBA)
description: Python pipeline and data used to compare potential evapotranspiration (PET) with and without the stomatal effect of CO₂ over MATOPIBA, Brazil (964 cells of 0.25°, about 736,000 km²). title: Reshuihe watershed, Liangshan (China): online household survey, fire-prevention burden and greening — data and code
description: De-identified data, analysis code and analysis outputs for a study of ecological restoration ("greening"), wildfire and fire-prevention duties in the Reshuihe watershed (174.7 km²), Xide County, Liangshan Yi Autonomous Prefecture, Sichuan, China. Survey. 815 questionnaires submitted online (Tencent Questionnaire) between 26 April and 3 May 2026, with the link forwarded by local government staff, who asked that their office and channels not be named; respondents answered on their own phones and staff had no access to the answers. Convenience sample; 84 submissions came from IP addresses in Liangshan Prefecture, 17 from elsewhere in Sichuan and 714 from outside Sichuan (released as a three-level variable). 73 coded variables, including five three-item Likert constructs (hazard concern, fire-duty burden, project participation, project dependence, perceived welfare) and four post hoc data-quality flags. Bilingual codebook and questionnaire text included. Code and outputs. Structural equation models with robustness checks, measurement-invariance and equivalence tests, and heterogeneity by IP location (R, lavaan); a Google Earth Engine pipeline for Landsat-only NDVI 2000–2025, a 200-basin donor pool, MODIS MCD64A1 burned area, FIRMS active fire, GLC_FCS30D land cover and CHIRPS/ERA5-Land climate; Python scripts for pixel-wise trends with FDR control, synthetic control / synthetic difference-in-differences with placebo inference, and fire activity relative to donor basins. Remote-sensing results. Growing-season NDVI rose across the watershed (median Sen's slope +0.0058 per year, 2000–2025), but no more than in 104 comparable basins: synthetic difference-in-differences estimate of the effect of the 2008 works −0.028 (95% CI −0.068 to 0.012, placebo p = 0.17). Version 2 corrects the description of how the survey data were collected, releases all 815 responses with collection date, completion time and IP-location group, replaces the version 1 remote-sensing files with the exports and outputs of a new Landsat-only pipeline, and corrects two specification issues of the version 1 SEM analysis. See CHANGELOG.md.
keywords: remote sensing; NDVI; environmental governance; ethnic minority; China; ecological restoration; wildfire; fire prevention; Liangshan; Yi; online survey; structural equation modelling; measurement invariance; synthetic control; Landsat NDVI; MODIS MCD64A1; FIRMS

title: Reproducibility package for "Damming the delta: cross-border attribution of coastal-delta sediment starvation for transboundary river governance"
description: Reproducibility package for "Damming the delta: cross-border attribution of coastal-delta sediment starvation for transboundary river governance" (Yiran Li), revision 1 (R1) of the manuscript under review at the Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies. This version supersedes version 1, which accompanied the original submission. The package contains the analysis code, the derived data tables and the figures underlying the paper, which presents a global source–receptor accounting of cross-border delta sediment starvation. Local sediment production is routed along the HydroBASINS river network; each dam's trapping is computed from its Brune efficiency and regulated-flow share; large natural lakes retain sediment with and without dams; natural loads are anchored to observed pre-dam values (39 rivers) or to the pristine loads of the Nienhuis et al. (2020) delta inventory; and each delta's dam-induced deficit is split into a domestic and a cross-border part and attributed to the upstream countries responsible. Key results (R1): dams withhold about 5,100 Mt yr⁻¹ of sediment from the world's inventoried deltas, of which about 1,130 Mt yr⁻¹ (22.1%) is withheld by dams in another country; 46 countries are net downstream bearers (25 of them bearing at least 1 Mt yr⁻¹); about 156 million people live on national delta parts that have lost at least a tenth of their sediment supply, mostly to foreign dams, 87% of them in Bangladesh and Egypt. Leading upstream sources: India, the United States, China, Ethiopia and Brazil. Contents: the analysis scripts (sediment_routing.py and the revision scripts run by run_all_r1.sh), the builders of the manuscript, Supplementary Material and response letter (build_all.sh), all derived CSV and JSON tables, Figures 1–5 and the graphical abstract. README_R1.md documents the input data, the run order, the method and all changes from version 1. A clean-room run from the public raw inputs (HydroBASINS, BasinATLAS, Global Dam Watch, the GlobalDeltaData of Nienhuis et al., the delta extents of Edmonds et al., the WorldPop 2020 grid, Natural Earth and World Bank GDP) reproduces every derived table byte for byte. The reviewer reports are confidential and are not included. No generative-AI tools were used to produce any figure or graphical artwork; all figures are data plots generated by the included code.

title: SOCOMv2: Experiment 2 (GOBM subsampling experiment) full experimental dataset
description: Dataset Information Current Version: v2 (changelog at end of repository Contacts: Daniel J. Ford (d.ford@exeter.ac.uk) and Alizée Roobaert (alizee.roobaert@vliz.be) The Surface Ocean CO2 Mapping program entered its second phase (SOCOMv2) with a range of experiments which provides a coordinated, community-driven framework to evaluate surface ocean fugacity of CO2 in seawater (sfCO2) reconstructions and derived air–sea CO2 fluxes under present-day observational constraints. This repository holds the dataset used within a Global Ocean Biogeochemical Model (GOBM) subsampling experiment designated Experiment 2, where nine fugacity of CO2 (fCO2) reconstruction methodologies reconstructed five GOBMs from the Global Carbon Budget 2023 (and one from 2024). The analysis and results of the study are presented in Roobaert et al. (in prep). How to reference? If you use these data for a new analysis or publication, we request that you contact Alizée Roobaert (alizee.roobaert@vliz.be) and Daniel J. Ford (d.ford@exeter.ac.uk). This will allow the authors, and the SOCOM community the opportunity to contribute and be considered for co-authorship, depending on their level of involvement. If these data are used please reference the orginial study (Roobaert et al. 2026) and the repository with the version. Data format This dataset includes five individual zip files which contain a single netCDF file. Within each netCDF, the model fCO2sw and air-sea CO2 fluxes alongside the sfCO2 reconstructions and resulting air-sea CO2 fluxes. Ancillary information including for example model sea surface tmeperature and salinity, gas transfer, wind speed and a consistent mask where all data products provide an fCO2 estimate, are included within each file to aid interpretation of the data. title: A global dataset of potential habitat areas in populated landscapes
description: A global dataset of potential habitat areas in populated landscapes This dataset maps potential habitat within populated, human-used landscapes on a ~1 km² hexagonal discrete global grid (ISEA3H, resolution 16; 1.18491 km² cells). Spatial domain: all files cover the 114,791,301 land cells whose centroid lies at or north of 60°S. Antarctica and other land south of 60°S are not included. For each cell, the dataset provides: the cell centroid; country (FAO GAUL 2024, with de facto assignment for disputed areas); counts of 10 m land-cover pixels: Dynamic World 2024, ESA WorldCover 2021, Global Pasture Watch and the Spatial Database of Planted Trees v2.0; land area, habitat area and habitat fraction of land; population: WorldPop R2025A, 2024, 100 m; classification into 'Populated' and 'Shared' Landscapes. 'Populated Landscapes' are cells where more than 1% of land is non-habitat (crop, built-up, pasture or tree crops) and population density is at least 1 person per km² of land. 'Shared Landscapes' are Populated Landscapes in which at least 20% of land is habitat. Globally: Populated Landscapes cover 26.14 million km² (20.5% of land); Shared Landscapes cover 18.87 million km² (14.8% of land; 72.2% of Populated Landscapes); 37.75% of the population lives in Shared Landscapes. Files dgg_isea3h16_land_shapefiles.zip : the land grid as 377 zipped shapefiles (10° tiles). Cells touch Natural Earth 10m or OpenStreetMap land, with a 200 m buffer. dgg_cells_shared_landscapes_dataset.csv.gz : per-cell results: centroid, country assignment, pixel counts, population, land and habitat areas and fractions, and landscape classes (gzip CSV, 33 columns). dataset_summaries.zip : global_summary.csv and country_summary.csv , with areas, fractions and the fraction of population in Shared Landscapes. DATA_DICTIONARY.md : definitions of every column and file format. Code: https://github.com/njdepsky/SharedLandscapes (MIT). The grid script accepts any bounding box, for example a global grid. Article: Ellis et al., Data in Brief (2026). Licence and attribution: Open Database License (ODbL) v1.0. The grid is derived from OpenStreetMap data, © OpenStreetMap contributors. Dynamic World: "This dataset is produced for the Dynamic World Project by Google in partnership with National Geographic Society and the World Resources Institute." title: Code and derived results: river-size association of Palaeolithic findspots in the Wainganga-Wardha basin, Nagpur and Chandrapur districts, Central India
description: R code, unit tests, saved summary tables and figure-source tables for a spatial analysis of 197 Palaeolithic findspots (59 source references) in Nagpur and Chandrapur districts, Central India (Wainganga-Wardha basin). The primary analysis estimates how site intensity varies with distance to drainage of increasing river size (WRIS stream order >= k, k = 3 to 9), using a down-weighted Poisson point-process likelihood with a ridge prior, spatial cluster-bootstrap inference, spatial cross-validation, a lineament-distance negative control and a robustness matrix. The analysis design was frozen and checksummed before the site-water models were fitted; the manifest is included. The primary hypothesis (intensity falls with distance to larger rivers) was not supported; the association depends on site classification, and exploratory analyses are labelled as such. Contents: scripts S01-S19, tests, saved result tables, figure-source tables, PDF figures, renv lockfile (R 4.5.2). Not included: exact site coordinates, the 1 km coarsened site table, and raw third-party data layers (WRIS, HydroRIVERS, ESA WorldCover, OpenStreetMap, Global Dam Watch), which must be obtained from their providers. Limitations: modern water bodies are a proxy for Pleistocene water; legacy survey bias; mixed coordinate quality; undated typology; no field validation.
keywords: palaeolithic; nagpur; chandrapur; central india; archaeological survey; river size; spatial point process

title: Global patterns and stocks of particulate and mineral-associated organic carbon across grasslands

Grassland_Scenario_A.csv : Grassland SOC, POC and MAOC observations, geographic coordinates and environmental predictors for Scenario A, combining CHELSA climate and HWSD soil data. Grassland_Scenario_B.csv : The same observation database with environmental predictors for Scenario B, combining CHELSA climate and SoilGrids soil data. Grassland_Scenario_C.csv : The same observation database with environmental predictors for Scenario C, combining WorldClim climate and HWSD soil data. Grassland_Scenario_D.csv : The same observation database with environmental predictors for Scenario D, combining WorldClim climate and SoilGrids soil data. run_POC_A_QRF.r : R script for training, evaluating and applying the Scenario A quantile regression forest model to predict grassland POC concentrations. title: Three Registries, Two Rivers — Oyapock zone (Z-OYA): results at D-OYA, 14 October 2026
description: Confirmatory results for the Oyapock zone (Z-OYA) of IAS Pre-registration No. 1, "Three Registries, Two Rivers", protocol v1.1 (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23348565). The French (Camino) and Brazilian (ANM SIGMINE, Amapá) mining-title registries were each downloaded once on D-OYA, 14 October 2026 (UTC), and processed with the code deposited with v1.1, unchanged. Verdict. P3 is not supported (band-sensitive). Within 10 km of the Oyapock, on each sovereign's own bank, neither Brazil nor France holds a small-scale gold-mining title (class S: 0 km² on each side). The 25-km band contains one Brazilian lavra garimpeira (9.66 km²) and no French AEX, hence the label. Other outcomes in the 10-km band. No granted gold title of any class (research, small-scale or long exploitation) lies on either bank. On the Brazilian bank, pending applications cover 208.44 km² (9 SIGMINE records, 8 processes) and one area listed for re-allocation (Apto para disponibilidade) covers 73.63 km². The French bank has neither. French titles within the bands are unchanged since T0 (22 September 2026). Contents. A results record (PDF): verdict, outcomes D1 to D6, checks, extraction record and deviations table. A data archive: run record, outcome tables, the Camino extract of D-OYA, the download log, the SIGMINE Amapá layer without holder names, and a supplementary area check. A file of fingerprints. Deviations are listed in section 7 of the PDF, including an extraction made outside the protocol on 13 October 2026, which is not scored. Titled area is not extraction or production, and no inference of illegality is drawn.

title: Ocean acidification and aragonite saturation, compounding anthropogenic stressors on marine life
description: Analysis scripts and derived data products behind the figures and numerical claims of Dryden & Duncan, "Ocean acidification, compounding anthropogenic stressors and marine water chemistry: evidence, regime-shift risk and implications for marine life". Contents: the winter aragonite threshold classification for all three zonation schemes; the same pipeline restricted to the polar and subpolar zone; the MODIS-Aqua equatorial Atlantic chlorophyll trend test; the figure build scripts; the derived 1-degree winter saturation and trend grids; the PyCO2SYS recomputation of aragonite saturation at the study sites with its per-point uncertainty; and the independent verification block. Primary datasets are not redistributed. OceanSODA-ETHZ v2025, SPOTS, GLODAP, CODAP-NA, World Ocean Atlas 2023 and the MODIS-Aqua ocean-colour products are public, carry their own DOIs, and are listed in README.md with the accessions needed to obtain them. Each script run against the original file reproduces the published values exactly. Expected outputs are tabulated in README.md so that any discrepancy is immediately visible. The polar-zone script deliberately reports the measured present state and no projection; the reason, a coverage artefact caused by seasonal ice in the trend mask, is documented in both the script header and the paper's Methods. Version 7 (October 2026) adds GOES_R1_graded_threshold_package.zip, the material behind the revised manuscript (revision R1 for BMC Marine Science): the graded ecological reference threshold (Omega 3.3 equatorward of 10 degrees to 1.6 poleward of 60 degrees), the winter aragonite saturation grids for 1982 to 2024 with the per-cell trend and the mask, the 1-degree block-mean MODIS-Aqua weights (net primary production, calcite and chlorophyll, 2019 to 2021) used to weight the water below its threshold, the month-by-month version of that weighting, the Monte Carlo, block-bootstrap and structural uncertainty with projections counted from 2023, the sea-surface-temperature variant of the threshold, and the scripts for Figures 1 to 3, S1 and S2 of the revised paper. Every script was re-run from the package before deposit: the numerical scripts reproduce the deposited results to rounding (two of them, run against the raw OceanSODA-ETHZ file, reproduce the deposited grids and JSON exactly), and the figure scripts reproduce the deposited PNG files byte for byte. Primary datasets are not redistributed; the README lists them with their accessions. CC BY 4.0.
