title: Climate Hazard Indicators (Extreme rainy days) Historical and SSP scenarios - Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu
description: ### Overview The dataset includes five major climatic indicators viz. annual values for minimum temperature (℃), maximum temperature (℃), mean temperature (℃), total precipitation (mm/year), and the number of rainy days (represented as integers) for two Indian states, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. It features decadal averages from 2020-2100 for Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs), including SSP5-8.5, which reflects a high emissions scenario, and SSP2-4.5, representing moderate challenges to both mitigation and adaptation. Additionally, the dataset provides historical data for all the five indicators averaged over the period from 2005 to 2014. ### Methodology **Pre-Processing**: The decadal time periods were labeled as follows: 2020-2029 as 2020, 2030-2039 as 2030, 2040-2049 as 2040, 2050-2059 as 2050, 2060-2069 as 2060, 2070-2079 as 2070, 2080-2089 as 2080, and 2090-2099 as 2090. **Layers of interest**: Annual averages of minimum temperature (℃), maximum temperature (℃), mean temperature (℃), Annual total precipitation (mm/year), and the annual total number of rainy days (represented as integers). **Data**: The ERA5 reanalysis dataset (ECMWF 2022), a satellite data product of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts with a spatial resolution of 31 kilometers (km), is used as a reference dataset. The ensemble of downscaled daily time series outputs from global climate models (GCMs). These time series include the historical years covered by the observation time series as well as the specified future years of interest. We have used the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 product, which includes outputs from 34 Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) models at approximately 25 km spatial resolution. ### Estimation Methods Out of the 35 models, we select the top 3 climate models that perform best for a specific weather variable in a particular geographic region, and present the ensemble mean of these models. The ERA5 dataset is used as a reference, and the comparison is made for the historical period between 1980 and 2014. After selecting the models, we apply a calibration/bias correction procedure to the future time series of the models. This involves aligning the model's frequency distribution with the historical data by shifting the percentiles of the model's distribution. For instance, if the 20th percentile of the model data corresponds to the 30th percentile of the observations, then the 30th percentile of the calibrated model data will match the 20th percentile of the uncalibrated model data. For the full documentation, please see the source methodology at Wong, T., and P Switzer. 2023. 'Estimating future local climate hazard probabilities.' Technical Note. Washington, DC: World Resources Institute. Available online at: doi.org/10.46830/writn.22.00074.v2. ### Description of the Layers **Annual Maximum Temperature (℃)**: The daily maximum temperature data for each year is extracted and averaged to calculate the yearly average maximum temperature. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years. **Annual Minimum Temperature (℃)**: The daily minimum temperature data for each year is extracted and averaged to calculate the yearly average minimum temperature. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years. **Annual Mean Temperature (℃)**: The daily mean temperature is calculated by averaging the daily minimum and maximum temperatures. The annual mean temperature is obtained by averaging the daily mean temperatures over the course of a year. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years. **Annual Total Precipitation (mm/year)**: The daily precipitation values are summed over the entire year to calculate the annual total precipitation. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years. **Annual Rainy Days (represented as integers)**: A rainy day is defined as a day with precipitation exceeding 2.5 mm (as per the India Meteorological Department). The total number of rainy days in a year is calculated by summing the rainy days throughout the year. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years. ### Visualizing the Data The data is provided at a 25-km resolution and is presented as a raster with a time slider with a separate layer for each variable. The values are visualized using a gradient based on the selected year in the slider, ranging from lighter shade (indicating low values) to darker shade (representing higher values). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source

Admissions of residents to out-of-state hospitals are excluded for most states. Admissions for border counties may be under estimated. The inclusion of these admissions by some states can affect state to state comparability. Rates were age-adjusted by the direct method using 2000 US standard population. These data are smoothed. Smoothing borrows information from neighboring areas to stabilize results from sparsely populated areas. Smoothing is used to reduce variability in the data, allowing patterns to emerge. description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](5c5e654e-182b-4ab4-8a3c-edff79cc68ea) as a replacement.**_ This data set, a collaboration between the GLAD (Global Land Analysis & Discovery) lab at the University of Maryland, Google, USGS, and NASA, measures areas of tree cover loss across all global land (except Antarctica and other Arctic islands) at approximately 30 × 30 meter resolution. The data were generated using multispectral satellite imagery from the Landsat 5 thematic mapper (TM), the Landsat 7 thematic mapper plus (ETM+), and the Landsat 8 Operational Land Imager (OLI) sensors. Over 1 million satellite images were processed and analyzed, including over 600,000 Landsat 7 images for the 2000-2012 interval, and more than 400,000 Landsat 5, 7, and 8 images for updates for the 2011-2017 interval. The clear land surface observations in the satellite images were assembled and a supervised learning algorithm was applied to identify per pixel tree cover loss. In this data set, “tree cover” is defined as all vegetation greater than 5 meters in height, and may take the form of natural forests or plantations across a range of canopy densities. Tree cover loss is defined as “stand replacement disturbance,” or the complete removal of tree cover canopy at the Landsat pixel scale. Tree cover loss may be the result of human activities, including forestry practices such as timber harvesting or deforestation (the conversion of natural forest to other land uses), as well as natural causes such as disease or storm damage. Fire is another widespread cause of tree cover loss, and can be either natural or human-induced. This data set has been updated five times since its creation, and now includes loss up to 2017 (Version 1.5). The analysis method has been modified in numerous ways, including new data for the target year, re-processed data for previous years (2011 and 2012 for the Version 1.1 update, 2012 and 2013 for the Version 1.2 update, and 2014 for the Version 1.3 update), and improved modelling and calibration. These modifications improve change detection for 2011-2017, including better detection of boreal loss due to fire, smallholder rotation agriculture in tropical forests, selective losing, and short cycle plantations. Eventually, a future “Version 2.0” will include reprocessing for 2000-2010 data, but in the meantime integrated use of the original data and Version 1.5 should be performed with caution. description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. MHTs reflect groupings of ecoregions with similar biological, chemical, and physical characteristics. The MHTs refer to the dynamics of ecological systems and the broad habitat structures that define them. These groupings can provide a structured framework for examining and comparing the diversity of life in terrestrial systems. MHTs are broadly broken down by latitude, ranging from boreal and tundra, temperature, and tropical regions. Temperate and tropical forests are further broken down into broadleaf and conifers. Finally, shrublands are distinguished by elevation, from high altitude montane shrublands to flooded lowlands. Coral Reef Fisheries Relative Catch
description: ### Overview The Coral Reef Fisheries Relative Catch dataset shows a basic estimate of the relative size of coral reef fisheries catch. This catch is determined as a function of estimated reef productivity and fishing effort. This global data set reflects the world's coral reefs as a 500 meter (m) grid, classified by a relative estimate of the annual fish harvest as of 2014. Reef areas are classified by decile of estimated fisheries catch by weight (biomass). The estimates do not account for variability in the economic or social value of these fisheries. Coral reef fisheries are an important source of food for local populations. They also generate revenue and exports. Furthermore, while most fishing on reefs is artisanal, some coral reefs host a proportion of very high-value target species which attract distant-water fleets. The relative productivity and composition of different reef fisheries is thus both socially and economically significant, and a relevant input to marine management. These estimates represent an important aspect of coral reef value—the relative size and spatial distribution of catch coming from coral reef fisheries—and represent an important incentive for sustainable reef management. The dataset was created by researchers from The Nature Conservancy (TNC), the University of Cambridge (Cambridge), and the World Resources Institute (WRI). ### Methodology Catch is determined as a function of estimated reef productivity and fishing effort. A minor modifier to this basic model makes allowance for no-take fishing areas: within these zones, fishing is not allowed and catches are presumed to be zero; in adjacent waters, a small buffer of enhanced fishery productivity reflects anticipated spillover from these protected areas. The authors do not account for variability in the economic or social value of these fisheries. The estimation of coral-reef associated fisheries involves 4 steps: 1. Estimate the pristine potential maximum sustainable yield (MSY) of coral reefs—the potential sustainable production of fish on healthy reefs. This estimate was based on a review of numerous published estimates of fisheries yields or maximum sustainable yield per unit area world-wide. 2. Estimate the realistic potential MSY on coral reefs, in light of current reef condition (degradation), which can reduce productivity. A proportional reduction was made based on the [Reefs at Risk](https://www.wri.org/publication/reefs-risk-revisited) model of integrated local threat to reefs, along with other studies. 3. Estimate catch based on the potential MSY, adjusted by nearby population and available fishing area, using a model adapted from previous field-based studies: reefs are recorded as reaching maximum fishing effort at population levels greater than 600 persons within reach of each square kilometre of reef. 4. This catch layer was modified for strictly protected no-take zones. Catch values were reduced to zero (no catch) in the no-take zones, while the potential catch in a surrounding 1 km buffer was raised to the maximum value, reflecting anticipated spillover. For more information, please see the source [methodology](https://www.nature.org/content/dam/tnc/nature/en/documents/Atlas-of-Ocean-Wealth.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Minimum Antarctic Sea Ice
description: ### Overview The Minimum Antarctic Sea Ice dataset shows the annual minimum extent of sea ice in the Antarctic for select years between 1980-2020. Antarctic sea ice typically reaches its minimum extent in February. In this map, light blue represents locations where sea ice was present during February for each year. Sea ice extent data was collected by satellite microwave sensing instruments at a spatial resolution of 25 kilometers (km). This dataset is derived from two products: a near real-time daily dataset and a separate daily dataset that is processed yearly. For the most recent 6-18 months, sea ice extents were derived from near real-time data; all older data was derived from the separate daily dataset. This dataset can be used to understand changes in annual minimum Antarctic sea ice extent over the past 40 years. Although Antarctic sea ice extent varies significantly from year to year, the average ice extent has not changed over the past 40 years. According to the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration](https://www.climate.gov/news-features/understanding-climate/understanding-climate-antarctic-sea-ice-extent), natural variability in the Southern Ocean and in atmospheric circulation patterns have a greater impact on Antarctic sea ice extent than climate change. However, climate change is disrupting wind patterns, currents and ocean temperatures across the globe. These changes may eventually impact Antarctic sea ice extent. The [National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC)](https://nsidc.org/) was founded in 1976 as the World Data Center for Glaciology. Over time, the NSIDC evolved to become a data distribution and research center specializing in remote sensing of cryospheric data such as snow, sea ice, frozen ground, ice sheets and glaciers. In addition to managing and distributing this data, the NSIDC creates and supports data access tools for its users. They also use the datasets for climate research and education. The NSIDC is part of University of Colorado Boulder’s [Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences (CIRES)](https://cires.colorado.edu/). It is supported by the [National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)](https://www.nasa.gov/), the [National Science Foundation (NSF)](https://www.nsf.gov/) and the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)](https://www.noaa.gov/). ### Methodology Minimum Antarctic Sea Ice was produced from two sources: NASA's [Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC)](https://nsidc.org/data/nsidc-0051) and NSIDC’s [Near-Real-Time DMSP SSMIS Daily Polar Gridded Sea Ice Concentrations (NRTSI)](https://nsidc.org/data/nsidc-0081). Data for the GSFC and NRTSI datasets was collected by the following six sensors: - GSFC data: - [Nimbus-7 Satellite](https://eospso.nasa.gov/missions/nimbus-7) Scanning Multichannel Microwave Radiometer (SMMR) from October 1978 to August 1987 - [Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP)](https://www.ospo.noaa.gov/Operations/DMSP/index.html) F8 Special Sensor Microwave/Imager (SSM/I) from August 1987 to December 1991 - DMSP-F11 SSM/I from December 1991 to September 1995 - DMSP-F13 SSM/I from September 1995 to December 2007 - DMSP-F17 Special Sensor Microwave Imager/Sounder (SSMIS) from January 2008 to present - NRTSI data: - DMSP-F18 SSMIS from April 2016 to present The SMMR, SSM/I, and SSMIS instruments sense emitted microwave radiation. Data was collected daily by the SSM/I and SSMIS sensors and on alternate days by the SMMR sensor. An object's physical properties, such as atomic composition and crystalline structure, determine the amount of microwave radiation it emits. The crystalline structure of ice typically emits more microwave energy than liquid ocean water. Thus, the microwave sensors can easily distinguish sea ice from the ocean. The satellite data was converted to [brightness temperature](https://glossary.ametsoc.org/wiki/Brightness_temperature), a descriptive measure of an object's radiation. Brightness temperature data was then converted to gridded ice concentration using the [NASA Team algorithm](https://nsidc.org/support/faq/nasa-team-vs-bootstrap-algorithm#NASATeam1) at a spatial resolution of 25 km. Gridded ice concentration is the percentage of ice (relative to water) in a given cell. Each cell’s daily ice concentrations were averaged to produce monthly concentrations. Sea ice extent is delineated by the location where ice ends and water (open ocean) begins. Cells were classified as water if their average monthly ice concentration was below 15%, and as ice if the concentration was above 15%. Images of sea ice extent were created for each month, with ice shown in light blue. The process was the same for both the NRTSI and GSFC datasets. GSFC data had a tighter quality control than NRTSI data. However, GSFC data is only released once per year. NRTSI data was available at the end of each month, so it was used to produce sea ice extents while GSFC data was being processed. GSFC data replaced NRTSI data once it was available. Thus, data from the most recent 6-18 months was derived from the NRTSI dataset and older data was derived from the GSFC dataset. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows additional NSIDC sea ice extent data: [Historical Sea Ice Medians](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/b1ebea96-5963-4c2c-9273-7d08536ac07d), [Minimum Arctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/a99c5cf5-f141-4bed-a36d-b04c8e171dfa), [Maximum Arctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/15a0b176-8313-4859-af90-5c198e50a605), [Arctic Sea Ice Extent](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/484fbba1-ac34-402f-8623-7b1cc9c34f17), [Maximum Antarctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7667bdd8-9adb-44de-b51c-d2d26e461af1) and [Antarctic Sea Ice Extent](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e740efec-c673-431a-be2c-b214613f641a). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/cli_005_polar_sea_ice_extents). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

Temperature Suitability for Disease-Carrying Mosquito Aedes albopictus
description: ### Overview This dataset shows the number of months per year when disease transmission by one of the most common disease-carrying mosquitoes is possible under baseline conditions, as well as in the years 2050 and 2080. The mosquito is *Aedes albopictus*, and it transmits diseases to humans such as zika, dengue, chikungunya, and yellow fever. The baseline data used to represent current conditions is calculated using climate data from the years 1960-1990. In addition to the baseline temperature suitability for disease-carrying mosquitoes, the researchers used four climate change scenarios to predict where temperatures will be suitable for mosquitoes to thrive in the years 2050 and 2080. On Resource Watch, we display the RCP 8.5 which is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. According to the [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/neglected_diseases/vector_ecology/mosquito-borne-diseases/en/), millions of people die each year from mosquito-borne diseases. Temperature is the main factor in mosquito survival and disease transmission. This dataset is crucial because governments and health organizations can use it to prevent and prepare for the viruses. The dataset was published by researchers from the University of Florida, Georgetown University, the University of Maryland, Stanford University, and Virginia Polytechnic and State University. The dataset has global coverage with a 5 arc minute resolution. Resource Watch also shows temperature suitability data for one of the other most common-disease-carrying mosquitoes, [*Aedes aegypti*](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/bio047a-Temperature-Suitability-for-Disease-Carrying-Mosquitoe-Aedes-aegypti). ### Methodology Researchers used a model to predict disease transmission by fitting the thermal responses of mosquitoes as results of several parameters. The parameters included temperature, mosquito traits such as biting rate per mosquito and mosquito mortality rate, human population size, and human recovery rate. This model of disease transmission was based on experiments and validated with empirical data. As for temperature, current mean monthly temperature data was derived from the WorldClim dataset. To predict future temperatures, researchers used four general circulation models (GCMs) that are most commonly used by studies forecasting species distributional shifts. Each of the four models can respectively be forecasted for four representative concentration pathways (RCPs): RCP 2.6, RCP 4.5, RCP 6.0, and RCP 8.5. These RCPs are standardized scenarios in predicting how future climate will respond to emission output. RCP 8.5 represents the worst-case, business-as-usual fossil fuel emissions scenario. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for three other climate change scenarios (RCP 2.6, RCP 4.5, and RCP 6.0), as well as results produced by different climate models, is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: Land Cover Map
description: ### Overview The global land use and land cover maps were created by the Global Land Analysis and Discovery Lab (GLAD) laboratory, and the data is available at 30 m spatial resolution for 2000 and 2020. The GLAD laboratory used the spatiotemporally consistent [Landsat Analysis Ready Data (GLAD ARD)](https://glad.umd.edu/ard) to quantify changes in forest extent and height, cropland, built-up lands, surface water, and perennial snow and ice extent over the twenty year period. Each thematic product was independently derived using state-of-the-art, locally and regionally calibrated machine learning tools. The dataset was validated using a statistical sampling which confirms its high accuracy. The Global Land Analysis and Discovery Lab (GLAD) laboratory in the Department of Geographical Sciences at UMD investigates methods, causes, and impacts of global land surface change. Earth observation imagery is the primary data source, and the land cover extent and change is the primary topic of interest. GLAD aspires to generate new science insights concerning land resources, educate the next generation of remote sensing-based land change scientists, and disseminate land monitoring capabilities to operational settings nationally and internationally. ### Methodology The Global Land Analysis and Discovery (GLAD) laboratory derived most global thematic products, except open water, using consistently processed [Landsat Analysis Ready Data (GLAD ARD)](https://glad.umd.edu/ard). The annual GLAD ARD data time series were integrated into a set of phenological metrics that enabled global model calibration and application. The water mapping was performed using the Landsat data processed in the Google Earth Engine using an approach similar to the GLAD ARD. GLAD used a separate supervised classification model to map each thematic class. The decision tree models calibrated with manually collected training data were implemented for water, cropland, and perennial snow and ice mapping. Forest height was estimated using the regression tree model calibrated with Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation Lidar (GEDI) forest structure measurements. The built-up lands were mapped using a deep learning convolutional neural network (CNN) algorithm trained using Open Street Map (OSM) data. The models were calibrated locally (for forest height and cropland mapping) or regionally (all other products). GLAD independently validated each global thematic product using statistical sample analysis. The sample reference data were collected through visual image interpretation using the best available high-resolution satellite data and Landsat time series. The GLAD ARD product consists of 16-day global Landsat normalized surface reflectance and brightness temperature composites combined from the best quality observations. Each 16-day composite includes the normalized surface reflectance for visible, near-infrared, and shortwave infrared Landsat bands and brightness temperature, along with the data quality layer. GLAD integrated the annual GLAD ARD 16-day clear-sky time series into a set of rank-based statistics, hereafter named phenology metrics, that enabled the application of the multitemporal classification and regression models. GLAD augmented the Landsat reflectance metrics with topographic metrics, including elevation and slope. GLAD defined forest as wildland, managed, and planted tree cover, including agroforestry and orchards. The forest extent was defined as an area with tree cover ≥ 5 m, to ensure consistency with the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) forest definition. Nevertheless, their forest definition differs from the one used by the FAO by the inclusion of trees outside forests (agroforestry, orchards, parks) and the exclusion of temporally unstocked forest areas. GLAD employed the global Landsat-based forest height model calibrated for the year 2019 using GEDI observations. For the boreal forests north of 52°N, where GEDI data are absent, GLAD used a regional model approach. Three separate models were calibrated for North America, Europe, and Northern Asia. The model calibrated for the year 2019 was applied to 2000, 2001, 2003, 2017, 2019, and 2020 annual metrics.The forest height values for the years 2000 and 2020 were calculated as the median of 2000, 2001, 2003, and 2017, 2019, 2020 products, respectively, unless forest loss for the years 2001-2003 or 2017-2020 was indicated by the forest disturbance data (in such case, only the year 2000 or 2020 product value was used, respectively). GLAD produced the year 2000 and 2020 forest extent maps by attributing pixels with ≥ 5 m forest height as the “forest” land cover class. The forest extent change (net forest extent loss and gain) was derived directly from the year 2000 and 2020 map comparison. Cropland was defined as land used to produce annual and perennial herbaceous crops for human consumption, forage, and biofuel. The definition excludes tree crops, permanent pastures, and shifting cultivation. Consistent with the FAO arable land category, the fallow length was limited to four years for the cropland class. The cropland mapping was performed for two four-year epochs, 2000-2003 and 2016-2019. For each epoch, they attributed a GLAD ARD pixel as cropland if a growing crop was detected during any year within the interval. The cropland mapping model was calibrated with manually delineated training areas which were extrapolated in space and time through a three-stage algorithm. Supervised classification (bagged decision tree ensembles) was implemented at each of these three steps. The final products were filtered by removing artifacts and cropland patches smaller than 0.5 ha. Built-up land consists of man-made land surfaces associated with infrastructure, commercial and residential land uses. At the Landsat spatial resolution, GLAD defined the built-up land class as pixels that include man-made surfaces, even if such surfaces do not dominate within the pixel. Due to the contextual nature of built-up lands, particularly settlements, they employed a deep learning convolutional neural network (CNN) algorithm to map this thematic class. Final 2000 and 2020 per-pixel class presence probabilities were generated, and validation data were used to assist in the final thresholding of the layers in depicting 2000 and 2020 extents and 2000-2020 gain in built-up lands. Loss of built-up lands, which represents a small proportion of the year 2000 class area, was not mapped by this provisional product. Open surface water, or simply water, is defined as inland water that covers ≥ 50% of a pixel and is not obscured by objects above the surface.The presented multidecadal surface water change product is based on the annual water presence dataset produced by Pickens et al. (2020). Water presence is a percent of Landsat observations classified as surface water of all annual clear-sky observations calculated per pixel. Instead of the GLAD ARD, the algorithm employed the original Collection 1 Tier 1 Landsat 5, 7, and 8 scenes from 1999-2020. GLAD classified each Landsat scene into the land, water, and unusable data classes using an ensemble of hierarchical, bagged classification trees developed for ARD data processing. The perennial snow and ice layer includes land covered by glaciers and snow which remains during the entire year. The map is limited to the GLAD ARD tiles where perennial snow and ice areas were detected using the ARD observation quality layer. GLAD mapped permanent snow and ice using regionally calibrated supervised classification models (decision tree ensembles). Overall, they used fourteen models, one model per mountain system or a geographic region. Each classification model was calibrated with manually collected training data from multitemporal Landsat metrics. Wetlands are treated as a landform containing multiple land cover classes. Topographical metrics, including slope, curvature, and a series of relative elevation layers from variably sized catchments were used to determine wetland versus terra firma. Percent bare ground was included from a previous assessment. GLAD validated each thematic product separately using an independently collected reference data sample. GLAD used different strata designs for each thematic product to target not only the LCLU class of interest but also the potential class omission errors. For product validation, the map and reference data were presented as discrete LCLU classes. The map accuracy metrics include overall accuracy (the proportion of correctly mapped sample pixels), user’s accuracy of the LCLU class (which reflects the thematic class commission), and producer’s accuracy of the LCLU class (which reflects the thematic class omission). Map accuracy statistics were accompanied by the standard error of the estimate (s.e.). We also estimated sample-based areas of LCLU classes and changes with the corresponding s.e. The global composite maps were created by layering an annual vegetation fraction layer with the bare land, wetland landform, followed by the superseding classes of ice, water, cropland, and built-up. The 2019 global composite map can be viewed and downloaded [here](https://glad.umd.edu/dataset/global-land-cover-land-use-v1). For the full documentation of the [landform classes](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1748-9326/ac46ec) and other [thematic classes](https://doi.org/10.3389/frsen.2022.856903), please see the original methodology. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows datasets from the GLAD laboratory for [Cropland Extent](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/50634b51-ea2e-4cc1-9e4b-8f26a389a301), [Cropland Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ec282483-4f5c-4fb8-ace7-8e557826781a), [Tree Height Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/64a3e126-000b-46fb-aaf4-8ac765a8263b), [Water Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/b83ad197-eb95-44e2-8ec3-3351ab926421), [Snow/Ice Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/5a796ce9-71d4-42b0-922d-056a86e5eb72), and [Built-Up Area Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e6a3f803-1222-46c2-8e6c-0ae94b3d80c8). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: Uttarakhand Change in Rainfall
description: The data represents annual and seasonal change in the rainfall for baseline (1981-2010) and mid-century (2021-2050) under RCP 4.5 & 8.5 emission scenarios in millimetre (mm). This data is an output from a hydrologic model, SWAT (Soil and Water Assessment Tool) which has been use to assess the impact of projected climate change on water resources. The SWAT model (Arnold et al., 1981, Neitsch et al., 2022) is a distributed parameter and continuous time simulation model. The SWAT model has been developed to predict the hydrological response of un-gauged catchments to natural inputs as well as the manmade interventions. The model (a) is physically based; (b) uses readily available inputs; (c) is computationally efficient to operate and (d) is continuous time and capable of simulating long periods for computing the effects of management changes. The major advantage of the SWAT model is that unlike the other conventional conceptual simulation models it does not require much calibration and therefore can be used on un-gauged watersheds (in fact the usual situation). The SWAT model is a long-term, continuous model for watershed simulation. It operates on a daily time step and is designed to predict the impact of land management practices on water, sediment, and agricultural chemical yields. The model is physically based, computationally efficient, and capable of simulating a high level of spatial details by allowing the watershed to be divided into a large number of sub-watersheds. Major model components include weather, hydrology, soil temperature, plant growth, nutrients, pesticides, and land management. The model has been validated for several watersheds. Input data used are terrain, landuse, soil, daily weather data (rainfall, maximum and minimum temperature, wind speed,, relative humidity and wind speed), cropping pattern, reservoirs and any man made structure with their characteristics. The outputs provided by the model are very exhaustive covering all the components of water balance spatially and temporally. The sub components of the water balance that are more significant and were used for analyses include: • Precipitation. • Total flow (Water yield) consisting of surface runoff, lateral and base flow. • Actual evapotranspiration (Actual ET). • Base flow. • Ground water recharge. PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link.

title: Global Soil Properties
description: ### Overview This dataset describes select global soil parameters regridded and upscaled from the Harmonized World Soil Database v1.2. The HWSD provides information for addressing land competition for food production, bio-energy demand, and biodiversity threats. It is also used as an input to model global carbon cycles. The data are presented as a series of five critical layers at 0.05-degree (~5 km) spatial resolution. ### Methodology **Data Sources:** The Harmonized World Soil Database integrates over 15,000 different soil mapping units, combining global, regional, and national updates (SOTER, ESD, Soil Map of China, WISE) with the FAO-UNESCO Soil Map of the World (FAO, 1971-1981). **Estimation Methods:** HWSD v1.2 (FAO 2012) provides the most comprehensive database of soil characteristics available for global analysis. Soil characteristics are derived from real soil profiles considering pedogenic development, land use, land use history, and disturbances. Properties in HWSD are available for both surface soil horizons (0-30 cm) and deeper soil profiles (30-100 cm). ### Description of the Layers **Topsoil Clay Fraction (% weight):** Percentage clay in the topsoil (0-30 cm). Clay consists of fine-grained particles (<0.002mm) that exhibit plasticity when wet and harden when dried or fired. **Topsoil Silt Fraction (% weight):** Percentage silt in the topsoil (0-30 cm). Silt results from mechanical weathering of rocks through glacial grinding, wind abrasion, or river erosion. It is primarily composed of quartz and feldspar. **Topsoil Sand Fraction (% weight):** Percentage sand in the topsoil (0-30 cm). Sand particles range from 0.0625 mm to 2 mm and feel gritty when touched. Classified into very fine, fine, medium, coarse, and very coarse based on size. **Topsoil pH (-log(H+)):** The acidity or alkalinity of topsoil (0-30 cm) measured in a soil-water solution. Categories include: - Extremely Acidic (pH < 4.5): Found in Acid Sulfate Soils (e.g., mangrove soils, cat clays). - Very Acidic (pH 4.5–5.5): Often influenced by aluminum toxicity. - Acidic to Neutral (pH 5.5–7.2): Optimal for nutrient availability and most crops. - Carbonate-Rich (pH 7.2–8.5): May reduce nutrient availability like phosphorus and iron. - Highly Alkaline (pH > 8.5): Typically sodic with high sodium, affecting soil structure. **Topsoil Organic Carbon Content (% weight):** Indicator of soil fertility and health. Classified as: - Very Low (<0.2%): Requires significant soil amendments. - Low (0.2%–0.6%): Poor in organic matter. - Moderate (0.6%–1.2%): Better fertility and structure. - High (1.2%–2.0%): Favorable conditions for crop growth. - Very High (>2.0%): Highly fertile and well-structured. ### Visualizing the Data The dataset is available at ~5 km resolution. Lighter shades indicate lower values, while brighter shades (orange-red) indicate higher values. ### Excerpts of this description were taken from the source.

title: Projected Cooling Degree Days (RCP8.5)
description: The Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset shows the change in annual cooling degree days (CDDs) at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. CDD is the number of degrees that a day's average temperature is above 65 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). For example, if a day's average temperature is 80°F, the CDD would be 15. If this happened 10 times in a year the annual CDD would be 150. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the CDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual CDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. CDD projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP). RCP 4.5 is a stabilization scenario where total radiative forcing is stabilized around 2050 by employment of a range of technologies and strategies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.25°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades and how this may affect future energy demands. For example, CDDs are often used as a proxy to estimate energy requirements for cooling buildings. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference. The annual CDD for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. Daily CDDs were calculated by subtracting the baseline temperature of 65°F from daily average temperature values. If the daily average temperature was below 65°F, it was counted as zero. Then, annual CDD was calculated by summing all daily CDD values over a given year. Annual CDDs were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in cooling degree days. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the CDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual CDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

title: Global Material Flows
description: ### Overview The Global Material Flows Database holds a variety of datasets on material extraction and consumption. The dataset displayed on Resource Watch shows global material consumption and extraction of nonmetallic minerals, biomass, fossil fuels, and metal ores at a national scale. This data is available at the source for every year between 1970 and 2017, but only the 2017 data is mapped on Resource Watch. The dataset also contains additional data on the overall consumption and extraction for each country at a per capita rate for the year 2015. Consumption and extraction are expressed in units of metric tons. This dataset was created using national statistics from a combination of local government organizations and international organizations like the United Nations, Eurostat, and the United States Geological Survey. This dataset was developed to assist governments in creating strategies to increase efficiency of material production and consumption activities. The dataset can help in better understanding how economic growth patterns influence resource use. It can also be used to evaluate the impacts of policies that have been adopted in the past. Additionally, the dataset can be used to develop effective strategies to minimize future resource use through targeted consumption and production policies. This database is used by academics around the world, integrated into several multi-regional input-output databases such as [EXIOBASE](https://www.exiobase.eu/) and featured in reports by international organisations, such as the United Nations Environmental Program and the European Economic Area. This database was created by the United Nations Environment Programme International Resource Panel (UNEP IRP) and developed as part of a collaborative effort by the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation, the Sustainable Resource Use research group of the Vienna University of Economics and Business, the Institute of Social Ecology Vienna, the Nagoya University, and University of Sydney’s Integrated Sustainability Analysis. ### Methodology This dataset was created by combining data from multiple sources. Data for all categories of extraction were taken from national production statistics. These datasets were collected from individual government ministries, industrial associations, and Eurostat's production statistics (PRODCOM) whenever available. Additional available data from international organizations, like the British Geological Survey and United States Geological Survey, were also used. Some categories, like metal ore extraction, were estimated using techniques in the [Eurostat: Economy-wide Material Flow Accounts Compilation Guide 2013](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/1798247/6191533/2013-EW-MFA-Guide-10Sep2013.pdf/). Data reported using different units was converted to a standard unit by using category-specific conversion factors. Data on domestic material consumption was calculated by finding the sum of each country’s domestic extraction and import values and subtracting total exports. Data on imports and exports was taken from national offices when available and United Nations reports when not available. Both per capita datasets were created by dividing each country’s total extraction and consumption by its population. The final datasets were produced in tabular format at a national level. A country's ND-GAIN score is composed of a vulnerability score and a readiness score. Vulnerability and readiness are based on compiled indicators. Vulnerability measures a country's exposure, sensitivity, and capacity to adapt to the negative effects of climate change. ND-GAIN measures overall vulnerability by considering 6 life-supporting sectors—food, water, health, ecosystem service, human habitat, and infrastructure—and 36 indicators. Readiness measures a country's ability to leverage investments and convert them to adaptation actions. ND-GAIN measures overall readiness by considering 3 components—economic readiness, governance readiness, and social readiness—and 9 indicators. Each indicator comes from a public data source. Infrastructure Investment Outlook
description: ### Overview This dataset from the Global Infrastructure Hub (GI Hub) shows national infrastructure investment gaps in 2015 U.S. dollars for the following sectors: energy, telecommunications, airports, ports, rail, road, and water. The dataset also includes a layer for the sum of all sectors, as total sectors. An investment gap represents the difference between the amount of money a country would need to invest in infrastructure to match the performance of other countries within the same income group and the amount that countries would be likely to spend if trends continued.The investment gap of a country where the investment trends meet their future investment needs is zero. This dataset was developed by the Global Infrastructure Hub. The data covers a total of 56 countries for the years 2016 to 2040. ### Methodology The Global Infrastructure Outlook was calculated using a “top-down” approach, beginning with existing cross-country datasets on infrastructure spending and filling in data gaps, where necessary. Sources for the initial cross-country datasets include the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), Infrastructure in Latin America (INFRALATAM), and Eurostat. The infrastructure investment gap for each year was calculated as the difference between the amount of money a country would need to invest in infrastructure to match the performance of other countries within the same income group and the amount that countries would be likely to spend if trends continued for that year. Gaps in national data were filled using data from national statistics agencies and major infrastructure companies. In areas where no data sources could be identified, econometric estimation was used to compute values. In countries where a time series existed but was incomplete, further manipulation was often required to fill in the gaps in that series. For data gaps in the middle of a time series, interpolation was used to fill the gaps. When data was missing from the beginning or the end of the time series, forecasting and/or backcasting were used to develop a longer time series. In the case where data was attributed to a broader sector, secondary data sources were used to align the data with the preferred sector definition. In some countries, data related to investment in utilities was used to attribute the investment into more detailed sectors like water and energy. For example, if energy accounts for 60% of the country's utilities investment, then 60% of the utilities investment would be allocated to the energy sector. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://cdn.gihub.org/outlook/live/methodology/Global+Infrastructure+Outlook+-+July+2017.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Wetlands
description: This data set estimates large-scale wetland distributions and important wetland complexes, including areas of marsh, fen, peatland, and water (Lehner and Döll 2004). Large rivers are also included as wetlands (lotic wetlands); it is assumed that only a river with adjacent wetlands (floodplain) is wide enough to appear as a polygon on the coarse-scale source maps. Wetlands are a crucial part of natural infrastructure as they help protect water quality, hold excess flood water, stabilize shoreline, and help recharge groundwater (Beeson and Doyle 1995, Stuart and Edwards 2006). Limited by sources, the data set refers to lakes as permanent still-water bodies (lentic water bodies) without direct connection to the sea, including saline lakes and lagoons as lakes, while excluding intermittent or ephemeral water bodies. Lakes that are manmade are explicitly classified as reservoirs. The Global Lakes and Wetlands Database combines best available sources for lakes and wetlands on a global scale. This data set includes information on large lakes (area ≥ 50 km2) and reservoirs (storage capacity ≥ 0.5 km3), permanent open water bodies (surface area ≥ 0.1 km2), and maximum extent and types of wetlands. title: Amphibian and Mammalian Richness and Threat Levels
description: ### Overview The Amphibian and Mammalian Richness and Threat Levels dataset shows the species richness and number of threatened species for amphibians and mammals. Species richness is defined by the number of mammal or amphibian species present in a given area. The International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN) [Red List](https://www.iucnredlist.org/about/background-history) defines a [threatened species](https://www.iucn.org/resources/conservation-tools/iucn-red-list-threatened-species) as one that is threatened with global extinction (critically endangered, endangered, or vulnerable). The Red List is the world’s most comprehensive list of species status and extinction risk, with assessments for over 120,000 species. The data shown here evaluated 5,198 amphibian species and 5,488 mammalian species in 2013. Gridded data is available at a spatial resolution of 30 arc seconds, which is approximately 1 kilometer (km) x 1 km at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. Biodiversity – the variety of life on earth – is essential to a healthy and stable environment. Biodiversity conservation is critical for food supply, fighting climate change, and providing natural resources for humans. However, human activities such as pollution, farming and deforestation have negatively impacted biodiversity, causing the loss of species and their habitats. Amphibians are facing the highest rates of decline: almost 50% of amphibian species are threatened, primarily in South America and Southeast Asia. Similarly, almost 50% of mammal species are in decline and 20% are threatened. Marine mammals are among the most threatened species. The Amphibian and Mammalian Richness and Threat Levels dataset is an important tool for wildlife conservation efforts. Understanding the magnitude and geographic focus of threatened species is important for making policy decisions and allocating conservation resources. Additionally, this dataset can be used for biodiversity modeling studies and understanding human interactions with the environment. Founded in 1948, the [International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN)](https://www.iucn.org/about) comprises more than 1,400 governmental and civil member organizations. Its mission is to influence, encourage and assist conservation of natural diversity, and ensure that the use of any natural resources is equitable and sustainable. The IUCN provides the Red List as a tool to inform conservation decisions and protect the natural resources necessary for human life. The Amphibian and Mammalian Richness and Threat Level dataset was aggregated by [Columbia University’s Center for International Earth Science Information Network (CIESIN)](http://www.ciesin.columbia.edu/) using data from the IUCN Red List. CIESIN specializes in online data management and spatial data integration for interdisciplinary research related to human interactions with the environment. ### Methodology The Amphibian and Mammalian Richness and Threat Levels dataset was created from species distribution shapefiles from the IUCN Red List. The shapefile data is from 2013 and has a spatial resolution of 30 arc seconds (approximately 1 km at the equator). The number in each grid cell represents the number of species present or the number of species threatened within that cell. CIESIN created the richness and threat level rasters by converting the shapefiles to GeoTIFF rasters based on attributes from the IUCN data. Amphibian and mammalian richness maps were created by aggregating individual species maps with the **Extant** class attribute. This attribute refers to species that are currently surviving in the wild. Threat level maps were created in the same way using the **All Threats** IUCN threat category. The All Threats category includes species classified as Critically Endangered (extremely high risk of extinction in the wild), Endangered (very high risk of extinction in the wild ) or Vulnerable (high risk of extinction in the wild). Species within these categories are undergoing reversible declines in population, geographic extent, habitat, and mature individuals. Red List species assessments follow a specific set of guidelines and undergo review before publication. More information about the Red List assessment process can be found [here](https://www.iucnredlist.org/assessment/process). Projected Change in Frost Free Season in the U.S.
description: ### Overview The Projected Change in Frost Free Season in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average frost free season at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. A frost free season is the largest number of consecutive days in a year where the minimum daily temperatures are above 32 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the frost free season in 2000 is actually an average of the annual frost free seasons between the years 1985 and 2015. Frost free season projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The change in frost free season is shown as the number of days difference between the frost free season during the projected decade and the baseline time period. The dataset is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. In particular, it can be used to understand and adapt to changing agricultural growing seasons and productivity in individual regions. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. ### Methodology The Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference. The annual average frost free season for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting daily minimum temperature values for a given year and finding the largest number of consecutive days where the minimum temperature exceeded 32°F. The average annual frost free seasons were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then the baseline average was subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in dry spells The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the frost free season in 2000 is actually an average of the annual frost free seasons between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows LOCA RCP 8.5 data for [Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/a9567364-e5ba-415e-a834-310e279326b6), [Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/4c6ba704-12f3-4954-92af-6c248c584233), [Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7ec68890-34a9-427c-907e-2f646f0dd9c8), [Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/412a8589-4887-44f2-9f45-3db5fb3937e7), [Projected Change in Dry Spells in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cd91e8d6-2e3d-46c1-9601-0dd7f524c7ba), [Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c985d4f6-9a03-4158-9955-e9f96db109ab), [Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/9e9b465a-bb0f-4047-ad72-9b8fabc0fd09), [Projected Change in Heating Degree Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6114c6fa-0ca6-4e06-ae23-413be0677503), [Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c5cbedcd-8cf5-4140-ac21-6791f6786f22). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data. Additional data is available for emissions scenario RCP 4.5. title: Heating Degree Days
description: A heating degree day (HDD) is defined as the number of degrees that a day's mean temperature is below 65°F. For example, if a day's average temperature is 50°F, the HDD would be 15. If a second day's average temperature were the same, the combined HDD for those two days would be 30. HDDs are often used as a proxy to estimate heating and cooling needs in buildings. While degree days can be calculated using any reference temperature, this data set uses 65°F (18.3°C), a common threshold for climate indicators, and a temperature at which people are generally comfortable. This indicator is useful in determining energy demands resulting from heating in different regions and assessing projected climate change impacts. This data set shows HDDs under RCP 8.5, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

title: Environmental Democracy Index
description: The Environmental Democracy Index (EDI) was developed by The Access Initiative (TAI) and World Resources Institute (WRI) in collaboration with partners around the world. The index evaluates 70 countries, across 75 legal indicators, based on objective and internationally recognized standards established by the Bali Guidelines of the UN Environment Programme (UNEP). Legal indicators test both the extent of provisions that promote environmental democracy and the strength of a given provision in providing an enforceable legal right for the public. Each of these indicators is scored on a range from 0 (lowest) to 3 (highest). A score of 3 means that the respective provision exemplifies accepted good practice. A score of 2 indicates that a majority—but not all—of environmental decision-making includes a certain provision, or indicates moderately strong provision. A score of 1 translates to a weaker provision that grants significant discretion to government agencies to fulfil these rights, or that a right only applies to a minority of environmental decision-making processes. A score of 0 indicates that the law is either silent or prohibits some aspect of procedural rights, depending on the indicator. The overall EDI score is the average of the scores of the 75 legal indicators. The EDI also includes a supplemental set of 24 limited practice indicators that provide insight on a country’s performance in implementation. The national laws and practices were assessed and scored by more than 140 lawyers around the world. Country assessments were conducted in 2014 and will be updated every 2 years. title: Gender Gap Index
description: ### Overview The Gender Gap Index quantifies the gaps between women and men in four key areas: health, education, economy, and politics. Data is available from 149 countries for select years between 2010-2021. Scores are based on the level of access women have to resources and opportunities relative to men. Countries are given a score from 0-1. A score of 1 indicates full equality between women and men and a score of 0 indicates full inequality. The Gender Gap Index is published annually by the World Economic Forum (WEF) and is designed to capture the magnitude of gender-based disparities and track progress over time. Gender equality is a necessity for a peaceful, prosperous and sustainable world. Women represent half of the world’s population but continue to be underrepresented in leadership and in the workplace. According to the 2021 Gender Gap Index, only 27% of global managerial positions were held by women in 2021. The largest gap between women and men was in political empowerment, where only 26.1% of about 35,500 parliament seats and 22.6% of over 3,400 ministers globally are held by women. The Gender Gap Index serves as a benchmark for comparing countries and their progress to gender equality over time. Based on current trends, the WEF estimates that it will take 135.6 years to close the global gender gap. However, the 2021 Gender Gap Index shows that many countries have made significant progress towards closing the gender gap. These countries include Iceland, Finland, Norway, New Zealand, Sweden, Namibia, Rwanda, and Lithuania. The WEF Centre for the New Economy and Society published the Gender Gap Index. The WEF is an international NGO founded in 1971. Focused on public-private cooperation, the WEF brings together political, business and cultural leaders at their annual meetings, workshops and seminars. The WEF’s primary aim is to drive positive change for the world by conducting research, producing data and leading collaborative projects and initiatives. The Centre for the New Economy and Society is focused on closing economic gender gaps, fostering diversity and promoting inclusive growth. ### Methodology The Gender Gap Index quantified the gaps between men and women across four subindexes: economic participation and opportunity, educational attainment, health and survival, and political empowerment. Indicators were scored within each subindex. The Gender Gap Index was based on three underlying concepts that determined how indicators were chosen, how the data was treated and how the index can be used. These concepts can be thought of as the “rules” for how the subindexes were scored. First, the index measured gender-based gaps in access to resources and opportunities in countries, rather than the actual levels of the available resources and opportunities. This rewarded countries with smaller gaps in access to these resources, regardless of the overall level of resources. Second, the index evaluated countries based on outcomes rather than inputs. Inputs – indicators related to country-specific policies, rights or customs – were not included in the index. For example, the gap between women and men in high-skilled jobs (an outcome indicator) was measured, but the length of maternity leave (a country-specific policy) was not. Third, the index evaluated countries based on their proximity to gender equality, rather than their level of women’s empowerment. The index rewarded countries in which outcomes for women equaled those for men, but it neither rewarded nor penalized countries in which women outperformed men. The four subindexes were scored based on the following indicators: - Economic participation and opportunity: This subindex measured gender-based gaps in workforce participation, remuneration and advancement. The remuneration gap was measured by the ratio of estimated female-to-male earned income and a qualitative assessment of wage equality for similar work. The advancement gap was captured through two hard data statistics: the ratio of women to men among legislators, senior officials and managers, and the ratio of women to men among technical and professional workers. Data was provided by the [International Labour Organization ILOSTAT database](https://ilostat.ilo.org/) and the WEF. - Educational attainment: Gender-based gaps in educational attainment were measured with the ratio of women to men enrolled in primary, secondary and tertiary education. The ratio of female to male literacy was also used as an indicator of a country’s long-term ability to educate women and men. Data was provided by the [United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) Institute for Statistics Education Indicators database](http://uis.unesco.org/). - Health and survival: The differences between women’s and men’s health were measured using the sex ratio at birth and the gap between women’s and men’s healthy life expectancy. Sex ratio at birth is the measure of male births for every female birth and was included to capture the phenomenon of [“missing women.”](https://www.weforum.org/agenda/2015/10/where-are-all-the-women/) This refers to the observation of a low ratio of women to men, particularly in countries with a strong son preference. Data for this subindex was provided by the [United Nations (UN) World Population Prospects dataset](https://population.un.org/wpp/) and the [World Health Organization (WHO) Global Health Observatory database](https://www.who.int/data/gho). - Political empowerment: The gap between women and men at the highest level of political decision-making was measured by the ratio of women to men in ministerial positions and the ratio of women to men in parliamentary positions. The ratio of women to men in terms of years in executive office (prime minister or president) for the last 50 years was also included. Data was provided by the Inter-Parliamentary Union [Women in National Parliaments](http://archive.ipu.org/wmn-e/classif.htm). [Women in Politics](https://www.ipu.org/resources/publications/infographics/2020-03/women-in-politics-2020) datasets and the WEF. All data was converted to female-to-male ratios. Ratios were then truncated at the “equality benchmark”. The equality benchmark was 1 for all indicators except the two in the health subindex. The sex ratio at birth equality benchmark was 0.9445 and the healthy life expectancy benchmark was 1.06. Truncating ratios at 1 assigns the same score to a country that has reached equality between women and men (a ratio of 1) and one in which women have surpassed men (a ratio greater than 1). This method measured how close women were to achieving equality with men in a country, but did not reward or penalize countries with a gender gap in the opposite direction. The total score for each subindex was a weighted average of the scores for each indicator. A weighted average was used to make sure each indicator had the same relative impact on the total score.The overall score for each country was a simple average of the subindex scores. A score of 0 indicated complete inequality between women and men and a score of 1 indicated complete equality. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://reports.weforum.org/global-gender-gap-report-2018/measuring-the-global-gender-gap/). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](c37b0b21-3d11-46ea-ba5d-4be4c0caa8ae) as a replacement.**_ ### Overview The Global Hunger Indices show the state of hunger worldwide in 2019, along with three reference years in 2000, 2005, and 2010. The indices capture the multidimensional nature of hunger by calculating Global Hunger Index (GHI) scores comprised of four indicators: undernourishment, child wasting, child stunting, and child mortality. The 2019 Global Hunger Index is published jointly by Concern Worldwide and Welthungerhilfe to measure and track hunger and to spotlight areas with the greatest need to eliminate hunger. The GHI scores are calculated on a 0-100 scale, where 0 indicates no hunger and 100 demonstrates complete hunger. A high GHI score, broadly speaking, can indicate a lack of food, a low-quality diet, insufficient child caregiving practices, an unhealthy environment, or all of these factors. The GHI classifies countries by the following severity layers: low, moderate, serious, alarming, or extremely alarming scales of hunger. ### Methodology GHI scores were calculated using a three-step process that draws on available data from various sources to capture the multidimensional nature of hunger. First, for each country, values were determined for four indicators: 1. Undernourishment: the share of the population that is undernourished (that is, whose caloric intake is insufficient); 2. Child wasting: the share of children under the age of five who are wasted (that is, who have low weight for their height, reflecting acute undernutrition); 3. Child stunting: the share of children under the age of five who are stunted (that is, who have low height for their age, reflecting chronic undernutrition); and 4. Child mortality: the mortality rate of children under the age of five (in part, a reflection of the fatal mix of inadequate nutrition and unhealthy environments). Second, each of the four component indicators was given a standardized score on a 100-point scale based on the highest observed level for the indicator on a global scale in recent decades. Third, standardized scores were aggregated to calculate the GHI score for each country, with each of the three dimensions (inadequate food supply, child mortality, and child undernutrition, which is composed equally of child stunting and child wasting) given equal weight. This three-step process results in GHI scores on a 100-point GHI Severity Scale, where 0 is the best score (no hunger) and 100 is the worst. In practice, neither of these extremes is reached. A value of 0 would mean that a country had no undernourished people in the population, no children younger than five who were wasted or stunted, and no children who died before their fifth birthday. A value of 100 would signify that a country’s undernourishment, child wasting, child stunting, and child mortality levels were each at approximately the highest levels observed worldwide in recent decades. The GHI Severity Scale shows the severity of hunger - from low to extremely alarming - associated with the range of possible GHI scores.
