title: Snow Cover
description: The MODIS Normalized Difference Snow Index (NDSI) snow cover layer, from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), shows the presence of snow cover over land and water bodies as an index related to the presence of snow. NDSI snow cover is derived from the cloud free snow reflectance sensed by the MODIS instrument, and hence this layer shows presence of snow during day time and under cloud clear condition only. NDSI snow cover though could be retrieved in the valid range of (0, 1.0) at every pixel, additional tests like surface temperature screening linked with the surface height is used for accurate detection. Snow is precipitation that forms from water vapor in the atmosphere where temperatures are below 0° Celsius. If the ground temperature is also below freezing, snow will accumulate on the ground as bright, white layer of snowpack. Snow cover reflects sunlight back into the atmosphere, helping to cool the Earth’s surface. Snowmelt is used for drinking water and crop irrigation, and can moisturize soil to reduce the risk of wildfire in many areas in the world. When snow melts in the spring, too much snow can cause springtime flooding. The MODIS Snow Cover (Normalized Difference Snow Index) layer is available from both the Terra (MOD10) and Aqua (MYD10) satellites. The sensor and imagery resolution is 500 m, the geographic coverage is global, and the temporal resolution is daily. Monthly averages for each CMG cell are calculated from the corresponding 28 – 31 days of observations in the MOD10C1 daily maximum snow cover extent data set. The input data are filtered to utilize only the clearest surface views in the average and to remove low magnitude snow cover fractions in the output that likely reflect erroneous snow detections.Algorithm Description Average snow cover is calculated for each cell in the CMG using the 28 – 31 days of MOD10C1 (daily snow cover) for the month. Data is filtered so that the most relevant days of snow cover are used to calculate the average and to filter out data that is of low magnitude i.e. low occurrence of snow during the month. The latter filter works to remove some occurrences of erroneous snow from the monthly snow average. The daily snow data is used to compute the monthly average snow cover. A daily cell must have a Clear Index (CI) of > 70% to be included in the average. Clear index is defined as the number of cells without clouds divided by the total number of cells.That filter is applied so that only the clearest of the daily observations are included in the average. (See the MOD10C1 section for description of the CI.) A daily observation contributes to the monthly average for a cell as follows: Daily contribution to monthly mean = 100 * snow%/CI For daily observations that are cloud free the snow contribution to the mean is the observed snow fraction in a grid cell. For daily observations of mixed snow and cloud fractions with a high CI it is assumed that there is some fraction of snow cover obscured by cloud. In that case the daily snow observation is increased in that equation so that the contribution to the monthly mean will be greater than the daily snow observation. For example, a cell has 25% snow cover and the CI = 75 then the cell is determined to have (25%/75 * 100) = 33% fractional snow cover. Daily observations with a CI ≤ 70 are assigned either as 100% cloudy, night, missing or no decision. There must be at least one day in the month for each cell with the CI > 70 in order for the mean snow cover to be computed for that cell of the monthly CMG. If that restriction is not met then the cell is reported as no decision. A second filter is applied to the calculated mean fractional snow cover of each cell to filter out those cells in which the magnitude of snow cover is less than 10%. Cells failing the filter are assigned 0% snow for the month. Cells with a low magnitude are considered suspect of being erroneous snow originating in the MOD10_L2 algorithm and being propagated through the sequence of snow products. The magnitude of snow is calculated as an average snow for all days with snow passing the first filter of CI > 70. Data displayed on Resource Watch is filtered to only show snow cover greater than 20 percent. title: World Database on Protected Areas
description: The World Database on Protected Areas (WDPA) is the most comprehensive global spatial data set on marine and terrestrial protected areas available. Protected area data are provided via Protected Planet, the online interface for the WDPA. The WDPA is a joint initiative of the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) and the UN Environment Programme's World Conservation Monitoring Centre (UNEP-WCMC) to compile spatially referenced information about protected areas. The data are provided as shapefiles and updated monthly. Not all protected areas receive the same degree of protection. While some have strict guidelines designed to preserve intact ecosystems, others allow for sustainable land use, often including limited resource extraction. In addition, not all countries use the same terminology when designating a protected area. Universal management categories are designated by the IUCN that stipulate the level of protection for most protected areas. These categories are defined as follows: (Ia) Strict Nature Reserves: protected areas designed to preserve biodiversity and all geological features. Limited human use (e.g., scientific study, education) is allowed and carefully monitored. Strict nature reserves are often used to understand the impact of indirect human disturbance (e.g., burning fossil fuels) because of the area’s high level of preservation. (Ib) Wilderness Areas: protected areas managed to preserve ecosystem processes with limited human use. Wilderness areas cannot contain modern infrastructure (e.g., a visitor’s center), but they allow for local indigenous groups to maintain subsistence lifestyles. These areas are often established to restore disturbed environments. (II) National Parks: protected areas designed to preserve large-scale ecosystems and support human visitation. With conservation as a priority, these areas allow infrastructure and contribute to the local economy by providing opportunities for environmental educational and recreation. (III) National Monuments or Features: areas established to protect a specific natural feature (e.g., cave, grove) or human-made monument with significant historical, spiritual, or environmental importance and the immediate surroundings. Accordingly, natural monuments or features are typically smaller in area and have high human impact resulting from visitor traffic. (IV) Habitat and Species Management Areas: areas designed to conserve specific wildlife populations and/or habitats. Habitat and species management areas often exist within a larger ecosystem or protected area and are carefully managed (e.g., through hunting abatement or habitat restoration) to conserve a target species or habitat. (V) Protected Landscapes and Seascapes: protected areas with ecological, biological, or cultural importance that have been shaped by human use of the landscape. Protected landscapes and seascapes typically cover entire bodies of land or ocean and allow for a number of for-profit activities (e.g., ecotourism) in accordance with the region’s management plan. (VI) Protected Areas with Sustainable Use of Natural Resources: areas designed to manage natural resources and uphold the livelihoods of surrounding communities. These regions have a low level of human occupation, small-scale developments (i.e., not industrial), and part of the landscape in its natural condition. title: Vegetation Condition Index
description: The STAR Vegetation Health Index is a product from NOAA's National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service (NOAA-NESDIS) Global and Regional Vegetation Heath (VH) system estimating vegetation health, moisture condition, and thermal condition. VH products can be used as proxy data for monitoring vegetation health, drought, soil saturation, moisture and thermal conditions, fire risk, greenness of vegetation cover, vegetation fraction, leaf area index, start/end of the growing season, crop and pasture productivity, teleconnection with El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO), desertification, mosquito-borne diseases, invasive species, ecological resources, land degradation, etc. The VH indices range from 0 to 100 characterizing changes in vegetation conditions from extremely poor (0) to excellent (100). Fair conditions are coded by green color (50), which changes to brown and red when conditions deteriorate and to blue when they improve. The VH reflects indirectly a combination of chlorophyll and moisture content in the vegetation health and also changes in thermal conditions at the surface. Monitoring vegetation health (condition), including drought detection and watch, is based on radiance measurements in the visible (VIS), near infrared (NIR), and 10.3-11.3 micrometers thermal (T) bands (channels) of the Advanced Very High Resolution Radiometer (AVHRR). These measurements are processed to reduce long-term noise. The VIS and NIR values were converted to the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI=(NIR-VIS)/(NIR+VIS)) and the T to brightness temperature (BT) using a look-up table. The NDVI and BT were filtered in order to eliminate high frequency noise. They were also adjusted for a non-uniformity of the land surface due to climate and ecosystem differences using multi-year NDVI and BT data. The NDVI and BT were converted to the Vegetation Condition Index (VCI), Temperature Condition Index (TCI), and Vegetation Health Index (VHI). The Vegetation Condition Index (VCI) is a proxy for moisture conditions. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Water Conflict Map
description: In an ongoing effort to understand the connections between water resources, water systems, and international security and conflict, the Pacific Institute initiated a project in the late 1980s to track and categorize events related to water and conflict, which has been continuously updated since. This map shows the geographic location where conflicts over water have occurred and information about each conflict. The data is global and covers the time period from 3000 BC through 2019. Events are included when there is violence (injuries or deaths) or threats of violence (including verbal threats, military maneuvers, and shows of force). This data set does not include instances of unintentional or incidental adverse impacts on populations or communities that occur associated with water management decisions, such as populations displaced by dam construction or impacts of extreme events such as flooding or droughts. (Based on this new definition, some previous entries were removed in May 2018.) Events are categorized based on the use, impact, or effect that water had within the conflict. 1) Trigger: Water as a trigger or root cause of conflict, where there is a dispute over the control of water or water systems or where economic or physical access to water, or scarcity of water, triggers violence; 2) Weapon: Water as a weapon of conflict, where water resources, or water systems themselves, are used as a tool or weapon in a violent conflict; 3) Casualty: Water resources or water systems as a casualty of conflict, where water resources, or water systems, are intentional or incidental casualties or targets of violence. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Air Quality: Nitrogen Oxide (NOₓ) Estimated Emissions
description: ### Overview This dataset from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) shows global anthropogenic emissions of nitrogen oxides (NOₓ) in 2018 from the following sectors: agriculture, animal agriculture, power generation, residential, ship, road transportation, off-road transportation, and industrial processes. The dataset also includes a layer for the sum of all sectors, as total emissions. Nitrogen oxides are a family of highly reactive air pollutants, produced by fossil fuel combustion from power plants and gasoline-burning vehicles. Nitrogen oxides are also an important precursor to ground-level ozone (O₃), an air pollutant and a major component of smog, which can worsen bronchitis and asthma and damage lung tissue. “Nitrogen oxides” is used to collectively describe the larger group of similar pollutants, which includes nitrogen dioxide, nitrous acid, and nitric acid. Resource Watch also shows CAMS global anthropogenic emissions data for [black carbon](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6bf069ff-a3b6-4b58-b4b8-eb1ac6354e89), [methane (CH₄)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/85936c69-b773-458b-90c4-b47d5d3b5f0d), and [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/92cb0e3c-369e-4c66-908c-5723f608e35b). Each compound shows the emissions by sector for up to 11 sectors, depending on the atmospheric compound. The CAMS global anthropogenic emissions dataset was developed by Emissions of Atmospheric Compounds and Compilation of Ancillary Data (ECCAD-AERIS). The data has global coverage at a 0.1 degree resolution, which is approximately 11 kilometers x 11 kilometers at the equator, but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. Emissions are provided as an annual sum for the years 2000 to 2019. This dataset shows annual emissions for the year 2018. ### Methodology The CAMS global anthropogenic emissions are based on the data provided by the Community Emissions Data System (CEDS) and Emissions Database for Global Atmospheric Research version 4.3.2 (EDGARv4.3.2) historical data. In preparing the dataset, the 0.5 degree global CEDS emissions dataset for the years 2011 to 2014 was used to calculate a linear trend in emissions. These trends were then disaggregated onto the same 0.1 degree grid as in EDGARv4.3.2. The sectors were then merged and aligned between the CEDS and EDGARv4.3.2 datasets. The 2011 to 2014 trends were applied to the EDGARv4.3.2 2010 emissions to estimate the emissions up to the year 2018. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://atmosphere.copernicus.eu/sites/default/files/2019-05/cams_emissions_general_document_apr2019_v6.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows CAMS global anthropogenic emissions data for [black carbon](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6bf069ff-a3b6-4b58-b4b8-eb1ac6354e89), [methane (CH₄)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/85936c69-b773-458b-90c4-b47d5d3b5f0d), and [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/92cb0e3c-369e-4c66-908c-5723f608e35b). title: Cooling Degree Days
description: A cooling degree day (CDD) is defined as the number of degrees that a day's mean temperature is above 65°F. For example, if a day's average temperature is 80°F, the CDD would be 15. If a second day's average temperature were the same, the combined CDD for those two days would be 30. CDDs are often used as a proxy to estimate heating and cooling needs in buildings. While degree days can be calculated using any reference temperature, this data set uses 65°F (18.3°C), a common threshold for climate indicators, and a temperature at which people are generally comfortable. This indicator is useful in determining energy demands resulting from cooling in different regions and assessing projected climate change impacts. This data set shows CDDs under RCP 8.5, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

title: Coral Reef Tourism Value
description: ### Overview The Coral Reef Tourism Value dataset estimates the annual economic value of coral reefs to the tourism sector. These values reflect the individual and combined value of on-reef and reef-adjacent tourism. The former includes recreational diving and snorkelling, while the latter encompasses the provision of calm waters, coral sand beaches, views and seafood. Economic value (in 2013 U.S. dollars) is estimated around the globe for every 500 meter (m) grid cell containing reefs with tourism activity, based on data from approximately 2005 through 2012. Coral reef tourism is a critical, undervalued ecosystem service. Coral reefs attract foreign and domestic visitors and generate revenue, including foreign exchange earnings, in over 100 countries and territories. Maps of value assigned to specific coral reef locations show considerable spatial variability across distances of just a few kilometers (km). About 30% of the world's reefs are of value to the tourism sector—the remainder being too remote for tourism—with an estimated total value of nearly $36 billion, or over 9% of _all_ coastal tourism value in the relevant countries. Understanding the full value of coral reefs to tourism, and the spatial distribution of these values, provides an important incentive for sustainable reef management. The dataset was created by researchers from The Nature Conservancy (TNC), World Resources Institute (WRI), the University of Washington (UWash), and the University of Cambridge (Cambridge). ### Methodology The value of coral reef tourism was explored using metrics of monetary value (i.e., expenditures) and visitor numbers (specifically, tourist trip equivalents: a term used to account for the fact that many of the statistics are built up from fractions of total arrivals, acknowledging that reefs are only part of most destination choices). Two components of coral reef tourism were distinguished: on-reef or _in situ_ values are derived from direct non-extractive reef uses including diving, snorkelling and glass-bottom boat tours; reef-adjacent or _ex situ_ values are not derived from in-water activities, but are indirectly linked to the presence of nearby reefs. The latter may include the role of reefs in generating clear calm waters and beach sand, outstanding views, fresh seafood and even their widespread use in advertising, all of which help to draw people to coral reef regions. Tourism was examined in the over 100 jurisdictions (countries and territories) around the world which have coral reefs. National statistics on travel and tourism for each jurisdiction were used as initial inputs. “Big data” from commercial, crowdsourced, and social media platforms were then used to prorate and spatially distribute the tourism expenditure and visitation to non-urban areas that could reasonably be linked to coral reefs. Paired, independent datasets were used to strengthen the robustness of the model, and the outputs were cross-referenced to existing studies. Tourism values were estimated as a proportion of the total visits and spending by coastal tourists within 30 km of reefs (excluding urban areas). On-reef values were based on the relative abundance of dive-shops and underwater photos in different countries and territories, which determined the proportion of that local coastal spending that was attributed to reefs. Reef-adjacent values were estimated as a fixed 10% of total local tourism expenditure. Finally, these tourism values were linked back and assigned to the reefs that were considered to be generating these values. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0308597X17300635). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. This methodology also yielded estimates of on-reef, reef-adjacent, and total "tourist trip equivalents." description: The Political Violence Risk Assessment dataset was originally published by The Hague Centre for Strategic Studies (HCSS). Its purpose is to forecast the onset of large-scale political violence. Countries are evaluated to determine their "risk" of experiencing a large-scale political violence event in the next month using structural data (infant mortality, regime type, conflicts in neighboring countries, and state-led discrimination) and automated event data (protests, assaults, and expressions of disapproval) from the previous month, which are combined in a logistic regression model. The score is normalized between 0 and 100 and indicates the percentile rank of probability of onset. Infant mortality data are from World Development Indicators; other structural data are from the Center for Systemic Peace; event data are from the Global Database of Events, Language, and Tone; and normalization and aggregation were done by the HCSS. title: Air Quality: Carbon Monoxide (CO) Modeled Next-day Forecast
description: ### Overview This dataset shows forecasted carbon monoxide (CO) concentrations at Earth's surface, modeled by the Whole Atmosphere Community Climate Model (WACCM). Carbon monoxide is a colorless, odorless gas that is toxic when inhaled in large amounts. Carbon monoxide exposure can be fatal. According to the U.S. [Center for Disease Control](https://www.cdc.gov/co/faqs.htm) (CDC), carbon monoxide is released when fossil fuels are burned. Common household sources include grills, cars, fireplaces, and gas stoves that aren’t properly ventilated. Major sources of carbon monoxide to outdoor air include cars, trucks and other fossil-fuel-burning machinery. Breathing air with a high concentration of carbon monoxide reduces oxygen availability in the bloodstream for critical organs like the heart and brain. Symptoms of carbon monoxide poisoning include headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain, and confusion. WACCM creates global forecasts for a variety of other air quality indicators, as well. While this dataset shows forecasted carbon monoxide concentrations, Resource Watch also shows WACCM forecasts for [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-SO), [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-PM-25), [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-Black-Carbon), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-O), and [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-NO). WACCM runs the model daily, and on their website you can find forecasted concentrations for each compound up to nine days into the future at three-hour time steps. WACCM was developed by the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) and the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research (UCAR). The data has global coverage at 1.9 x 2.5 degree resolution. ### Methodology WACCM is a comprehensive numerical model, driven by meteorological fields from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration’s (NASA) Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO) Goddard Earth Observing System Model, Version 5 (GEOS-5) model. The development of WACCM is an inter-divisional collaboration that unifies modeling from the High Altitude Observatory ([HAO](http://www2.hao.ucar.edu/)), the Atmospheric Chemistry Observations and Modeling ([ACOM](https://www2.acom.ucar.edu/)) Laboratory, and the Climate and Global Dynamics ([CGD](http://www2.cgd.ucar.edu/)) Laboratory. Upper atmospheric modeling from HAO, middle atmospheric modeling from ACOM, and tropospheric modeling from CGD are combined using the NCAR [Community Earth System Model (CESM)](http://www.cesm.ucar.edu/) as a common numerical framework. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://opensky.ucar.edu/islandora/object/articles%3A12836). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows WACCM forecasts for [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-SO), [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-PM-25), [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-Black-Carbon), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-O), and [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-NO). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional forecasted data for other compounds, times, and levels of the atmosphere are also produced by WACCM. Tree Cover
description: ### Overview The Tree Cover dataset measures areas of tree cover in 2000. Tree cover is defined as all vegetation greater than 5 meters (m) in height and may take the form of natural forests or plantations across a range of canopy densities. The dataset has a spatial resolution of 1 arc second which is approximately 30 m × 30 m at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. Forests provide a wide range of ecosystem services that are [critical to biodiversity richness, climate regulation, carbon storage, and water supplies](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/309/5734/570?ijkey=493d3bb49264119aa5ed9175119f7e221b2093d6&keytype2=tf_ipsecsha). They provide shelter to a variety of wildlife species and supply humans with [essential products including lumber, paper, and firewood]( https://www.fs.fed.us/forestmanagement/products/#:~:text=Forest%20products%20include%20materials%20derived,nuts%2C%20and%20other%20natural%20products). In the global fight against climate change, the forest ecosystem is playing an incredibly important role since it [absorbs and stores large amounts of carbon](https://www.undp.org/content/undp/en/home/blog/2018/Forests-A-natural-solution-to-climate-change-crucial-for-a-sustainable-future.html). Through measuring the tree cover density of global forests, this dataset provides decision makers with a consistent basis on which to understand the [causes of tree cover loss](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/342/6160/850). It also helps to quantify other critical environmental issues, such as the economic drivers of [natural forest conversion to more intensive land uses](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1549-0831.1998.tb00691.x) and the effectiveness of [protected areas around the globe](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature02422) to represent species diversity. The dataset was created through a collaboration among the Global Land Analysis & Discovery (GLAD) lab at the University of Maryland (UMD), Google, United States Geological Survey (USGS), and National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) with the aim to provide a spatially and temporally detailed quantification of global forest change. ### Methodology The data was generated using multispectral satellite imagery from three sources: the Landsat 5 thematic mapper, the Landsat 7 thematic mapper plus and the Landsat 8 Operational Land Imager sensors. [Images captured during growing seasons](https://doi.org/10.14358/PERS.70.3.313) were used since they are more appropriate for mapping land cover. More than 1 million satellite images were processed, including over 600,000 Landsat 7 images for the 2000-2012 interval and 400,000 Landsat 5, 7 and 8 images for the 2011-2019 interval. The following steps were taken to pre-process the images: 1. Pixel values were recalculated if image resolutions were changed. 2. Images were screened for clouds, shadows and water. 3. Images were [calibrated and normalized](http://gsp.humboldt.edu/OLM/Courses/GSP_216_Online/lesson4-1/radiometric.html) to make them comparable with one another. Land surface observations in the satellite images were assembled with a supervised learning algorithm, which involved [using labeled data to develop a machine learning model](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/problem-framing/cases#what-is-supervised-learning) to identify per pixel tree cover. To facilitate processing, each continent was characterized individually: North America, South America, Eurasia, Africa, and Australia using [Google Earth Engine](https://earthengine.google.com/), a cloud platform for earth observation data analysis that combines a public data catalog with a large-scale computational facility capable of handling large volumes of geospatial data. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows [Tree Cover Loss](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/5c5e654e-182b-4ab4-8a3c-edff79cc68ea) and [Tree Cover Gain](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/426fe3f0-12de-4adb-b3aa-850eb04f75b4) from the same dataset. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for the reference multispectral imagery from 2000 and 2019 is available from the data provider. title: Uttarakhand Change in Evapotranspiration
description: The data represents annual change in the evapotranspiration for baseline (1981-2010) and mid-century (2021-2050) under RCP 4.5 & 8.5 emission scenarios in millimetre (mm). This data is an output from a hydrologic model, SWAT (Soil and Water Assessment Tool) which has been use to assess the impact of projected climate change on water resources. The SWAT model (Arnold et al., 1981, Neitsch et al., 2022) is a distributed parameter and continuous time simulation model. The SWAT model has been developed to predict the hydrological response of un-gauged catchments to natural inputs as well as the manmade interventions. The model (a) is physically based; (b) uses readily available inputs; (c) is computationally efficient to operate and (d) is continuous time and capable of simulating long periods for computing the effects of management changes. The major advantage of the SWAT model is that unlike the other conventional conceptual simulation models it does not require much calibration and therefore can be used on un-gauged watersheds (in fact the usual situation). The SWAT model is a long-term, continuous model for watershed simulation. It operates on a daily time step and is designed to predict the impact of land management practices on water, sediment, and agricultural chemical yields. The model is physically based, computationally efficient, and capable of simulating a high level of spatial details by allowing the watershed to be divided into a large number of sub-watersheds. Major model components include weather, hydrology, soil temperature, plant growth, nutrients, pesticides, and land management. The model has been validated for several watersheds. Input data used are terrain, landuse, soil, daily weather data (rainfall, maximum and minimum temperature, wind speed,, relative humidity and wind speed), cropping pattern, reservoirs and any man made structure with their characteristics. The outputs provided by the model are very exhaustive covering all the components of water balance spatially and temporally. The sub components of the water balance that are more significant and were used for analyses include: • Precipitation. • Total flow (Water yield) consisting of surface runoff, lateral and base flow. • Actual evapotranspiration (Actual ET). • Base flow. • Ground water recharge. PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link.

description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](79f16b9a-a062-4820-822d-7858609a8fd5) as a replacement.**_ ### Overview This dataset shows the locations of seasonal water and permanent water for each year between 1984 and 2018. A permanent water surface is an area that is underwater for all 12 months of the year, while a seasonal water surface is underwater for less than 12 months of the year. This dataset has a 30 meter resolution. Water is essential for Earth’s plant and animal life, as well as for many human activities. Surface water also affects the exchange of heat, gas, and water vapor between Earth’s surface and atmosphere. The dataset can be used to support sectors such as water resource management, climate modeling, biodiversity conservation, and food security. This data is a part of the Global Surface Water dataset, created by the European Commission’s Joint Research Center. ### Methodology Water coverage was detected using satellite imagery from Landsat 5, 7, and 8 that was collected between 1984 and 2018. To detect water, researchers used big data exploration and information extraction techniques such as expert systems, visual analytics, and evidential reasoning. An expert system is a classification process that can account for data uncertainty and incorporate image interpretation expertise. In some places, observations for all 12 months of the year were not available. For example, some parts of the world experience a polar night during parts of the year, in which the night lasts for more than 24 hours. These areas do not have adequate imagery to detect surface water coverage for all 12 months. In cases where 12 months of data was not available, water is considered to be permanent if the number of months where water is present is equal to the number of months where valid observations were acquired. Likewise, if the number of months where water is present is less than the number of months of valid observations, water is considered to be seasonal. Ice is treated as a nonvalid observation. If water is present throughout the unfrozen period, the lake is considered to be a permanent water surface. If the area of the lake contracts during the unfrozen period, then the pixels along the borders of the lake will be considered as seasonal water. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature20584). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for monthly recurrence and monthly water history are available from the data provider. title: Urban Expansion Probabilities
description: The Global Grid of Probabilities of Urban Expansion to 2030 by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration Socioeconomic Data and Applications Center (NASA SEDAC) presents spatially explicit probabilistic forecasts of global urban land cover change from 2000 through 2030 at a 2.5 arc-minute resolution. For each grid cell that is nonurban in 2000, a Monte Carlo model assigned a probability of becoming urban by the year 2030. The authors first extracted urban extent circa 2000 from the NASA MODIS Land Cover Type Product, Version 5, which provides a conservative estimate of global urban land cover. The authors then used population densities from the Global Rural-Urban Mapping Project, Version 1 (GRUMP v1), to create the population density driver map. They estimated the amount of new urban land in each UN region by 2030 in a Monte Carlo fashion based on present empirical distribution of regional urban population densities and probability density functions of projected regional population and GDP values for 2030. Change in Snowmelt Timing
description: The Change in Snowmelt Timing, 1975-2040, by Freshwater Ecoregion data set from the Nature Conservancy was developed by summarizing weekly averages of snowmelt for each 0.5-degree cell. Weekly snowmelt averages were derived using the Variable Infiltration Capacity (VIC) macroscale hydrologic model, which simulates spatially distributed total runoff and snowmelt over all global land areas for two time periods (past period covers 1961-1990; future period, 2025-2054). These modeled data were provided by the Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering at the University of Washington in Seattle and Washington State University in Pullman. The change in snowmelt peak is represented as the number of weeks' difference between past peak week and future peak week for each 0.5-degree cell and then averaged these values across each ecoregion. Areas where past snow cover was consistently absent over a ten-year period were excluded by using a snow cover mask derived from the 0.5-degree Nimbus-7 SMMR satellite data. Areas where peak snowmelt varied little throughout the averaged year were also excluded by using a mask of cells greater than one standard deviation of the past peak snowmelt range. The Upper Amur River (Shilka) has very high results largely due to extreme decadal shifts in precipitation. Local peak time shifts within ecoregions can be longer than this summarized map relates. title: Distribution of Consumer Spending by Sector
description: ### Overview The Distribution of Consumer Spending by Sector dataset estimates the share of household income that is spent on various types of products and services. Spending was analyzed for four consumption segments: lowest, low, middle, and higher. The four levels of consumption segments were based on income per capita: - Lowest: below $2.97 per capita a day - Low: between $2.97 and $8.44 per capita a day - Middle: between $8.44 and $23.03 per capita a day - Higher: above $23.03 per capita a day This dataset shows the percent of the household income that is spent on each type of product or service within each of these consumption segments. This dataset was developed by the World Bank Group as part of its Global Consumption Database. The data covers both urban and rural households in developing countries and is reported at the national level for the year 2010. ### Methodology The Distribution of Consumer Spending by Sector dataset was developed using multiple different surveys, depending on data availability, including household budget survey, living standard measurement surveys, and various kinds of country-specific socioeconomic surveys. All surveys measure consumption at the household level; however, different surveys collected data over different time periods. Some conducted surveys over a period of 12 months to account for seasonality, while others collected data over a shorter period (a few weeks or a few months). Most surveys rely on the "recall method," in which households are asked to report what they can recall spending over a given period. The choice of recall period may have a significant impact on the level of consumption reported by the households. Data was collected for households in various developing countries. These households were categorized by their consumption segments for the Global Consumption Database. The consumption segments are based on the global income distribution data, which rank the global population by income per capita. The lowest consumption segment corresponds to the bottom half of the global distribution, or the 50th percentile and below; the low consumption segment to the 51st-75th percentiles; the middle consumption segment to the 76th-90th percentiles; and the higher consumption segments to the 91st percentile and above. The purchasing power parity (PPP) US dollar threshold was converted into annual expenditure in local currency (as of 2010). The Global Consumption Database draws on a diverse array of data surveys, so standardization was applied, to the extent possible, through a six-step process. The first step consisted of annualizing each household's consumption or expenditure data for each commodity. The second step was to detect and fix outliers. The third step was to map commodities found in each survey dataset to a standard classification of products and services. In the fourth step, extrapolations were done to convert all consumption and population data to a common reference year. In the fifth and sixth step, the resulting data was compared with data from other sources and used to generate a standard set of tables for each country showing consumption and demographic patterns across consumption segments. title: National Populations
description: The 'Population, total' dataset released by the World Bank data catalog is based on the de facto definition of population, which counts all residents regardless of legal status or citizenship. The values shown are midyear estimates. Population estimates are usually based on national population censuses. Estimates for the years before and after the census are interpolations or extrapolations based on demographic models. Errors and undercounting occur even in high-income countries. The spatial coverage of this data set is global and on the national level, and the temporal coverage runs from 1960 through present day. In developing countries errors may be substantial because of limits in the transport, communications, and other resources required to conduct and analyze a full census. The quality and reliability of official demographic data are also affected by public trust in the government, government commitment to full and accurate enumeration, confidentiality and protection against misuse of census data, and census agencies' independence from political influence. Moreover, comparability of population indicators is limited by differences in the concepts, definitions, collection procedures, and estimation methods used by national statistical agencies and other organizations that collect the data. The currentness of a census and the availability of complementary data from surveys or registration systems are objective ways to judge demographic data quality. Some European countries' registration systems offer complete information on population in the absence of a census. The United Nations Statistics Division monitors the completeness of vital registration systems. Some developing countries have made progress over the last 60 years, but others still have deficiencies in civil registration systems. International migration is the only other factor besides birth and death rates that directly determines a country's population growth. Estimating migration is difficult. At any time many people are located outside their home country as tourists, workers, or refugees or for other reasons. Standards for the duration and purpose of international moves that qualify as migration vary, and estimates require information on flows into and out of countries that is difficult to collect. Population projections, starting from a base year are projected forward using assumptions of mortality, fertility, and migration by age and sex through 2050, based on the UN Population Division's World Population Prospects database medium variant. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Subnational Infant Mortality
description: ### Overview This dataset includes estimated infant mortality rates (IMR) for 234 countries and territories at a spatial resolution of 30 arc-seconds (about one kilometer at the equator) for the year 2015. 143 countries are recorded with subnational units and 91 countries include only national units. IMR is defined as the number of children who die before their first birthday for every 1,000 live births. IMR can be used as a proxy measurement for poverty and wellbeing within a population. This dataset can also be useful for a wide user community in interdisciplinary studies of health, development, sustainability, and the environment. This dataset was compiled by the Center for International Earth Science Information Network (CIESIN) of Columbia University and is managed by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration Socioeconomic Data and Applications Center (NASA SEDAC). ### Methodology Infant mortality rate (IMR) data were either acquired or calculated by CIESIN. Acquired means that IMRs were collected from trusted sources. Calculated by CIESIN means that IMRs were calculated by taking the number of infant deaths, dividing them by the number of live births, and multiplying the results by 1,000. Researchers collected the most recent IMR data from national offices, Demographic Health Surveys (DHS), Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (MICS) and other sources. Data collected from national offices included information from either a national Human Development Report, National Statistical Office (NSO), or ministry of health. Since the IMR input data spanned from 2006 to 2014, researchers adjusted the rate for the year 2015 based on the United Nations Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation. Boundary data came from the IMR data source when possible and when not available the Gridded Population of the World, Version 4 (GPWv4), was used. Against the boundary data, IMR data were assigned to grid cells at a spatial resolution of 30 arc-seconds to allow for easy integration with other spatial data like demographic and environmental datasets. Water features were collected from GPWv4 and categorized as no population or uninhabited areas. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://sedac.ciesin.columbia.edu/data/set/povmap-global-subnational-infant-mortality-rates-v2/docs). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Ramsar Internationally Important Wetlands
description: Ramsar wetlands refer to "internally important" wetlands as defined by the Convention on Wetlands and are designated by each contracting party. At the time of joining the Convention, each contracting party must designate at least one wetland site within their territory for inclusion in the List of Wetlands of International Importance (the Ramsar List). These Ramsar sites acquire a new national and international status. They are recognized as being of significant value not only for the country or the countries in which they are located but for humanity as a whole. There are currently over 2,400 Ramsar sites around the world. They cover over 2.1 million km2, an area larger than Mexico. Parties continue to designate wetlands for inclusion on the list. They select suitable wetlands for designation by referring to the criteria for identifying wetlands of international importance. The Convention has provided guidance to contracting parties on the management of Ramsar sites, in addition to its guidance on the wise use of all wetlands. The inclusion of a wetland on the list signifies the government’s commitment to take the steps necessary to ensure that the site’s ecological character is maintained. The Convention includes various measures to respond to threats to the ecological character of sites. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: Air Quality: Fine Paritculate Matter (PM2.5) Station Measurements
description: OpenAQ is an open-source project to surface live, real-time air quality data from around the world. Its “mission is to enable previously impossible science, impact policy and empower the public to fight air pollution.” The data include air pollutant measurements for [PM10](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003bnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-10), [PM2.5](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003anrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-25), [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cairqualityso2), [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003fnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-CO), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003dnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-NO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-O), and [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/0c3ed5b9-94b4-4fc5-9208-bf749f0a5052) from over 5,400 locations in 48 countries as of June 2017. Scientists, researchers, developers, and citizens can use these data to understand how air quality in different locations changes over time. OpenAQ has 5 criteria for including data sources in its platform: 1) Data must represent one of these pollutant types: PM10, PM2.5, SO₂, CO, NO₂, O₃, or BC; 2) Data must be from an official-level stationary, outdoor air quality source, defined as data produced by a government entity or international organization; 3) Data must be "raw" and reported in physical concentrations on their originating site; 4) Data must be at the "station-level," not aggregated into a higher (e.g., city) level; 5) Data must be from measurements averaged between 10 minutes and 24 hours. PM2.5 are fine inhalable particles, with diameters that are generally 2.5 micrometers and smaller. These particles come in many sizes and shapes and can be made up of hundreds of different chemicals. Some are emitted directly from a source, such as construction sites, unpaved roads, fields, smokestacks or fires. Most particles form in the atmosphere as a result of complex reactions of chemicals such as sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, which are pollutants emitted from power plants, industries and automobiles. The size of these particles allows them to get deep into your lungs, and some may even get into your bloodstream. Exposure to such particles can affect both your lungs and your heart. Numerous scientific studies have linked particle pollution exposure to a variety of problems, including: premature death in people with heart or lung disease, nonfatal heart attacks, irregular heartbeat, aggravated asthma, decreased lung function, increased respiratory symptoms, such as irritation of the airways, coughing or difficulty breathing. People with heart or lung diseases, children, and older adults are the most likely to be affected by particle pollution exposure. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Extreme Precipitation Days
description: Extreme precipitation days represent the annual average count of days with precipitation greater than the 99th percentile of the baseline, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

title: Air Quality: Nitrogen Dioxide (NO₂) Modeled Next-day Forecast
description: ### Overview This dataset shows forecasted nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) concentrations at Earth's surface, modeled by the Whole Atmosphere Community Climate Model (WACCM). NO₂ is a highly-reactive air pollutant, produced by fossil fuel combustion from power plants and gasoline-burning vehicles. NO₂ is used as the indicator for the larger group of nitrogen oxides (NOx), which includes nitrous acid and nitric acid. NO₂ emissions contribute to the [formation of smog](https://www.environment.gov.au/protection/publications/factsheet-nitrogen-dioxide-no2) and can significantly harm human health. According to the [U.S. Environmental Protection Agency](https://www.epa.gov/no2-pollution/basic-information-about-no2) (EPA), breathing air with a high concentration of NO₂ can irritate airways in the respiratory system and long-term exposures can contribute to asthma development. Even exposures to elevated NO₂ concentrations over short periods can aggravate respiratory diseases, particularly asthma, leading to respiratory symptoms (such as coughing, wheezing or difficulty breathing), hospital admissions and visits to emergency rooms. People with asthma, as well as children and the elderly are generally at greater risk for the health effects of NO₂. WACCM creates global forecasts for a variety of other air quality indicators, as well. While this dataset shows forecasted O₃ concentrations, Resource Watch also shows WACCM forecasts for [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-SO), [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-PM-25), [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-Black-Carbon), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-O), and [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-CO). WACCM runs the model daily, and on their website you can find forecasted concentrations for each compound up to nine days into the future at three-hour time steps. WACCM was developed by the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) and the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research (UCAR). The data has global coverage at 1.9 x 2.5 degree resolution. ### Methodology WACCM is a comprehensive numerical model, driven by meteorological fields from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration’s (NASA) Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO) Goddard Earth Observing System Model, Version 5 (GEOS-5) model. The development of WACCM is an inter-divisional collaboration that unifies modeling from the High Altitude Observatory ([HAO](http://www2.hao.ucar.edu/)), the Atmospheric Chemistry Observations and Modeling ([ACOM](https://www2.acom.ucar.edu/)) Laboratory, and the Climate and Global Dynamics ([CGD](http://www2.cgd.ucar.edu/)) Laboratory. Upper atmospheric modeling from HAO, middle atmospheric modeling from ACOM, and tropospheric modeling from CGD are combined using the NCAR [Community Earth System Model (CESM)](http://www.cesm.ucar.edu/) as a common numerical framework. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://opensky.ucar.edu/islandora/object/articles%3A12836). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows WACCM forecasts for [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-SO), [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-PM-25), [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-Black-Carbon), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-O), and [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-CO). description: Increased mortality is associated with increased heat. Climate change is projected to increase the number of heat related deaths. As such, tracking the number of heat related deaths may help public health professionals design targeted adaptation and response options for their specific regional requirements. The Heat-Related Mortality: Number of summertime (May-Sep) heat-related deaths by year is derived by the Center for Disease Control and Prevetnion's (CDC) Environmental Health Tracking Branch using National Center for Health Statistics mortality data with appropriate ICD-10 codes to calculate the total number of deaths by year during summer (May - September) period by year for the United States. Deaths from excessive heat exposure are defined based on codes from the tenth revision of International Classification of Diseases (ICD-10). Such deaths included those in which exposure to excessive natural heat (code X30) was reported as either the underlying or a contributing cause of death. Deaths due to exposure to excessive heat of man-made origin (W92) were excluded. Blanks or missing data within the maps, tables, and charts may be due to one of the following reasons: (1) data were not collected, (2) data were collected but were not provided to CDC, or (3) data were incomplete or did not meet data quality standards.

title: Energy Intensity
description: ### Overview This dataset shows energy intensity in 259 countries from 1990 to 2015. Energy intensity indicates how much primary energy (energy that comes directly from nature and has not been converted to a different form) is used to produce one unit of gross domestic product (GDP). GDP is a key economic indicator that measures the monetary value of goods and services provided within an area. Energy intensity is expressed as megajoules (MJ) of primary energy available per GDP produced, based on [purchasing power parity (PPP)](https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/fandd/basics/ppp.htm) in 2011 U.S. dollars (USD). PPP is a factor used to convert local currencies to one comparable unit of measure based on the local cost of goods and services in each country. Low energy intensity is desirable, as it means that less energy is used to produce one more unit of economic output. Having a low energy intensity indicates that a country can increase its economic growth without having to rely as heavily on energy consumption. The dataset was published as part of the Sustainable Energy for All (SE4ALL) initiative. The database is intended to help policymakers in government, business, and civil society work toward doubling the share of renewable energy in the global energy mix by 2030. Resource Watch also shows [renewable energy consumption](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene021a-Renewable-Energy-Consumption) and [percentage of energy consumption from renewable sources](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/bced4001-425a-4fad-8c22-8214d9340ea4) data from the SE4ALL Database. ### Methodology Energy intensity was measured as the ratio of total primary energy supply to the value added to the economy. Primary energy supply data came from the International Energy Agency (IEA) and the United Nations (UN) Energy Statistics Database. The value added to the economy was expressed in 2011 USD, adjusted for PPP. The data for GDP PPP came from the World Bank’s World Development Indicators. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://trackingsdg7.esmap.org/methodology). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows [renewable energy consumption](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/431f7c9e-7ef5-4f00-a5dc-8845fcb3a9a9) and [percentage of energy consumption from renewable sources](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/bced4001-425a-4fad-8c22-8214d9340ea4) data from the SE4ALL Database. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data related to electricity access and renewable energy electricity is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. Temperature Suitability for Disease-Carrying Mosquitoes
description: ### Overview This dataset shows the number of months per year when disease transmissions by two of the most common disease-carrying mosquitoes is possible, under current conditions, as well as in the years 2050, and 2080. The two mosquitoes are *Aedes aegypti* and *Aedes albopictus*. They transmit diseases to humans such as zika, dengue, chikungunya, and yellow fever. The baseline data used to represent current conditions is calculated using climate data from the years 1960-1990. In addition to the current temperature suitability for disease-carrying mosquitoes, the researchers used four climate change scenarios to predict where temperatures will be suitable for mosquitoes to thrive in the years 2050 and 2080. The dataset was published by researchers from the University of Florida, Georgetown University, the University of Maryland, Stanford University, and Virginia Polytechnic and State University. The dataset has global coverage with a 5 arc minute resolution. According to the [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/neglected_diseases/vector_ecology/mosquito-borne-diseases/en/), millions of people die each year from mosquito-borne diseases. Temperature is the main factor in mosquito survival and disease transmission. This dataset is crucial because governments and health organizations can use it to prevent and prepare for the viruses. ### Methodology Researchers used a model to predict disease transmission by fitting the thermal responses of mosquitoes as results of several parameters. The parameters included temperature, mosquito traits such as biting rate per mosquito and mosquito mortality rate, human population size, and human recovery rate. This model of disease transmission was based on experiments and validated with empirical data. As for temperature, current mean monthly temperature data was derived from the WorldClim dataset. To predict future temperatures, researchers used four general circulation models (GCMs) that are most commonly used by studies forecasting species distributional shifts. Each of the four models can respectively be forecasted for four representative concentration pathways (RCPs): RCP 2.6, RCP 4.5, RCP 6.0, and RCP 8.5. These RCPs are standardized scenarios in predicting how future climate will respond to emission output. RCP 2.5 represents the best-case scenario for mitigation and adaptation, and RCP 8.5 represents the worst-case, business-as-usual fossil fuel emissions scenario. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for the other three general circulation models (GCMs) besides the Had-GEM2-ES model is available from the data provider. Agricultural Trade Statistics
description: ### Overview The Agricultural Trade data and statistics compiled by the Food and Agricultural Organization of the United Nations (FAO) are key economic indicators, used to track trade flows between nations. Metrics are aggregated annually at the country level. The dataset comprises four categories: import quantity, import value, export quantity, and export value, and are available for all food and agricultural products for each country in the world. Quantity data is measured in weight (tonnes), while value is measured in 1,000 United States Dollars (USD). Agricultural commodity flows are especially important for actors along the agricultural supply chain. The metrics included in this dataset are standardized across countries, enabling comparisons to be made. This provides important information about what commodities are in surplus/deficit at the national level and elucidate linkages in the global flow of agricultural goods. The FAO has an institutional mandate to “collect, analyze, interpret, and disseminate information relating to nutrition, food and agriculture.” A primary purpose of this dataset is to ensure that there is a source of current, relevant, and reliable statistics for crop and livestock products that is applicable on the global scale. ### Methodology The FAO collects trade data from various entities including the United Nations Statistics Division (UNSD), Eurostat, and other national authorities. Trade data is collected, processed, and disseminated according to the standards outlined by the International Merchandise Trade Statistics (IMTS) [Methodology](https://unstats.un.org/unsd/trade/default.asp). The database includes annual information on the import quantity, export quantity, import value, and export value of all crop and livestock products for all countries in the world. Our data catalog only shows certain products that are derived from three crops: coffee, cotton, and rice. Additionally, only data from 1990 to 2020 is shown here , as it provides a firm historical understanding of these metrics. Trade quantity refers to the net weight (in tonnes) of the commodity and excludes containers. Export quantities are defined by IMTS methodology as the physical quantity of crop products originating or manufactured in and shipped out of the reporting country and include [re-exports](https://unstats.un.org/wiki/display/comtrade/Re-exports+and+Re-imports). Import quantity is essentially the reverse: referring to the import of products for domestic consumption or processing within that country and includes re-imports. Trade values (measured in one thousand USD) are reported as the value of the products or goods as well as the value of the services performed to deliver the goods from border to border. Trade data is compiled by the domestic customs office. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://unstats.un.org/wiki/display/comtrade/Re-exports+and+Re-imports). ### Additional Information Our data catalog shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for every year between 1961 and 2020 and more crops and livestock products are available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data See the documentation on how our team retrieved the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/com_039_rw0_agricultural_trade_statistics). Current Account Balance (BoP, current US$)
description: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) publishes annual national account balance in the form of balance of payments (BoP), that is, the sum of net exports of goods and services, net primary income, and net secondary income. BoP is a double-entry accounting system that shows all flows of goods and services into and out of an economy; all transfers that are the counterpart of real resources or financial claims provided to or by the rest of the world without a quid pro quo, such as donations and grants; and all changes in residents' claims on and liabilities to nonresidents that arise from economic transactions. All transactions are recorded twice—once as a credit and once as a debit. In principle, the net balance should be zero, but in practice the accounts often do not balance, requiring inclusion of a balancing item, net errors and omissions. The concepts and definitions underlying the data are based on the 6th edition of the Balance of Payments Manual (BPM6), published by the IMF. Balance of payments data for 2005 onward will be presented in accord with the BPM6. The historical BPM5 data series will end with data for 2008, which can be accessed through the World Development Indicators archives. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: Coral Reef Connectivity
description: ### Overview This dataset estimates the level of connectivity between each area containing coral reefs and other such areas. Connectivity refers to the extent to which populations are linked by the exchange of eggs, larval recruits, juveniles, or adults—an exchange which is primarily conducted via ocean currents. A coral larvae dispersal probability model developed by Wood et al. was applied by the 50 Reefs Project to simulate coral exchange between 2003 and 2011, ultimately yielding connectivity estimates globally at 0.05° resolution. These estimates were based on potential dispersal only; settlement and post-settlement survival were not modelled. Connectivity within and between protected areas is important for maintaining diversity, fish stocks, and especially important for maintaining ecological resilience. While poorly understood, it is a key factor to consider in marine reserve design as it may enhance resilience to disturbance and be important for the persistence of populations. Both of these are important processes in the context of conservation planning under climate change, the dominant threat to coral reefs in the coming decades. Even if the goals of the Paris Climate Agreement are achieved, 70-90% of coral reef areas are likely to cease to be suitable for coral growth by mid-century. Coral communities that survive will play a key role in the regeneration of reefs by mid-to-late century. The purpose of the 50 Reefs Project was to develop a long-term strategic plan for the conservation of coral reefs by identifying 50 large (500 km²) regions that are the least vulnerable to climate change and which are positioned to facilitate natural coral reef regeneration. These locations constitute important opportunities for novel conservation investments to secure less vulnerable yet well-connected coral reefs that may help to repopulate degraded areas after the climate has stabilized. The strategy and actions proposed by the project should strengthen and expand existing conservation efforts for coral reefs as the world faces the long-term consequences of intensifying climate change. ### Methodology The authors used a coral larvae dispersal probability model developed by [Wood et al.](https://doi.org/10.1111/geb.12101), basing their findings on simulations of larvae dispersal over a 93 month period. Within this modeling, 115 million particles (representing larvae from a generic broadcast spawning coral) were released from each of 12,397 habitat cells on a monthly basis between 2003-2011. Again following Wood et al., the authors used two measures of connectivity: (i) outgoing settlement, which is the proportion of particles that reached any habitat cell, including the source cell, and (ii) export, which is the proportion of particles reaching any cell other than the source cell, hence omitting self-seeding. These were combined into an overall "connectivity" score. The dataset contains entries for each of the approximately 54,586 0.05° degree (approximately 25 km² but [changes with distance from the equator](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616)) raster cells identified as containing coral habitat by a dataset from [Coral Reef Watch](https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/). The values were standardized to mean 0 unit variance for subsequent analysis by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation. The resulting scores reflect how far the values were below or above the population mean. The data table also contains: (1) an ID field that assigns a unique numeric identification number to each cell; (2) two fields representing the latitude and longitude of the center of the cell; (3) scores corresponding to other essential components of the 50 Reefs assessment; and (4) one final variable representing the aggregate score of the 50 Reefs analysis. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://conbio.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/conl.12587). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. The 50 Reefs initiative generated scores for several other factors crucial to their assessment: thermal history and recent thermal conditions, predicted future thermal conditions, and cyclone and storm risk. In total, the component scores were derived from 174 separate variables relevant to these topics; these components were also combined into one final assessment score using a custom weighting. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/ocn_017_coral_reef_connectivity). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.
