title: Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days in the U.S.
description: ### Overview The Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual cooling degree days (CDDs) at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. CDD is the number of degrees that a day's average temperature is above 65 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). For example, if a day's average temperature is 80°F, the CDD would be 15. If this happened 10 times in a year the annual CDD would be 150. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the CDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual CDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. CDD projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades and how this may affect future energy demands. For example, CDD is often used as a proxy to estimate energy requirements for cooling buildings. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. ### Methodology The Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference. The annual CDD for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. Daily CDDs were calculated by subtracting the baseline temperature of 65°F from daily average temperature values. If the daily average temperature was below 65°F, it was counted as zero. Then, annual CDD was calculated by summing all daily CDD values over a given year. Annual CDDs were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in cooling degree days. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the CDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual CDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows LOCA RCP 8.5 data for [Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/a9567364-e5ba-415e-a834-310e279326b6), [Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/4c6ba704-12f3-4954-92af-6c248c584233), [Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7ec68890-34a9-427c-907e-2f646f0dd9c8), [Projected Change in Dry Spells in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cd91e8d6-2e3d-46c1-9601-0dd7f524c7ba), [Projected Change in Frost Free Season in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/09e43293-98f1-4618-8e7e-d9f72cd5a4d7), [Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c985d4f6-9a03-4158-9955-e9f96db109ab), [Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/9e9b465a-bb0f-4047-ad72-9b8fabc0fd09), [Projected Change in Heating Degree Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6114c6fa-0ca6-4e06-ae23-413be0677503), [Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c5cbedcd-8cf5-4140-ac21-6791f6786f22). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data. Additional data is available for emissions scenario RCP 4.5. For access to the original LOCA dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. title: Historical Imagery
description: ### Overview The Historical Imagery dataset is a compilation of high quality Landsat imagery for each year from 2013-2016. These images show a detailed picture of the landscape at the Earth’s surface, e.g., forests, ice, freshwater, grasslands, desert and urban areas. Landsat data was collected continuously by satellite sensors. These sensors collected approximately 22 complete pictures of the Earth per year, with a spatial resolution of 30 meters (m). The satellite imagery was processed with Google Earth Engine’s Simple Composite algorithm. This algorithm converts the images to [top of atmosphere (TOA) reflectance](https://un-spider.org/node/10958) values and removes cloud-covered pixels. Understanding the Earth’s changing landscape is critical to many environmental issues: agriculture, water usage, forest coverage and natural disasters. In agriculture, Landsat data can be used to predict crop production, help farmers make planting decisions and settle water usage disputes. Landsat imagery shows changes in forest coverage, which is crucial to forest management and protection. Forest coverage influences the environment in many ways, including carbon storage and flood control. Landsat imagery is also a valuable tool for analyzing natural disasters such as floods, fires, droughts and volcanic eruptions. In areas affected by natural disasters, before and after imagery can be used to map damage, plan recovery efforts, and assess future risk. The Historical Imagery dataset was generated by [Google Earth Engine](https://earthengine.google.com/). Earth Engine is a tool for visualizing and analyzing geospatial datasets. The platform hosts satellite imagery in a public data archive for academic, non-profit, business and government users. In addition to hosting data, Earth Engine provides a variety of algorithms and processed datasets, including climate, surface temperature, weather and land cover. Earth Engine is part of Google’s overall mission to organize the world’s information and make it universally accessible. The satellite data used to generate the Historical Imagery dataset was provided by [Landsat](https://www.usgs.gov/core-science-systems/nli/landsat). Landsat is a joint effort between the [United States Geological Survey (USGS)](https://www.usgs.gov/) and the [National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)](https://www.nasa.gov/). Founded in 1972, Landsat manages satellites that continuously acquire images of the Earth. Landsat’s mission is to provide uninterrupted data and imagery of the Earth to help with decision-making about natural resources and the environment. ### Methodology The Historical Imagery dataset was generated from images of the Earth collected by instruments aboard the [Landsat satellites](https://www.usgs.gov/core-science-systems/nli/landsat/landsat-satellite-missions?qt-science_support_page_related_con=0#qt-science_support_page_related_con). These satellites crossed every point on Earth once every 16 days and each provided 22 complete pictures of the Earth each year. Each pixel in these images has a resolution of 30 m. The satellite imagery was processed using [Google Earth Engine’s Simple Composite algorithm](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/apidocs/ee-algorithms-landsat-simplecomposite). This algorithm selected a subset of pixels at each location and converted them to top of atmosphere (TOA) reflectance. This conversion is a linear transformation used to correct satellite data for variations in solar angle and the scattering of light that occurs as light travels through the atmosphere and reflects off the Earth. The simple cloud score was used to find the images with the least cloud cover. This algorithm scored TOA data pixels by their relative cloudiness from 0 (least cloudy) to 100 (most cloudy). After the pixels were scored, the median of the least cloudy pixels were used, thus selecting the least cloudy images. These images were used to generate the Historical Imagery composites. description: The Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS) collects and prepares satellite and ground-based observation data products for use in Land Surface Models (LSMs). The GLDAS is developed and distributed by NASA and the Goddard Earth Sciences Data and Information Services Center (GES DISC). This selection of GLDAS contains data on the amount of water stored as root-level soil moisture. [Archived] Boat Detection
description: ### Overview This dataset shows boats detected using satellite data collected by the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) instrument. VIIRS only detects the activity of lit boats. The data shows patterns of vessel activity and can provide indications of fishing activity within marine protected areas (MPAs) and across exclusive economic zone (EEZ) boundaries. Generally, EEZs are defined as the area within 200 nautical miles of a country’s coastline. The dataset is published by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Association (NOAA) and the National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI). The dataset has global spatial coverage, gives point location (latitude and longitude) of boat detections. The data collection began in 2017 and is updated daily. ### Methodology Lit fishing boat features detected by the VIIRS day/night band (DNB) data show up as spikes of light. A set of algorithms has been developed for automatic detection of spikes and characterization of the sharpness of spike features. A spike detection algorithm generates a list of candidate boat detections. A second algorithm measures the height of the spikes for the discard of ionospheric energetic particle detections and to rate boat detections as either strong or weak. A sharpness index is used to label boat detections that appear blurry due to the scattering of light by clouds. The candidate spikes are then compared with a separate VIIRS gas flares data set to identify detections that were also found to be gas flares. Based on the sharpness index, scan properties, and the gas flare indication, each candidate spike is assigned a quality flag that separates the detections into boats, blurry detections, and gas flares. Based on the location of the boat detections, they are also assigned information such as whether it is in an exclusive economic zone (EEZ) or a marine protected area (MPA). For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/7/3/3020). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. description: ### Overview The Tree Cover Gain dataset measures areas of tree cover gain from 2001 through 2012. Tree cover is defined as all vegetation greater than 5 meters (m) in height and may take the form of natural forests or plantations across a range of canopy densities. Gain is mapped for all areas that did not have tree cover in 2000 and had ≥ 50% cover in 2012. Longer-lived regrowing stands of tree cover that did not begin as non-forest within the study period were not mapped as forest gain. The dataset has a spatial resolution of 1 arc second which is approximately 30 m × 30 m at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. Forests provide a wide range of ecosystem services that are [critical to biodiversity richness, climate regulation, carbon storage, and water supplies](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/309/5734/570?ijkey=493d3bb49264119aa5ed9175119f7e221b2093d6&keytype2=tf_ipsecsha). They provide shelter to a variety of wildlife species and supply humans with [essential products including lumber, paper, and firewood]( https://www.fs.fed.us/forestmanagement/products/#:~:text=Forest%20products%20include%20materials%20derived,nuts%2C%20and%20other%20natural%20products). In the global fight against climate change, the forest ecosystem is playing an incredibly important role since it [absorbs and stores large amounts of carbon](https://www.undp.org/content/undp/en/home/blog/2018/Forests-A-natural-solution-to-climate-change-crucial-for-a-sustainable-future.html). Through measuring the gain in tree cover of global forests, this dataset provides decision makers with a consistent basis on which to understand the [causes of tree cover loss](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/342/6160/850). It also helps to quantify other critical environmental issues, such as the economic drivers of [natural forest conversion to more intensive land uses](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1549-0831.1998.tb00691.x) and the effectiveness of [protected areas around the globe](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature02422) to represent species diversity. The dataset has been created through a collaboration among the Global Land Analysis & Discovery (GLAD) lab at the University of Maryland (UMD), Google, United States Geological Survey (USGS), and National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) with the aim to provide a spatially and temporally detailed quantification of global forest change. ### Methodology The data was generated using multispectral satellite imagery from three sources: the Landsat 5 thematic mapper, the Landsat 7 thematic mapper plus and the Landsat 8 Operational Land Imager sensors. [Images captured during growing seasons](https://doi.org/10.14358/PERS.70.3.313) were used since they are more appropriate for mapping land cover. More than 1 million satellite images were processed, including over 600,000 Landsat 7 images for the 2000-2012 interval and 400,000 Landsat 5, 7 and 8 images for the 2011-2019 interval. The following steps were taken to pre-process the images: 1. Pixel values were recalculated if image resolutions were changed. 2. Images were screened for clouds, shadows and water. 3. Images were [calibrated and normalized](http://gsp.humboldt.edu/OLM/Courses/GSP_216_Online/lesson4-1/radiometric.html) to make them comparable with one another. Land surface observations in the satellite images were assembled with a supervised learning algorithm, which involved [using labeled data to develop a machine learning model](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/problem-framing/cases#what-is-supervised-learning) to identify per pixel tree cover gain. To facilitate processing, each continent was characterized individually: North America, South America, Eurasia, Africa, and Australia using [Google Earth Engine](https://earthengine.google.com/), a cloud platform for earth observation data analysis that combines a public data catalog with a large-scale computational facility capable of handling large volumes of geospatial data. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows the [Tree Cover](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/027799db-c161-462a-9c20-aeb97b84e06e) and the [Tree Cover Loss](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/5c5e654e-182b-4ab4-8a3c-edff79cc68ea) from the same dataset. description: Increases in the rates of hospital admission for heat stress are one potential impact of rising global temperatures. Tracking Crude Rate of Hospitalization for Heat Stress per 100,000 Population can help document changes over place and time, monitor vulnerable areas, and evaluate the results of local climate-adaptation strategies. Heat stress can manifest in a number of clinical outcomes, and people with chronic health problems (e.g., cardiovascular disease, diabetes, obesity) are more susceptible to the effects of heat than healthy individuals. For these reasons, heat stress may not be listed as the primary diagnosis. This indicator therefore includes all cases where heat stress is explicitly listed as the primary diagnosis or any other diagnosis. The hospital data shown here are provided by state and/or local public health departments to the National Environmental Public Health Tracking Program. Data are based on the date of admission rather than the date of discharge. For these measures, admission date is limited to between May 1 and September 30 for each year. These data represent number of admissions rather than number of individuals admitted to the hospital. The Center for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) Tracking Network suppresses data for counties with non-zero counts less than 6 and population less than 100,000 to protect confidentiality. This data set covers the United States from 2000 to 2016. Data on states designated as 'unstable', or counties corresponding with relative standard error greater than 30%, have been excluded in this visualization. title: Renewable Energy Consumption
description: ### Overview This dataset shows renewable energy consumption in 259 countries from 1990 to present. In this dataset, renewable energy sources are defined as hydropower, solid and liquid biofuels, wind, solar, biogas, geothermal, marine, and waste to energy. The dataset was published as part of the Sustainable Energy for All (SE4ALL) initiative, and the data was compiled by the International Energy Agency (IEA) and the United Nations Statistics Divisions (UNSD). IEA and UNDC are the primary developers of internationally comparable national energy statistics. This dataset tracks the progress of Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) indicator 7.2, to advance the target of increase substantially the share of renewable energy in the global energy mix by 2030. Resource Watch also shows [energy intensity](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene029a-Energy-Intensity) and [percentage of energy consumption from renewable sources](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/bced4001-425a-4fad-8c22-8214d9340ea4) data from the SE4ALL Database. ### Methodology This dataset was compiled using data from the International Energy Agency (IEA) energy statistics, complemented by the United Nations (UN) database when IEA data was not available. IEA data contained the most comprehensive and accurate data for countries that were a part of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), as well as 75 non-OECD countries. In the case of smaller non-OECD countries, extrapolations of country data provided by the UN Statistics Division were used. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.seforall.org/sites/default/files/l/2013/09/9-gtf_ch4.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows [energy intensity](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene029a-Energy-Intensity) and [percentage of energy consumption from renewable sources](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/bced4001-425a-4fad-8c22-8214d9340ea4) data from the SE4ALL Database. title: [Archived] Global Hunger Index
description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](c37b0b21-3d11-46ea-ba5d-4be4c0caa8ae) as a replacement.**_ ### Overview The Global Hunger Indices show the state of hunger worldwide in 2018, along with three reference years in 2000, 2005, and 2010. The indices capture the multidimensional nature of hunger by calculating Global Hunger Index (GHI) scores comprised of four indicators: undernourishment, child wasting, child stunting, and child mortality. The 2018 Global Hunger Index is published jointly by Concern Worldwide and Welthungerhilfe to measure and track hunger and to spotlight areas with the greatest need to eliminate hunger. The GHI scores are calculated on a 0-100 scale, where 0 indicates no hunger and 100 demonstrates complete hunger. A high GHI score, broadly speaking, can indicate a lack of food, a low-quality diet, insufficient child caregiving practices, an unhealthy environment, or all of these factors. In the GHI by Severity layers, countries are classified as having low, moderate, serious, alarming, or extremely alarming scales of hunger. ### Methodology GHI scores were calculated using a three-step process that draws on available data from various sources to capture the multidimensional nature of hunger. First, for each country, values were determined for four indicators: 1. Undernourishment: the share of the population that is undernourished (that is, whose caloric intake is insufficient); 2. Child wasting: the share of children under the age of five who are wasted (that is, who have low weight for their height, reflecting acute undernutrition); 3. Child stunting: the share of children under the age of five who are stunted (that is, who have low height for their age, reflecting chronic undernutrition); and 4. Child Mortality: the mortality rate of children under the age of five (in part, a reflection of the fatal mix of inadequate nutrition and unhealthy environments). Second, each of the four component indicators was given a standardized score on a 100-point scale based on the highest observed level for the indicator on a global scale in recent decades. Third, standardized scores were aggregated to calculate the GHI score for each country, with each of the three dimensions (inadequate food supply, child mortality, and child undernutrition, which is composed equally of child stunting and child wasting) given equal weight. This three-step process results in GHI scores on a 100-point GHI Severity Scale, where 0 is the best score (no hunger) and 100 is the worst. In practice, neither of these extremes is reached. A value of 0 would mean that a country had no undernourished people in the population, no children younger than five who were wasted or stunted, and no children who died before their fifth birthday. A value of 100 would signify that a country’s undernourishment, child wasting, child stunting, and child mortality levels were each at approximately the highest levels observed worldwide in recent decades. The GHI Severity Scale shows the severity of hunger - from low to extremely alarming - associated with the range of possible GHI scores. description: The Consultative Group for International Agricultural Research Consortium for Spatial Information (CGIAR-CSI) supported the development of the Global-Aridity Database. This database is designed for use in models of sustainable development, biodiversity and environmental conservation, poverty alleviation, and adaption to climate change globally, in particular in developing countries, and provides data for each month between 1970 and 2000 at a spatial resolution of 30 arc seconds. This data set is the aridity index (AI), which is calculated as the ratio of mean annual precipitation to mean annual potential evapotranspiration (PET), using data from the WorldClim Global Climate Database. The yearly precipitation values are available directly from the WorldClim database, and the PET values are derived from a selection of WorldClim variables. PET is a measure of the rate at which water evaporates from the Earth's surface into the atmosphere. It is influenced by several factors, including solar radiation, temperature, air humidity, and wind speed. Other contributing factors include the leaf area index of an area, as water pooling on top of leaves and tree canopies can lead to faster evaporation than if precipitating water entered the soil layer. title: Groundwater Vulnerability to Floods and Droughts
description: The German Federal Institute for Geosciences and Natural Resources (BGR) partnered with UNESCO's International Hydrological Programme and the International Association of Hydrogeologists to coordinate the World-wide Hydrogeological Mapping and Assessment Programme (WHYMAP). The Map of Global Groundwater Vulnerability (GWV) to Floods and Droughts at the scale of 1:25,000,000 is a WHYMAP product that rates groundwater systems on a scale of 1 to 7 according to their vulnerability to drought and flood events. Vulnerability is defined as a system's sensitivity to natural and/or human impacts, and the ability of the system to cope with these impacts. This information can be used to prioritize which groundwater resources can be relied on in case of a natural disaster. The maps of groundwater systems were sourced from national, regional, and global sources. Many aquifer boundaries were sourced from the WHYMAP Groundwater Resources Map (GRM). The GRM includes major groundwater basins, areas with complex hydrogeological structures, and local and shallow aquifers. These were complemented by aquifers in fluvial deposits of large rivers from the Geological Map of the World, aquifers in carbonate rocks—usually karstified—from the World Map of Carbonate Rock Outcrops, and the WHYMAP database for aquifers with nonrenewable groundwater. The extent of the impact of different natural disasters on aquifers and their groundwater resources differs depending on factors such as the origin of the disaster, its intensity and frequency, the hydrogeological conditions and geographical position of the aquifer (coastal area or a floodplain), and other factors affecting vulnerability (shallow or deep, whether groundwater is nonrenewable). The GWV uses a simplified version of the DRASTIC index for assessing groundwater vulnerability, measuring aquifer vulnerability according to the type of aquifer and the aquifer’s groundwater recharge rate. Aquifer types are assessed according to the map sources mentioned above. Groundwater recharge rates are calculated using the WaterGAP hydrogeological model and categorized as < 20 mm/year, 20-100 mm/year, or > 100 mm/year. A total vulnerability range (TVR) is assigned to each aquifer based on its type and recharge rate. Aquifer type is weighted more than rate of recharge in this calculation, since aquifers in carbonate rocks (often karstified) or in fluvial deposits of large rivers and shallow and local aquifers are all highly vulnerable to natural disasters—particularly floods, storms, and tsunamis—and are also highly vulnerable to droughts in arid and semiarid regions. Natural disasters include 1) hydro-climatic events (floods, droughts, storms); 2) geological events (earthquakes, volcanic activity); and 3) events caused by a combination of hydroclimatic and geological factors (tsunamis, landslides). The GWV focuses on hydroclimatic events, and the vulnerability of each aquifer is assessed for floods and droughts. The map assigns 7 categories of vulnerability based on the combination of flood and drought vulnerability (low, low; low, moderate; etc). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Fully and Highly Protected Marine Areas
description: ### Overview The Fully and Highly Protected Marine Areas dataset as shown on Resource Watch presents marine protected areas (MPAs) that are fully or highly protected. The [Marine Protection Atlas (MPAtlas)](https://mpatlas.org/) uses the [World Database on Protected Areas](https://www.protectedplanet.net/en/thematic-areas/marine-protected-areas) as a starting point, then assesses the current protection status of listed MPAs based on additional sources and research. This global dataset was first created in 2020 and in the future will be regularly updated, as new MPAs are created, protections change, and currently designated areas are implemented. MPAs are essential for safeguarding biodiversity and the health of marine ecosystems. They provide sanctuary for species to mature and reproduce, and they help restore healthy populations within and beyond their borders. MPAs also build resilience against threats such as climate change and pollution by maintaining vital natural processes, storing carbon, buffering coastlines, and ensuring sustainable food supplies for coastal communities. However, different MPAs may offer different levels of protection, from minor restrictions to the full exclusion of most commercial activity. Robust scientific evidence indicates that no-take zones (where no extractive activities are allowed) and highly protected areas yield the greatest conservation benefits. The MPAtlas brings together the best available information on marine protection around the world, so that the marine conservation community can work together to protect at least [30% of the world's oceans by 2030](https://www.campaignfornature.org/science-page). This more detailed approach to MPA data provides a more nuanced look at progress toward conservation goals and the outcomes that can be expected from existing protections. ### Methodology MPAtlas takes the WDPA as its starting point and examines the listed MPAs in depth, adding to or replacing WDPA records with information from original research using more detailed or up-to-date sources, such as national or regional databases, official documentation, or management plans. These additions can include more accurate spatial data, such as the addition of boundaries for individual zones within an MPA. It can also include more detailed information about site regulations and management, both of which are directly related to conservation outcomes. MPAtlas coverage numbers differ from those of other sources for two primary reasons: 1. MPAtlas attempts to identify and distinguish protected areas that are legally designated but are still awaiting implementation from those that are fully in effect on the water. The project also identifies committed or proposed protected areas that have not yet achieved legal or authoritative recognition. 2. MPA coverage data is reported by protection level, as no-take and fully and highly protected areas are those which afford the greatest conservation benefits. The project accomplishes this by conducting detailed assessments using widely-accepted, scientifically-based criteria for measuring an MPA’s protection level and associated conservation outcomes. Detailed information about the assessment process [can be found here](https://marine-conservation.org/mpatlas-assessments/). For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://mpatlas.org/methods). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows [the full WDPA](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/bio007-World-Database-on-Protected-Areas_replacement) and [the MPA subset](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/bio007b-Marine-Protected-Areas), on which the MPAtlas is based. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the Marine Protected Atlas. The MPAtlas includes all MPAs in the WDPA, but because these are already mapped elsewhere, Resource Watch displays only those MPAtlas entries with confirmed partial or complete protections from fishing and extractive commercial activity. description: The global Landslide Hazard Assessment for Situational Awareness (LHASA) model is developed by NASA to provide situational awareness of landslide hazards for a wide range of users. Precipitation is a common trigger of landslides. The Integrated Multisatellite Retrievals for the Global Precipitation Measurement mission (IMERG) data shows recent precipitation, updated every 30 minutes. A LHASA landslide “nowcast” is created by comparing GPM data from the last 7 days to the long-term precipitation record provided by the Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission (TRMM) Multisatellite Precipitation Analysis (TMPA). Because IMERG data are only available starting in 2014, the record of historical rainfall was established by the TMPA, comparing 2001 to the present. The TMPA rainfall probability distributions were then compared to those of IMERG, and the rainfall thresholds were adjusted so that the IMERG data more closely mapped to those of the TMPA archive. The past 7 days of rainfall are considered, with each day weighted according to its date before present, with the last 24 hours having the most impact. In places where precipitation is unusually high, the susceptibility of the terrain is evaluated based on the global landslide susceptibility map, which includes quantitative information on whether (1) roads have been built, (2) trees have been cut down or burned, (3) a major tectonic fault is nearby, (4) the local bedrock is weak, or (5) the hillsides are steep. title: Biodiversity Hotspots
description: ### Overview Biodiversity hotspots, a classification system created by the Critical Ecosystem Partnership Fund (CEPF), include some of our planet’s most biologically diverse yet threatened terrestrial areas. An area is qualified as a hotspot if it contains at least 1,500 species of vascular plants found nowhere else on Earth (known as “endemic” species) and it has lost at least 70 percent of its primary native vegetation. Between 1988 and 2016, 36 biodiversity hotspots have been identified globally. ### Methodology Hotspots were defined by Norman Myers in 1988 when he published a seminal paper identifying 10 tropical forest “hotspots.” These regions were characterized both by exceptional levels of plant endemism, meaning plants found nowhere else on Earth, and serious levels of habitat loss. Conservation International (CI) adopted Myers’s hotspots as its institutional blueprint in 1989. In 1999, CI undertook a global review, which introduced quantitative thresholds for the designation of biodiversity hotspots and resulted in the identification of 25. In 2005, an additional analysis brought the total number of biodiversity hotspots to 34, based on the work of nearly 400 specialists. In 2011, the Forests of East Australia were identified as the 35th hotspot by a team of researchers from the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organization working with CI. In February 2016, the North American Coastal Plain was recognized as meeting the criteria and became the world’s 36th hotspot. description: Potential Natural Vegetation is a data set created by EarthStat to identify what vegetation would be most likely to exist now in the absence of human activities. In regions not dominated by human land use, the vegetation types are those currently observed from a satellite. This differs from presettlement natural vegetation to the extent that vegetation types have changed because of changing environmental conditions such as climate and CO₂ concentrations. 1 km resolution DISCover data were classified under the Olson Global Ecosystems (OGE) framework to derive the potential vegetation data set. First the 94 OGE classes were reclassified into 15 potential vegetation types and 3 additional classes: land use, wetlands, and water. Wetlands are poorly characterized in the DISCover data and were thus ignored; only upland natural vegetation was considered. Each 5 minute resolution grid cell was searched among the 1 km pixels for the dominant potential upland vegetation class and was assigned to be the potential vegetation. Some grid cells had 2 dominant potential vegetation classes, or none. In these cases, the search was iterated to the adjacent 1 km pixels until a dominant potential vegetation class was found. title: Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days U.S. (RCP8.5)
description: The Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual cooling degree days (CDDs) at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. CDD is the number of degrees that a day's average temperature is above 65 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). For example, if a day's average temperature is 80°F, the CDD would be 15. If this happened 10 times in a year the annual CDD would be 150. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the CDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual CDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. CDD projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades and how this may affect future energy demands. For example, CDD is often used as a proxy to estimate energy requirements for cooling buildings. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference. The annual CDD for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. Daily CDDs were calculated by subtracting the baseline temperature of 65°F from daily average temperature values. If the daily average temperature was below 65°F, it was counted as zero. Then, annual CDD was calculated by summing all daily CDD values over a given year. Annual CDDs were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in cooling degree days. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the CDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual CDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

title: Water Stress Country Ranking
description: ### Overview This dataset shows the baseline water stress rating at a national scale. Baseline water stress is a measure of the level of competition for available freshwater. The dataset was calculated by comparing water withdrawals in a region to the quantity of water available. Higher water stress values indicate that there is more competition among people for available freshwater. The dataset was grouped by water usage for different sectors (agricultural, domestic, and industrial) to help understand which sectors had the greatest impact on water stress. The results were projected on a global map in five water stress risk categories: low, low to medium, medium to high, high, and extremely high. Understanding water stress is integral for human wellbeing. Water is a limited resource and a necessity for life. Water stress can have serious environmental consequences, with damage occurring to natural ecosystems reliant on a steady water supply. Additionally, water stress can lead to human and business conflicts, particularly between industrial and agricultural users that rely on water supply for production. This dataset was created by the World Resources Institute (WRI) to assist companies, investors, and governments in creating water use policies. ### Methodology The Water Stress Country Ranking is based on baseline water stress measurements. Baseline water stress measures the ratio of total water withdrawals to available renewable surface and groundwater supplies. Gridded output data from the [PCRaster Global Water Balance](https://gmd.copernicus.org/articles/11/2429/2018/) (PCRGLOBWB 2) hydrological model was used for both water withdrawal and available water. The water withdrawal output data from PCRGLOBWB 2 included monthly data from January 1960 to December 2014 for four sectors: domestic, industrial, irrigation, and livestock. Output data for available water was also available over the same time frame. Data from the model was then aggregated spatially to the sub-basin level using the World Wildlife Fund’s (WWF) [HydroBASINS level 6](https://hydrosheds.org/page/hydrobasins) hydrological sub-basins. Next, the data was regressed at the sub-basin level using an ordinary least square (OLS) regression with a trailing moving window size of 10 years to reduce noise in the data. This process resulted in gross water withdrawal and available water for each month for each sub-basin in the dataset. Next, the overall baseline water stress per month, per year, per sub-basin was determined. This was done by dividing the gross total water withdrawal by the difference between the available water and consumptive water withdrawal. This resulted in 12 time series of baseline water stress for each sub-basin: one time series for each month, with each time series spanning the years 1960-2014. Then, a single baseline water stress value for each month in each sub-basin was calculated by fitting a second OLS regression to each of the 12 time series and using the value for 2014 as the baseline water stress for that month. While the 2014 regression value is used, this value actually represents the baseline value, rather than an estimate of the water stress in 2014. To compute national baseline water stress scores, the sub-basins had to be aggregated to a national scale. Aggregation was made possible by following the steps outlined on page 4 of the [2013 version](https://files.wri.org/s3fs-public/aqueduct_coutnry_rankings_010914.pdf) of the methodology. This resulted in raw country score percentages in which water stress was classified as follows: - Low (0-1): <10% - Low to medium (1-2): 10-20% - Medium to high (2-3): 20-40% - High (3-4): 40-80% - Extremely high (4-5): >80% Each category represents the risk of water stress in the country. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://files.wri.org/s3fs-public/aqueduct-30-updated-decision-relevant-global-water-risk-indicators_1.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows [interannual variability](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/wat052-Aqueduct-Interannual-Variability) and [seasonal variability](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/wat053-Aqueduct-Seasonal-Variability) in water supply from the same dataset. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional information on drought risk and riverine flood risk is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/wat_036_rw1_water_stress_country_ranking). This data has been mapped on Resource Watch by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: [Archived] PRODES deforestation
description: The PRODES deforestation dataset was developed by Global Forest Watch (GFW) at the World Resources Institute (WRI) using data from the PRODES project, which is operated by the National Institute of Space Research (INPE) in collaboration with the Minister of the Environment (MMA) and the Brazilian Institute of Environment and Renewable Natural Resources (IBAMA). The dataset shows annual deforestation in the Brazilian Legal Amazon between 2000 and 2015. Since 2002, all PRODES data is publicly available online. Input images for each of the 220 Landsat footprints that cover the Brazilian Amazon are selected based on their lack of cloud cover and their capture date. The PRODES system uses the seasonal year, starting on August 1st, to calculate annual deforestation, so images are selected as near to this date as possible (generally from July, August, and September). From 2003 to 2005, analysts used image transformation to determine the components of vegetation, soil, and shadow using the program SPRING. These components were segmented and classified into the classes of forest, non-forest, deforestation in the target year, previous deforestation, clouds, and water, which are then manually corrected by experts. Starting in 2005, a new methodology was implemented which makes use of the open source TerraAmazon platform. The platform allows the PRODES analysis to be more uniform and can incorporate imagery from a variety of satellites. As before, images are selected to be as cloud free as possible. The images are then masked to exclude non-forest, previous deforestation, and water using the previous year’s analysis. Analysts then delineate deforested polygons in the intact forest of the previous year. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Global Peace Index
description: ### Overview The Global Peace Index (GPI) is a quantification of the absence of violence or the fear of violence to assess a nation’s level of peace. This lack of violence is defined as Negative Peace. A higher GPI represents a higher level of violence in a country. The Global Peace Index dataset was created by the Institute for Economics & Peace to measure global peacefulness. Its goal is to create understanding on the effects of violence and help countries develop the means to create peaceful societies. It measures a country’s level of Negative Peace using three domains of peacefulness: 1. *The extent of Ongoing Domestic and International Conflict:* This investigates the extent to which countries are involved in internal and external conflicts, as well as their role and duration of involvement in conflicts. This is based on six indicators, such as the number and duration of internal conflicts, number of deaths from external organized conflicts, and relationships with neighboring countries. 2. *The level of Societal Safety and Security:* It evaluates the level of harmony or discord within a nation using ten indicators. These indicators include topics like the level of perceived criminality in society, impact of terrorism, and political instability. 3. *The degree of Militarisation:* Militarisation refers to a country’s military build-up and access to weapons. This is determined by using seven indicators, such as military expenditure as a percentage of GDP, number of armed services personnel per 100,000 people, and nuclear and heavy weapons capabilities. The GPI data is reported at a national level with global coverage. Data is updated annually and is available from 2008 to 2019 for 163 countries or independent territories covering 99.7% of the world’s population. This data can help to understand the economic value and trends of peace, and how to develop peaceful societies. ### Methodology The Global Peace Index uses 23 indicators in three domains to quantify the absence of violence or fear of violence. An international panel of independent experts helped to select the indicators in 2007 and reviews them on an annual basis. These 23 indicators were weighted and combined into two categories to create an overall score for GPI out of 100. The total GPI score was then simplified into a value of 1-5, with 5 being the highest amount of violence or fear being present within a country. The two overarching categories were a measure of how peaceful a country is internally and a measure of how peaceful a country is externally. The value of these two categories out of the total GPI value was 40% for external peace and 60% for internal peace. The weighting scheme was selected based on the relative importance of each indicator to achieve global peace. All scores for each indicator were normalized on a scale of 1-5. Qualitative indicators were banded into five groupings relevant to the indicator. Quantitative indicators were scored continuously based on relevant data and rounded to the third decimal point. The Economist Intelligence Unit’s team of country analysts scored seven of the eight qualitative indicators and also provided estimates about the gaps in the quantitative data. Scoring for qualitative indicators followed a strict set of guidelines to ensure reliability between values. Quantitative values were taken from a variety of international and government organizations. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://visionofhumanity.org/app/uploads/2019/07/GPI-2019web.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](c12446ce-174f-4ffb-b2f7-77ecb0116aba) as a replacement.**_ The STAR Vegetation Health Index is a product from NOAA's National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service (NOAA-NESDIS) Global and Regional Vegetation Heath (VH) system estimating vegetation health, moisture condition, and thermal condition. VH products can be used as proxy data for monitoring vegetation health, drought, soil saturation, moisture and thermal conditions, fire risk, greenness of vegetation cover, vegetation fraction, leaf area index, start/end of the growing season, crop and pasture productivity, teleconnection with ENSO, desertification, mosquito-borne diseases, invasive species, ecological resources, land degradation, etc. The VH indices range from 0 to 100 characterizing changes in vegetation conditions from extremely poor (0) to excellent (100). Fair conditions are coded by green color (50), which changes to brown and red when conditions deteriorate and to blue when they improve. The VH reflects indirectly a combination of chlorophyll and moisture content in the vegetationhealth and also changes in thermal conditions at the surface.Monitoring vegetation health (condition), including drought detection and watch, is based on radiance measurements in the visible (VIS), near infrared (NIR), and 10.3-11.3 micrometers thermal (T) bands (channels) of the Advanced Very High Resolution Radiometer (AVHRR). These measurements are processed to reduce long-term noise. The VIS and NIR values were converted to the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI=(NIR-VIS)/(NIR+VIS)) and the T to brightness temperature (BT) using a look-up table. The NDVI and BT were filtered in order to eliminate high frequency noise. They were also adjusted for a non-uniformity of the land surface due to climate and ecosystem differences using multi-year NDVI and BT data. The NDVI and BT were converted to the Vegetation Condition Index (VCI), Temperature Condition Index (TCI), and Vegetation Health Index (VHI).The Vegetation Health Index (VHI) is a proxy characterizing vegetation health or a combined estimation of moisture and thermal conditions. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Marine Protected Areas
description: ### Overview The Marine Protected Area (MPA) dataset contains officially designated parks, reserves, and other formal conservation areas around the world that have a substantial maritime component. Protected area data are provided via [Protected Planet](https://www.protectedplanet.net/en/thematic-areas/marine-protected-areas), the online interface for the World Database for Protected Areas (WDPA). The WDPA is a joint initiative of the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) and the UN Environment Programme's World Conservation Monitoring Centre (UNEP-WCMC) to compile spatially referenced information about protected areas. The data is provided as shapefiles and updates monthly. Each record is either represented as a polygon boundary, or if unavailable, a point location, along with descriptive information, such as the name, legal designation, and mode of administration. As of May 2019, the WDPA included data on 242,784 protected areas, of which 91% were polygons and 9% were points. Over 70% of the surface of Earth is ocean, comprised of highly diverse ecosystems, and providing a wide range of marine ecosystem services that support human society, health and the economy. Much of the recent growth in MPA coverage has been driven by the establishment of very large MPAs over 100,000 (square kilometers) km². These vast MPAs each contribute a significant part of the total global ocean coverage, with the 20 largest making up the majority of the world’s MPA coverage. While these represent huge commitments to conservation, there is a need for international collaboration to ensure that MPAs achieve their desired conservation value. The information contained in the MPA dataset contributes to the UNEP-WCMC's mission to place biodiversity at the heart of environment and development decision-making to enable enlightened choices for people and the planet. The mandate of the database dates back to 1959 when the UN Economic and Social Council called for a list of national parks and equivalent reserves in recognition that they "are valuable for economic and scientific reasons and also as areas for the future preservation of fauna and flora and geologic structures in their natural state." The first UN List of Protected Areas was published in 1962, and subsequently evolved into the WDPA. The database is also used to generate indicators to track progress towards the Convention on Biological Diversity Aichi Biodiversity Target 11 and UN Sustainable Development Goals 14 and 15. ### Methodology Data for protected area records in the WDPA have been obtained from nearly 500 sources. Along with information on the data verifier, these sources are listed in the source table that is included with each monthly release. Data for protected areas designated under international agreements and conventions are often sourced from the relevant convention secretariats. Data for national-level protected areas have been sourced from national authorities wherever possible. Information may also be supplemented by data from other agencies, organizations or individuals. All data in the WDPA have been verified either by the national authorities or by non-government expert partners, with the exception of some data included before the verification process was established. Data in the WDPA must meet the Protected Planet data standards. These were developed in 2010, regularly updated and subsequently revised in 2015 to ensure consistency in the way the WDPA is compiled, checked, managed, and presented. Standards are important to ensure all information is supplied in a common format that is interoperable and useful for a wide variety of reporting and analytical purposes. There are four key requirements: 1. All sites must meet the IUCN definition of a protected area 2. Spatial data from Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and an associated list of attributes must be provided 3. Source of information must be provided 4. The WDPA Data Contributor Agreement must be signed The Protected Planet data standards also encompass standards specific to other databases, such as the Global Database on Protected Area Management Effectiveness. The MPA dataset comprises protected areas in the WDPA that intersect with the marine part of an internal base layer—generally, the ocean or seas, but not lakes. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.protectedplanet.net/en/resources/wdpa-manual). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows [the full WDPA dataset](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/bio007-World-Database-on-Protected-Areas_replacement) as accessed through the [Protected Planet API](https://api.protectedplanet.net/documentation#get-v3protectedareas). ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. title: Arctic Sea Ice Extent
description: ### Overview The Arctic Sea Ice Extent dataset shows the extent of sea ice in the Arctic for the latest month. Sea ice extent data was collected by satellite microwave sensing instruments at a spatial resolution of 25 kilometers (km). Data was collected daily and averaged at the end of each month to produce monthly ice extents. In this map, light blue represents locations where sea ice is currently present in the Arctic region. This dataset can be used to understand the current Arctic sea ice extent. Typically, Arctic sea ice extent reaches its maximum in March and minimum in September. However, Arctic sea ice extent has been declining since 2000. Melting sea ice can have [dramatic effects on global climate](https://nsidc.org/cryosphere/seaice/environment/global_climate.html). Because of its white color, sea ice reflects sunlight back into space. This property - albedo - keeps polar regions cold. However, as sea ice continues to melt, the Earth’s surface absorbs more sunlight, causing an increase in temperature. When sea ice melts, it changes the ocean’s salinity and temperature, disrupting currents and weather patterns. The [National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC)](https://nsidc.org/) was founded in 1976 as the World Data Center for Glaciology. Over time, the NSIDC evolved to become a data distribution and research center specializing in remote sensing of cryospheric data such as snow, sea ice, frozen ground, ice sheets and glaciers. In addition to managing and distributing this data, the NSIDC creates and supports data access tools for its users. They also use the datasets for climate research and education. The NSIDC is part of University of Colorado Boulder’s [Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences (CIRES)](https://cires.colorado.edu/). It is supported by the [National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)](https://www.nasa.gov/), the [National Science Foundation (NSF)](https://www.nsf.gov/) and the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)](https://www.noaa.gov/). ### Methodology Data was collected daily at a spatial resolution of 25 km. The Special Sensor Microwave Imager/Sounder (SSMIS) instrument aboard the [Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP) satellites](https://www.ospo.noaa.gov/Operations/DMSP/index.html) measured the data. NSIDC used this satellite data to create the [Near-Real-Time DMSP SSMIS Daily Polar Gridded Sea Ice Concentrations (NRTSI)](https://nsidc.org/data/nsidc-0081) dataset. The Monthly Arctic Sea Ice Extent dataset was generated from the NRTSI dataset. The SSMIS instrument senses microwave radiation emitted from the Earth's surface. The amount of microwave radiation emitted from an object depends on its physical properties, such as atomic composition and crystalline structure. The crystalline structure of ice typically emits more microwave energy than liquid ocean water, allowing SSMIS to easily distinguish sea ice from ocean water. SSMIS data was converted to [brightness temperature](https://glossary.ametsoc.org/wiki/Brightness_temperature), which is a measure of an object's radiation. Brightness temperature data was then converted to gridded ice concentration using the [NASA Team algorithm](https://nsidc.org/support/faq/nasa-team-vs-bootstrap-algorithm#NASATeam1). Gridded ice concentrations are the percentage of ice in a given cell. Each cell’s daily ice concentrations were averaged to produce monthly concentrations. If a cell contained more than 15% ice concentration, it was classified as ice. Otherwise, it was classified as water. Sea ice extent was delineated by the location where ice ends and the open ocean begins. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows additional NSIDC sea ice extent data: [Historical Sea Ice Medians](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/b1ebea96-5963-4c2c-9273-7d08536ac07d), [Minimum Arctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/a99c5cf5-f141-4bed-a36d-b04c8e171dfa), [Maximum Arctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/15a0b176-8313-4859-af90-5c198e50a605), [Minimum Antarctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/05fd2614-325b-460a-8b52-3155fa9dd98f), [Maximum Antarctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7667bdd8-9adb-44de-b51c-d2d26e461af1) and [Antarctic Sea Ice Extent](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e740efec-c673-431a-be2c-b214613f641a). description: These data were used to create Figure 17.4 in the Third National Climate Assessment report. See: http://nca2014.globalchange.gov/report/regions/southeast#graphic-17055 This figure shows the average of projections of the number of days over 95 degrees Fahrenheit from several climate models. On the global scale, climate model simulations show consistent projections of future temperature conditions under a range of emissions scenarios. All models show warming by late this century that is much larger than historical variations nearly everywhere globally. For the U.S., models unequivocally project large and historically unprecedented future warming in every region of the U.S. under all of the scenarios used in this assessment. The amount of warming varies substantially between higher versus lower scenarios, and moderately from model to model, but the amount of projected warming is much larger than historical variations. Likewise, the models project unequivocal increases in the number of days over 95 degrees Fahrenheit that are larger than historical variations. title: Drivers of Deforestation
description: This data set on deforestation drivers was adapted from Hosonuma et al. (2012) and illustrates the contribution of various industries ("drivers") to deforestation in Africa, the Americas and Asia (including Oceania). The driver data are summarized and analyzed for each of the 3 continents. Agriculture is the main driver of deforestation, but with geographic differences in the importance of commercial versus subsistence agriculture. The data include continental-level estimations for the relative area proportion and absolute net forest area change in km2 yr−1 (FAO 2010) for the period 2000–2010, deforestation drivers, and the relative disturbed forest area fraction of degradation drivers. The estimates are based on data from 46 tropical and subtropical countries and were obtained by the authors from REDD+ reports as well as Center for International Forestry Research country profiles (which include driver and activity information for deforestation and forest degradation), United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change National Communications, and other reports. In total, driver data were available for 46 of the 100 (sub)tropical non-Annex I countries. These 46 countries account for 78% of the total forest area (in 2010) and 81% of forest loss (in 2000–2010) of the 100 countries under consideration, according to 2010 data from the UN Food and Agriculture Organization Forest Resources Assessment (FAO 2010), and cover a range of forest transition (FT) phases on each continent. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Inflation
description: ### Overview The Inflation dataset shows national annual rates of inflation for each year from 1960-2019. Inflation reflects the annual percentage change in cost to the average consumer of acquiring specific goods and services. The dataset calculates inflation using the consumer price index (CPI), which is a weighted average of prices of a basket of consumer goods and services that can be measured and compared yearly. The dataset includes all countries that have CPI data available and has a national spatial resolution. It uses the units of percent change (% change) to compare how consumer prices have changed compared to previous years. The dataset is created by The World Bank with data from the International Monetary Fund (IMF). Inflation affects the purchasing power of a currency, so when inflation increases, each unit of currency buys fewer goods and services. Understanding and monitoring national inflation rates is important for governments and financial institutions in creating economic policies that reflect the state of their economy. ### Methodology The dataset was created by comparing CPI between years for each country. The CPI and inflation rate for each country was calculated using the Laspeyres formula. When a large range of goods and services are used in the formula it can be used to measure changes in a country’s cost of living. The Laspeyres formula was calculated by working out the cost of a group of commodities at the target year, dividing this by the cost of the same group of commodities at the previous year prices, and then multiplying by 100. The Laspeyres formula uses a base value of 100, so a value of 102 actually means there was an inflation rate of 2%. CPI data was taken from the International Monetary Fund, International Financial Statistics and data files. description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](c5a62289-bdc8-4821-83f0-6f05e3d36bdc) as a replacement.**_ The International Soil Reference and Information Centre - World Soil Information (ISRIC-WIS) uses machine learning techniques to develop global maps of soil properties at various soil depths, as well as characterizing bedrock depth. Soil organic carbon stocks are reported in tons per hectare for six standard depth intervals: depths of 0-5 cm, 5-15 cm, 15-30 cm, 30-60 cm, 60-100 cm, and 100-200 cm. Soil organic carbon stocks are important because they are correlated with the productive capacity of land to generate food and other plant life. Soil property estimates are generated using machine learning techniques that combine soil samples, expert opinion, and remote-sensing data. 150,000 soil profiles from a variety of reporting organizations are used in conjunction with a stack of 158 remote sensing-based soil covariates (primarily derived from MODIS land products, SRTM DEM derivatives, climatic images and global landform and lithology maps) to fit an ensemble of machine learning methods—random forest and gradient boosting and/or multinomial logistic regression—as implemented in the R packages ranger, xgboost, nnet and caret. The results of 10–fold cross-validation show that the ensemble models explain between 56% (coarse fragments) and 83% (pH) of variation with an overall average of 61%. Improvements in the relative accuracy considering the amount of variation explained, in comparison to the previous version of SoilGrids at 1 km spatial resolution, range from 60 to 230%. Improvements can be attributed to: (1) the use of machine learning instead of linear regression, (2) to considerable investments in preparing finer resolution covariate layers and (3) to insertion of additional soil profiles. Further development of SoilGrids could include refinement of methods to incorporate input uncertainties and derivation of posterior probability distributions (per pixel), and further automation of spatial modeling so that soil maps can be generated for potentially hundreds of soil variables. title: Projected Extreme Precipitation Days U.S. (RCP8.5)
description: The Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average days of extreme precipitation at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. An extreme precipitation day is defined as a day where precipitation is greater than the 99th percentile precipitation compared to the baseline period. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of extreme precipitation days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual number of extreme precipitation days between the years 1985 and 2015. Precipitation projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. Days of extreme precipitation are divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change. Values greater than 1 indicate that extreme precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. Data is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and the resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation dataset provides projections on how extreme precipitation patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. Generally, extreme precipitation events are expected to become more frequent worldwide. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation dataset was created with precipitation data from LOCA. The LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference. The annual average extreme precipitation days for each year, climate model, and scenario were calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting the daily precipitation values for a given year and summing the number of days where precipitation was greater than the 99th percentile precipitation during the baseline period. The annual average extreme precipitation days were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then each of the nine projected decades were divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change in extreme precipitation. Values greater than 1 indicate that extreme precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the extreme precipitation days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual extreme precipitation days between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.

title: Index of Coastal Protection by Coral Reefs
description: ### Overview This dataset is an index that estimates the relative value provided by coral reefs that protect coastlines through reduction of wave height and wave energy. The value as of 2014 is modeled as a function of exposed populations and infrastructure that received some level of protection from coastal and barrier reefs, and is described in relative terms, classified by decile (i.e., grouped into the most valuable ten percent of reefs for protection, the second-most valuable tenth of reefs, etc.). It was calculated at 1 kilometer (km) resolution globally, encompassing all countries and territories containing coral reefs. During storms, low-lying coastal areas are particularly exposed to ocean water and waves, which can threaten human inhabitants and damage infrastructure. Coastal and barrier reefs can reduce erosion as well as inundation, thereby substantially reducing the risk to lives and livelihoods—a valuable ecosystem service. These estimates represent one part of a concerted effort to quantify the value of coral reefs, as well as the spatial distribution of those values, thereby providing an important incentive for sustainable reef management. The dataset was created by researchers from The Nature Conservancy (TNC), World Resources Institute (WRI), and the University of Cambridge (Cambridge). ### Methodology This global examination of the relative value of the shoreline protection service provided by coral reefs proceeded in four main steps. First, the authors identified the areas vulnerable to inundation and erosion during storms. This was primarily based on the dataset "Low Elevation Coastal Zone Urban and Rural Population and Land Area Estimates, Version 2" (LECZ) from the Center for International Earth Science Information Network (CIESIN), which denotes coastal areas at elevations of less than 10 m above sea level (at approximately 1 km resolution). These zones were augmented to maximize shoreline inclusion (further detail is provided in the Cautions section). Second, the resulting map of vulnerable areas was used to assess exposure: the people and infrastructure in those areas potentially at risk. These were considered separately, as there were significant differences in their distributions. Population information was drawn from the LandScan 2007 gridded dataset from Oak Ridge National Laboratory. The stable Nighttime Lights Time Series from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) served as a proxy for the presence of infrastructure. Both of these datasets were also obtained at 1 km resolution. In quantifying the combined exposure, population was weighted as twice as important as infrastructure. Next, the authors calculated which coastal areas were protected by coral reefs. The protected shoreline map used for this purpose was originally created under the social vulnerability analysis of WRI's Reefs at Risk Revisited project, but was updated slightly for this effort. In general, the estimated level of protection offered by a coral reef was inversely proportional to the distance of the reef from the shore (meaning that the closer the reef was to the shore, the more protection it provided). Finally, the authors combined these different analytic elements in order to estimate the relative value of protection of the shoreline by reefs, within each relevant 1 km grid cell. For more information, please see the [source](https://www.nature.org/content/dam/tnc/nature/en/documents/Atlas-of-Ocean-Wealth.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch.
