title: Projected Cumulative Precipitation U.S. (RCP8.5)
description: The Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average total precipitation at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the total precipitation in 2000 is actually an average of the cumulative precipitation between the years 1985 and 2015. Cumulative average precipitation is divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change. Values greater than 1 indicate that cumulative precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. Data is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation dataset provides projections on how precipitation patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. Precipitation changes are projected to be more varied across the world, generally showing increases in mean precipitation in high-latitude regions and a pole-ward shift of subtropical arid regions. In addition, precipitation is projected to occur in fewer, but more intense events. Except in the few areas that are projected to see substantial drying, historically extreme precipitation events are expected to become more frequent worldwide. Even as precipitation increases, dry periods are projected to increase in length and frequency. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation dataset was created with precipitation data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference. The cumulative precipitation for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by adding all daily precipitation data over a given year. The cumulative precipitations were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then each of the nine projected decades were divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change in cumulative precipitation. Values greater than 1 indicate that cumulative precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that cumulative precipitation is decreasing. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the cumulative precipitation in 2000 was calculated as an average of the cumulative precipitation between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.

title: Temperature Suitability for Disease-Carrying Mosquito Aedes aegypti
description: ### Overview This dataset shows the number of months per year when disease transmission by one of the most common disease-carrying mosquitoes is possible under baseline conditions, as well as in the years 2050 and 2080. The mosquito is *Aedes aegypti*, and it transmits diseases to humans such as zika, dengue, chikungunya, and yellow fever. The baseline data used to represent current conditions is calculated using climate data from the years 1960-1990. In addition to the baseline temperature suitability for disease-carrying mosquitoes, the researchers used four climate change scenarios to predict where temperatures will be suitable for mosquitoes to thrive in the years 2050 and 2080. On Resource Watch, we display the RCP 8.5 “business as usual” scenario, which represents how the climate is predicted to change if we continue our current emissions trends. According to the [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/neglected_diseases/vector_ecology/mosquito-borne-diseases/en/), millions of people die each year from mosquito-borne diseases. Temperature is the main factor in mosquito survival and disease transmission. This dataset is crucial because governments and health organizations can use it to prevent and prepare for the viruses. The dataset was published by researchers from the University of Florida, Georgetown University, the University of Maryland, Stanford University, and Virginia Polytechnic and State University. The dataset has global coverage with a 5 arc minute resolution. Resource Watch also shows temperature suitability data for one of the other most common-disease-carrying mosquitoes, [*Aedes albopictus*](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/bio047b-Temperature-Suitability-for-Disease-Carrying-Mosquitoe-Aedes-albopictus). ### Methodology Researchers used a model to predict disease transmission by fitting the thermal responses of mosquitoes as results of several parameters. The parameters included temperature, mosquito traits such as biting rate per mosquito and mosquito mortality rate, human population size, and human recovery rate. This model of disease transmission was based on experiments and validated with empirical data. As for temperature, current mean monthly temperature data was derived from the WorldClim dataset. To predict future temperatures, researchers used four general circulation models (GCMs) that are most commonly used by studies forecasting species distributional shifts. Each of the four models can respectively be forecasted for four representative concentration pathways (RCPs): RCP 2.6, RCP 4.5, RCP 6.0, and RCP 8.5. These RCPs are standardized scenarios in predicting how future climate will respond to emission output. RCP 8.5 represents the worst-case, business-as-usual fossil fuel emissions scenario. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for three other climate change scenarios (RCP 2.6, RCP 4.5, and RCP 6.0), as well as results produced by different climate models, is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: Certified Commodity Crops
description: The Certified Commodity Crops Map, created through the research of Chadburn et al. (2017), is the first global data set showing the distribution of commodity crop certification. Crop certification helps consumers purchase more ethical products that come from farms that promote social equality and sustainability. However, these certifications are not well represented in some of the poorest countries of the world or in the tropical rainforests that are at the greatest risk. This map allows users to view the spatial distribution of global crop certification. The locations of certified farms came from publicly available datasets or by directly contacting standards bodies. Certification data from all major standards and codes of practice were included (4C, Bird-friendly coffee, Bonsucro, Etanol Verde, Fairtrade, ISCC, Rainforest Alliance, Roundtable Responsible Soy, Roundtable on Sustainable Biomaterials, Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil, Starbucks C.A.F.E. Practices and UTZ). The seven most certified crops (banana, cocoa, coffee, tea, soybean, sugar and palm oil) were mapped. Coordinates and postal addresses were used to identify point locations of each scheme. Postal addresses were converted to coordinates using ESRI Online World Geocode service. Data cleaning was performed to ensure points were located in their listed country and fell within the crop growing area, identified by a crop cover map. Some data permissions were granted under the condition that they be aggregated with other standards so that specific certification schemes and crop producers could not be identified. Therefore, data were aggregated at a 30 km x 30 km resolution. Certification data came from the years 2013, 2014 and 2015. PREPdata shows only a subset of the data set. Tree Cover Loss
description: ### Overview The Tree Cover Loss dataset measures areas of tree cover loss from 2000 through 2020. Tree cover is defined as all vegetation greater than 5 meters (m) in height and may take the form of natural forests or plantations across a range of canopy densities. Tree cover loss may be the result of human activities, including forestry practices such as timber harvesting or deforestation (the conversion of natural forest to other land uses), as well as natural causes such as disease or storm damage. Fire is another widespread cause of tree cover loss, and can be either natural or human-induced. It has a spatial resolution of global coverage (except Antarctica and other Arctic islands) at a 1 arc second resolution, which is approximately 30 meters × 30 meters at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. Forests provide a wide range of ecosystem services that are [critical to biodiversity richness, climate regulation, carbon storage, and water supplies](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/309/5734/570?ijkey=493d3bb49264119aa5ed9175119f7e221b2093d6&keytype2=tf_ipsecsha). They not only provide shelter to a variety of wildlife species, but also supply humans with [essential products including lumber, paper, and firewood]( https://www.fs.fed.us/forestmanagement/products/#:~:text=Forest%20products%20include%20materials%20derived,nuts%2C%20and%20other%20natural%20products). In the global fight against climate change, the forest ecosystem is [playing an incredibly important role since it absorbs and stores large amounts of carbon](https://www.undp.org/content/undp/en/home/blog/2018/Forests-A-natural-solution-to-climate-change-crucial-for-a-sustainable-future.html). Through measuring the loss in global forests, this dataset provides decision makers with a consistent basis on which to understand the [causes of tree cover loss](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/342/6160/850). It also helps to quantify other critical environmental issues, such as the economic drivers of [natural forest conversion to more intensive land uses](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1549-0831.1998.tb00691.x) and the effectiveness of [protected areas around the globe](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature02422) to represent species diversity. The dataset has been created through a collaboration among the Global Land Analysis & Discovery (GLAD) lab at the University of Maryland (UMD), Google, United States Geological Survey (USGS), and National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) with the aim to provide a spatially and temporally detailed quantification of global forest change. ### Methodology The data was generated using multispectral satellite imagery from three sources: the Landsat 5 thematic mapper, the Landsat 7 thematic mapper plus and the Landsat 8 Operational Land Imager sensors. [Images captured during growing seasons](https://doi.org/10.14358/PERS.70.3.313) were used since they are more appropriate for mapping land cover. More than 1 million satellite images were processed, including over 600,000 Landsat 7 images for the 2000-2012 interval and 400,000 Landsat 5, 7 and 8 images for the 2011-2020 interval. The following steps were taken to pre-process the images: 1. Pixel values were recalculated if image resolutions were changed. 2. Images were screened for clouds, shadows and water. 3. Images were [calibrated and normalized](http://gsp.humboldt.edu/OLM/Courses/GSP_216_Online/lesson4-1/radiometric.html) to make them comparable with one another. Land surface observations in the satellite images were assembled with a supervised learning algorithm, which involved [using labeled data to develop a machine learning model](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/problem-framing/cases#what-is-supervised-learning) to identify per pixel tree cover loss. To facilitate processing, each continent was characterized individually: North America, South America, Eurasia, Africa, and Australia using [Google Earth Engine](https://earthengine.google.com/), a cloud platform for earth observation data analysis that combines a public data catalog with a large-scale computational facility capable of handling large volumes of geospatial data. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. This dataset has been updated annually since its creation, and now includes loss up to 2020. The development of the algorithm has been modified in numerous ways, such as the addition of new data, reprocessed data from 2011 onward, and improved modelling and calibration. These modifications improve the dataset for 2011-2020, including better detection of boreal loss due to fire, smallholder rotation agriculture in tropical forests, selective losing, and short cycle plantations. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows the [Tree Cover](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e00ed8ca-ee7a-4539-b6b5-0bf2c30ee0d8) and the [Tree Cover Gain](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d305958d-3468-4a35-9660-5e18aa3e3190) from the same dataset. title: Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature in the U.S.
description: ### Overview The Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average maximum temperature at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average maximum temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the maximum temperature between the years 1985 and 2015. Average maximum temperature projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. ### Methodology The Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference. The annual average maximum temperature for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCAdata on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting and averaging all daily maximum temperature data over a given year. The average annual maximum temperatures were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in annual average maximum temperature. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average maximum temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the annual maximum temperatures between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows LOCA RCP 8.5 data for [Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/a9567364-e5ba-415e-a834-310e279326b6), [Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7ec68890-34a9-427c-907e-2f646f0dd9c8), [Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/412a8589-4887-44f2-9f45-3db5fb3937e7), [Projected Change in Dry Spells in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cd91e8d6-2e3d-46c1-9601-0dd7f524c7ba), [Projected Change in Frost Free Season in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/09e43293-98f1-4618-8e7e-d9f72cd5a4d7), [Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c985d4f6-9a03-4158-9955-e9f96db109ab), [Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/9e9b465a-bb0f-4047-ad72-9b8fabc0fd09), [Projected Change in Heating Degree Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6114c6fa-0ca6-4e06-ae23-413be0677503), [Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c5cbedcd-8cf5-4140-ac21-6791f6786f22). title: Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature
description: ### Overview The Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature dataset shows the change in annual average temperature at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the temperature between the years 1985 and 2015. Average temperature projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.25°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Average Annual Temperature dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. ### Methodology The Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference. The annual average temperature for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis using the following steps: All daily low temperature data over a given year was extracted and averaged to produce a yearly average low temperature value. All daily high temperature data over a given year was extracted and averaged to produce a yearly average high temperature value. Average annual temperature was calculated by taking the mean of the average daily temperature over a given year. Average daily temperature was calculated by dividing the sum of daily low temperature and daily high temperature by 2. The average annual temperatures were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in annual average temperature. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the annual average temperatures between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows projected change NEX-GDDP RCP 8.5 data for [Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3d8e2e82-b33a-4898-90e5-6e4a1d007b82), [Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c4b12251-2d61-458f-a2c0-096c37901ade), [Projected Change in Heating Degree Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/1d2f4eae-10e1-4ea6-980c-501b34106de2), [Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6fa000b5-8d91-46c8-8502-07427bc5eafc), [Projected Change in Frost Free Season](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d3f512c0-fbb0-47d5-9ac9-a452574c8e58), [Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3941bbba-181b-434a-84c3-fcdfa5234735), [Projected Change in Annual Precipitation](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/faf79d2c-5e54-4591-9d70-4bd1029c18e6), [Projected Change in Dry Spells](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d0f46576-411d-48aa-8df8-d89a3792cdce), [Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/66d28bbc-1e6e-4156-9ba2-875ecab665af). Vulnerability to Climate Change Index
description: ### Overview The University of Notre Dame Global Adaptation Initiative (ND-GAIN) produces an annual index that measures a country’s vulnerability to climate change along with its readiness to respond and adapt. The index assesses 192 countries annually from 1995-2019. The index is on a scale from 0-100, with higher numbers indicating that the country is better poised to respond to climate disruptions. Every country around the world will experience and respond differently to climate disruptions. Due to the unique socioeconomic and geographic locations of each country, some will be more vulnerable from the impacts of climate change and will have differing capacities to adapt. ND-GAIN’s index combines a vulnerability score with a readiness score to assess each country. Vulnerability measures a country's exposure, sensitivity, and capacity to adapt to the negative effects of climate change. Readiness measures a country's ability to leverage investments and convert them to adaptation actions. This index provides a standardized way to estimate a country's adaptation risk and opportunity. ND-GAIN is a program within the Notre Dame Environmental Change Initiative with the goal of heightening awareness and understanding of adaptation, providing products and services to spur action, and enhance investments in vulnerable communities. ### Methodology The ND-GAIN index measures both a country's vulnerability to climate change and its readiness to take adaptation actions. Vulnerability is assessed by considering six sectors: food, water, health, ecosystem services, human habitat, and infrastructure. Each sector is composed of six indicators (36 total) that relate to three components: exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity. - Exposure measures the extent to which society and its supporting sectors are stressed by future climate conditions. - Sensitivity relates to the degree to which people and the sectors they depend on are affected by climate related disturbances. - Adaptive capacity measures the ability of society to respond and decrease the negative consequences of climate related events. Similarly, readiness is assessed by three core components - economic readiness, governance readiness, and social readiness - and nine indicators to produce an overall readiness metric that gauges a country's ability to leverage investments and adaptation actions. - Economic readiness represents the investment environment which is needed to marshal funds from the private sector. - Governance readiness relates to the conditions (stability of society, institutional arrangements) that contribute to investment risk. - Social readiness measures the social conditions that enable society to make efficient and equitable use of and benefit from an investment. 74 data sources are used to construct the 45 indicators that make up the readiness and vulnerability scores. 20 indicators come directly from raw data sources, the other 25 are computed by the underlying data. The following steps outline how the index is created: 1. Collect the raw data and process 2. Interpolate missing data or denote certain indicators as “missing” for specific countries 3. Identify the baseline minimum and maximum values from the raw data 4. Define a reference point for each indicator (e.g. reference point for child malnutrition is 0%) 5. Scale the raw data to score, from 0 to 1, to allow for comparison 6. Compute the vulnerability and readiness scores 7. Compute ND-GAIN and scale scores to give a value from 0 to 100 (higher values representing greater readiness and lower vulnerability) ### Additional Information Our data catalog shows only a subset of the dataset. The ND-GAIN dataset also includes data for each vulnerability sector (food, ecosystem services, health, human habitat, infrastructure, water), readiness sector (economic, governance, social), all 45 indicators, and trends. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on WRI’s data catalog. See the documentation on how we processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/cli_029_rw2_vulnerability_to_climate_change). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: Burned Areas
description: ### Overview The Burned Areas dataset shows areas that have experienced fire events in near real-time. The dataset provides the approximate date in which the burning occurred for each of the 500 meter (m) grid cells. Data is available starting in November 2000 and is updated on a monthly basis. [According to the United States Geological Survey (USGS)](https://www.usgs.gov/land-resources/nli/landsat/landsat-burned-area?qt-science_support_page_related_con=0#qt-science_support_page_related_con), data on burned areas is needed to characterize drivers of fire occurrence, project future fire behavior, and help with assessments of fire impacts on both natural and social systems. The dataset was created by the USGS using satellite imagery. The final product has a resolution of 500 m. ### Methodology The Burned Areas dataset was produced and is continually updated by combining data from both 500 m Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) Surface Reflectance imagery and 1 kilometer (km) MODIS active fire observations. This hybrid algorithm uses a burn-sensitive vegetation index derived from MODIS short-wave infrared bands 5 and 7. In addition, the active fire maps are used to guide the selection of burned and unburned training samples. If a grid cell has been marked as burned, the dataset identifies the date when the burn occurred within that cell. The dataset also includes special values for missing data, unburned cells, and water grid cells. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://lpdaac.usgs.gov/documents/114/MCD64_User_Guide_V6.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional information on the uncertainty of burn date data, quality assurance indicators, and the first and last days of the burn for each burned area can be found in the original source data. title: Cooling Degree Days
description: A cooling degree day (CDD) is defined as the number of degrees that a day's mean temperature is above 65°F. For example, if a day's average temperature is 80°F, the CDD would be 15. If a second day's average temperature were the same, the combined CDD for those two days would be 30. CDDs are often used as a proxy to estimate heating and cooling needs in buildings. While degree days can be calculated using any reference temperature, this data set uses 65°F (18.3°C), a common threshold for climate indicators, and a temperature at which people are generally comfortable. This indicator is useful in determining energy demands resulting from cooling in different regions and assessing projected climate change impacts. This data set shows CDDs under RCP 8.5, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

NLCD 2001 percent developed imperviousness was developed for all 50 states and Puerto Rico / U.S. Virgin Islands. NLCD 2011 percent developed imperviousness was created on a path/row basis and mosaicked to create a seamless national product. The data in NLCD 2011 are completely integrated with NLCD 2001 and NLCD 2006. As part of the NLCD 2011 project, the NLCD 2001 and 2006 percent developed imperviousness data products were revised and reissued to provide full compatibility with the new NLCD 2011 products. title: Biodiversity Intactness
description: ### Overview The biodiversity intactness map shows global estimates of how land use pressures have affected the numbers of species and individuals found in an area. This data is important because if biodiversity loss goes unchecked, it will undermine efforts toward long-term sustainable development. The data, created by [Newbold et al. (2016)](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/353/6296/288), represents intactness in 2005 at a 1 kilometer resolution. ### Methodology The Biodiversity Intactness dataset shows global estimates of how land use pressures have affected the numbers of species and individuals found in samples from local terrestrial ecological assemblages. The map represents the average losses of originally present species. The datasets used 2,382,624 data points from the Projecting Responses of Ecological Diversity in Changing Terrestrial Systems (PREDICTS) database, a global database of how local terrestrial biodiversity responds to human impacts. The map modeled how richness and abundance respond to land use pressures. The models included 4 pressure variables—land use, land use intensity, human population density, and proximity to the nearest road. The values of the response variables were expressed relative to an intact assemblage undisturbed by humans. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/353/6296/288). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](609487de-0a23-4783-bafc-4335b6fe7d4b) as a replacement.**_ The Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI) Global Drought Monitor offers near real-time information about drought conditions at the global scale, with a 0.5 degrees spatial resolution and a monthly time resolution. SPEI provides a measure of change in water availability in a region by accounting for increases in available water through precipitation and decreases in available water through a process known as evapotranspiration, which includes both evaporation of water from the Earth's surface and transpiration of water which results during plants' photosynthesis. SPEI is calculated relative to historical seasonal averages. Different SPEIs can be calculated by accounting for water available change over different lengths of time. SPEI time-scales between one and 48 months are available through the CSIC website.The calibration period for the SPEI is January 1950 to December 2010. The dataset is updated during the first days of the following month based on the most reliable and updated sources of climatic data. Mean temperature data are obtained from the NOAA NCEP CPC GHCN CAMS gridded dataset. Monthly precipitation sums data are obtained from the Global Precipitation Climatology Centre (GPCC). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Aqueduct Unimproved or No Sanitation Access
description: ### Overview Unimproved/No sanitation access reflects the percentage of the population using pit latrines without a slab or platform, hanging/bucket latrines, or directly disposing human waste in fields, forests, bushes, open bodies of water, beaches, other open spaces, or with solid waste [(WHO and UNICEF 2017)](https://washdata.org/data). Specifically, the indicator aligns with the unimproved and open defecation categories of the Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP)—the lowest tiers of sanitation services. Higher values indicate areas where people have less access to improved sanitation services. These values were then converted into risk scores based on the thresholds defined in the methodology. These risk scores range from low (<2.5%) to extremely high water stress (>20%). The JMP statistics have been disaggregated from the country level to the sub-basin scale (HydroBASIN level 6) using gridded urban and rural population data. ### Methodology Data for this indicator came from the 2015 sanitation access rates published by JMP [(WHO and UNICEF 2017)](https://washdata.org/data) for urban and rural populations per country. Specifically, this indicator used the unimproved and open defecation statistics. First, country level data were matched to the Aqueduct sub-basin scale using a one-to-one geospatial intersection between Aqueduct sub-basins and countries (henceforth called intersect). Next, the gridded 2010 population data [(van Vuuren et al. 2007)](https://www.pbl.nl/en/publications/2006/DownscalingDriversOfGlobalEnvironmentalChangeScenarios) was parsed into urban and rural classes using a 2010 urban extent data layer [(van Huijstee et al. 2018)](https://www.pbl.nl/en/publications/towards-an-urban-preview). The total urban and rural populations were then summed per intersect. Within each intersect, the urban and rural rates of access were multiplied by the urban and rural populations, respectively, and then were added together to find the number of people with access to unimproved/no sanitation. Results were aggregated up from the intersect scale to the HydroBASIN 6 scale. Within each HydroBASIN 6 sub-basin, the population with access to unimproved/no sanitation was divided by the total population to find the percent of population with access to unimproved/no sanitation. Finally, raw unimproved/no sanitation access values were converted to risk scores between 0 and 5, based on quantiles. These scores were placed into categories indicating how high the risk for this indicator is. The thresholds for raw unimproved/no sanitation access values and the corresponding risk scores that were used in each category are defined below as Risk Category (Risk Scores): Raw Value Thresholds. - Low (0-1): < 2.5% - Low to medium (1-2): 2.5 - 5.0% - Medium to high (2-3): 5.0 - 10.0% - High (3-4): 10.0 - 20.0% - Extremely high (4-5): >20.0% For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/aqueduct-30). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Undiscovered Oil and Gas Resources
description: ### Overview The Undiscovered Oil and Gas Resources dataset shows the locations of the Assessment Units (AUs) in the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) World Assessment of Undiscovered Oil and Gas Resources. The assessment was conducted in 2012 and evaluated 313 AUs within 171 geologic provinces (areas where oil and gas occur in commercial quantities). An AU is a mappable volume of rock with homogenous geologic properties. Each AU was assessed for undiscovered oil and gas resources using data from published literature. In each geologic province, total petroleum systems (TPS) were also defined. A TPS is the group of geologic elements needed for oil and gas formation. The Undiscovered Oil and Gas Resources dataset provides an understanding of the quantity, quality and distribution of global conventional oil and gas resources. Conventional oil and gas resources, such as crude oil and natural gas, are found in high porosity/permeability reservoirs. Unconventional oil and gas resources are found in low porosity/permeability reservoirs, such as shale and tar sands. Conventional resources are relatively easy to extract from the earth and do not require fracking. The [USGS World Assessment of Undiscovered Oil and Gas Resources](https://certmapper.cr.usgs.gov/data/apps/we-data/) determined that a total of 565,298 million barrels of oil, 5,605,626 billion cubic feet of gas and 166,668 million barrels of natural gas liquids remained undiscovered as of 2011. All of these resources are conventionally extractable. However, conventional oil and gas resources are dwindling. Knowing where and how much conventional oil and gas remains undiscovered is important for understanding the world’s energy future. The Undiscovered Oil and Gas Resources dataset is a geologic basis for making decisions about energy. It can help predict future energy production trends and increase understanding of the social and environmental consequences of oil and gas resource exploitation. Established in 1879, the [USGS](https://www.usgs.gov/) is a scientific organization within the U.S. Department of the Interior. The USGS’s purpose is to collect, monitor, analyze and provide science about natural resource conditions and issues. The Undiscovered Oil and Gas Resources dataset was generated from data published by the [USGS Central Energy Resource Science Center (CERSC)](https://www.usgs.gov/centers/cersc), a group that conducts interdisciplinary research on global geoscience and energy systems. The CERSC studies the geological processes critical to the formation of natural resources. They also evaluate the environmental and socioeconomic effects of the production and usage of oil and gas resources. ### Methodology The Undiscovered Oil and Gas Resources dataset shows the locations of areas assessed in the 2012 USGS World Assessment of Undiscovered Oil and Gas Resources. Data is available for the entire world, excluding the U.S. The study evaluated 313 AUs within 171 geologic provinces. Geologic provinces are areas that encompass a natural geologic setting, such as a sedimentary basin or delta, and are contiguous for hundreds to thousands of kilometers. Geologic provinces contain valuable quantities of oil and gas resources. Each province contains at least one TPS. A TPS are areas that contain all the necessary essential geologic elements and processes required for oil and gas to form. The geologic elements are source rock, reservoir, seal and overburden. In each province, these elements were mapped, described and modeled based on data from published literature. The data source provides [a viewer](https://certmapper.cr.usgs.gov/data/apps/world-energy/?resource=conventional) where you can select an AU and reference the published literature. AUs were defined within each TPS. A TPS typically contains only one AU, although some TPSs were divided into more than one AU. An AU is a homogeneous package of rock that contains oil and gas resources from a single TPS. Any given AU has the same set of geologic processes that led to the generation, migration and storage of oil and gas. All AUs were analyzed to determine their quantities of undiscovered, technically recoverable oil and gas resources. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://pubs.usgs.gov/fs/2012/3042/). ### Additional Information Approximately 75% of the undiscovered oil and gas resources are in the following four regions: South America and the Caribbean, sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East and North Africa, and the Arctic regions of North America. The full assessment and data for each AU is available [here](https://certmapper.cr.usgs.gov/data/apps/world-energy/?resource=conventional). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: Global Cropland Extent
description: ### Overview The Global Cropland Extent dataset at 30 m spatial resolution was developed by the Global Land Analysis and Discovery Lab (GLAD) at the University of Maryland (UMD) using Landsat satellite data time-series. Cropland is defined as land used to produce herbaceous crops for human consumption, forage, and biofuel. Perennial woody crops, permanent pastures, and shifting cultivation are excluded from the definition. The map is based on the machine learning classification of the global Landsat data archive using locally calibrated models. Model calibration data were collected through visual interpretation of Landsat and high spatial resolution satellite images. The mapping was performed for 2000-2003, 2004-2007, 2008-2011, 2012-2015, and 2016-2019 time intervals. For each four-year interval, a 30x30 m pixel was mapped as cropland if a growing crop was detected during any of these years. **Cropland change data are available**[here](https://bit.ly/34QydNx). Global population growth and increasing standards of living inevitably cause the expansion and intensification of global agricultural land use to fulfill growing demands for food, biofuel, and other commodities. In turn, agriculture expansion and intensification threaten ecosystem functioning and lead to species extinction through habitat loss and fragmentation. The [United Nations 2030 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)](https://www.undp.org/sustainable-development-goals) call for balancing increasing agricultural production with maintenance of ecosystem services. Implementation of SDGs to improve food security, protect freshwater and terrestrial ecosystems, and mitigate climate change require national policies and international cooperation that are based on consistent, independent, and timely data on agriculture extent and productivity. The Cropland Extent and Change dataset can serve as a tool for monitoring national and global progress towards SDGs. The GLAD laboratory in the Department of Geographical Sciences at UMD investigates methods, causes, and impacts of global land surface change. Earth observation imagery is the primary data source and land cover extent and change is the primary topic of interest. GLAD aspires to generate new science insights concerning land resources, educate the next generation of remote sensing-based land change scientists, and disseminate land monitoring capabilities to operational settings nationally and internationally. ### Methodology Cropland is defined as land used for the production of annual and perennial herbaceous crops for human consumption, forage (including hay), and biofuel. Perennial woody crops, permanent pastures, and shifting cultivation are excluded from the definition. The fallow length is limited to four years for the cropland class. The cropland class definition is largely consistent with the arable land category reported by the [Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations](https://www.fao.org/3/Y4171E/Y4171E20.htm). The analysis was performed in four-year epochs, 2000-2003, 2004-2007, 2008-2011, 2012-2015, and 2016-2019. One cropland map per epoch was created. Using a four-year interval (rather than a single year) increased the number of clear-sky satellite observations in the time-series, which improves the representation of land surface phenology and the accuracy of cropland detection. For each four-year interval, an area was mapped as cropland if a growing crop was detected during any of these years. This way, the criterion of the maximum fallow length was implemented: if an area was not used as cropland for more than four years, it was not included in the cropland map for the corresponding time interval. The global 16-day normalized surface reflectance Landsat Analysis Ready Data (Landsat ARD) was employed as input data for cropland mapping [(Potapov et al., 2020)](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/12/3/426). For each four-year interval, a single annualized gap-free 16-day observation time-series was created. For each 16-day interval, the observation with the highest near-infrared reflectance value was selected (to prioritize observations with the highest vegetation cover) from four years of Landsat data. The annualized 16-day time series within each four-year interval was transformed into a set of multitemporal metrics that provide consistent land surface phenology inputs for global cropland mapping. The Landsat metrics were augmented with elevation data. Global cropland mapping included three stages that enabled extrapolation of visually delineated cropland training data to a temporally consistent global cropland map time-series using machine learning. At all three stages, bagged decision tree ensembles were employed as a supervised classification algorithm that uses class presence and absence data as the dependent variable and a set of multitemporal metrics as independent variables at a Landsat ARD pixel scale. The first stage consisted of performing individual cropland classifications for a set of 924 Landsat ARD 1°×1° tiles for the 2016-2019 interval. At the second stage, the 924 tiles that had been classified as cropland/other land and the 2016-2019 metric set were used to train a series of regional cropland mapping models. At the third stage, the preliminary global cropland maps were used as training data to generate temporally consistent global cropland data. The goal of this third stage was to create a robust spatiotemporally consistent set of locally calibrated cropland detection models. For each 1°×1° Landsat ARD tile (13,451 tiles total) training data for each four-year interval was collected from the preliminary cropland extent maps within a 3° radius of the target tile, with preference to select stable cropland and non-cropland pixels as training. Training data from all intervals were used to calibrate a single decision tree ensemble for each ARD tile. The per-tile models were then applied to each time interval, and the results were post-processed to remove single cropland class detections and omissions within time-series and eliminate cropland patches below 0.5 ha. Manual masks to remove map artifacts (e.g., cropland overestimation over temperate wetlands and flooded grasslands) were applied in some regions to improve the final map. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows datasets from the GLAD laboratory for [Cropland Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ec282483-4f5c-4fb8-ace7-8e557826781a), [Tree Height Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/64a3e126-000b-46fb-aaf4-8ac765a8263b), [Water Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/b83ad197-eb95-44e2-8ec3-3351ab926421), [Snow/Ice Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/5a796ce9-71d4-42b0-922d-056a86e5eb72), [Built-Up Area Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e6a3f803-1222-46c2-8e6c-0ae94b3d80c8), and [Land Cover Map](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/06e734af-66f0-4c3e-ac71-1b99f3cbfe1d). Air Quality: Carbon Monoxide (CO) Station Measurements
description: ### Overview The Air Quality: Carbon Monoxide (CO) Station Measurements dataset is a global dataset that shows real-time air quality data from around the world for carbon monoxide (CO) . It presents data collected from government and international organizations at the station level. This means the data is more accurate to specific areas than national or regional data. As of June 2017 OpenAQ data was available for 5,400 locations in 48 countries and is being continually updated with new sources. Carbon monoxide (CO) is a colorless, odorless gas that can be harmful when inhaled in large amounts. CO is released during combustion, so the largest outdoor sources of CO are cars, trucks and other vehicles, and machinery that burn fossil fuels. Breathing air with a high concentration of CO reduces the amount of oxygen that can be transported in the bloodstream to critical organs like the heart and brain. At very high levels, which are possible indoors or in other enclosed environments, CO can cause dizziness, confusion, unconsciousness, and death. Very high levels of CO are not likely to occur outdoors. However, when CO levels are elevated outdoors it can be of particular concern to people with preexisting heart disease. These people already have a reduced ability for getting oxygenated blood to their heart. They are especially vulnerable to the effects of CO when exercising or under increased stress. In these situations, short-term exposure to elevated CO may result in reduced oxygen to the heart accompanied by chest pain also known as angina. OpenAQ is an open-source project to surface live, real-time air quality data from around the world. Its “mission is to enable previously impossible science, impact policy, and empower the public to fight air pollution.” Scientists, researchers, developers, and citizens can use these data to understand how air quality in different locations changes over time. Resource Watch also shows continually updated air quality data from OpenAQ on [inhalable particulates (PM10)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003bnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-10), [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cairqualityso2), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003dnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-NO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-O), [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003anrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-25), and [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003gnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-BC_1). ### Methodology The carbon monoxide station measurement dataset was produced and is continually updated by aggregating data from permanent outdoor air quality measures. Data was collected only from official sources, including government entities and international organizations. As of June 2017 OpenAQ data was available for 5,400 locations in 48 countries. For data to be included it had to meet three criteria: 1. The “raw” measurement data on physical particle concentration had to be available on the originating site. 2. The data needed to be at the “station level.” It is unacceptable if it is presented in an aggregated form for a city or region. 3. The data needed to be continuously updated at intervals between 10 minutes and 24 hours. After the data was collected it was put into tables. Data was collected using the source organization’s Air Quality Index (AQI) classifications. The final dataset was mapped in vector format at a subnational level with each measurement station showing local particle concentration. OpenAQ continually reviews each data source website for updated values and updates the dataset every hour. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows continually updated air quality data from OpenAQ on [inhalable particulates (PM10)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003bnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-10), [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cairqualityso2), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003dnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-NO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-O), [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003anrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-25), and [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003gnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-BC_1). title: Madhya Pradesh Agriculture Vulnerability
description: The data layers indicate a district-wise comparison of agricultural vulnerability in Madhya Pradesh in the baseline and mid-century based on two different emission scenarios RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5. The analysis is based on an agriculture vulnerability index (AGVI) that was arrived at by aggregating and weighing a cross section 15 indicators (such as crop yields, net sown area, net irrigated area, fertiliser consumption, livestock units, small landholdings etc]. According to the analysis the overall agriculture vulnerability of the Madhya Pradesh districts is projected to decrease towards mid-century as compared to the current conditions for both emission scenarios of RCP4.5 and RCP8.5. description: The World Bank Group International Comparison Program compiles gross domestic product (GDP) data based on purchasing power parity (PPP) converted to international dollars by country. An international dollar has the same purchasing power over GDP as the U.S. dollar has in the United States. GDP is the sum of gross value added by all resident producers in the economy plus any product taxes and minus any subsidies not included in the value of the products. It is calculated without making deductions for depreciation of fabricated assets or for depletion and degradation of natural resources. Data are in current international dollars. For most economies PPP figures are extrapolated from the 2011 International Comparison Program (ICP) benchmark estimates or imputed using a statistical model based on the 2011 ICP. For 47 high- and upper-middle-income economies conversion factors are provided by Eurostat and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). Because exchange rates do not always reflect differences in price levels between countries, GDP and GDP per capita estimates are converted into international dollars using purchasing power parity rates. PPP rates provide a standard measure allowing comparison of real levels of expenditure between countries, just as conventional price indexes allow comparison of real values over time. PPP rates are calculated by simultaneously comparing the prices of similar goods and services among a large number of countries. In the most recent round of price surveys conducted by the International Comparison Program (ICP) in 2011, 199 economies participated. The PPP conversion factors come from 3 sources. For 47 high- and upper-middle-income countries conversion factors are provided by Eurostat and the OECD. For the remaining 2011 ICP countries the PPP estimates are extrapolated from the 2011 ICP benchmark results, which account for relative price changes between each economy and the United States. For countries that did not participate in the 2011 ICP round, the PPP estimates are imputed using a statistical model. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: Heating Degree Days
description: A heating degree day (HDD) is defined as the number of degrees that a day's mean temperature is below 65°F. For example, if a day's average temperature is 50°F, the HDD would be 15. If a second day's average temperature were the same, the combined HDD for those two days would be 30. HDDs are often used as a proxy to estimate heating and cooling needs in buildings. While degree days can be calculated using any reference temperature, this data set uses 65°F (18.3°C), a common threshold for climate indicators, and a temperature at which people are generally comfortable. This indicator is useful in determining energy demands resulting from heating in different regions and assessing projected climate change impacts. This data set shows HDDs under RCP 8.5, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

title: Crop Land Area and Production
description: ### Overview The Crop Land and Production dataset shows the global harvested area, production, and yield for six major crops: wheat, soybean, rice, maize, coffee, and cotton. The dataset was derived from the 2010 Spatial Production Allocation Model (SPAM). The SPAM model aimed to disaggregate (downscale) national and sub-national crop statistics using a variety of inputs, such as cropland surface, location of irrigated areas, crop suitability and potential yields, rural population densities, production systems characteristics and crop prices. Crop data was downscaled to a spatial resolution of 5 arc minutes. This spatial resolution is approximately 10 kilometers x 10 kilometers at the equator, but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. Together, maize, rice, soybean, and wheat account for nearly two-thirds of global agricultural calories. Global demand for these crops is rising as a result of diet shifts, rising population levels, and increased biofuel demand. Increased demand for these resources will significantly affect land and resource use, climate change, political agendas, and technological developments. A comprehensive understanding of the current spatial distribution of the world’s crops is necessary in order to preemptively address these effects. The Crop Land Area and Production dataset can be used to understand the extent and productivity of key global crops, which will help address food crop demand and its effects. The Crop Land Area and Production dataset was generated by the [Consultative Group on International Agricultural Research Program on Policies, Institutions, and Markets (CGIAR-PIM)](https://pim.cgiar.org/about/). CGIAR-PIM provides support for policies that help farmers improve their lives, produce nutritious and affordable foods, and protect the soil, water and biodiversity in rural landscapes. The program is led by the [International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI)](https://www.ifpri.org/about), a CGIAR-PIM research center. IFPRI provides research-based policy solutions to sustainably reduce poverty and end hunger in developing countries. The Crop Land Area and Production dataset was part of the larger SPAM dataset, which was developed for the HarvestChoice research initiative. Conducted by IFPRI, [HarvestChoice](https://www.ifpri.org/project/harvestchoice) generated knowledge products to help guide strategic investments to improve the well-being of poor people in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia through more productive and profitable farming. ### Methodology The main purpose of SPAM is to disaggregate crop statistics (e.g., harvested area, production quantity, and yield) by different farming systems and to further allocate such disaggregated statistics into spatially gridded units. The whole procedure entails a data fusion approach that combines information from different sources and at different spatial scales by deploying various matching and calibration processes. Then all the data elements are processed by the optimization model, which generates results at the grid level. There are three submodules in a standardized SPAM model: disaggregation, optimization, and allocation. The SPAM2010 is conceptualized based on this general setting, while it adds further methodological and data improvements, which mainly include the update of base year, the expansion of subnational administrative-unit coverage, the extension of crop list, and the substitution of the latest hybrid cropland map as the basic allocation layer. The first step for SPAM is to disaggregate crop statistics of agricultural production (e.g., the yield, harvested area, and total production) by administrative-unit levels (k), crop type (j), and farming system (l) from coarser scale to finer scale. The four production systems were defined by water and management type: - Irrigated – high input (I) - Rainfed – high input (H) - Rainfed – low input (L) - Rainfed – subsistence (S) The four conceptualized farming systems are mainly delineated by the water supply system and inputs used by farmers, despite global data on farming system shares for each crop being largely absent. For a small number of large countries, e.g., Brazil, China, India, Russia, the United States, the authors have data on farming system shares at the ADM1 level. For the other countries the authors assigned the national farming system shares to each ADM1 level and then adjusted individual ADM1 farming system shares in light of the supporting evidence. For irrigated farming systems, the crop-specific shares are derived by dividing the harvested area cultivated under full control irrigation obtained from [Global Information System on Water and Agriculture (AQUASTAT)](https://www.fao.org/aquastat/en/), [MIRCA](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2008GB003435), and country-level statistics by the overall harvested area. The optimization module in SPAM2010 is almost the same as that in previous versions. The authors applied a cross-entropy process in the General Algebraic Modeling System (GAMS), which ensures that the optimization procedure iterates until a solution is found. Once the allocation is successful, meaning that an optimal or locally optimal solution has been found, the routine immediately returns the allocated physical area by grid, crop and farming system, and the program continues with post-processing automatically. The SPAM model used additional biological and economic inputs to allocate the statistics within each pixel. Input data included (among several others): - Administrative units - Crop Type - Farming system - Adjusted harvested area - Total suitable area in each grid by crop and farming system - Crop prices - Market accessibility in each grid - Population density Our data catalog provides three of the SPAM2010 essential output indicators: - Harvested Area: also measured in hectares, harvested area is at least as large as physical area but sometimes more since it also accounts for multiple harvests of a crop on the same plot. Like for physical area, the harvested area is calculated for each production system, and the sum of all harvested areas of all production systems in a pixel amounts to the total harvested area of the pixel. The sum of all the harvested areas of the crops in a pixel can be larger than the pixel size. - Production: for each production system and crop, production is calculated by multiplying the area harvested by its corresponding yield. It is measured in metric tons. The total production of a crop includes the production of all production systems of that crop. - Yield: is the amount of production per harvested area and measured in kilograms per hectare. It is a measure of productivity. The total yield of a crop, when considering all production systems, is the weighted average of the four systems’ yields. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://essd.copernicus.org/articles/12/3545/2020/essd-12-3545-2020.pdf). ### Additional Information Our data catalog shows only a subset of the dataset. The Global Spatially-Disaggregated Crop Production Statistics Data for 2010 Version 2.0 has data for 36 other crops (42 total). The full dataset also includes physical area and value of production for all 42 crops. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click the “Learn more” button. Our data catalog has previously shown data for [2005](https://bit.ly/3CjoFYc). This dataset was archived because the methodology has been changed. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on WRI’s data catalog. See the documentation on how we retrieved the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/foo_005_rw1_crop_area_production). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

description: The Certified Commodity Crops Map, created through the research of Chadburn et al. (2017), is the first global data set showing the distribution of commodity crop certification. Crop certification helps consumers purchase more ethical products that come from farms that promote social equality and sustainability. However, these certifications are not well represented in some of the poorest countries of the world or in the tropical rainforests that are at the greatest risk. This map allows users to view the spatial distribution of global crop certification. The locations of certified farms came from publicly available datasets or by directly contacting standards bodies. Certification data from all major standards and codes of practice were included (4C, Bird-friendly coffee, Bonsucro, Etanol Verde, Fairtrade, ISCC, Rainforest Alliance, Roundtable Responsible Soy, Roundtable on Sustainable Biomaterials, Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil, Starbucks C.A.F.E. Practices and UTZ). The seven most certified crops (banana, cocoa, coffee, tea, soybean, sugar and palm oil) were mapped. Coordinates and postal addresses were used to identify point locations of each scheme. Postal addresses were converted to coordinates using ESRI Online World Geocode service. Data cleaning was performed to ensure points were located in their listed country and fell within the crop growing area, identified by a crop cover map. Some data permissions were granted under the condition that they be aggregated with other standards so that specific certification schemes and crop producers could not be identified. Therefore, data were aggregated at a 30 km x 30 km resolution. Certification data came from the years 2013, 2014 and 2015. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: Daily Nighttime Lights
description: Nighttime Imagery (Day/Night Band, Enhanced Near Constant Contrast) is available from the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) on the joint NASA/NOAA Suomi National Polar orbiting Partnership (SNPP) satellite. The VIIRS Nighttime Imagery layer shows the earth’s surface and atmosphere using a sensor designed to capture low-light emission sources, under varying illumination conditions. It is displayed as a grey-scale image. Sources of illumination include both natural and anthropogenic sources of light emissions. Lunar reflection can be used to highlight the location and features of clouds and other terrestrial features such as sea ice and snow cover when there is partial to full moon conditions. When there is no moonlight, natural and anthropogenic night time light emissions are highlighted such as city lights, lightning, auroras, fires, gas flares, and fishing fleets. The VIIRS sensor collects imagery as it orbits the Earth every 100 minutes. Passing over the poles 14 times per day, it crosses the equator at at 1:30am local time, photographing the entire world each day. The sensor resolution is 750 m at nadir and the imagery resolution is 500 m. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set.
