title: Climate Hazard Indicators (Total rainfall) Historical and SSP scenarios - Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu
description: ### Overview The dataset includes five major climatic indicators viz. annual values for minimum temperature (℃), maximum temperature (℃), mean temperature (℃), total precipitation (mm/year), and the number of rainy days (represented as integers) for two Indian states, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. It features decadal averages from 2020-2100 for Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs), including SSP5-8.5, which reflects a high emissions scenario, and SSP2-4.5, representing moderate challenges to both mitigation and adaptation. Additionally, the dataset provides historical data for all the five indicators averaged over the period from 2005 to 2014. ### Methodology **Pre-Processing**: The decadal time periods were labeled as follows: 2020-2029 as 2020, 2030-2039 as 2030, 2040-2049 as 2040, 2050-2059 as 2050, 2060-2069 as 2060, 2070-2079 as 2070, 2080-2089 as 2080, and 2090-2099 as 2090. **Layers of interest**: Annual averages of minimum temperature (℃), maximum temperature (℃), mean temperature (℃), Annual total precipitation (mm/year), and the annual total number of rainy days (represented as integers). **Data**: The ERA5 reanalysis dataset (ECMWF 2022), a satellite data product of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts with a spatial resolution of 31 kilometers (km), is used as a reference dataset. The ensemble of downscaled daily time series outputs from global climate models (GCMs). These time series include the historical years covered by the observation time series as well as the specified future years of interest. We have used the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 product, which includes outputs from 34 Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) models at approximately 25 km spatial resolution. ### Estimation Methods Out of the 35 models, we select the top 3 climate models that perform best for a specific weather variable in a particular geographic region, and present the ensemble mean of these models. The ERA5 dataset is used as a reference, and the comparison is made for the historical period between 1980 and 2014. After selecting the models, we apply a calibration/bias correction procedure to the future time series of the models. This involves aligning the model's frequency distribution with the historical data by shifting the percentiles of the model's distribution. For instance, if the 20th percentile of the model data corresponds to the 30th percentile of the observations, then the 30th percentile of the calibrated model data will match the 20th percentile of the uncalibrated model data. For the full documentation, please see the source methodology at Wong, T., and P Switzer. 2023. 'Estimating future local climate hazard probabilities.' Technical Note. Washington, DC: World Resources Institute. Available online at: doi.org/10.46830/writn.22.00074.v2. ### Description of the Layers **Annual Maximum Temperature (℃)**: The daily maximum temperature data for each year is extracted and averaged to calculate the yearly average maximum temperature. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years. **Annual Minimum Temperature (℃)**: The daily minimum temperature data for each year is extracted and averaged to calculate the yearly average minimum temperature. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years. **Annual Mean Temperature (℃)**: The daily mean temperature is calculated by averaging the daily minimum and maximum temperatures. The annual mean temperature is obtained by averaging the daily mean temperatures over the course of a year. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years. **Annual Total Precipitation (mm/year)**: The daily precipitation values are summed over the entire year to calculate the annual total precipitation. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years. **Annual Rainy Days (represented as integers)**: A rainy day is defined as a day with precipitation exceeding 2.5 mm (as per the India Meteorological Department). The total number of rainy days in a year is calculated by summing the rainy days throughout the year. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years. ### Visualizing the Data The data is provided at a 25-km resolution and is presented as a raster with a time slider with a separate layer for each variable. The values are visualized using a gradient based on the selected year in the slider, ranging from lighter shade (indicating low values) to darker shade (representing higher values). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source

title: Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days
description: ### Overview The Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset shows the change in annual cooling degree days (CDDs) at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. CDD is the number of degrees that a day's average temperature is above 65 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). For example, if a day's average temperature is 80°F, the CDD would be 15. If this happened 10 times in a year the annual CDD would be 150. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the CDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual CDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. CDD projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.25°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades and how this may affect future energy demands. For example, CDDs are often used as a proxy to estimate energy requirements for cooling buildings. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. ### Methodology The Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference. The annual CDD for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. Daily CDDs were calculated by subtracting the baseline temperature of 65°F from daily average temperature values. If the daily average temperature was below 65°F, it was counted as zero. Then, annual CDD was calculated by summing all daily CDD values over a given year. Annual CDDs were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in cooling degree days. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the CDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual CDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows projected change NEX-GDDP RCP 8.5 data for [Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/4ca6826c-718d-457d-b4e2-e9277d7ed62c), [Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3d8e2e82-b33a-4898-90e5-6e4a1d007b82), [Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c4b12251-2d61-458f-a2c0-096c37901ade), [Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6fa000b5-8d91-46c8-8502-07427bc5eafc), [Projected Change in Frost Free Season](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d3f512c0-fbb0-47d5-9ac9-a452574c8e58), [Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3941bbba-181b-434a-84c3-fcdfa5234735), [Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/faf79d2c-5e54-4591-9d70-4bd1029c18e6), [Projected Change in Dry Spells](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d0f46576-411d-48aa-8df8-d89a3792cdce), [Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/66d28bbc-1e6e-4156-9ba2-875ecab665af). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data. Additional data is available for emissions scenario RCP 4.5. For access to the original NEX-GDDP dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/cli_050-059_066-075_nexgddp_and_loca). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: Environmental Impact by Food Type (Calories)
description: The Environmental Impact by Food Type (Calories) data set, produced by World Resources Institute in its 2018 World Resources Report: _Creating a Sustainable Food Future_, illustrates the variations in impact of various food products on land use, freshwater use, and greenhouse gas emissions per million kilocalories consumed. Land use is separated into cropland use and pasture land use. Freshwater use is specified as either from rainwater or irrigation. Greenhouse gas emissions are categorized as occurring during land-use change (e.g., converting forested land to pasture or cropland) or during agricultural production. The impact is measured by the hectares used, thousand cubic meters of freshwater used, or tons of carbon dioxide equivalent produced per million of kilocalories consumed. Both plant-based and animal-based food products are examined in this data set. The plant-based products examined are sugar, rice, rapeseed and mustard seed oil, palm oil, maize, roots and tubers, wheat, soybean oil, fruits and vegetables, sunflower seed oil, and pulses; the animal-based products are pork, eggs, fish (farmed, includes all aquatic animal products), poultry, dairy, beef, and sheep and goat meat. The data set clearly illustrates that animal products overwhelmingly use more land and water, and produce greater quantities of greenhouse gas emissions, than plant-based products. The data used in this data set are global means for land use, water use, and GHG emissions and were derived from the GlobAgri-WRR model (land use and greenhouse gas emissions), authors’ calculations from Mekonnen and Hoekstra (2011, 2012) (freshwater consumption), and Waite et al. (2014) (farmed fish freshwater consumption). Freshwater use for farmed fish products is shown as rainwater and irrigation combined. Land use and greenhouse gas emissions estimates are based on a marginal analysis (i.e., additional agricultural land use and emissions per additional million calories or ton of protein consumed). Based on the approach taken by the European Union for estimating emissions from land-use change for biofuels, land-use change impacts are amortized over a period of 20 years and then shown as annual impacts. Land use and greenhouse gas emissions estimates for beef production are based on dedicated beef production, not beef that is a coproduct of dairy. Tons of harvested products were converted to quantities of calories and protein using the global average edible calorie and protein contents of food types as reported in the Food and Agriculture Organization's FAOSTAT (2017). description: The Intact Forest Landscapes (IFL) data set identifies unbroken expanses of natural ecosystems within the zone of forest extent that show no signs of significant human activity and are large enough that all native biodiversity, including viable populations of wide-ranging species, could be maintained. To map IFL areas, a set of criteria was developed and designed to be globally applicable and easily replicable, the latter to allow for repeated assessments over time as well as verification. IFL areas were defined as unfragmented landscapes, at least 50,000 ha in size, and with a minimum width of 10 km. These were then mapped from Landsat satellite imagery for the year 2000. Changes in the extent of IFLs were identified within year 2000 IFL boundary using the global wall-to-wall Landsat image composite for year 2013 and the global forest cover loss data set (Hansen et al. 2013). Areas identified as “reduction in extent” met the IFL criteria in 2000 but no longer met the criteria in 2013. The main causes of change were clearing for agriculture and tree plantations, industrial activity such as logging and mining, fragmentation due to infrastructure and new roads, and fires assumed to be caused by humans. These data can be used to assess forest intactness, alteration, and degradation at global and regional scales. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. Forest Landscape Integrity Index
description: ### Overview The Forest Landscape Integrity Index (FLII) dataset describes the degree of anthropogenic forest modification as of the beginning of 2019. The dataset is global with 300 m resolution. The FLII was calculated from data covering forest extent, observed and inferred human pressures, and alterations in forest connectivity. Deforestation is a major environmental issue, but far less attention has been given to the degree of anthropogenic modification of remaining forests. Human modification of remaining forests reduces ecosystem integrity, diminishes many of the benefits that these remaining forests provide, and is potentially as significant as outright forest loss in determining overall environmental outcomes. Many global environmental agendas, including halting biodiversity loss, reversing land degradation, and limiting climate change, depend upon retaining forests with high ecological integrity, yet the scale and degree of forest modification remain poorly quantified and mapped. Mapping and monitoring forest modification globally will provide essential information for coordinated global, national, and local policy-making, planning, and action, to help nations and other stakeholders achieve the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and implement other shared commitments. Created by [47 forest experts from across the world](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-020-19493-3#author-information), the FLII offers a timely indicator of the status and management needs of Earth’s remaining forests, and demonstrates there has been a huge loss of forest integrity. Globally, only 17.4 million km2 of forest (40%) can be considered having high integrity and only 27% of this area is found in nationally-designated protected areas ([Grantham et al. 2020](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-020-19493-3)). ### Methodology To produce the Forest Landscape Integrity Index, four datasets were combined representing: 1. forest extent 2. ‘observed’ pressure from high impact, localized human activities for which spatial datasets exist, specifically: infrastructure, agriculture, and recent deforestation 3. ‘inferred’ pressure associated with edge effects, and other diffuse processes, (e.g. activities such as hunting and selective logging) modelled using proximity to observed pressures 4. anthropogenic changes in forest connectivity due to forest loss These datasets were combined to produce an index score for each forest pixel (300m), with the highest scores reflecting the highest forest integrity, as of the start of 2019.For the full documentation, please see the accompanying article [Grantham et al. 2020](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-020-19493-3). ### Additional Information For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. description: ### Overview This dataset shows potential climate change impacts on world crop production and yield from 1970-2000 to 2080 under different emissions scenarios. The impact under different emissions scenarios is reported as the percentage change from this baseline. This dataset includes the years 2020, 2050, and 2080; the crops maize, rice, wheat, and grain; and the emissions scenarios from the Special Report on Emissions Scenarios (SRES) A1F1, A2A, A2B, A2C, B1A, B2A, and B2B. This dataset is an update to a major crop modeling study by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Goddard Institute for Space Studies (GISS). ### Methodology The initial study was published in 1997, based on output of the HadCM2 model forced with greenhouse gas (GHG) concentration from the IS95 emission scenarios in 1997. Results of the initial study are presented in “Potential Impacts of Climate Change on World Food Supply: Data Sets from a Major Crop Modeling Study,” released by the NASA Socioeconomic Data and Applications Center (SEDAC) in 2001. The co-authors developed and tested a method for investigating the spatial implications of climate change on crop production. The Decision Support System for Agrotechnology Transfer dynamic process crop growth models were specified and validated for 127 sites in the major world agricultural regions. Results from the crop models, calibrated and validated in the major crop-growing regions, were then used to test functional forms describing the response of yield changes in the climate and environmental conditions as a percent change by country. The baseline year for crop yield changes is the average yield simulated under current climate (1970-2000 baseline). The resulting yield change data was then fed into trade models to assess impacts on prices and overall food production. Optimal yield is the potential yield not limited by water or fertilizer and without management constraints. Adapted yields are evaluated in each country as a fraction of the potential yield. The weighting factor combines the ratio of current yields to current yield potential and the economic limitation of the economic country’s agricultural systems. This updated version is based on HadCM3 model output along with GHG concentrations from the Special Report on Emissions Scenarios (SRES). The crop yield estimates incorporate some major improvements: (1) consistent crop simulation methodology and climate change scenarios; (2) weighting of model site results by contribution to regional and national, and rainfed and irrigated, production; (3) quantitative foundation for estimation of physiological CO₂ effects on crop yields; (4) explicit consideration of adaptation; and (5) reporting of results by country rather than by Basic Linked System region. For full documentation, please read the source [methodology](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0959378003000827?via%3Dihub). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data is available from the data provider for the years 2020, 2050, and 2080; the crops maize, rice, wheat, and grain; and the emissions scenarios from the Special Report on Emissions Scenarios (SRES) A1F1, A2A, A2B, A2C, B1A, B2A, and B2B. description: The Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) active fires data (VNP14IMGT) constitute the latest fire monitoring product to be added to FIRMS (Fire Information for Resource Management System), which identifies global fire locations in near-real time. Information is collected from the VIIRS sensor and processed with a fire detection algorithm to flag active fires. Each dot on the map represents the center of a 375 m pixel that has been flagged by the algorithm. The VIIRS data provides a higher resolution data set than the active fires data from MODIS. The VIIRS data have higher spatial resolution (375 m pixels vs. 1 km pixels), which improves detection of smaller fires and provides a more reliable estimate of fire perimeters. The VIIRS data are also better calibrated to detect fires at night. The active fires data are available to view and download for the past 24 hours, 48 hours, or 7 days. Older fire data will be available for download from the NASA FIRMS website beginning in mid-2016. Each fire alert has a confidence value of low, nominal, or high to help users gauge the quality of individual hotspot /fire pixels. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. description: The Global Volcano Hazard Frequency and Distribution data are created by the World Bank Group, the Columbia University Center for Hazards and Risk Research (Columbia CHRR), and the Columbia University Earth Institute Center for International Earth Science Information Network (CIESIN). The data are released in a 2.5 minute gridded data set based on the National Geophysical Data Center (NGDC) Volcano Database spanning the period 1979 through 2000. This database includes nearly 4,000 volcanic events categorized as moderate or above (values 2 through 8) according to the Volcano Explosivity Index (VEI). Most volcanoes are georeferenced to the nearest 10th or 100th of a degree, with a few to the nearest 1,000th of a degree. To produce the final output, the frequency of a volcanic hazard is computed for each grid cell, with the data set consequently being classified into deciles (10 classes consisting of an approximately equal number of grid cells). The higher the grid cell value in the final output, the higher the relative frequency of hazard posed by volcanoes. This data set is the result of collaboration between the CHRR and CIESIN. title: U.S. Monthly Precipitation Normals
description: The Parameter-elevation Relationships on Independent Slopes Model (PRISM) Climate Group monthly climate normals are baseline data sets describing average monthly conditions over the most recent three full decades. The most recent PRISM normals are for the period 1981-2010. Spatial climate data sets for mean monthly precipitation and minimum and maximum temperature were developed for the conterminous United States. These 30-arcsec (∼800-m) grids are the official spatial climate data sets of the U.S. Department of Agriculture. The PRISM interpolation method was used to develop data sets that reflected, as closely as possible, the current state of knowledge of spatial climate patterns in the United States. PRISM calculates a climate–elevation regression for each digital elevation model (DEM) grid cell, and stations entering the regression are assigned weights based primarily on the physiographic similarity of the station to the grid cell. Factors considered are location, elevation, coastal proximity, topographic facet orientation, vertical atmospheric layer, topographic position, and orographic effectiveness of the terrain. Surface stations used in the analysis numbered nearly 13,000 for precipitation and 10,000 for temperature. Station data were spatially quality controlled, and short-period-of-record averages adjusted to better reflect the 1981–2010 period.

title: U.S. Heat Stress Emergency Department Visits
description: The Crude Rate of Emergency Department Visits for Heat Stress per 100,000 Population data set contains case counts of heat stress illness emergency department (ED) visits using admission date among residents of the United States. These data are stratified by year of admission, state, and gender. Emergency department visit records are selected using primary and other diagnosis codes and emergency department visit date between May 1 and September 30 for each year. Annual Crude rates are calculated using Midyear and postcensal resident population, by age and sex, for state and county. Age-adjusted rates are calculated by method to Year 2000 US Standard Population. ED visits data were submitted by 25 states and 1 city: California, Colorado, Connecticut, Florida, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, New York City, Oregon, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Utah, Vermont, Washington, and Wisconsin. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) Tracking Network suppresses data for counties with non-zero counts less than 6 and population less than 100,000 to protect confidentiality. Increases in the rates of ED visits for heat stress are one potential impact of rising global temperatures. Tracking these data can help document changes over place and time, monitor vulnerable areas, and evaluate the results of local climate-adaptation strategies. description: ### Overview Gross domestic product (GDP) is a key economic indicator that measures the monetary value of goods and services provided within that area. The gridded GDP dataset used national GDP, gridded population data, and other factors to estimate GDP at a 30 arc-second resolution for 1990, 2000 and 2015. This gridded GDP dataset is important because it can be used for research at the sub-national level. GDP measurements are in purchasing power parity (PPP) in 2011 U.S. dollars. The data was created at Aalto University. The authors also created the [GDP per capita](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/soc073a) dataset. ### Methodology To create a high resolution, complete picture of GDP, the author first calculated GDP per capita using the World bank Development Indicators database. For missing countries, they used data from the Central Intelligence Agency World Factbook. The temporal coverage of both the national and sub-national data varied considerably. To fill in the missing values, temporal interpolation and extrapolation approaches were used. To be consistent between the sub-national and national datasets, and to ensure the data set would represent official national statistics, the authors did not use the sub-national GDP per capita directly, but instead used the sub-national data to scale national GDP per capita. This was done for each year by first calculating population-weighted national GDP per capita from sub-national GDP per capita data and the HYDE 3.2 population data set. This output was then used in each sub-national unit to calculate the ratio between population-weighted national GDP and reported sub-national GDP. The final sub-national GDP per capita (in PPP) was calculated by multiplying the ratio with the reported national GDP per capita. Reported sub-national data were used preferentially, followed by interpolated and extrapolated sub-national data, together with national averages. To estimate the total GDP of each grid cell, the authors multiplied the GDP per capita by grid specific population data using two different spatial resolutions: 5 arc-minutes (10 km at equator) and 30 arc-seconds (1 km at equator). Lower resolution population data were taken from HYDE 3.2 which includes annual data for the year 1990 and for the years 2000-2015 with a resolution of 5 arc-min. Thus, for the years 1991-1999 they needed to use the interpolated population between 1990 and 2000. Higher resolution population data were adapted from the Global Human Settlement (GHS) population grid which has data for the years 1990, 2000 and 2015 with a resolution of 30 arc-seconds. title: Air Quality: Sulfur Dioxide (SO₂) Station Measurements
description: ### Overview The Air Quality: Sulfur Dioxide (SO₂) Station Measurements dataset is a global dataset that shows real-time air quality data from around the world for sulfur dioxide (SO₂). It presents data collected from government and international organizations at the station level. This means the data is more accurate to specific areas than national or regional data. As of June 2017 OpenAQ data was available for 5,400 locations in 48 countries and is being continually updated with new sources. Sulfur dioxide (SO₂) is a colorless air pollutant with a strong odor. The main sources of sulfur dioxide emissions are from fossil fuel combustion and natural volcanic activity. Additionally, it can react in the atmosphere to form other harmful compounds, like sulfuric acid, and causes acid rain. It can be a threat to human health, animal health, and plant life. Sulfur dioxide irritates the skin and mucous membranes of the eyes, nose, throat, and lungs. High concentrations of SO₂ can cause inflammation and irritation of the respiratory system, especially during heavy physical activity. The resulting symptoms can include pain when taking a deep breath, coughing, throat irritation, and breathing difficulties. High concentrations of SO₂ can affect lung function, worsen asthma attacks, and worsen existing heart disease in sensitive groups. People with preexisting respiratory issues and children are most affected by SO₂ exposure. OpenAQ is an open-source project to surface live, real-time air quality data from around the world. Its “mission is to enable previously impossible science, impact policy, and empower the public to fight air pollution.” Scientists, researchers, developers, and citizens can use these data to understand how air quality in different locations changes over time. Resource Watch also shows continually updated air quality data from OpenAQ on [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003anrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-25), [inhalable particulates (PM10)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003bnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-10), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003dnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-NO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-O), [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003fnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-CO), and [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003gnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-BC_1). ### Methodology The sulfur dioxide station measurements dataset was produced and is continually updated by aggregating data from permanent outdoor air quality measures. Data was collected only from official sources, including government entities and international organizations. As of June 2017 OpenAQ data was available for 5,400 locations in 48 countries. For data to be included it had to meet three criteria: 1. The “raw” measurement data on physical particle concentration had to be available on the originating site. 2. The data needed to be at the “station level.” It is unacceptable if it is presented in an aggregated form for a city or region. 3. The data needed to be continuously updated at intervals between 10 minutes and 24 hours. After the data was collected it was put into tables. Data was collected using the source organization’s Air Quality Index (AQI) classifications. The final dataset was mapped in vector format at a subnational level with each measurement station showing local particle concentration. OpenAQ continually reviews each data source website for updated values and updates the dataset every hour. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows continually updated air quality data from OpenAQ on [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003anrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-25), [inhalable particulates (PM10)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003bnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-10), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003dnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-NO), [ozone (O₃)]https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-O), [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003fnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-CO), and [black carbon (BC)]https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003gnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-BC_1). title: Aqueduct Riverine Flood Hazard
description: ### Overview The Aqueduct Riverine Flood Hazard dataset shows the projected inundation depth for river basins around the world, in a business as usual climate scenario. In this dataset, the inundation depth represents the depth of water over normally dry ground that would occur during 100-year floods. Inundation depths are calculated for the baseline year 2010 and predicted for future years 2030, 2050, and 2080. The dataset has a spatial resolution of 30 arc seconds, which is approximately 1 km x 1 km at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. Flooding is likely to intensify in the coming decades due to climate change. It is among the most serious of all global risks, causing loss of life and damage to property, livelihoods, and economies. As urbanization and economic growth put more people and assets into flood-prone areas, it is important to calculate flood risks and hazards around the world. However, these hazards are usually underestimated due to lack of data and information. This dataset helps change that by providing high resolution inundation depth data. The Aqueduct Riverine Flood Hazard dataset was created by the World Resource Institute (WRI) to assist in creating water use policies and assessing flood risks. This dataset is part of WRI’s Aqueduct datasets. Aqueduct helps to identify and evaluate water risks around the world. ### Methodology The Aqueduct Riverine Flood Hazard dataset was created using a Global Flood Risk with IMAGE Scenarios (GLOFRIS) framework. GLOFRIS combines a global hydrological model called PCRaster Global Water Balance (PCR-GLOBWB) with river and floodplain routing scheme to make long-term simulations of river discharges and flood levels for a variety of climate conditions. In addition, meteorological datasets from European Water and Global Change (EUWATCH) were used to force PCR-GLOBWB over various time periods. Floodplain water volumes were then calculated using the PCR-GLOBWB outputs for a 2010 baseline, along with future climate scenarios in 2030, 2050, and 2080. The output flood volumes were converted to high resolution inundation maps using a volume spreading flood model. The “Riverine” hazard represents flooding from river overflow and occurs in river basins with an area of at least 10,000 kilometers squared. However, smaller floods do occur more regularly than larger floods. The data on Resource Watch shows what a 100-year flood (1% probability of occurrence per year) will look like for the selected years (2030, 2050, and 2080). For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Aqueduct also provides datasets on coastal hazards and other water risks. description: ### Overview The Maximum Antarctic Sea Ice dataset shows the annual maximum extent of sea ice in the Antarctic for select years between 1980-2020. Antarctic sea ice typically reaches its maximum extent in September. In this map, light blue represents locations where sea ice was present during September for each year. Sea ice extent data was collected by satellite microwave sensing instruments at a spatial resolution of 25 kilometers (km). This dataset is derived from two products: a near real-time daily dataset and a separate daily dataset that is processed yearly. For the most recent 6-18 months, sea ice extents were derived from near real-time data; all older data was derived from the separate daily dataset. This dataset can be used to understand changes in annual maximum Antarctic sea ice extent over the past 40 years. Although Antarctic sea ice extent varies significantly from year to year, the average ice extent has not changed over the past 40 years. According to the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration](https://www.climate.gov/news-features/understanding-climate/understanding-climate-antarctic-sea-ice-extent),natural variability in the Southern Ocean and in atmospheric circulation patterns have a greater impact on Antarctic sea ice extent than climate change. However, climate change is disrupting wind patterns, currents and ocean temperatures across the globe. These changes may eventually impact Antarctic sea ice extent. The [National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC)](https://nsidc.org/) was founded in 1976 as the World Data Center for Glaciology. Over time, the NSIDC evolved to become a data distribution and research center specializing in remote sensing of cryospheric data such as snow, sea ice, frozen ground, ice sheets and glaciers. In addition to managing and distributing this data, the NSIDC creates and supports data access tools for its users. They also use the datasets for climate research and education. The NSIDC is part of University of Colorado Boulder’s [Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences (CIRES)](https://cires.colorado.edu/). It is supported by the [National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)](https://www.nasa.gov/), the [National Science Foundation (NSF)](https://www.nsf.gov/) and the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)](https://www.noaa.gov/). ### Methodology Maximum Antarctic Sea Ice was produced from two sources: NASA's [Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC)](https://nsidc.org/data/nsidc-0051) and NSIDC’s [Near-Real-Time DMSP SSMIS Daily Polar Gridded Sea Ice Concentrations (NRTSI)](https://nsidc.org/data/nsidc-0081). Data for the GSFC and NRTSI datasets was collected by the following six sensors: - GSFC data: - [Nimbus-7 Satellite](https://eospso.nasa.gov/missions/nimbus-7) Scanning Multichannel Microwave Radiometer (SMMR) from October 1978 to August 1987 - [Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP)](https://www.ospo.noaa.gov/Operations/DMSP/index.html) F8 Special Sensor Microwave/Imager (SSM/I) from August 1987 to December 1991 - DMSP-F11 SSM/I from December 1991 to September 1995 - DMSP-F13 SSM/I from September 1995 to December 2007 - DMSP-F17 Special Sensor Microwave Imager/Sounder (SSMIS) from January 2008 to present - NRTSI data: - DMSP-F18 SSMIS from April 2016 to present The SMMR, SSM/I, and SSMIS instruments sense emitted microwave radiation. Data was collected daily by the SSM/I and SSMIS sensors and on alternate days by the SMMR sensor. An object's physical properties, such as atomic composition and crystalline structure, determine the amount of microwave radiation it emits. The crystalline structure of ice typically emits more microwave energy than liquid ocean water. Thus, the microwave sensors can easily distinguish sea ice from the ocean. The satellite data was converted to [brightness temperature](https://glossary.ametsoc.org/wiki/Brightness_temperature), a descriptive measure of an object's radiation. Brightness temperature data was then converted to gridded ice concentration using the [NASA Team algorithm](https://nsidc.org/support/faq/nasa-team-vs-bootstrap-algorithm#NASATeam1) at a spatial resolution of 25 km. Gridded ice concentration is the percentage of ice (relative to water) in a given cell. Each cell’s daily ice concentrations were averaged to produce monthly concentrations. Sea ice extent is delineated by the location where ice ends and water (open ocean) begins. Cells were classified as water if their average monthly ice concentration was below 15%, and as ice if the concentration was above 15%. Images of sea ice extent were created for each month, with ice shown in light blue. The process was the same for both the NRTSI and GSFC datasets. GSFC data had a tighter quality control than NRTSI data. However, GSFC data is only released once per year. NRTSI data was available at the end of each month, so it was used to produce sea ice extents while GSFC data was being processed. GSFC data replaced NRTSI data once it was available. Thus, data from the most recent 6-18 months was derived from the NRTSI dataset and older data was derived from the GSFC dataset. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows additional NSIDC sea ice extent data: [Historical Sea Ice Medians](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/b1ebea96-5963-4c2c-9273-7d08536ac07d), [Minimum Arctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/a99c5cf5-f141-4bed-a36d-b04c8e171dfa), [Maximum Arctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/15a0b176-8313-4859-af90-5c198e50a605), [Arctic Sea Ice Extent](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/484fbba1-ac34-402f-8623-7b1cc9c34f17), [Minimum Antarctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/05fd2614-325b-460a-8b52-3155fa9dd98f) and [Antarctic Sea Ice Extent](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e740efec-c673-431a-be2c-b214613f641a). title: Watersheds Transporting Wastewater to Coastal Ocean
description: ### Overview The Watersheds that Transport Wastewater to Coastal Ocean dataset, produced by National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis, maps human sewage inputs into coastal waters for the year 2015. This dataset displays the size and shape of nearly 135,000 watersheds across the globe that contribute to nitrogen and pathogen input from wastewater to the coastal ocean. Nitrogen concentration in each watershed is measured in grams/year. Human sewage is considered both an ecological and a human health issue, because it contributes both increased levels of nitrogen and pathogens to coastal waters. Excess nitrogen plays a key role in the ecological degradation of coastal ecosystems through a process called [eutrophication](https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/eutrophication.html). Eutrophication leads to harmful algal blooms and low-oxygen waters, which can kill fish, and degrade essential fish habitats. Pathogens in coastal waters can promote disease in marine organisms, such as coral reefs, and can cause human health impacts. It is important to monitor both nitrogen and pathogen concentrations, to understand trends and inform management. The National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis created this map of pourpoints, along with a model of nitrogen dispersion into the ocean, to inform marine conservation and public health work. The data allows for the comparison of global models of nitrogen sources and traditional water quality monitoring to identify priority hotspots. In-depth local monitoring can then pinpoint the true sources of and quantities of pollutants like nitrogen to benefit conservation and management. The model also links nitrogen inputs with data on pathogens in coastal waters to inform policy decisions around wastewater treatment options. ### Methodology High-resolution watershed vector data and pourpoints were used with an automated flow-accumulation process to determine the boundaries for ~135,000 global basins that drain into the ocean. Population and settlement data for each basin were used to estimate the levels of nitrogen and pathogen inputs to coastal waters. Nitrogen concentrations in grams per year (g/yr) were modeled from data on three types of wastewater (treated, septic, and open defecation) and the estimated amount of nitrogen removed by each treatment type. The inputs to coastal waters were determined by totaling the estimates that fell within the watershed boundary. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0258898#sec002). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also provides data on the location of ‘pourpoints’, the location at which water drains into the ocean, in [Wastewater Inputs to Coastal Areas](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/5bf349ec-3b14-4021-a7d4-fc4b8104bd74) and the dispersion of nitrogen into the coastal ocean at each pourpoint in [Wastewater Plumes in Coastal Areas](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/11804f04-d9c7-47b9-8d27-27ce6ed6c042). title: Air Quality: Aerosol Index Satellite Measurements
description: ### Overview The Air Quality: Aerosol Index Satellite Measurements dataset provides global monthly averages of an index that measures the presence of aerosols that absorb ultraviolet (UV) radiation in the atmosphere, such as dust and smoke. This index may be referred to as the absorbing aerosol index (AAI) or the UV Aerosol Index (UVAI). Absorbing Aerosols are solid and liquid particles suspended in the atmosphere. They are made up of primary aerosols and secondary aerosols. Primary aerosols are emitted directly, whereas secondary aerosols are formed by gases reacting in the atmosphere. Absorbing aerosols are mostly made of dust and smoke. The main sources of aerosols are combustion, like burning biomass, and natural sources, like volcanoes. The AAI can show dust and smoke particles coming from events like dust storms, volcanic eruptions, fires, and biomass burning around the world. The dataset is made up of data collected from the Sentinel-5 Precursor (S5p) mission, a low Earth orbit polar satellite system.The S5p mission is part of the Global Monitoring of the Environment and Security (GMES/COPERNICUS) space component program headed by the European Commission (EC) in partnership with the European Space Agency (ESA). Its goal is to provide information and services on air quality, climate, and the ozone layer. The S5p mission includes the TROPOspheric Monitoring Instrument (TROPOMI), which takes daily global observations of key atmospheric components, such as absorbing aerosols, at a 5.5 x 3.5 kilometer (km) resolution. Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-NO), [ozone (O₃)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-O), and [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-CO). ### Methodology The TROPOMI AAI dataset was created with data collected by the S5P satellite mission. UV-absorbing aerosol data was collected by determining the amount of Rayleigh scattering that occured in the UV spectral range for a pair of wavelengths. A spectral range is the range of light wavelengths that a specific spectrometer can measure, and in this case it refers to the wavelength of light that UV-absorbing aerosol molecules emit in the atmosphere. Rayleigh scattering is the scattering of light particles without causing a change in their wavelength. The UV-absorbing aerosol data collected was then compared with a calculated theoretical Rayleigh scattering value based on no UV-absorbing aerosols being present in the troposphere. The difference in scattering between the two data points represents the amount of UV-absorbing aerosols present and is the absorbing aerosol index. A positive AAI value indicates that UV-absorbing aerosols are present. The dataset was mapped by the Google Earth Engine team using the [harpconvert] (https://cdn.rawgit.com/stcorp/harp/master/doc/html/harpconvert.html) tool. For more information on this conversion please see the Google Earth Engine documentation. The offline version of this data is displayed on Resource Watch, which is more complete than its near real-time counterpart, but is released on a greater delay due to the additional processing time needed. For the full documentation, please see the [source methodology](https://sentinel.esa.int/web/sentinel/technical-guides/sentinel-5p/products-algorithms) associated with the “UV-Aerosol Index”. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-NO), [ozone (O₃)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-O), and [carbon monoxide (CO)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-CO). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset.Additional data for formaldehyde (CH₂O), sulphur dioxide (SO₂), methane (CH₄) and clouds are available from the data provider. Both a near real-time and an offline version of each of these compounds are available. Please see the [Google Earth Engine data catalog](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/tags/tropomi) to access this data. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/cit_035_tropomi_atmospheric_chemistry_model). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: Global Conflict Risk Index
description: The Global Conflict Risk Index (GCRI), created by the European Commission's Joint Research Centre (EC JRC), is an index of the statistical risk of violent conflict in the next 1-4 years for each country in the world. It assumes that structural conditions in a country are linked to the occurrence of violent conflict. The GCRI is exclusively based on quantitative indicators from open sources. It is calculated for 24 indicators across 5 dimensions: Political (Regime Type, Lack of Democracy, Government Effectiveness, Level of Repression, Empowerment Rights); Security (Recent Internal Conflict, Neighbors with Highly Violent Conflict, Years since Highly Violent Conflict); Social (Corruption, Ethnic Power Change, Ethnic Compilation, Transnational Ethnic Bonds, Homicide Rate, Infant Mortality); Economy (GDP per Capita, Income Inequality, Openness, Food Security, Unemployment); Geography and Environment (Water Stress, Oil Production, Structural Constraints, Population Size, Youth Bulge). The GCRI uses a linear regression model including historical data to train the model. Its creators at the EC JRC first determined the predictive value of the 24 variables regarding conflict onsets in the past 20 years. They then applied the results to the final model and derived the weights for the indicators from their significance regarding the model performance. Countries were scored on a 10-point scale for each of the 24 indicators. Data were obtained from open source resources such as the World Bank Group, United Nations, or Uppsala Data Conflict Program (UCDP). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Soil Carbon
Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature U.S. (RCP8.5)
description: The Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average temperature at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the temperature between the years 1985 and 2015. Average temperature projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Average Annual Temperature dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference. The annual average temperature for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis using the following steps: All daily low temperature data over a given year was extracted and averaged to produce a yearly average low temperature value. All daily high temperature data over a given year was extracted and averaged to produce a yearly average high temperature value. Average annual temperature was calculated by taking the mean of the average daily temperature over a given year. Average daily temperature was calculated by dividing the sum of daily low temperature and daily high temperature by 2. The average annual temperatures were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in annual average temperature. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the annual average temperatures between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

title: Annual Surface Water Coverage
description: ### Overview This dataset shows the locations of seasonal water and permanent water for each year between 1984 and 2020. A permanent water surface is an area that is underwater for all 12 months of the year, while a seasonal water surface is underwater for less than 12 months of the year. This dataset has a 30 meter resolution. Water is essential for Earth’s plant and animal life, as well as for many human activities. Surface water also affects the exchange of heat, gas, and water vapor between Earth’s surface and atmosphere. The dataset can be used to support sectors such as water resource management, climate modeling, biodiversity conservation, and food security. This data is a part of the Global Surface Water dataset, created by the European Commission’s Joint Research Center. ### Methodology Water coverage was detected using satellite imagery from Landsat 5, 7, and 8 that was collected between 1984 and 2020. To detect water, researchers used big data exploration and information extraction techniques such as expert systems, visual analytics, and evidential reasoning. An expert system is a classification process that can account for data uncertainty and incorporate image interpretation expertise. In some places, observations for all 12 months of the year were not available. For example, some parts of the world experience a polar night during parts of the year, in which the night lasts for more than 24 hours. These areas do not have adequate imagery to detect surface water coverage for all 12 months. In cases where 12 months of data was not available, water is considered to be permanent if the number of months where water is present is equal to the number of months where valid observations were acquired. Likewise, if the number of months where water is present is less than the number of months of valid observations, water is considered to be seasonal. Ice is treated as a nonvalid observation. If water is present throughout the unfrozen period, the lake is considered to be a permanent water surface. If the area of the lake contracts during the unfrozen period, then the pixels along the borders of the lake will be considered as seasonal water. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature20584). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for monthly recurrence and monthly water history are available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: Rainfall (5-day)
description: CHIRPS data, production led by the Climate Hazards Group at UCSB, can be used as a quasi-global rainfall data set for trend analysis and seasonal drought monitoring. This data set spans 50°S-50°N (and all longitudes), starting in 1981 and spanning to near-present. As of February 12, 2015, version 2.0 of CHIRPS is complete and available to the public. CHIRPS incorporates 0.05° resolution satellite imagery with on-the-ground precipitation station data to create gridded rainfall time series, measured in millimeters of precipitation / time period. Satellite data are derived from both microwave and infrared sensors. On-the-ground precipitation station data come from the Agromet Group of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and the Global Historical Climate Network (GHCN). A detailed description of the methodology behind CHIRPS can be found in this Naturearticle: http://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201566 http://dx.doi.org/10.3133/ds832. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.
