title: [Archived] Current and Projected Food Insecurity
description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](ac6dcdb3-2beb-4c66-9f83-565c16c2c914) as a replacement.**_ The Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) Food Security Outlook shapefiles are created by FEWS NET, led by U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), National Aeronautic and Space Administration (NASA), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Kimetrica, and Chemonics. Food security for a region is determined according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification approach. This is a standardized approach to classifying the level of food insecurity in a region. Classifications are typically released 4 times a year, each with a short-term (0-3 months from publication) and medium-term (4-7 months from publication) evaluation of food insecurity at the subnational level. The approach revolves around a consensus-building process. Food security experts review the available evidence to determine a food security classification on a scale of 1 to 5, with phase 1 corresponding to minimal food insecurity, and phase 5 corresponding to famine-level food insecurity. Evidence used includes satellite data measuring precipitation anomalies (CHIRPS SPI), vegetation anomalies (NDVI), and expert opinion based on knowledge of market and trade functioning and socioeconomic dynamics in each region of interest, among others. The data covers select regions from East, West, and Central Africa, Central America, and Afghanistan. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Historical Gridded Population
description: ### Overview The History Database of the Global Environment (HYDE version 3.2), is a combination of gridded historical population and land use estimates. The authors used historical records to model population at the province level and land use areas at the national level through time; then used algorithms to spatially distribute the total population and land use areas to 5 arc minute pixels (about 10 kilometers at the equator). HYDE is the first spatially explicit estimate of population and land use going back to 10,000 BC. Population is represented by maps of total, urban, and rural population, population density and built-up area. This dataset on Resource Watch describes the population data of HYDE, and the land use data can be viewed [here](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/soc088c-HYDE-Anthromes). The dataset has global coverage from 10,000 BC to 2017 AD at a resolution of 5 arc minutes (about 10 km). HYDE was developed by the PBL Netherlands Environmental Assessment Agency, and is used by the World Climate Research Program Coupled Model Intercomparison Project ([CMIP6](https://www.wcrp-climate.org/wgcm-cmip/wgcm-cmip6)). ### Methodology The authors estimated population totals at the state or province level by using a variety of historical sources and then used algorithms to spatially distribute the state level population to 5 arc minute pixels. The basis for the state level population data is the United Nations World Populations Prospects (2008 Revision) for the 1950–2017 period. The pre-1950 historical estimates were largely taken from McEvedy and Jones (1978), Livi-Bacci (2007), and Maddison (2001). The authors supplemented these sources with the sub-national population numbers of Populstat (Lahmeyer, personal communication, 2004) and many other country specific sources. The country specific sources of population estimates are outlined in the supplementary information of their [methodology](https://www.earth-syst-sci-data.net/9/927/2017/). The authors then used interpolation techniques to fill in gaps between population sources. For the present population spatial distribution, the authors used the spatial patterns from the Gridded Population of the World (GPW v3) and LandScan (2014) for the year 2012 to allocate the total population for each administrative unit to the 5 arc minute pixel level. LandScan is a global population database with information on population totals at 1 km resolution from the Department of Energy’s Oak Ridge National Laboratory. In order to distribute the state level population to the pixel resolution (5 arc minutes), the 2012 population patterns from LandScan are gradually replaced with weighting maps based on various proxies such as soil suitability, slope, distance to water and case studies from several disciplines (e.g. history, archaeology). For simplicity, current administrative level boundaries (town, county, etc.) were kept constant over time, and every historical source was adjusted to match the current subnational boundaries (e.g. by taking fractions of former larger empires). Country and regional totals were then checked against other historical estimates. For the full documentation, please see the [source methodology](https://www.earth-syst-sci-data.net/9/927/2017/). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows data from the HYDE dataset with land use data categorized under [Anthropogenic Biomes](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/soc088c-HYDE-Anthromes). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. The HYDE dataset has additional population data including population count, rural population count, urban population count, and urban built-up area. HYDE also provides data on land use including pasture areas, irrigated crops and rainfed crops. The HYDE dataset covers 10,000 BC to 2017 at the following time intervals: every 1000 years from 10,000 BC to 0 AD, every 100 years from 0 AD to 1700 AD, every 10 years from 1700 AD to 2000, and every year from 2000 to 2017. description: Annual average total precipitation, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

description: Global sea level is expected to change due to climatic and non-climatic factors. Here, sea level change for selected locations for the years 2050 and 2100 and RCP 4.5 and 8.5 scenarios are shown in units of cm above levels in the year 2000. Two models, K14 and DP16, are mapped. The Kopp et al. (2014), or K14, framework combines multiple lines of information to construct probability distributions for key contributors to global mean sea level and relative sea level change. Factors in this model include: thermal expansion; regional ocean dynamics; glacier and ice sheet mass-balance; anthropogenic changes in land-waterstorage; and non-climatic effects such as glacio-isostatic adjustment, tectonics, and sediment compaction. The DeConto and Pollard (2016), or DP16, model found that the inclusion in a physical model of previously omitted processes such as ice-shelf hydrofracturing and structural collapse of tall, marine-terminating ice cliffs has the potential to drive a large increase in Antarctic mass-loss rates. The K14 and DP16 projections utilize different statistical methods, the former using a more robust probabilistic model. Therefore, both models are included for comparison. title: Unemployment Rate
description: ### Overview This dataset includes the estimated unemployment rate in 208 countries from 1991 to present and is updated annually. The unemployment rate is the percentage of the labor force that is without work but available for and seeking employment. The unemployment rate is an indicator of an economy’s efficiency and effectiveness to absorb its labor force. High and consistent unemployment suggests serious inefficiencies in resource allocation. The dataset is published by the International Labour Organization (ILO), through its Department of Statistics (ILOSTAT). ### Methodology Country-level estimations of unemployment rates came from several data sources. Nationally representative labor force surveys were first consulted for this data. In the case that this survey data was not available, other sources like population censuses and nationally reported estimates were used. In cases of missing values, an ILO econometric model was used. This model ensured that data was comparable across countries and over time by accounting for differences in data sources, the scope of coverage, methodology, and other country-specific factors. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.ilo.org/ilostat-files/Documents/TEM.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. These raw data are analyzed using methods that account for the varied spacing of temperature stations around the globe and for urban heating effects that could skew the calculations. title: Air Quality: Mexico City Nitrogen Dioxide (NO₂) Forecast
description: ### Overview The Air Quality: Mexico City Nitrogen Dioxide (NO₂) Forecast dataset provides weather and air quality forecasts for Mexico City. This dataset represents the forecasted density for Nitrogen Dioxide in parts per billion (ppb). The forecast offers an hourly estimate on Nitrogen Dioxide density with a spatial resolution of 1 kilometer (km), encompassing Mexico CIty and its Metropolitan Area (MCMA). A number of hazards related to pollutants is known, which depends on the physical characteristics of the individual exposed to pollution, the time of exposure and the type of pollutant. Effects can range from respiratory discomfort to the worsening of pre-existing conditions like asthma, particularly in children and the elderly. NO₂ is a highly reactive air pollutant, produced by fossil fuel combustion from power plants and gasoline-burning vehicles. According to the [U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)] (https://www.epa.gov/no2-pollution/basic-information-about-no2), breathing air with a high concentration of NO₂ can irritate airways in the respiratory system and long-term exposures can contribute to asthma development. Even exposure to elevated NO₂ concentrations over short periods can aggravate respiratory diseases, leading to respiratory symptoms (such as coughing, wheezing, or difficulty breathing), hospital admissions, and visits to emergency rooms. People with asthma as well as children and the elderly are generally at greater risk for the health effects of NO₂. In the MCMA the main source of NO₂ comes from vehicles that burn fossil fuels. In addition,the pollutant has a strong seasonal behavior with higher concentrations during the cold-dry months of the year. According to the [Mexico City Ministry of the Environment (SEDEMA)](http://www.aire.cdmx.gob.mx/descargas/publicaciones/flippingbook/informe_anual_calidad_aire_2017/mobile/informe_anual_calidad_aire_2017v3.pdf), NO₂ concentrations in the MCMA have remained below the limit levels indicated in Mexican regulations, as well as those recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) and EPA, though higher concentrations have occasionally been recorded in the areas of the city with greater mobility. Showcasing the spatial distribution of NO₂ in the MCMA will help provide insights about the way a city can produce information according to its needs while complementing global air quality models. The forecast helps the Mexico CIty government to issue health warnings based on the expected air quality for a given day, like recommending citizens to avoid open-air exercise or to limit their use of fossil fuel vehicles. The forecast was generated by SEDEMA with help from the Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC). SEDEMA provides a tool for the inhabitants of MCMA to make well-informed decisions about dangerous air pollution activity on a given day. SEDEMA works on five environmental issues: air quality and climate change, land conservation and biodiversity, sustainable urban infrastructure, water supply and quality, and environmental communication and education. ### Methodology The dataset is comprised of the following models: Weather: Estimates the weather conditions of the MCMA using data from global systems. It harnesses the [Weather Research and Forecasting Model-Advanced Research (WRF-ARW)](https://www.mmm.ucar.edu/weather-research-and-forecasting-model), which is a mesoscale numerical weather prediction system designed for both atmospheric research and operational forecasting applications. The model generates temperature, wind, rainfall and solar radiation, among other weather related indicators.among others. Emissions: This model makes use of emission inventories for the MCMA to estimate NO₂ levels on an hourly basis, as well as its geospatial distribution. Chemical Transport: This model harnesses the outputs from the weather and emissions models as well as other chemical and physical mechanisms to simulate transformations in the atmosphere and the influence of weather dynamics in these processes. For this purpose, the [Community Multiscale Air Quality Modeling System (CMAQ)] (https://www.cmascenter.org/cmaq/) is employed to forecast the behavior of the pollutants in the MCMA. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows forecasts for [Air Quality: Mexico City Carbon Monoxide (CO) Forecast](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e39f5910-a9b8-4ef1-b4b4-f6b141b15541), [Air Quality: Mexico City Sulfur Dioxide (SO₂) Forecast](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/59790e64-d95d-43fa-a124-5c7eb1cb4456), [Air Quality: Mexico City Ozone (O₃) Forecast](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/00d6bae1-e105-4165-8230-ee73a8128538) and [Air Quality: Mexico City Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) Forecast](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7a34b770-83f9-4c6a-acb8-31edcff7241e) Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. The source also includes the outputs for their weather model as well as the measurements of the Mexico City Weather Monitoring System (SIMAT) using their air quality index. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. title: U.S. Particulate Matter Concentrations
description: The annual PM2.5 Level (Monitor Only) data set is provided by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), and offers a general indication of the overall trend in annual PM2.5 concentrations. It can be used to inform policy makers and the public about the degree of potential exposures to fine particles within a state during a year and over time (trends), based on the annual National Ambient Air Quality Standard (NAAQS) of 15 µg/m³ for PM2.5 developed by EPA. The annual average measures of PM2.5 are created using the site-level daily monitoring data. Only monitors that have at least 11 observations for each of the four calendar quarters are considered complete. The annual averages are computed only for monitors that satisfy the completeness criteria. Annual averages are calculated using seasonal (quarterly) averages. title: [Archived] Gridded Livestock
description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](6b523d76-ca2d-4059-b0a6-d90a6b8ba5a6) as a replacement.**_ The GLW is a global livestock mapping project by the Food and Agriculture Organization's Animal Production and Health Division (FAO-AGA). The data shows livestock distributions for the year 2006 at a 0.05° resolution.The methodology and sources of data are fully described in a document entitled: "The Gridded Livestock of the World. FAO (2007)". In summary, for each country the most recent available sub-national livestock census data and corresponding administrative boundaries have been collected. These are then converted into densities, excluding land unsuitable for livestock (either monogastric or ruminant), to provide the 'observed' data. The data are then disaggregated based on statistical relations with some environmental variables in similar agro-ecological zones to produce the 'predicted' distribution. The predicted data are further manipulated to match national census totals for the year 2000 according to the FAOSTAT database. The project also includes: a global network of data providers on livestock and sub-national boundaries; an Oracle database in which these data are managed and processed; a system for predicting livestock distributions based on environmental data and an interactive web application, the Global Livestock Production and Health Atlas (GLiPHA), through which data are viewed and disseminated. The files are in a raster GRID format. Pixel values represent actual densities (per square kilometre). These data have been produced by FAO's Animal Production and Health Division in collaboration with ERGO and the TALA research group, University of Oxford, UK. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Predicted Vulnerability of Fisheries to Climate Change
description: ### Overview The Predicted Vulnerability of Fisheries to Climate Change dataset shows the predicted vulnerability of marine capture fishing industries in 147 coastal countries for the time period of 2016-2050. Fishery vulnerabilities are presented at a national resolution with each country receiving a vulnerability score between 0 and 1, with the latter being the highest vulnerability. The dataset utilizes the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) definition of vulnerability, which is based on three variables: exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity. Additionally, the dataset used future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the IPCC’s Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5 to include the effect of climate change. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in current greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. Marine ecosystems and fisheries provide a crucial foundation for human well-being and development, yielding 81.5 million tons of catch in 2014, valued at over $90 billion. For many [low-income food-deficit countries](http://www.fao.org/countryprofiles/lifdc/en/#:~:text=Three%20countries%20have%20graduated%20out,the%20net%20food%2Dexporter%20criterion) and local communities in developing countries, near-shore marine fisheries also provide a crucial source of micronutrients, which are necessary for early childhood development and influence long-term public health outcomes. The goal of this dataset is to provide a useful tool for understanding which countries are most at risk to the negative effects of climate change on the fishing industry in the coming decades. It can help prioritize the allocation of [climate finance](https://unfccc.int/topics/climate-finance/resources/biennial-assessment-of-climate-finance), as well as activities aimed at capacity building and the transfer of marine technology. The dataset was created by [Blasiak et al.](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article/file?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0179632&type=printable), with additional help and grants from Stockholm University, University of Tokyo, James Cook University, and University of Waterloo. ### Methodology The Fisheries Vulnerability to Climate Change dataset was created by using the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) definition of vulnerability. Vulnerability was calculated by finding the difference between adaptive capacity and the sum of exposure and sensitivity. The **exposure** of countries to the impacts of climate change on marine capture fisheries was calculated based on projected sea surface temperature (SST) anomalies. SST anomalies were calculated by subtracting future SST average estimates by historical SST averages. Future SST estimates were taken from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) climate model for RCP 8.5 and averaged for the time period between 2016 to 2050. Historical reference climatology was also taken from the CMIP5 model from the year 1900 to 1950. SST anomaly data was then averaged among country boundaries to provide SST anomaly data by country. The index was then normalized on a scale of zero to one. The **sensitivity** or dependence of countries on marine capture fisheries was calculated as an index of five variables: number of fishers, share of marine fisheries exports in total exports, percentage of fishers in the economically active population, weight of total fisheries landings, and share of marine fish protein in total protein consumption. Data for the five variables was collected from the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the World Bank Group and the World Factbook by the Central Intelligence Agency. Values for each variable were normalized on a scale from zero to one, and the five variables were averaged with equal weights. The total average value was then normalized on a scale from zero to one to create the sensitivity index. The **adaptive capacity** of countries represents the ability to modify or adjust fisheries and livelihoods in order to cope with the negative impacts of climate change and pursue any emerging opportunities. Six variables were combined to calculate the index of adaptive capacity: - Fisheries subsidies, collected from the Sea Around Us - Ratio of industrial to small-scale fisheries, collected from the Sea Around Us - Healthy life expectancy, taken from the World Health Organization (WHO) - Governance capacity (averaging six dimensions of governance), taken from the World Bank Group’s Worldwide Governance Indicators - Education levels (literacy rates or school enrollment rates), taken from the World Bank Group - Gross domestic product (GDP) per capita, taken from the World Bank Group’s Development Indicators database The mean of the two fisheries-related variables, fisheries subsidies and ratio of industrial to small-scale fisheries, made up one half of the adaptive capacity index. The four remaining socio-economic variables made up the other half of the adaptive capacity index. This gave the fisheries-related variables a greater weight than the socio-economic variables. The adaptive capacity index was then normalized on a scale from zero to one. The vulnerability index was calculated by finding the difference between the adaptive capacity and the sum of exposure and sensitivity, in line with the IPCC framework. The resulting vulnerability index was normalized on a scale from zero to one. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Indices for this same time period are available from the data provider for RCPs 2.6 and 4.5. Additionally, for the time period of 2066-2100, indices were calculated under the same three emissions scenarios (RCPs 2.6, 4.5, and 8.5). title: Ocean Nitrate Concentration
description: ### Overview This dataset shows global daily and monthly mean nitrate (NO₃) concentrations in seawater from the surface to 5.1 meters in depth. The data are a product of the Global Ocean and Biogeochemistry Analysis system, a global biogeochemical simulation using the [PISCES model](https://www.nemo-ocean.eu/framework/components/engines) and are displayed at a 0.25° by 0.25° resolution. Nutrients, such as nitrogen and phosphorus, are essential for plant and animal growth and nourishment, but the overabundance of these nutrients can drive phase shifts in coastal ecosystems. Nitrogen, in the form of nitrate, is naturally abundant in the environment, but high concentrations in water are usually an indicator of pollution. The [main sources of nitrogen pollution](https://www.wri.org/our-work/project/eutrophication-and-hypoxia/sources-eutrophication) are agriculture nutrient sources. These include chemical fertilizer run-off, manure from cattle farms, and aquaculture operations. Other sources include fossil fuel combustion and wastewater. Nitrogen flows from rivers into the ocean, where it disrupts the nutrient balance in marine systems and drives the growth of aquatic plants and algae. Excessive growth of these organisms can block light to deeper waters and use up dissolved oxygen as they decompose. This process is known as [eutrophication](https://www.wri.org/our-work/project/eutrophication-and-hypoxia/impacts). If enough oxygen is removed the water can become hypoxic, where there is not enough oxygen to sustain most forms of life. The complete removal of oxygen creates an anoxic area, or oxygen “dead zone.” The [Copernicus Marine Service](https://marine.copernicus.eu/) is the marine component of the Copernicus Programme of the European Union. It provides free, regular and systematic authoritative information on the state of the ocean, on a global and regional scale. It is funded by the European Commission (EC) and implemented by [Mercator-Ocean International](https://www.mercator-ocean.fr/). It is designed to serve policy and commitments related to Ocean Governance, to cater for the needs of society at large for global ocean knowledge and to boost the Blue Economy across all maritime sectors by providing free-of-charge state-of-the-art ocean data and information. ### Methodology The data shown are based on the PISCES biogeochemical model available on the [Nucleus for European Modelling of the Ocean (NEMO)](https://www.nemo-ocean.eu/) modelling platform. The model includes 24 predictor variables and simulates biogeochemical cycles of oxygen, carbon, and the main nutrients controlling phytoplankton growth (nitrate, ammonium, phosphate, silicic acid, and iron). Mean nutrient concentrations are interpolated on a standard regular grid in NetCDF format. The output product is validated by comparing systematically the biogeochemical modeled fields with available observations datasets. The data isdisplayed with a 1/4 degree horizontal resolution with regular longitude/latitude equirectangular projection. For the full documentation and additional information about the PISCES model, please see the source [methodology](http://marine.copernicus.eu/documents/QUID/CMEMS-GLO-QUID-001-028.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows daily and monthly nitrate concentration averaged from a depth of 0 to 5.1 meters. CMEMS provides 50 vertical levels covering a depth profile of 0 to 5500 meters from the surface. Resource Watch also shows CMEMS averages for [phosphates](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/f1aa9ec7-c3b6-441c-b395-96fc796b7612) and [dissolved oxygen](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/877cdf39-5536-409c-bcba-2220e1b72796). Additional biogeochemical fields for chlorophyll concentration, silicate, dissolved iron, primary production, phytoplankton, pH, and surface partial pressure of carbon dioxide are also included in the Global Ocean and Biogeochemistry Analysis and Forecast system. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. title: Glacier Locations
description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](926e6be3-8699-4a0c-8214-b8c05b7e0083) as a replacement.**_ The GLIMS: Global Glacier Database managed by the NSIDC is an international collaborative project that includes more than 60 institutions worldwide. Its goal is to create this globally comprehensive inventory of land ice including measurements of glacier area, geometry, surface velocity, and snow line elevation. To perform these analyses, the GLIMS project uses satellite data, primarily from the Advanced Spaceborne Thermal Emission and Reflection Radiometer (ASTER) and the Landsat Enhanced Thematic Mapper Plus (ETM+), as well as historical information derived from maps and aerial photographs. The analysis results are submitted to the GLIMS database at the National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC) in Boulder, CO. The GLIMS database is designed to be a logical extension of the World Glacier Inventory (WGI) of the World Glacier Monitoring Service (WGMS) and stores the full complement of the WGMS-defined glacier characteristics. Each analysis received by the GLIMS team at the NSIDC is ingested into the GLIMS Glacier Database. New glacier data are continually being added to the database. title: Air Quality: Sulfur Dioxide (SO₂) Estimated Emissions
description: ### Overview This dataset from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) global anthropogenic shows sulfur dioxide (SO₂) emissions in 2018 for the agriculture, power generation, residential, ship, road transportation, off-road transportation, and industrial processes sectors. The dataset also includes a layer for the sum of all sectors, as total emissions. Sulfur dioxide is a colorless air pollutant with a strong odor. The gas is a respiratory irritant that can harm human health. According to the [Australian Department of Environment and Energy](https://www.environment.gov.au/protection/publications/factsheet-sulfur-dioxide-so2), sulfur dioxide irritates the nose, throat, and airways. It can cause shortness of breath, coughing, wheezing, or a tight feeling around the chest. High concentrations of sulfur dioxide can affect lung function, worsen asthma attacks, and worsen existing heart disease in sensitive groups. Most sulfur dioxide emissions come from the burning of coal, oil, or gas for electricity and transportation; these fossil fuels contain sulfur, which is emitted as sulfur dioxide when burned. Sulfur dioxide does not contribute to global warming, but it reacts easily with other substances to form harmful compounds such as sulfuric acid and small sulfate particles. When sulfur dioxide reacts with water and oxygen, it [creates acid rain](https://www.epa.gov/acidrain/what-acid-rain). Acid rain has a number of [environmental impacts](https://www.ucsusa.org/clean-energy/coal-and-other-fossil-fuels/hidden-cost-of-fossils), including making lakes, rivers, wetlands, and other water bodies more acidic, which can be harmful to fish and other aquatic wildlife. Resource Watch also shows CAMS Global Anthropogenic Emissions for [black carbon](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6bf069ff-a3b6-4b58-b4b8-eb1ac6354e89), [nitrogen oxides (NOₓ)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/249cb5ff-0ad1-461c-bcaa-15fb44f45d72), and [methane (CH₄)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/85936c69-b773-458b-90c4-b47d5d3b5f0d). Each compound shows the emissions by sector for up to 11 sectors, depending on the atmospheric compound. CAMS global anthropogenic emissions was developed by Emissions of Atmospheric Compounds and Compilation of Ancillary Data (ECCAD-AERIS). The data has global coverage at a 0.1 degree resolution, which is approximately 11 kilometers x 11 kilometers at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. Emissions are provided as an annual sum for the years 2000 to 2019. This dataset shows annual emissions for the year 2018. ### Methodology The CAMS global anthropogenic emissions are based on the data provided by the Community Emissions Data System (CEDS) and Emissions Database for Global Atmospheric Research version 4.3.2 (EDGARv4.3.2) historical data. In preparing the dataset, the 0.5 x 0.5 degree global CEDS emissions dataset for the years 2011 to 2014 was used to calculate a linear trend in emissions. These trends were then disaggregated onto the same 0.1 x 0.1 degree grid as in EDGARv4.3.2. The sectors were then merged and aligned between the CEDS and EDGARv4.3.2 data sets. The 2011 to 2014 trends were applied to the EDGARv4.3.2 2010 emissions to estimate the emissions for the year 2018. For full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://atmosphere.copernicus.eu/sites/default/files/2019-05/cams_emissions_general_document_apr2019_v6.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows CAMS Global Anthropogenic Emissions for [black carbon](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6bf069ff-a3b6-4b58-b4b8-eb1ac6354e89), [nitrogen oxides (NOₓ)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/249cb5ff-0ad1-461c-bcaa-15fb44f45d72), and [methane (CH₄)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/85936c69-b773-458b-90c4-b47d5d3b5f0d). title: Crop Suitability Classes
description: ### Overview The Global Agro-Ecological Zoning version 4 (GAEZ v4) dataset assesses current and future agricultural resources and their potential. It is a standardized framework allowing for the characterization of climate, soil, and terrain conditions that are relevant for agricultural production. Data from the Fourth theme, Suitability and Attainable Yield, is displayed here. It combines multiple inputs ranging from climatic conditions, water supply, and agricultural input levels to spatially map the suitability of 4 different crops globally. Outputs are presented at 5 arc minutes resolution, which is approximately 9 km x 9 km at the equator but [changes with distance from the equator](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616). ​​Information on the current and future use of land resources are important for agricultural decision-making with implications on food security, sustainability of land and water resources, and agricultural development and policies. The GAEZ v4 dataset brings together multiple data sources to provide information on current crop suitability and assess its potential impact from climate change. Coffee, Cotton, Dryland Rice, and Wetland Rice are important commodities around the globe and the Crop Suitability Class provides important spatial information on where these commodities will thrive or face challenges in future timeframes and under different climate scenarios. Understanding what changes may occur in the future will enable different actors the ability to increase resilience, develop techniques or policies to alleviate potential challenges, and maintain food security. The Food and Agricultural Organization of the United Nations (FAO) together with the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) began developing the GAEZ modeling framework in the early 1980s to provide current data on the state of agricultural resources. It has since expanded to support sustainable agricultural development and provide key information on current and future risks to agricultural production, crop development, land productivity, and impacts from climate change. ### Methodology Multiple datasets were used as inputs to the GAEZ v4 modeling framework and provide data on historic and future climate attributes, soil and terrain resources, land cover, protected land, biodiversity areas, water resources, administrative units, population, and livestock. Historical climate data comes from the Climatic Research Unit TS v3.21 datasets which include monthly climate information. Future climate data is derived from multiple climate model outputs for four (2.6, 4.5, 6, 8.5) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) from the Fifth Assessment Report (AR5) of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. Data processing was broken into several steps and seven main modules summarize the necessary steps within the GAEZ v4 modeling framework. Outputs from each of the modules are categorized into six main themes: 1) Land and Water Resources, 2) Agro-climatic Resources, 3) Agro-climatic Potential Yield, 4) Suitability and Attainable Yield, 5) Actual Yields and Production, and 6) Yield and Production Gaps. The Suitability Class sub-theme falls under Theme Four of the outputs and Module V of the modeling framework. Module V integrates results from the first four modules and combines agro-climatic potential yields with soil and terrain evaluation results. This Module identifies in each grid cell its respective soil types and slope classes and then assesses and assigns a suitability rating and simulated potential yield. Results are then aggregated and mapped for each historic and future 30-year period by crop, input level, and water source and have a spatial resolution of 5 arc minutes (approximately 9 km at the equator). Suitability classes are calculated from the normalized Suitability Index (SI), where: SI = 100 x (90 x VS + 70 x S + 50 x MS + 30 x mS + 15 x VmS + 0 x NS) / 0.9 SI values can range from 0 to 10,000 and the acronyms that are underlying suitability classes are defined as follows: VS = very suitable, S = suitable, MS = moderately suitable, mS = marginally suitable, VmS = very marginally suitable, and NS = not suitable. These six categories represent the shares of area extents of the different suitability classes in a grid cell. SI is calculated for each of the 53 crops by the level of input, management, and water supply system. The resultant SI in each grid cell is then grouped into eight classes depicting the aggregate crop suitability as: - Very high: SI > 8,500 - High: 7,000 < SI ≤ 8,500 - Good: 5,550 < SI ≤ 7,000 - Medium: 4,000 < SI ≤ 5,500 - Moderate: 2,500 < SI ≤ 4,000 - Marginal: 1,000 < SI ≤ 2,500 - Very marginal: 0 < SI ≤ 1,000 - Not suitable: SI = 0 For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.fao.org/3/cb4744en/cb4744en.pdf). ### Additional Information Our data catalog shows only a subset of the dataset. The Global Agro-Ecological Zoning version 4 Crop Suitability Index full dataset has data for 53 crops, additional timeframes (1961-1990, 1971-2000, and 2071-2100), RCPs (2.6 and 6.0), water supply (rainfed all phases, gravity irrigation), a low input level option, and a without CO2 fertilization option. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on WRI’s data catalog. See the documentation on how we retrieved the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/blob/master/foo_067_rw0_crop_suitability_class). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: Projected Change in Dry Spells (RCP4.5)
description: The Projected Change in Dry Spells dataset shows change in average annual dry spells at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. A dry spell is a five day period with less than 1 millimeter (mm) of precipitation. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of dry spells in 2000 is actually an average of the annual number of dry spells between the years 1985 and 2015. Precipitation projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP). RCP 4.5 is a stabilization scenario where total radiative forcing is stabilized around 2050 by employment of a range of technologies and strategies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. Change in dry spells is shown as the multiplicative difference between annual average dry spells during the projected decade and the baseline time period. Values greater than 1 indicate that the number of dry spells is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. The dataset is shown at a spatial resolution of 0.25°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and the resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Dry Spells dataset provides projections on how precipitation patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Dry Spells dataset was created with precipitation data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference. The average annual number of dry spells for each year, climate model, and scenario were calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting precipitation data for a given year and summing the number of 5-day periods with less than 1 mm of precipitation. If a dry period lasted longer than 5 days, each additional day without precipitation was counted as a fractional (1/5) dry period. For example, a dry period of 8 days would count as 8/5 of a dry period (1 + 3/5). The average annual number of dry spells were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then each of the nine projected decades were divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change in dry spells. Values greater than 1 indicate that the number of dry spells is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of dry spells in 2000 is actually an average of the annual number of dry spells between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.

title: Near-Term climate hazard indicators across India – Early Century Projection - SSP 585
description: ### Overview This dataset provides insights into India’s climate projections for the period 2021–2040, focusing on extreme weather events such as heat waves, droughts, and intense rainfall. The data is essential for understanding the regional risks posed by climate change and for supporting targeted strategies to safeguard lives and livelihoods across the country. The data is provided at district level. ### Methodology **Layers of interest**: Average Annual Maximum Temperature Change (℃), Average Annual Minimum Temperature Change (℃), Average Annual Precipitation Change (%), Average Annual Relative Humidity (%), Average Southwest Monsoon Precipitation Change (%), Average Northeast Monsoon Precipitation Change (%), Average Change in Number of Heavy Precipitation Days during Southwest Monsoon (number of days), Average Change in Number of Heavy Precipitation Days during Northeast Monsoon (number of days). **Data sources**: The dataset integrates outputs from 34 Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) models. The daily precipitation dataset (grid resolution: 0.25° × 0.25°), maximum, minimum and mean temperature datasets (grid resolution: 1°×1°) developed by the India Meteorological Department (IMD) have been used as observed data. ### Estimation Methods The India Meteorological Department (IMD) have been used for statistical downscaling of the coarser resolution CMIP6 model simulations to 25 km. The study employed bias-correction procedure for daily datasets for precipitation, maximum temperature, and minimum temperature, as developed by Mishra et al. (2020). Climate projections are analysed for various temperature and precipitation changes under both SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios. The projections include two key scenarios: SSP2-4.5 (Middle of the Road): Moderate emissions and adaptation. SSP5-8.5 (Fossil-Fueled Development): High emissions and heavy reliance on fossil fuels. The historical simulation period 1951 – 1970 was selected as the ‘baseline period’ and for future climate projections, the time period 2021–2040 was used. In the present format, all the model simulations and observations have been maintained to a uniform grid resolution of 0.25°×0.25° for making them consistent for computing the Multi-Model Mean (MMM). For precise diagnosis of precipitation and temperature changes on a space and time scale in the present and future climate, the final parameters are presented at district level through district level mean aggregates. For the full documentation, please see the source methodology at Mishra V, Bhatia U, Tiwari AD (2020) Bias corrected climate projections from CMIP6 models for Indian sub-continental river basins. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.3874046 and https://azimpremjiuniversity.edu.in/data-and-methods. ### Description of the Layers **Average Annual Maximum Temperature Change (℃):** The daily maximum temperature data for each year is extracted and averaged to calculate the yearly average maximum temperature. The average from climate projections for the period 2021–2040 was compared against the historical simulation period 1951–1970 and the change in temperature was calculated. **Average Annual Minimum Temperature Change (℃):** The daily minimum temperature data for each year is extracted and averaged to calculate the yearly average minimum temperature. The average from climate projections for the period 2021–2040 was compared against the historical simulation period 1951–1970 and the change in temperature was calculated. **Average Annual Precipitation Change (%):** The annual precipitation total for each year is extracted and averaged across years to calculate the yearly average precipitation. The yearly average from climate projections for the period 2021–2040 was compared against the historical simulation period 1951–1970 and the change in precipitation was calculated. **Average Annual Relative Humidity (%):** The annual average relative humidity for each year is calculated considering all the parallel to the temperatures available and presented for the period 2021–2040. **Average Southwest Monsoon Precipitation Change (%):** The annual precipitation total for the southwest monsoon season covering June-July-August-September of every year is extracted. The yearly average from climate projections for the period 2021–2040 was compared against the historical simulation period 1951–1970 and the change in precipitation for the season was calculated. **Average Northeast Monsoon Precipitation Change (%):** The annual precipitation total for the northeast monsoon season covering October-November-December of every year is extracted. The yearly average from climate projections for the period 2021–2040 was compared against the historical simulation period 1951–1970 and the change in precipitation for the season was calculated. **Average Change in Number of Heavy Precipitation Days during Southwest Monsoon (number of days):** A heavy rainfall day as per IMD is whenever daily rainfall exceeds 64.5 mm. The number of heavy precipitation days for the southwest monsoon season covering June-July-August-September of every year is extracted. The yearly average from climate projections for the period 2021–2040 was compared against the historical simulation period 1951–1970 and the change in number of heavy rainy days for the season was calculated. **Average Change in Number of Heavy Precipitation Days during Northeast Monsoon (number of days):** A heavy rainfall day as per IMD is whenever daily rainfall exceeds 64.5 mm. The number of heavy precipitation days for the southwest monsoon season covering October-November-December of every year is extracted. The yearly average from climate projections for the period 2021–2040 was compared against the historical simulation period 1951–1970 and the change in number of heavy rainy days for the season was calculated. ### Visualizing the Data The data is presented district wise with a time slider with a dropdown selector for changing between the layers. The values are visualized using a gradient based on the selected year in the slider, ranging from lighter shades of yellow (indicating low values) to darker shades of green (representing higher values). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source.

title: U.S. Monthly Minimum Temperature Normals
description: The Parameter-elevation Relationships on Independent Slopes Model (PRISM) Climate Group monthly climate normals are baseline data sets describing average monthly conditions over the most recent three full decades. The most recent PRISM normals are for the period 1981-2010. Spatial climate data sets for mean monthly precipitation and minimum and maximum temperature were developed for the conterminous United States. These 30-arcsec (∼800-m) grids are the official spatial climate data sets of the U.S. Department of Agriculture. The PRISM interpolation method was used to develop data sets that reflected, as closely as possible, the current state of knowledge of spatial climate patterns in the United States. PRISM calculates a climate–elevation regression for each digital elevation model (DEM) grid cell, and stations entering the regression are assigned weights based primarily on the physiographic similarity of the station to the grid cell. Factors considered are location, elevation, coastal proximity, topographic facet orientation, vertical atmospheric layer, topographic position, and orographic effectiveness of the terrain. Surface stations used in the analysis numbered nearly 13,000 for precipitation and 10,000 for temperature. Station data were spatially quality controlled, and short-period-of-record averages adjusted to better reflect the 1981–2010 period.

description: The "Terrestrial Protected Areas (% of Total Land Area)" data set was published on the World Bank's open access data portal. It was created using data from the UN Environment Programme and the World Conservation Monitoring Centre and compiled by World Resources Institute. Terrestrial protected areas are defined in this instance as "totally or partially protected areas of at least 1,000 hectares that are designated by national authorities as scientific reserves with limited public access, national parks, natural monuments, nature reserves or wildlife sanctuaries, protected landscapes, and areas managed mainly for sustainable use." Marine areas, unclassified areas, littoral (intertidal) areas, and sites protected under local or provincial law are excluded. Some sites are owned and managed by governments, others by private individuals, companies, communities, and faith groups. Currently about a 10th of the world's land surface is under some form of protected area, and the system represents a unique commitment to the future. Over the last 40 years the global protected area estate has increased from an area the size of the United Kingdom to an area the size of South America. Increasing the proportion of terrestrial and marine areas protected helps defend vulnerable plant and animal species and safeguard biodiversity. This indicator is calculated using all the nationally designated protected areas recorded in the World Database on Protected Areas (WDPA) whose location and extent is known and aggregated using a weighted average. A global protected area layer is created by combining the polygons and points recorded in the WDPA. Circular buffers are created around points based on the known extent of protected areas for which no polygon is available. Annual protected area layers are created by dissolving the global protected area layer by the known year of establishment of protected areas recorded in the WDPA. The annual protected area layers are overlaid with country/territory boundaries, coastlines, and buffered coastlines (delineating the territorial waters) to obtain the absolute coverage (in km2) of protected areas by country/territory per year from 1990 to the present. The total area of a country's/territory's terrestrial protected areas and marine protected areas in territorial waters is divided by the total area of its land areas (including inland waters) and territorial waters to obtain the relative coverage (percentage) of protected areas. title: Projected Coral Bleaching
description: ### Overview This dataset represents climate model projections of the year in which severe coral bleaching conditions will begin occurring twice per decade and ten times per decade (i.e., annually). The 4 kilometer (km) resolution projections are global, running from 2000 through 2100. Coral communities will start to change when bleaching becomes more frequent than twice per decade: corals susceptible to bleaching will be less common and the structural complexity of many coral reefs will decline. These changes will occur even more rapidly when bleaching events begin to occur annually. These projections are based on future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathway (RCP) 8.5. The RCP 8.5 scenario presumes no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. More information on these scenarios can be found [here](http://tntcat.iiasa.ac.at:8787/RcpDb/dsd?Action=htmlpage&page=about). Mass coral bleaching events due to unusually warm ocean water have increased in frequency and severity, and have become one of the most significant contributors to the deterioration of the world's coral reefs. Furthermore, bleaching events are expected to become more frequent and more severe in the decades ahead. Thermal stress that persists for several weeks with ambient water temperatures as little as 1 to 2 °C above a coral’s thermal tolerance level has been shown to cause bleaching, often on broad geographical scales. Corals can die if thermal stress is severe or long-lasting or if it leads to disease in the colony. Extensive bleaching events have dramatic long-term ecological and social impacts, including loss of reef-building corals, changes in benthic habitat, changes in associated fish populations and economic loss. Even under favorable conditions, it can take decades for severely bleached reefs to fully recover. As the climate continues to warm, bleaching is a major threat to the future of coral reefs. There is great variation in the projected timing of when severe bleaching conditions will become an annual occurrence in most coral reef regions. These large variations can even be seen within a single country’s coral reefs. Reefs projected to experience annual severe bleaching 10 or more years later than other reefs in the same country or territory are considered to be relative refugia: they may provide refuge for aquatic creatures living in surrounding areas with higher levels of bleaching. These relative refugia should therefore be conservation priorities. The projected timing of annual severe bleaching varies by 10 or more years in 71 of the 87 countries and territories with at least 500 square kilometers of reef area. This suggests that these projections should be taken into consideration in most reef areas during conservation and management planning. Coral reefs are among the most biologically rich and productive ecosystems on earth and provide valuable ecosystem benefits to millions of people in coastal areas. They are, however, widely threatened by both local threats (such as overfishing, pollution, and direct physical damage) and the global threats of ocean warming and acidification. These have already caused widespread damage to most of the world’s coral reefs, resulting in reduced areas of living coral, increased algal cover, diminished species diversity, and lower fish abundance, as well as degraded economic and social benefits to many coastal communities. ### Methodology Ensembles of climate models were used to generate projections of the year when severe coral bleaching events will start to occur annually, and of changes in aragonite saturation state. The models were used to generate projected monthly data for the following variables: sea surface temperature (SST), surface pressure of carbon dioxide (CO₂), pH, and salinity. Each model independently generated monthly data for the listed variables, and these model outputs were then adjusted to the mean (within the annual cycle) of observations of SST based on the [OISST V2 1982‐2005 climatology](https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/oisst/optimum-interpolation-sea-surface-temperature-oisst-v20). The sea water temperature stress that triggers bleaching is measured in degree heating weeks (DHWs). One degree heating week is equal to one degree above the long-term average summer maximum temperatures for one week. Severe bleaching is common when thermal stress exceeds 8 DHWs. Both bleaching frequency projections have been produced for emissions scenarios RCP8.5 and RCP4.5 (for a total of four projections). RCP8.5 is a "business-as-usual" scenario that assumes emissions increase unabated. At time of dataset production in May of 2016, emissions concentrations were greater than what RCP8.5 had projected for 2016. RCP4.5 assumes emissions stabilize just after 2100 due to successful implementation of climate policies that reduce emissions. These projections are unique in that they have been produced through statistical downscaling so have high resolution (4km) relative to raw climate model data (~1x1°), i.e. relative to the projections [here](https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/climate/projections/piccc_oa_and_bleaching/index.php). The final outputs represent the ensemble average, with 33 climate models from the [Coupled Model Intercomparison Project, Phase 5 (CMIP5)](https://pcmdi.llnl.gov/mips/cmip5/) of the [International Panel on Climate Change (IPCC)](http://www.ipcc.ch/) used for RCP8.5 and 35 used for RCP4.5. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only the subset of the dataset corresponding to severe bleaching under the RCP 8.5 scenario. The full dataset includes equivalent data layers about the onset of 2x and 10x per decade bleaching under the RCP 4.5 scenario. Projection results are available in the form of Google Earth files, map images, and ArcGIS-compatible spatial data. The projections can also be viewed on [the UNEPLive site](http://uneplive.unep.org/) under the Coral Reefs theme. The [About page](http://uneplive.unep.org/theme/index/19#about) on UNEPLive also describes the main findings of the research project and discusses the conservation, management and policy applications of the downscaled projections. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch retrieved the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/ocn_010_projected_coral_bleaching). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

Projected Frost Free Season U.S. (RCP8.5)
description: The Projected Change in Frost Free Season in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average frost free season at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. A frost free season is the largest number of consecutive days in a year where the minimum daily temperatures are above 32 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the frost free season in 2000 is actually an average of the annual frost free seasons between the years 1985 and 2015. Frost free season projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The change in frost free season is shown as the number of days difference between the frost free season during the projected decade and the baseline time period. The dataset is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. In particular, it can be used to understand and adapt to changing agricultural growing seasons and productivity in individual regions. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference. The annual average frost free season for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting daily minimum temperature values for a given year and finding the largest number of consecutive days where the minimum temperature exceeded 32°F. The average annual frost free seasons were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then the baseline average was subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in dry spells The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the frost free season in 2000 is actually an average of the annual frost free seasons between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.

title: Aqueduct Interannual Variability
description: ### Overview Interannual variability measures the average between-year variability of available water supply, including both renewable surface and groundwater supplies. Higher values indicate wider variations in available supply from year to year. These values were then converted into risk scores based on the thresholds defined in the methodology. These risk scores range from low variability (coefficient of variation <0.25) to extremely high variability (coefficient of variation >1.0). Interannual variability values are available per sub-basin (HydroBASIN level 6). ### Methodology Aqueduct used the global hydrological model, PCRaster Global Water Balance (PCR-GLOBWB 2), to calculate five indicators. Interannual variability is one of those indicators and was calculated using the available water supply time series from the default PCR-GLOBWB 2. Interannual or between-year variability is defined as the coefficient of variation (CV) of available water from year to year for each sub-basin. The CV was calculated by dividing the standard deviation (SD) of the available water across years by the mean. The CV per sub-basin was determined for each individual month, as well as annually. Finally, raw interannual variability values were converted to risk scores between 0 and 5, based on quantiles. These scores were placed into categories indicating how high the risk for this indicator is. The thresholds for raw interannual variability values and the corresponding risk scores that were used in each category are defined below as Risk Category (Risk Scores): Raw Value Thresholds. - Low (0-1): < 0.25 - Low to medium (1-2): 0.25 - 0.50 - Medium to high (2-3): 0.50 - 0.75 - High (3-4): 0.75 - 1.0 - Extremely high (4-5): > 1.0 For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/aqueduct-30). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](43d9dac0-88be-4db1-b71e-482756220817) as a replacement.**_ The Consultative Group for International Agricultural Research Consortium for Spatial Information (CGIAR-CSI) supported the development of the Global-Aridity Database. This database is designed for use in models of sustainable development, biodiversity and environmental conservation, poverty alleviation, and adaption to climate change globally, in particular in developing countries, and provides data for each month between 1950 and 2000 at a spatial resolution of 30 arc seconds. This data set is the aridity index (AI), which is calculated as the ratio of mean annual precipitation to mean annual potential evapotranspiration (PET), using data from the WorldClim Global Climate Database. The yearly precipitation values are available directly from the WorldClim database, and the PET values are derived from a selection of WorldClim variables. PET is a measure of the rate at which water evaporates from the Earth's surface into the atmosphere. It is influenced by several factors, including solar radiation, temperature, air humidity, and wind speed. Other contributing factors include the leaf area index of an area, as water pooling on top of leaves and tree canopies can lead to faster evaporation than if precipitating water entered the soil layer. title: Populations in Coastal Zones
description: The percentage of the total population living within 100 km of the coastline, created by CIESIN, also includes population living at or below 50 m above sea level. This indicator serves 2 purposes. It quantifies an important driver of coastal ecosystem pressure, and it also quantifies an important component of vulnerability to sea-level rise and other coastal hazards. Because of the economic benefits that accrue from access to ocean navigation, coastal fisheries, tourism, and recreation, human settlements are often more concentrated in the coastal zone than elsewhere. Presently about 40% of the world’s population lives within 100 km of the coast. As population density and economic activity in the coastal zone increases, pressures on coastal ecosystems increase. Among the most important pressures are habitat conversion, land cover change, pollutant loads, and introduction of invasive species. These pressures can lead to loss of biodiversity, coral reef bleaching, new diseases among organisms, hypoxia, harmful algal blooms, siltation, reduced water quality, and a threat to human health through toxins in fish and shellfish and pathogens such as cholera and hepatitis A residing in polluted water. Finally, it is important to recognize that a high population concentration in the low elevation coastal zone (defined as less than 10 m elevation) increases a country’s vulnerability to sea-level rise and other coastal hazards such as storm surges. To calculate the percentage of the population within those boundaries requires a disaggregated population data set so that the population within the zone can be distinguished from the rest of the country. Censuses usually offer population data disaggregated subnationally by administrative units, such as regions and districts. These smaller administrative units can be gridded and converted to a raster file, each cell having an equal population. A 100 m buffer can be created from an equidistant map projection of coasts and a low elevation mask from a gridded elevation set. The population within that zone can then be divided by the total country's population and multiplied by 100 to find the percentage. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: Average Temperature
description: Annual average temperature, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

U.S. Change in Leaf and Bloom Dates
description: The Climate Change Indicators: Leaf and Bloom Dates data set from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) shows trends in the timing of first leaf dates and first bloom dates in lilacs and honeysuckles across the contiguous 48 states. Because of their close connection with climate, the timing of these phenological events can be used as an indicator of the sensitivity of ecological processes to climate change. The first leaf dates and the first bloom dates of lilacs and honeysuckles, which have an easily monitored flowering season, a relatively high survival rate, and a large geographic distribution, are particularly useful indicators of the timing of spring events. The first leaf date in these plants relates to the timing of events that occur in early spring, while the first bloom date is consistent with the timing of later spring events, such as the start of growth in forest vegetation. Because many of the phenological observation records in the United States are less than 40 years long, and because these records may have gaps in time or space, computer models have been used to provide a more complete understanding of long-term trends nationwide. The models for this indicator were developed using data from the USA National Phenology Network, which collects ground observations from a network of federal agencies, field stations, educational institutions, and citizens who have been trained to log observations of leaf and bloom dates. For consistency, observations were limited to a few specific types of lilacs and honeysuckles. Next, models were created to relate actual leaf and bloom observations with records from nearby weather stations. Once scientists were able to determine the relationship between climate factors (particularly temperatures) and leaf and bloom dates, they used this knowledge to estimate leaf and bloom dates for earlier years based on historical weather records. They also used the models to estimate how leaf and bloom dates would have changed in a few areas (mostly in the far South) where lilacs and honeysuckles are not widespread. This indicator uses data from nearly 3,000 weather stations throughout the contiguous 48 states. The exact number of stations varies from year to year. For each year, the timing of first leaf and first bloom at each station was compared with the 1981 to 2010 average to determine the number of days’ “deviation from normal.” This indicator presents the average deviation across all stations, along with maps that compare the most recent 10-year period (2006–2015) with a mid-20th-century baseline (1951–1960) at individual stations. These time periods were chosen to match published studies. PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set. The data are generated using algorithms for the Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites (GOES) Imager, the Polar Operational Environmental Satellites (POES), Advanced Very High Resolution Radiometer (AVHRR), and Moderate-Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS).
