Minimum Arctic Sea Ice
description: ### Overview The Minimum Arctic Sea Ice dataset shows the annual minimum extent of sea ice in the Arctic for select years between 1980-2020. Arctic sea ice typically reaches its minimum extent in September. In this map, light blue represents locations where sea ice was present during September for each year. Sea ice extent data was collected by satellite microwave sensing instruments at a spatial resolution of 25 kilometers (km). This dataset is derived from two products: a near real-time daily dataset and a separate daily dataset that is processed yearly. For the most recent 6-18 months, sea ice extents were derived from near real-time data; all older data was derived from the separate daily dataset. This dataset can be used to understand changes in annual minimum Arctic sea ice extent over the past 40 years. Arctic sea ice extent has been declining since 2000. Melting sea ice can have [dramatic effects on global climate](https://nsidc.org/cryosphere/seaice/environment/global_climate.html). Because of its white color, sea ice reflects sunlight back into space. This property – albedo –keeps the polar regions cold. However, as sea ice continues to melt, the Earth’s surface absorbs more sunlight, causing an increase in temperature and ice melt. When sea ice melts, it changes the ocean’s salinity and temperature, disrupting currents and weather patterns. The [National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC)](https://nsidc.org/) was founded in 1976 as the World Data Center for Glaciology. Over time, the NSIDC evolved to become a data distribution and research center specializing in remote sensing of cryospheric data such as snow, sea ice, frozen ground, ice sheets and glaciers. In addition to managing and distributing this data, the NSIDC creates and supports data access tools for its users. They also use the datasets for climate research and education. The NSIDC is part of University of Colorado Boulder’s [Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences (CIRES)](https://cires.colorado.edu/). It is supported by the [National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)](https://www.nasa.gov/), the [National Science Foundation (NSF)](https://www.nsf.gov/) and the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)](https://www.noaa.gov/). ### Methodology Minimum Arctic Sea Ice was produced from two sources: NASA's [Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC)](https://nsidc.org/data/nsidc-0051) and NSIDC’s [Near-Real-Time DMSP SSMIS Daily Polar Gridded Sea Ice Concentrations (NRTSI)](https://nsidc.org/data/nsidc-0081). Data for the GSFC and NRTSI datasets was collected by the following six sensors: - GSFC data: - [Nimbus-7 Satellite](https://eospso.nasa.gov/missions/nimbus-7) Scanning Multichannel Microwave Radiometer (SMMR) from October 1978 to August 1987 - [Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP)](https://www.ospo.noaa.gov/Operations/DMSP/index.html) F8 Special Sensor Microwave/Imager (SSM/I) from August 1987 to December 1991 - DMSP-F11 SSM/I from December 1991 to September 1995 - DMSP-F13 SSM/I from September 1995 to December 2007 - DMSP-F17 Special Sensor Microwave Imager/Sounder (SSMIS) from January 2008 to present - NRTSI data: - DMSP-F18 SSMIS from April 2016 to present The SMMR, SSM/I, and SSMIS instruments sense emitted microwave radiation. Data was collected daily by the SSM/I and SSMIS sensors and on alternate days by the SMMR sensor. An object's physical properties, such as atomic composition and crystalline structure, determine the amount of microwave radiation it emits. The crystalline structure of ice typically emits more microwave energy than liquid ocean water. Thus, the microwave sensors can easily distinguish sea ice from the ocean. The satellite data was converted to [brightness temperature](https://glossary.ametsoc.org/wiki/Brightness_temperature), a descriptive measure of an object's radiation. Brightness temperature data was then converted to gridded ice concentration using the [NASA Team algorithm](https://nsidc.org/support/faq/nasa-team-vs-bootstrap-algorithm#NASATeam1) at a spatial resolution of 25 km. Gridded ice concentration is the percentage of ice (relative to water) in a given cell. Each cell’s daily ice concentrations were averaged to produce monthly concentrations. Sea ice extent is delineated by the location where ice ends and water (open ocean) begins. Cells were classified as water if their average monthly ice concentration was below 15%, and as ice if the concentration was above 15%. Images of sea ice extent were created for each month, with ice shown in light blue. The process was the same for both the NRTSI and GSFC datasets. GSFC data had a tighter quality control than NRTSI data. However, GSFC data is only released once per year. NRTSI data was available at the end of each month, so it was used to produce sea ice extents while GSFC data was being processed. GSFC data replaced NRTSI data once it was available. Thus, data from the most recent 6-18 months was derived from the NRTSI dataset and older data was derived from the GSFC dataset. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows additional NSIDC sea ice extent data: [Historical Sea Ice Medians](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/b1ebea96-5963-4c2c-9273-7d08536ac07d), [Maximum Arctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/15a0b176-8313-4859-af90-5c198e50a605), [Arctic Sea Ice Extent](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/484fbba1-ac34-402f-8623-7b1cc9c34f17), [Minimum Antarctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/05fd2614-325b-460a-8b52-3155fa9dd98f), [Maximum Antarctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7667bdd8-9adb-44de-b51c-d2d26e461af1) and [Antarctic Sea Ice Extent](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e740efec-c673-431a-be2c-b214613f641a). title: [Archived] Fires (MODIS)
description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](20cc5eca-8c63-4c41-8e8e-134dcf1e6d76) as a replacement.**_ The Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) Thermal Anomalies/Fire products are primarily derived from MODIS 4 and 11 micrometer radiances. The fire detection strategy is based on absolute detection of a fire (when the fire strength is sufficient to detect) and on detection relative to its background (to account for variability of the surface temperature and reflection by sunlight). The product includes fire occurrence (day/night), fire location, the logical criteria used for the fire selection, detection confidence, fire radiative power, and numerous other layers describing fire pixel attributes. The product distinguishes between fire, no fire, and no observation. Level 3 Daily fire products include 8 separate days of data detailing pixels according to their level of confidence as fires. This information will be used in monitoring the spatial and temporal distribution of fires in different ecosystems, detecting changes in fire distribution, and identifying new fire frontiers, wildfires, and changes in the frequency of the fires or their relative strength. MODIS data on Terra and Aqua are acquired from each platform twice daily at mid-latitudes. These 4 daily MODIS fire observations that are typically acquired serve operational fire management needs while also advancing global monitoring of the fire process and its effects on ecosystems, the atmosphere, and climate. description: The Crop Harvested Area and Production data set was created by EarthStat, the University of Minnesota's Institute on the Environment (UMN IonE) and the Land Use and Global Environment Lab at the University of British Columbia (LUGE Lab at UBC). It shows the harvested area, yield and production amount of 175 crops in 206 countries for the year 2000 (average of census data between 1997 and 2003). Harvested area represents the fractional proportion of hectares harvested per gridcell. Production is calculated by multiplying harvested area in hectares and crop yield in tons per hectare. The data were collected from agricultural census and survey information on the areas and yields of 175 crops from the smallest political units reasonably obtainable for 206 countries. Data availability varies for different crops within each country, with most countries having subnational statistics for some crops but national statistics for others. The largest single source of subnational data is Agro-MAPS, a joint project between the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, the International Food Policy Research Institute and the Center for Sustainability and the Global Environment. Croplands cover about 15 million km² of the planet and provide the bulk of the food and fiber essential to human well-being. Most global land cover data sets from satellites group croplands into just a few categories, thereby excluding information critical for answering key questions on subjects ranging from biodiversity conservation to food security to biogeochemical cycling. Information about agricultural land use practices like crop selection, yield and fertilizer use is even more limited. These EarthStat data present land use data sets created by combining national, state and county-level census statistics with a recently updated global data set of croplands on a 5 minute by 5 minute (~10 km x 10 km) latitude/longitude grid. title: Average Low Temperature
description: Annual average low temperature, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

The VIIRS data are also better calibrated to detect fires at night. Each fire alert has a confidence value of low, nominal, or high to help users gauge the quality of individual hotspots or fire pixels. Watersheds
description: ### Overview The HydroBASINS dataset depicts watershed boundaries and sub-basin delineations at a global scale. A watershed is an area of land that drains all surface and groundwater to a common body of water. The boundaries of watersheds provide important geospatial units for many applications, but at a global scale there is a lack of high-quality sources for watershed mapping and analysis. The HydroBasins dataset is part of the HydroSHEDS database ([Hydrological data and maps based on SHuttle Elevation Derivatives](http://www.hydrosheds.org)) which provides hydrographic data layers that allow for the derivation of watershed boundaries for any given location based on the near-global, high-resolution [Shuttle Radar Topology Mission](https://www2.jpl.nasa.gov/srtm/) digital elevation model. The goal of this product is to provide a seamless global coverage of consistently sized and hierarchically nested sub-basins at different scales (from tens to millions of square kilometers), supported by a coding scheme that allows for analysis of watershed topology such as up- and downstream connectivity. The HydroSHEDS database generates key data layers to support regional and global watershed analyses, hydrological modeling, and freshwater conservation planning at a quality, resolution and extent that has previously been unachievable. Watersheds in this database are delineated at 15 arc-second resolution with a hierarchical sub-basin breakdown. The HydroBASINS product was created in 2013. It was developed on behalf of the World Wildlife Fund US (WWF), with support from and in collaboration with the [EU BioFresh] (http://www.freshwaterbiodiversity.eu/contact/) project, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), and McGill University. ### Methodology All HydroBASINS layers were derived from World Wildlife Fund’s [HydroSHEDS data](http://www.hydrosheds.org) based on a grid resolution of 15 arc-seconds (approximately 500 m x 500 m at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator.). An important characteristic of any sub-basin delineation is the sub-basin breakdown, i.e. the decision of when and how to subdivide a larger basin into multiple tributary basins. Standard GIS tools offer the possibility to break out sub-watersheds at any confluence where the inflowing branches (i.e., a tributary and its main stem) exceed a certain size threshold, typically measured by the number of upstream pixels or the upstream catchment area. HydroBASINS divides a basin into two sub-basins at every location where two river branches meet which each have an individual upstream area of at least 100 km². A second critical feature of sub-basin delineations is the way the sub-basins are grouped or coded to allow for the breakout of nested sub-basins at different scales, or to navigate within the sub-basin network from up- to downstream. One of the easiest methods for navigation is to provide the ID of the next downstream object, which allows for moving from object to object in order to traverse the network. As for nesting and topological concepts, the ‘Pfafstetter’ coding system is frequently used due to its relative simplicity and ease of application. The basic principle of the Pfafstetter coding is that a larger basin is sequentially subdivided into 9 smaller units (the 4 largest tributaries, coded with even numbers, and the 5 inter-basins, coded with odd numbers). Thus, the next finer resolution of a sub-basin delineation is achieved at the next Pfafstetter level by adding one digit to the code of the previous level. A more detailed description of the Pfafstetter coding is provided in literature (e.g., [Verdin and Verdin 1999](https://www.bowdoin.edu/~ltoma/teaching/cs3225-GIS/fall16/Project-watershed/papers-watershed/1999-delineate-verdin.pdf)). The HydroBASINS product provides levels 1 to 12 globally. Level 1 distinguishes 9 continents. Level 2 splits each continent into up to 9 large sub-units. Level 3 corresponds to the largest river basins for each continent. From Level 4 onwards, the breakdown follows the Pfafstetter concept. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.hydrosheds.org/images/inpages/HydroBASINS_TechDoc_v1c.pdf) ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Delineations for all Pfafstetter levels (1-12) by region can be downloaded from the the source. A version of this dataset with inserted lakes as well as data for void-filled elevation, hydrologically conditioned elevation, drainage directions, flow accumulation, river networks, basin outlines, lake shorelines, and other hydro-environmental variables is also available from the data provider. title: Current and Projected Food Insecurity
description: The Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) Food Security Outlook shapefiles are created by FEWS NET, led by U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), National Aeronautic and Space Administration (NASA), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Kimetrica, and Chemonics. Food security for a region is determined according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification approach. This is a standardized approach to classifying the level of food insecurity in a region. Classifications are typically released 4 times a year, each with a short-term (0-3 months from publication) and medium-term (4-7 months from publication) evaluation of food insecurity at the subnational level. The approach revolves around a consensus-building process. Food security experts review the available evidence to determine a food security classification on a scale of 1 to 5, with phase 1 corresponding to minimal food insecurity, and phase 5 corresponding to famine-level food insecurity. Evidence used includes satellite data measuring precipitation anomalies (CHIRPS SPI), vegetation anomalies (NDVI), and expert opinion based on knowledge of market and trade functioning and socioeconomic dynamics in each region of interest, among others. The data covers select regions from East, West, and Central Africa, Central America, and Afghanistan. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. description: Global 30 Arc-Second Elevation (GTOPO30) is a global digital elevation model (DEM) with a horizontal grid spacing of 30 arc seconds (approximately 1 kilometer). Completed in late 1996, GTOPO30 was developed over a three year period through a collaborative effort led by staff at the U.S. Geological Survey's Center for Earth Resources Observation and Science (EROS). title: Coping Strategies for Food Insecurity
description: The World Food Programme Mobile Vulnerability Analysis and Mapping unit uses phone-based surveys to create a Coping Strategies Index for regions at risk of needing food aid or market assistance. The CSI is based on the many possible answers to a single question: "What do you do when you don't have adequate food, and don't have the money to buy food?" An advantage of the CSI is that it is often quicker and easier to observe coping strategies than actual food consumption profiles. The reduced CSI (rCSI) only accounts for coping strategies that are nearly universal in the areas where the WFP works. The CSI and rCSI have been shown to be well correlated with future food insecurity and are therefore useful metrics for organizations that offer food aid and market support. Designing a full CSI requires that program analysts engage focus groups in the area of interest to determine the list of unique coping strategies used by locals. The rCSI has been developed based on the most common coping strategies observed in the past CSI implementations. The rCSI has been shown to correlate nearly as well with food insecurity as the original, context-specific CSI, but it is easier and faster to create. The rCSI has the additional benefit of being comparable across geographic regions and cultural contexts, which is useful for developing objective methods for the allocation and geographic targeting of aid resources. There are 2 basic types of coping strategy: * Changing short-term consumption * Longer-term alteration of income earning or food production patterns, including asset sales The rCSI includes the following strategies and associated (severities): * Eating less-preferred foods (1.0) * Borrowing food/money from friends and relatives (2.0) * Limiting portions at mealtime (1.0) * Limiting adult intake (3.0) * Reducing the number of meals per day (1.0) The results of the rCSI can be incorporated into early warning systems to address acute food insecurity before it develops, or as part of postdistribution monitoring systems to evaluate the success of emergency and long-term interventions. title: Fishery Production
description: ### Overview The Fishery Production dataset on Resource Watch shows annual time series data of national aquaculture, capture, and total fishery production beginning in 1950. The data displayed cover capture fishery production related to catch of fish, crustaceans, molluscs and other aquatic animals taken for commercial, industrial, recreational and subsistence purposes from inland, brackish and marine waters. The data also cover aquaculture fishery production related to the farming of aquatic organisms including fish, molluscs, crustaceans and aquatic plants. Quantities are given in metric tons (=1000 kg). The fisheries and aquaculture sector contributes significantly to food security and nutrition, especially in some of the world’s most food-limited regions, while simultaneously supporting the livelihood of hundreds of millions of people around the world. It is critical to ensure fisheries are managed responsibly and sustainably around the world. This requires standardized, reliable and up-to-date information on fishery production and supply chain, as well as the consideration of social and economic aspects, for making sound policy and assessing the performance of responsible fisheries and aquaculture management systems. Furthermore, timely, trustworthy data are crucial for demonstrating progress towards the [2030 UN Agenda for Sustainable Development](https://www.un.org/sustainabledevelopment/development-agenda/). Attaining the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) will require a solid framework of indicators and statistical data to monitor progress, inform policy and ensure accountability of all stakeholders. The FAO works to achieve food security for all, and as the custodian agency of four indicators under SDG14, the FAO has an obligation to accelerate the global momentum to secure healthy and productive oceans. Underpinning these efforts is the need to rely on high quality national, regional and global statistics, while ensuring these data are freely accessible to all. To meet this need, the FAO provides the only source of global statistics on capture fisheries and aquaculture production—a unique global asset for sector analysis and monitoring. ### Methodology Data on Fisheries and Aquaculture Production are sourced annually from relevant national offices concerned with fishery statistics. Information is collected by means of a system of standardized forms, which list for each country the relative species items and fishing areas breakdown. In the case of some "aquatic products," data are also obtained from trade associations or other specialized international organizations to which data are also submitted. In this way the statistics are reviewed by subject matter specialists. Data concerning the nominal catch of certain major groups are generally reviewed in collaboration with the regional agency concerned. For example, data on tuna provided by the national correspondents are often replaced by the "best scientific estimates" produced by regional bodies collecting tuna catch statistics. For the period 1950–1995, capture and aquaculture were compiled together in the total production statistics. However, capture and aquaculture production quantities have since been extended back to 1950. Capture data relate to the nominal catches of fish, crustaceans, molluscs, aquatic mammals, other aquatic animals, residues (used for fishmeal and fish oil production) and plants. Catches from capture production are taken for commercial, industrial, recreational and subsistence purposes from inland, brackish and marine waters. Data include all quantities caught and landed for both food and feed purposes but exclude discards. Aquaculture data relate to the farming of aquatic organisms including fish, molluscs, crustaceans and aquatic plants. Farming implies some form of intervention in the rearing process to enhance production, such as regular stocking, feeding, protection from predators, etc. Farming also implies individual or corporate ownership of the stock being cultivated. For statistical purposes, aquatic organisms which are harvested by an individual or corporate body which has owned them throughout their rearing period contribute to aquaculture while aquatic organisms which are exploitable by the public as a common property resource, with or without appropriate licenses, are the harvest of fisheries. Catches of fish, crustaceans and molluscs are expressed in live weight, that is, the nominal weight of the aquatic organisms at the time of capture. The harvest of aquatic plants is given in wet weight. Data are given in metric tons (=1000 kg), except those for whales, seals and crocodiles, which are given in numbers. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://www.fao.org/cwp-on-fishery-statistics/handbook/capture-fisheries-statistics/en/). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows FAO yearbook data for [ocean-sourced dietary energy and protein supply](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/foo061rw0-Blue-Food-Supply). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for species and fishing areas as well as data on commodities, trade, catches, number of fishers, and consumption are provided by the FAO fisheries division. Food Price Spikes
description: ### Overview The Alert for Price Spikes (ALPS) dataset tracks the current prices of key staple food commodities and compares them to expected prices, which are calculated based on seasonal trends. An ALPS value is assigned to a given commodity at a particular market based on how much its current price differs from the expected price. This value is used to categorize a commodity’s price into one of four categories: normal, stress, alert, or crisis. Food prices on a local market often correlated with food security crises. Food price spikes can have devastating impacts for rural households in developing countries since they spend a large percentage of income on food. ALPS serves three main purposes for decision-making. First, it can serve as a price monitoring tool that allows users to identify price abnormalities. Second, ALPS can generate early warning information that enables users to prepare and act to reduce harm to households most vulnerable to food price fluctuations. Third, ALPS can trigger contingency planning by anticipating food price crises. The ALPS dataset is generated by the World Food Programme (WFP) and monitors markets spanning more than 60 countries. The time period over which prices have been tracked varies by location, but certain markets have food price data as early as 1994. The data is updated monthly for markets that are actively being monitored. ### Methodology Seasonal price trends were determined through reference to monthly commodity prices recorded in the WFP's Vulnerability Analysis and Mapping (VAM) Food and Commodity Price dataset. This dataset was collected by WFP country offices, national government agencies, and partner organizations. The ALPS indicator level was calculated in four steps: - **Estimation of seasonal price trends**: The seasonal price trend was calculated using a linear regression of market price data over the entire period for which data was available. Both the long-term trend and monthly fluctuations, related to the production or demand of a commodity, were included in the regression. - **Calculation of the difference between market price and estimated price**: The difference between the observed price and the expected price based on seasonal trends was calculated for each month. - **Calculation of the ALPS indicator considering price volatility**: Each month’s difference was divided by the standard deviation of the differences over all of the recorded months, producing the value of the ALPS indicator. - **Categorization of the ALPS indicator**: Based on the ALPS indicator value, markets were assigned to one of four situations: (1) Normal: ALPS < 0.25; (2) Stress: 0.25 ≤ ALPS < 1; (3) Alert: 1 ≤ ALPS < 2; (4) Crisis: ALPS ≥ 2. title: Glacier Locations
description: The GLIMS: Global Glacier Database managed by the NSIDC is an international collaborative project that includes more than 60 institutions worldwide. Its goal is to create this globally comprehensive inventory of land ice including measurements of glacier area, geometry, surface velocity, and snow line elevation. To perform these analyses, the GLIMS project uses satellite data, primarily from the Advanced Spaceborne Thermal Emission and Reflection Radiometer (ASTER) and the Landsat Enhanced Thematic Mapper Plus (ETM+), as well as historical information derived from maps and aerial photographs. The analysis results are submitted to the GLIMS database at the National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC) in Boulder, CO. The GLIMS database is designed to be a logical extension of the World Glacier Inventory (WGI) of the World Glacier Monitoring Service (WGMS) and stores the full complement of the WGMS-defined glacier characteristics. Each analysis received by the GLIMS team at the NSIDC is ingested into the GLIMS Glacier Database. New glacier data are continually being added to the database. title: Coral Reef Bleaching Alerts
description: The Coral Reef Watch (CRW) program of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAH) produces this daily 5 km product of coral reef bleaching alert areas, allowing direct monitoring of 95% of global coral reefs. This 7-day composite product shows the maximum stress level that an ocean pixel has experienced due to high sea surface temperature (SST) during the most recent 7 consecutive days, and are dated on the last day of the period. These data are used as the core of NOAA's CRW coral bleaching management program. These coral bleaching alerts are derived from the NOAA National Environmental Satellite Data and Information Service (NESDIS) 5 km Geo-Polar Blended Night-Only SST Analysis. Long-term satellite data of SST is used to define the "usual" SST for a given grid cell. This is taken to be the maximum monthly mean SST over that grid cell. For example, if September is the month with the hottest average SST, the September mean SST will be taken as that grid cell's "usual" value. A HotSpot is then defined as temperatures that are higher than this average. A Degree Heating Week is defined as a grid cell being week degree C hotter than usual for a period of one week. The Bleaching Alert Levels are defined as below. This product shows the maximum bleaching alert level that a grid square has reached in the past 7 consecutive days. Stress Level Definition Effect No Stress HotSpot <= 0 Bleaching Watch 0 < HotSpot < 1 Bleaching Warning 1 <= HotSpot and 0 < DHW < 4 Possible Bleaching Bleaching Alert Level 1 1 <= HotSpot and 4 <= DHW < 8 Bleaching Likely Bleaching Alert Level 2 1 <= HotSpot and 8 <= DHW Mortality Likely Full technical details on the types of satellites used, data collected, and analyses performed are available at the following sites: http://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/6/11/11579 and https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/satellite/methodology/methodology.php#sst. title: Anthropogenic Biomes
description: Anthropogenic Biomes, also known as Anthromes, are defined as “the globally significant ecological patterns created by sustained interactions between humans and ecosystems.” The Anthropogenic Biomes data set illustrates historical transformations within the terrestrial biosphere, land-based regions occupied by living organisms, illustrated through the changes in the anthromes. The data set reclassifies the terrestrial biosphere into 19 anthrome classes at 5-degree resolution for the years 1700, 1800, 1900, and 2000 to illustrate historical changes. The classification used a rule-based anthrome classification model based on human population density and land use data. The transformation of terrestrial biomes is assessed by comparing potential natural vegetation maps with anthrome maps using overlay analysis and other analytical geographic information system (GIS) software tools. The anthrome classes included in this data set are urban (urban, mixed settlements), villages (rice villages, irrigated villages, rainfed villages, pastoral villages), croplands (residential irrigated croplands, residential rainfed croplands, populated rainfed croplands, remote croplands), rangelands (residential rangelands, populated rangelands, remote rangelands), forested (residential woodlands, populated woodlands, remote woodlands, inhabited treeless and barren lands), and woodlands (wild woodlands, wild treeless and barren lands). The Anthropogenic Biomes data set was created by the Anthromes Working Group. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. Air Quality: Ozone (O₃) Satellite Measurements
description: ### Overview The Air Quality: O₃ Satellite Measurements dataset provides global monthly averages of ozone (O₃) densities in the total atmospheric column. Each value shown in the dataset represents the density of O₃ found between Earth’s surface and the top of the atmosphere. The O₃ density is reported with units of moles of O₃ per square meter of air (mol/m²). Unlike stratospheric ozone, which forms naturally in the upper atmosphere and protects us from the sun's harmful ultraviolet rays, ground-level (or tropospheric) ozone is created through the interactions of man-made (and natural) emissions of volatile organic compounds and nitrogen oxides in the presence of heat and sunlight. Cars and gasoline-burning engines are large sources of volatile organic compounds (VOCs). VOCs also come from consumer products such as paints, insecticides, and cleaners as well as industrial solvents and chemical manufacturing. High concentrations of ozone near ground level can be harmful to people, animals, crops, and other materials. Ozone can irritate the respiratory system, causing coughing and irritation. Ozone can aggravate pre existing respiratory problems like asthma, emphysema, and bronchitis and reduce the immune system's ability to fight off infections. Additionally, it can inflame and damage cells that line the lungs. It is possible for ozone to cause irreparable lung damage. These effects can be worse in children and exercising adults. The dataset is made up of data collected from the Sentinel-5 Precursor (S5p) mission, a low Earth orbit polar satellite system.The S5p mission is part of the Global Monitoring of the Environment and Security (GMES/COPERNICUS) space component program headed by the European Commission (EC) in partnership with the European Space Agency (ESA). Its goal is to provide information and services on air quality, climate, and the ozone layer. The S5p mission includes the TROPOspheric Monitoring Instrument (TROPOMI), which takes daily global observations of key atmospheric components, such as O₃, at a 5.5 x 3.5 kilometer (km) resolution. Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-NO), [carbon monoxide (CO)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-CO), and [absorbing aerosol index (AAI)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-AER-AI). ### Methodology The TROPOMI O₃ dataset was created with data collected by the S5P satellite mission. O₃ data was collected by determining the amount of radiation reflected by the troposphere in the UV Huggins bands (325-335 nanometers) spectral range of the solar spectrum. A spectral range is the range of light wavelengths that a specific spectrometer can measure and in this case it refers to the wavelength of light that O₃ molecules produce in the atmosphere. The O₃ data collected using this method was then input into the GODFIT (GOME Direct-FITting) algorithm, created by the European Space Agency. Along with O₃ data, the following information was input into GODFIT: - Relative profile of O₃ and sulfur dioxide (SO₂) in the atmosphere for a given region - Estimated surface albedo for the region - Solar/viewing geometry and geo-location of the S5P satellite - Surface pressure, elevation map, snow and ice maps for the earth’s surface, ozone temperature, cloud cover/pressure profiles, and the absorbing aerosol index for the tropospheric column being measured SO₂ profiles were required as SO₂ converts to sulfuric acid in the atmosphere and blocks incoming solar radiation. This interferes with O₃ readings by TROPOMI. The results from GODFIT were analyzed with the convective-cloud-differential method (CCD) combined with cloud measurement data to produce the final dataset. The final result produced was vertical total column density of O₃ (mol/m²). The dataset shown on Resource Watch was mapped by the Google Earth Engine team using the [harpconvert] (https://cdn.rawgit.com/stcorp/harp/master/doc/html/harpconvert.html) tool. For more information on this conversion please see the Google Earth Engine documentation. The offline version of this data is displayed on Resource Watch, which is more complete than its near real-time counterpart, but is released on a greater delay due to the additional processing time needed. For the full documentation, please see the [source methodology](https://sentinel.esa.int/web/sentinel/technical-guides/sentinel-5p/products-algorithms) associated with the “Ozone (O₃) Total Column”. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-NO), [carbon monoxide] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-CO), and [absorbing aerosol index (AAI)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-AER-AI). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for formaldehyde (CH₂O), sulphur dioxide (SO₂), methane (CH₄) and clouds are available from the data provider. Both a near real-time and an offline version of each of these compounds are available. Please see the [Google Earth Engine data catalog](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/tags/tropomi) to access this data. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. title: Cooling Degree Days
description: A cooling degree day (CDD) is defined as the number of degrees that a day's mean temperature is above 65°F. For example, if a day's average temperature is 80°F, the CDD would be 15. If a second day's average temperature were the same, the combined CDD for those two days would be 30. CDDs are often used as a proxy to estimate heating and cooling needs in buildings. While degree days can be calculated using any reference temperature, this data set uses 65°F (18.3°C), a common threshold for climate indicators, and a temperature at which people are generally comfortable. This indicator is useful in determining energy demands resulting from cooling in different regions and assessing projected climate change impacts. This data set shows CDDs under RCP 8.5, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

Air Quality: Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) Station Measurements
description: ### Overview The Air Quality: Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) Station Measurements dataset is a global dataset that shows real-time air quality data from around the world for fine particulate matter (PM2.5). It presents data collected from government and international organizations at the station level. This means the data is more accurate to specific areas than national or regional data. As of June 2017 OpenAQ data was available for 5,400 locations in 48 countries and is being continually updated with new sources. PM2.5 are fine inhalable particles, with diameters that are generally 2.5 micrometers and smaller. These particles come in many sizes and shapes and can be made up of hundreds of different chemicals. Some are emitted directly from a source, such as construction sites or smokestacks, while others are created from complex reactions in the atmosphere. The size of these particles allows them to get deep into the lungs, and some may even get into the bloodstream. Numerous scientific studies have linked particle pollution exposure to a variety of health problems, including: premature death in people with heart or lung disease, nonfatal heart attacks, irregular heartbeat, aggravated asthma, decreased lung function, and increased respiratory symptoms. People with heart or lung diseases, children, and older adults are most likely to be affected by particle pollution exposure. OpenAQ is an open-source project to surface live, real-time air quality data from around the world. Its “mission is to enable previously impossible science, impact policy, and empower the public to fight air pollution.” Scientists, researchers, developers, and citizens can use these data to understand how air quality in different locations changes over time. Resource Watch also shows continually updated air quality data from OpenAQ on [inhalable particulates (PM10)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003bnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-10), [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cairqualityso2), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003dnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-NO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-O), [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003fnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-CO), and [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003gnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-BC_1). ### Methodology The fine particulate matter (PM2.5) station measurement dataset was produced and is continually updated by aggregating data from permanent outdoor air quality measures. Data was collected only from official sources, including government entities and international organizations. As of June 2017 OpenAQ data was available for 5,400 locations in 48 countries. For data to be included it had to meet three criteria: 1. The “raw” measurement data on physical particle concentration had to be available on the originating site. 2. The data needed to be at the “station level.” It is unacceptable if it is presented in an aggregated form for a city or region. 3. The data needed to be continuously updated at intervals between 10 minutes and 24 hours. After the data was collected it was put into tables. Data was collected using the source organization’s Air Quality Index (AQI) classifications. The final dataset was mapped in vector format at a subnational level with each measurement station showing local particle concentration. OpenAQ continually reviews each data source website for updated values and updates the dataset every hour. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows continually updated air quality data from OpenAQ on [inhalable particulates (PM10)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003bnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-10), [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cairqualityso2), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003dnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-NO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-O), [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003fnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-CO), and [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003gnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-BC_1). City Expansion Index
description: ### Overview The city expansion index dataset shows outward and upward urban growth in 377 cities globally that have a population of over 1 million residents. Outward growth is the horizontal expansion of buildings and upward growth is the vertical expansion of buildings. The final dataset was normalized into comparable values called the Upward Growth Index and Outward Growth Index. A higher expansion index value means more growth is occurring. The dataset uses remote sensing data collected between 2000 and 2014. This dataset was created by the World Resources Institute (WRI) as part of the World Resources Report (WRR) Towards a More Equal City. It is intended to highlight regional trends in urban expansion and differences in urban structure within and between cities. Ultimately, it can be used to help governments understand how urban expansion can be managed in a way that achieves more equitable access to core services for the under-served while bringing wider economic and environmental benefits to cities. For the dataset to paint a complete picture it should ideally be used in conjunction with a matching dataset on the socioeconomic information of the city. ### Methodology This dataset was created using a combination of remote sensing data to determine upward and outward expansion in cities with a metropolitan population greater than 1 million. Remote sensing data was collected from mean summer backscatter power ratio (PR) from NASA's SeaWinds microwave scatterometer (Ku-band, 13.4 GHz) and built-up area from the multitemporal Global Human Settlement Layer (GHSL). The data showed the outward growth of urban built-up areas between 2000 and 2014 measured from the Global Human Settlement Layer (GHSL) and upward growth between 2001 and 2009 measured using the power ratio (PR) from NASA’s SeaWinds microwave scatterometer. Each dataset was reprocessed to have the same spatial resolution of 0.05 degrees (about 5.6 km at the equator). To determine which cities had a metropolitan population greater than 1 million, Landscan data created by the Oak Ridge National Laboratory was combined with the Oxford Economics database to create a combined dataset of 377 cities. Researchers overlayed an 11x11 pixel grid (121 total pixels) over each city using the dataset Populated Places from Natural Earth to create a unified boundary to measure the cities growth. The 11x11 grids were extracted and all grid cells with a built up value less than 20 percent were masked in GHSL. Total upward and outward growth were then calculated using the remaining pixels for each city by using a cluster analysis to group each pixel into similar urban growth patterns and structures. Finally, the values were converted into the upward urban growth index and outward urban growth index to allow for comparison of the values across cities. The final dataset was presented in raster format at a spatial resolution of 0.28 degrees (20.98 square kilometers at the equator). title: Projected Change in Heating Degree Days (RCP4.5)
description: The Projected Change in Heating Degree Days dataset shows the change in annual heating degree days (HDDs) at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. HDD is the number of degrees that a day's average temperature is below 65 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). For example, if a day's average temperature is 50°F, the HDD would be 15. If this happened 10 times in a year the annual HDD would be 150. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the HDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual HDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. HDD projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP). RCP 4.5 is a stabilization scenario where total radiative forcing is stabilized around 2050 by employment of a range of technologies and strategies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.25°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Heating Degree Days dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades and how this may affect future energy demands. For example, HDDs are often used as a proxy to estimate energy requirements for heating buildings. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Heating Degree Days dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference. The annual HDD for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. Daily HDDs were calculated by subtracting daily average temperature values from the baseline temperature of 65°F. If the daily average temperature was above 65°F, it was counted as zero. Then, annual HDD was calculated by summing all daily HDD values over a given year. Annual HDDs were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in heating degree days. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the HDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual HDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

title: Historical Sea Ice Medians
description: ### Overview The Historical Sea Ice Medians dataset shows monthly median sea ice extent over the period of 1981-2010. Sea ice extent data was collected by satellite microwave sensing instruments for both the Arctic and Antarctic regions. Satellite data was collected daily at a spatial resolution of 25 kilometers (km). Gridded ice concentration estimates were used to define the ice edge position that is typical for each month. This dataset shows the maximum (blue line) and minimum (yellow line) sea ice extent, and the typical sea ice extent for each month in between. In the Arctic, sea ice normally reaches its maximum extent in March and its minimum extent in September. Antarctic sea ice extent peaks in September and reaches its minimum in February. The lines in this dataset represent how sea ice expands and retreats between its maximum and minimum extent. This dataset is the [baseline](https://nsidc.org/data/noaa/baseline-change) for sea ice index products from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). Climate baselines are used as a historical reference to current trends and anomalies. A three-decade time period is ideal because it averages out short-term variability. This dataset can be used to understand how polar sea ice extent and melting season are changing. Antarctic sea ice behaves differently than Arctic sea ice, largely because the two regions have different land-ocean configurations. Although Antarctic sea ice extent varies significantly from year to year, the average ice extent has not changed over the past 40 years. Arctic sea ice extent has declined since 2000. Melting sea ice can have [dramatic effects on global climate](https://nsidc.org/cryosphere/seaice/environment/global_climate.html). Because of its white color, sea ice reflects sunlight back into space. This property – albedo – keeps the polar regions cold. However, as sea ice continues to melt, the Earth’s surface absorbs more sunlight, causing an increase in temperature and ice melt. When sea ice melts, it changes the ocean’s salinity and temperature, disrupting currents and weather patterns. Comparing current sea ice extent data to this baseline dataset can help define the rates and locations of sea ice retreat. The [National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC)](https://nsidc.org/) was founded in 1976 as the World Data Center for Glaciology. Over time, the NSIDC evolved to become a data distribution and research center specializing in remote sensing of cryospheric data such as snow, sea ice, frozen ground, ice sheets and glaciers. In addition to managing and distributing this data, the NSIDC creates and supports data access tools for its users. They also use the datasets for climate research and education. The NSIDC is part of University of Colorado Boulder’s [Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences (CIRES)](https://cires.colorado.edu/). It is supported by the [National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)](https://www.nasa.gov/), the [National Science Foundation (NSF)](https://www.nsf.gov/) and the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)](https://www.noaa.gov/). ### Methodology Historical Sea Ice Medians were generated from data collected by five sensors: - [Nimbus-7](https://eospso.nasa.gov/missions/nimbus-7) Scanning Multichannel Microwave Radiometer (SMMR) from October 1978 to August 1987 - [Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP)](https://www.ospo.noaa.gov/Operations/DMSP/index.html) F8 Special Sensor Microwave/Imager (SSM/I) from August 1987 to December 1991 - DMSP-F11 SSM/I from December 1991 to September 1995 - DMSP-F13 SSM/I from September 1995 to December 2007 - DMSP-F17 Special Sensor Microwave Imager/Sounder (SSMIS) from January 2008 to December 2017 The SMMR, SSM/I, and SSMIS instruments sense emitted microwave radiation. The SMMR sensor collected data on alternate days and the SSM/I and SSMIS sensor collected data on a daily basis. Daily satellite measurements were averaged each month to eliminate errors and smooth variations caused by short-term weather conditions. An object's physical properties, such as atomic composition and crystalline structure, determine the amount of microwave radiation it emits. The crystalline structure of ice typically emits more microwave energy than liquid ocean water. Thus, the microwave sensors can easily distinguish sea ice from ocean. The satellite data was converted to [brightness temperature](https://glossary.ametsoc.org/wiki/Brightness_temperature), which is a descriptive measure of an object's radiation. Brightness temperature data was then converted to gridded ice concentration using the [NASA Team algorithm](https://nsidc.org/support/faq/nasa-team-vs-bootstrap-algorithm#NASATeam1) at a spatial resolution of 25 km. Gridded ice concentration is the percentage of ice (relative to water) in a given cell. Sea ice extent is delineated by the location where ice ends and water (open ocean) begins. Cells were classified as water if their ice concentration was below 15%, and as ice if the concentration was above 15%. Median ice extents were calculated by applying the 15% cutoff to all gridded concentration data for each month between 1981 and 2010. Cells that classified as ice more than 50% of the time from 1981-2010 were designated as ice; cells that classified as ice less than 50% of the time were designated as water. This was done on a monthly basis: for example, the data from every January from 1981-2010 was analyzed together to create a single January dataset. Each month’s gridded concentration data was mapped and a contour line was drawn to mark the ice edge. This contour line represents the median sea ice extent. Because the sea ice extent varies considerably from year to year, the median extent is a better representation of the sea ice extent over time. The workflow was applied to both the Arctic and Antarctic regions. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows additional NSIDC sea ice extent data: [Minimum Arctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/a99c5cf5-f141-4bed-a36d-b04c8e171dfa), [Maximum Arctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/15a0b176-8313-4859-af90-5c198e50a605), [Arctic Sea Ice Extent](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/484fbba1-ac34-402f-8623-7b1cc9c34f17), [Minimum Antarctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/05fd2614-325b-460a-8b52-3155fa9dd98f), [Maximum Antarctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7667bdd8-9adb-44de-b51c-d2d26e461af1) and [Antarctic Sea Ice Extent](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e740efec-c673-431a-be2c-b214613f641a). The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5 from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on Resource Watch. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. Global Land Cover
description: ### Overview The Copernicus Global Land Service (CGLS) delivers a global Land Cover product at 100-meter spatial resolution (CGLS-LC100) on an annual basis from 2015-2019. Each pixel value corresponds to a different type (class) of physical coverage of the Earth's surface, e.g. forests, grasslands, croplands, lakes, wetlands. The classifications follow the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (UN-FAO) Land Cover Classification System (LCCS) scheme. Resource watch displays 11 discrete LCCS classifications, with all forests grouped into open or closed classes. Land cover plays a major role in the climate and biogeochemistry of the Earth system. Understanding patterns in land use and transitions of land cover classes over time is crucial to understand, monitor, and manage a number of processes at global level. Therefore, accurate and spatially detailed maps on land cover and land use are relevant to a broad range of issues including deforestation, desertification, urbanization, land degradation, loss of biodiversity and ecosystem functions, water resource management, agriculture and food security, urban and regional development, and climate change and are critical to make informed policy development, planning, and resource management decisions. The Copernicus Global Land Service (CGLS) is a component of the Land Monitoring Core Service (LMCS) of Copernicus, the European flagship programme on Earth Observation. The Global Land Service systematically produces a series of qualified bio-geophysical products on the status and evolution of the land surface, at global scale and at mid to low spatial resolution, complemented by the constitution of long term time series. The products are used to monitor the vegetation, the water cycle, the energy budget and the terrestrial cryosphere. ### Methodology For the global land cover 100-meter resolution data, the main inputs are PROBA-V satellite observations, organized into millions of Sentinel-2 equivalent tiles of 110x110-kilometers. These satellite observations are put through an algorithm, that includes: - pre-processing, sensor specific data cleaning, and outlier screening - data fusion between the 5-day 100-meter resolution and daily 300-meter resolution data; - extraction of 183 metrics, including the base reflectances, vegetation indicators, time series harmonics and descriptive statistics; - the use of 168K training points, collected at 10-meter resolution, from GeoWIKI’s crowd-sourcing, for year 2015 - the use of well-established, external datasets for the shoreline masking, ecological regionalisation, built-up (urban) cover, permanent and seasonal water cover, arctic vegetation, weather and topography; supervised classification and regression. The classified metrics are calculated over a three year period (epoch), in three processing modes: - base maps for epoch 2015, that serves as reference for the classifier and regression models, - consolidated maps (epochs 2016, 2017 and 2018) with full years of prior and pastor data and - the near-real time (nrt, 2019) maps with one year prior and only three months pastor data. The final maps are validated using an independent set of 21,700 validation points, also sourced from Geo-WIKI. For the full documentation, please see the source [user manual](https://land.copernicus.eu/global/sites/cgls.vito.be/files/products/CGLOPS1_PUM_LC100m-V3_I3.4.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows 11 of the 23 discrete LCCS classifications from the CGLS Land Cover Product. The 12 original forest classes are shown as two classes, open and closed. The ocean and unknown classes are not displayed. Historical data on global land cover from 1992 to 2019 can be found on Resource Watch [here](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/soc068brw2-Global-Land-Cover-IPCC-Classification). The products are provided as single-layer, internally compressed GeoTIFF files, per 20x20 degree on the [Land Cover viewer](https://lcviewer.vito.be/), as global files on [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/communities/copernicus-land-cover?page=1&size=20), and analyzed on [Google Earth Engine](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/catalog/COPERNICUS_Landcover_100m_Proba-V-C3_Global). The annual LC product also includes data for cover fractions (%) for the 10 base classes, an indicator to distinguish forest types, an indicator for the input Data Density, and a change confidence layer (after 2015) are available in the data from the provider. The Land Cover viewer also shows annual maps of change occurrence and of change processes. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. The products are provided as single-layer, internally compressed GeoTIFF files, per 20x20 degree on the [Land Cover viewer](https://lcviewer.vito.be/), as global files on [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/communities/copernicus-land-cover?page=1&size=20), and analyzed on [Google Earth Engine](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/catalog/COPERNICUS_Landcover_100m_Proba-V-C3_Global). ### Visualizing the Data See the documentation on how Resource Watch retrieved the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/soc_104_rw0_global_land_cover). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata. title: Irrigated Crop Water Requirement and Withdrawal
description: The Irrigated Water Requirement and Water Withdrawal data set is prepared by FAO AQUASTAT as part of its Irrigation Water Use study. The data can be used to estimate the amount of irrigation water needed to satisfy crop water demand and compare this with the amount of irrigation water actually used. This provides a measure of a country's shortfall in available irrigation water or irrigation infrastructure. The irrigated water requirement is calculated as irrigation consumptive water use (ICU), which is a function of potential crop evapotranspiration (ETc), effective precipitation (P), and change in soil moisture (DS): ICU = ETc - P - DS Written another way, the irrigation consumptive water use at a point in time (ICU(t)) can be represented as the difference between the potential crop evapotranspiration at time t (ETc(t)) and the actual crop evapotranspiration under nonirrigated conditions at time t (ETa(t)): ICU(t) = ETc(t) - ETa(t) The potential crop evapotranspiration of a grid cell is influenced by certain climatic conditions, such as solar radiation, wind speeds at 2 m, and daily temperatures, among others. The reference evapotranspiration (ETo(t)), determined by the FAO Penman-Monteith equations) in a given area at a given time is the amount of water that would be released into the atmosphere through evapotranspiration if the entire ground surface were covered in a certain crop, typically taken to be grass 12 cm tall, and there were no limits on available water. Each other crop (c) has a crop factor (Kc) that can be used to scale the ETo(t) to obtain ETc(t): ETc(t) = Kc x ETo(t) 118 out of 165 countries in the study report the volume of water used for irrigation to FAO AQUASTAT. For the remaining 47 countries, AQUASTAT developed a method for calculating regional (r) correction ratios (CRr) that relate the total irrigation water requirements for countries in that region (IWRr) to the total irrigation water withdrawn for countries in that region (IWWr). CRr = IWRr / IWWrWhen reliable data on a country's IWW (IWWc) are not available, these values are replaced using the IWRr and CRr of the country's relevant surrounding region: IWWc = IWRr / CRr Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Projected Change in Frost Free Season U.S. (RCP4.5)
description: The Projected Change in Frost Free Season in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average frost free season at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. A frost free season is the largest number of consecutive days in a year where the minimum daily temperatures are above 32 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the frost free season in 2000 is actually an average of the annual frost free seasons between the years 1985 and 2015. Frost free season projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The change in frost free season is shown as the number of days difference between the frost free season during the projected decade and the baseline time period. The dataset is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. In particular, it can be used to understand and adapt to changing agricultural growing seasons and productivity in individual regions. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference. The annual average frost free season for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting daily minimum temperature values for a given year and finding the largest number of consecutive days where the minimum temperature exceeded 32°F. The average annual frost free seasons were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then the baseline average was subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in dry spells The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the frost free season in 2000 is actually an average of the annual frost free seasons between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.

title: Cities with Bus Rapid Transit
description: ### Overview This dataset from Global BRT Data shows cities that have active bus rapid transit (BRT) systems and the year in which they commenced. Global BRT Data collects information on BRT and bus priority systems in cities around the world. BRT systems are characterized by median-aligned and segregated bus lanes, preboard fare collection, and platform-level boarding. Bus priority systems are similar in that they include dedicated bus lanes, but they may not include all of the features necessary to be classified as a BRT system. The Bus Rapid Transit Locations dataset is managed and updated monthly by the World Resources Institute (WRI) Brazil Ross Center for Sustainable Cities. The dataset covers 171 cities globally from 1968 to 2019. ### Methodology The Bus Rapid Transit dataset was created by Global BRT Data. The data is collected and aggregated from various sources, including transit agencies or associations of transit agencies, government, researchers, and nongovernmental organizations. The data may be collected from websites, publications, conversations with experts, or direct observations. In instances where sources of published data contradict each other, Global BRT Data defers to data from transit agencies, governments, or peer-reviewed publications.
