title: Climate Hazard Indicators (Annual minimum temperatures - mean) Historical and SSP scenarios - Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu
description: ### Overview The dataset includes five major climatic indicators viz. annual values for minimum temperature (℃), maximum temperature (℃), mean temperature (℃), total precipitation (mm/year), and the number of rainy days (represented as integers) for two Indian states, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. It features decadal averages from 2020-2100 for Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs), including SSP5-8.5, which reflects a high emissions scenario, and SSP2-4.5, representing moderate challenges to both mitigation and adaptation. Additionally, the dataset provides historical data for all the five indicators averaged over the period from 2005 to 2014. ### Methodology **Pre-Processing**: The decadal time periods were labeled as follows: 2020-2029 as 2020, 2030-2039 as 2030, 2040-2049 as 2040, 2050-2059 as 2050, 2060-2069 as 2060, 2070-2079 as 2070, 2080-2089 as 2080, and 2090-2099 as 2090. **Layers of interest**: Annual averages of minimum temperature (℃), maximum temperature (℃), mean temperature (℃), Annual total precipitation (mm/year), and the annual total number of rainy days (represented as integers). **Data**: The ERA5 reanalysis dataset (ECMWF 2022), a satellite data product of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts with a spatial resolution of 31 kilometers (km), is used as a reference dataset. The ensemble of downscaled daily time series outputs from global climate models (GCMs). These time series include the historical years covered by the observation time series as well as the specified future years of interest. We have used the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 product, which includes outputs from 34 Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) models at approximately 25 km spatial resolution. ### Estimation Methods Out of the 35 models, we select the top 3 climate models that perform best for a specific weather variable in a particular geographic region, and present the ensemble mean of these models. The ERA5 dataset is used as a reference, and the comparison is made for the historical period between 1980 and 2014. After selecting the models, we apply a calibration/bias correction procedure to the future time series of the models. This involves aligning the model's frequency distribution with the historical data by shifting the percentiles of the model's distribution. For instance, if the 20th percentile of the model data corresponds to the 30th percentile of the observations, then the 30th percentile of the calibrated model data will match the 20th percentile of the uncalibrated model data. For the full documentation, please see the source methodology at Wong, T., and P Switzer. 2023. 'Estimating future local climate hazard probabilities.' Technical Note. Washington, DC: World Resources Institute. Available online at: doi.org/10.46830/writn.22.00074.v2. ### Description of the Layers **Annual Maximum Temperature (℃)**: The daily maximum temperature data for each year is extracted and averaged to calculate the yearly average maximum temperature. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years. **Annual Minimum Temperature (℃)**: The daily minimum temperature data for each year is extracted and averaged to calculate the yearly average minimum temperature. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years. **Annual Mean Temperature (℃)**: The daily mean temperature is calculated by averaging the daily minimum and maximum temperatures. The annual mean temperature is obtained by averaging the daily mean temperatures over the course of a year. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years. **Annual Total Precipitation (mm/year)**: The daily precipitation values are summed over the entire year to calculate the annual total precipitation. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years. **Annual Rainy Days (represented as integers)**: A rainy day is defined as a day with precipitation exceeding 2.5 mm (as per the India Meteorological Department). The total number of rainy days in a year is calculated by summing the rainy days throughout the year. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years. ### Visualizing the Data The data is provided at a 25-km resolution and is presented as a raster with a time slider with a separate layer for each variable. The values are visualized using a gradient based on the selected year in the slider, ranging from lighter shade (indicating low values) to darker shade (representing higher values). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source

title: [Archived] Population (Grid, 250 m)
description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](d6e42176-90c4-429d-8cae-7619c545a458) as a replacement.**_ The European Commission Joint Research Centre (EC JRC) and the Columbia University Earth Institute Center for International Earth Science Information Network (CIESIN) created a 250-meter resolution population grid. Residential population estimates for 1975, 1990, 2000 and 2015 were generated by disaggregating census or administrative unit population data and re-mapping them to grid cells. The distribution and density of built-up area (from the Global Human Settlement Layer) informed the re-mapping of the population data. The model used raster-based density mapping relying on the Global Human Settlement – Built-Up Area data to define the distribution of people and inform the respective density. The Built-Up grid is the distribution of built-up areas displayed as the proportion of occupied area within each cell. Population estimates came from country-based census data and administrative polygons with estimated residential populations. Population grids were created using a volume-preserving density mapping approach: given population data and built-up area data: A. If the polygon generates 250 meter cells and contains built-up area data, disaggregate the population in proportion to density of built-up area; B. If the polygon generates 250-meter cells and does not contain built-up area data, disaggregate the population using areal weighting; C. If the polygon does not generate its own 250-meter cell, convert polygon to point (centroid within), sum al points within a cell, and sum to a mosaic of A and B. Option C was required because some populated source zones (polygons) were smaller than a 250 x 250 meter cell. This process preserved the full resolution of the Gridded Population of the World data set. All data came from the respective years. Air Quality: Nitrogen Dioxide (NO₂) Satellite Measurements
description: ### Overview The Air Quality: NO₂ Satellite Measurements dataset provides global monthly averages of nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) density in the troposphere. Each value shown in the dataset represents the density of NO₂ between Earth’s surface and the top of the troposphere. The NO₂ density is reported with units of moles of NO₂ per square meter of air (mol/m²). Nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) is one of the most common compounds in the nitrogen oxides (NOx) group. Other nitrogen oxides include nitric acid (HNO₃) and nitric oxide (NO). NO₂ is used as the indicator for the larger group of nitrogen oxides, meaning if NO₂ is present it is likely other nitrogen oxides are as well. NO₂ is primarily created by the burning of fuel, which can be from cars, trucks and buses, power plants, and off-road equipment. Breathing air with a high concentration of NO₂ can irritate airways in the human respiratory system. Acute exposures can aggravate respiratory diseases, particularly asthma, leading to respiratory symptoms, like coughing, wheezing or difficulty breathing. Longer chronic exposures to elevated concentrations of NO₂ may contribute to the development of asthma and potentially increase susceptibility to respiratory infections. People with asthma, as well as children and the elderly are generally at greater risk for the health effects of NO₂. The dataset is made up of data collected from the Sentinel-5 Precursor (S5p) mission, a low Earth orbit polar satellite system. The S5p mission is part of the Global Monitoring of the Environment and Security (GMES/COPERNICUS) space component program headed by the European Commission (EC) in partnership with the European Space Agency (ESA). Its goal is to provide information and services on air quality, climate, and the ozone layer. The S5p mission includes the TROPOspheric Monitoring Instrument (TROPOMI), which takes daily global observations of key atmospheric components, such as NO₂, at a 5.5 x 3.5 kilometer (km) resolution. Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-CO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-O), and [absorbing aerosol index (AAI)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-AER-AI). ### Methodology The TROPOMI NO₂ dataset was created with data collected by the S5P satellite mission. The data was retrieved and analyzed using a 3 step process. 1. Total NO₂ slant column density was determined from radiance and irradiance spectra measured by TROPOMI. It was analyzed using a Differential Optical Absorption Spectroscopy (DOAS) method. NO₂ slant column density is the amount of NO₂ found along an average path taken by photons traveling from the sun to the satellite sensor. 2. Slant column density data was then separated into stratospheric and tropospheric categories based on information coming from the satellite’s data assimilation system. Stratospheric data was then removed from the dataset. 3. Tropospheric slant column density was converted into tropospheric vertical column density and the average NO₂ density for the entire vertical column was calculated. This was determined by applying an appropriate air mass factor (AMF) and actual, daily information on the vertical distribution of NO₂ calculated by the TM5-MP global chemistry transport model. The altitude-dependent AMF used depended on the satellite geometry, terrain height, cloud fraction and height, and surface albedo. The dataset shown on Resource Watch was mapped by the Google Earth Engine team using the [harpconvert] (https://cdn.rawgit.com/stcorp/harp/master/doc/html/harpconvert.html) tool. For more information on this conversion please see the Google Earth Engine documentation. The offline version of this data is displayed on Resource Watch, which is more complete than its near real-time counterpart, but is released on a greater delay due to the additional processing time needed. For the full documentation, please see the [source methodology](https://sentinel.esa.int/web/sentinel/technical-guides/sentinel-5p/products-algorithms) associated with the “Nitrogen Dioxide (NO₂) Total Column”. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-CO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-O), and [absorbing aerosol index (AAI)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-AER-AI). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for formaldehyde (CH₂O), sulphur dioxide (SO₂), methane (CH₄) and clouds are available from the data provider. Both a near real-time and an offline version of each of these compounds are available. Please see the [Google Earth Engine data catalog](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/tags/tropomi) to access this data. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. Tropical Cyclones
description: ### Overview This dataset shows the paths cyclones have followed and their intensities, from 1980 to the present. The data includes information on tropical cyclones by location, ocean basin, scale, name, wind speed, and other intensity parameters. The International Best Track Archive for Climate Stewardship (IBTrACS) is run by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). According to NOAA, a tropical cyclone is a weather event that produces rotating clouds, high winds, and thunderstorms. These cyclones are called hurricanes in the North Atlantic, central North Pacific, and eastern North Pacific. Elsewhere they are called typhoons or tropical typhoons. The disruptions from tropical cyclones have significant impacts on human life, property, and ecology. By compiling data in one place, this dataset can support scientific research efforts in understanding the distribution, frequency, and intensity of tropical cyclones, and assist emergency managers with disaster mitigation efforts. ### Methodology Researchers obtained this data from various agencies either directly through agency websites or via personal communication. The data originated from satellite observations. The data files were then converted into a common format with two general steps. To solve the double-reporting issue with various data sources, step 1 identified each unique storm with an algorithm based on the storm’s position. Step 2 harmonized intensity estimates across data sources so that the intensity parameters are comparable. In cases of different sources having different positions and intensities, researchers calculated the average values from all available reports. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://journals.ametsoc.org/doi/pdf/10.1175/2009BAMS2755.1). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Water Change
description: ### Overview The global annual surface water percent and surface water dynamics maps were created by the Global Land Analysis and Discovery Lab (GLAD) laboratory, and the data is available at 30 m spatial resolution, globally, from 2000 to 2020. The GLAD laboratory classified all available Landsat 5, 7, and 8 scenes. Each scene was classified per pixel to identify land, water, and ground obscured by cloud, shadow, haze, or ice. Land and water observations were summed by month from all available images. These counts were aggregated to estimate the annual temporal percent of the year each pixel had water presence, resulting in values of 0-100, and pixels with no observations a no-data value of 255. In order to characterize the type of surface water dynamic over the 21 years, the annual water percent was estimated for each year and temporally filtered to provide greater consistency. A series of rules were applied to this time series to characterize it into permanent land or water, stable seasonal, unidirectional loss or gain, temporary dry or wet period, and high-frequency transitions between annual states of water and land. The pixels that experienced temporary dry or wet periods and high frequency transitions were mapped as variable water. The Global Land Analysis and Discovery Lab (GLAD) laboratory in the Department of Geographical Sciences at UMD investigates methods, causes, and impacts of global land surface change. Earth observation imagery is the primary data source, and the land cover extent and change is the primary topic of interest. GLAD aspires to generate new science insights concerning land resources, educate the next generation of remote sensing-based land change scientists, and disseminate land monitoring capabilities to operational settings nationally and internationally. ### Methodology Open surface water, or simply water, is defined as inland water that covers ≥50% of a pixel and is not obscured by objects on or above the water surface, for example, forest canopy, floating aquatic vegetation, bridges, or ice. The analysis had three major steps: (1) classify every Landsat scene 1999-2020; (2) create an annual percent water time-series; and (3) characterize the time-series into various dynamics classes. All Landsat 5, 7, and 8 scenes from 2000-2020 were classified into land, water, and unusable data. Due to the diversity of reflectance patterns for open surface water targets, an ensemble of hierarchical, bagged classification trees were used to discriminate clear observations from those contaminated by cloud, shadow, and ice and to discriminate water from land. These classification trees were developed from a training set of 150-180 fully labeled scenes per sensor [(Potapov et al., 2015)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2014.11.027). The classification models utilize all the Landsat bands, normalized difference ratios of each pair of spectral bands, and 3x3 pixel spatial averages of all bands and ratios, as well as, utilize topographic inputs of elevation and derived slope, aspect, and hillshade data. The annual water percent time series was derived from the counts of water and land observations. To account for intra-annual variation in clear observation frequency (e.g. fewer observations in the far north in winter due to low sun elevations or in tropical monsoon environments due to high cloud cover), the percent of land and water observations flagged as water (water / (water + land)) was first calculated per meteorological season (December-February, March-May, June-August, September-November) of each year. Then the average water percent of the seasons with data was assigned as the annual water percent. Temporal filters and manual masks were applied to remove noise and omission/commission errors. An inter-annual water dynamics model was developed to characterize and visualize the dynamics of water presence 2000-2020. The annual water percent time series was first smoothed using a 3-year mean moving window, and the range and mean were calculated per pixel. Pixels with a range of ≤33% and a mean of ≤10% or ≥90% were labeled permanent land and water, respectively, providing a stable target with low sensitivity to possible omission or commission effects due to image artifacts or atmospheric conditions. Change pixels were identified as pixels with a range of ≥50%, and all other pixels labeled as stable seasonal, characterized by having little or no inter-annual variation in water presence and consistent intra-annual variation. By an analysis of all local maxima and minima in the time-series, pixels labeled as change were further characterized into the following main change types: gain, loss, dry period (water-land-water), wet period (land-water-land), and high-frequency (3 or more) land-water transitions. For more details, please refer to Pickens et al. [(2020)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2020.111792). For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows datasets from the GLAD laboratory for [Cropland Extent](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/50634b51-ea2e-4cc1-9e4b-8f26a389a301), [Cropland Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ec282483-4f5c-4fb8-ace7-8e557826781a), [Tree Height Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/64a3e126-000b-46fb-aaf4-8ac765a8263b), [Snow/Ice Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/5a796ce9-71d4-42b0-922d-056a86e5eb72), [Built-Up Area Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e6a3f803-1222-46c2-8e6c-0ae94b3d80c8), and [Land Cover Map](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/06e734af-66f0-4c3e-ac71-1b99f3cbfe1d). Economic Capacity Categorization of Cities
description: ### Overview The Economic Capacity Categorization of Cities dataset shows the projected change in population and categorization of 769 cities based on their economic capacity to meet urban service needs between 2015 and 2030. Cities are categorized into four groups based on their current economic strength, projected population, and economic growth. Gross domestic product (GDP) per capita is used as an indicator of a city’s income. The four categories used in the dataset are: struggling, emerging, thriving, and stabilizing cities. This categorization can help identify cities that will likely face the greatest challenges in providing urban services in the future. It will also assist in locating cities that have the opportunity to avoid locking in unsustainable patterns of urban development. The dataset was created by the World Resources Institute (WRI) with data from Oxford Economics' Global Cities 2030 database in conjunction with the United Nations World Urbanization Prospects and the World Bank's World Development Indicators. Oxford Economics’ Global Cities 2030 service has been developed to explore market trends and opportunities among the world’s largest 750 cities. The service provides city (and corresponding national) annual historic estimates (back to 2000 where possible) and forecasts (to 2030) to support business decision making and strategy, research analysis, urban planning, and client consultation and engagements. This classification of cities can help to understand the challenges that cities will face in the years ahead. WRI believes that the pattern of urbanization will change in the future, and a new vision of how to build and manage cities is crucial in developing cities where everyone can live, move, and thrive. ### Methodology The Economic Capacity Categorization of Cities dataset was created by reviewing patterns in income, projected population, and economic growth data. The cities included in the dataset were from Oxford Economics’ Global Cities 2030 database and have at least 400,000 inhabitants or were deemed “strategically” important, like country capitals. Researchers collected data on current GDP per capita as a means of understanding a city’s current economic strength. This data was combined with projected growth in GDP per capita between 2015 and 2030 relative to the projected growth in urban population over the same time period. WRI proposed that these are good measures of how well a city’s resource base can serve its population into the future. These two measures were used to distribute cities into the following four categories: 1. Struggling Cities: These cities have a low GDP per capita today (i.e., GDP per capita less than $10,000), and a low ratio of projected growth in GDP per capita to projected growth in population between 2015 and 2030 (i.e., ratio less than 1), as compared to other cities. They are classified as struggling cities because, in the near future, they are likely to experience more rapid population growth than per capita economic growth, pointing to an impending resource gap. While this category includes predominantly sub-Saharan African cities, some cities in the Middle East and North Africa, and a few cities in South Asia, and Latin America and the Caribbean are also represented. 2. Emerging Cities: These cities have a low GDP per capita today, and a high ratio of projected growth in GDP per capita to projected growth in population between 2015 and 2030, as compared to other cities. They are classified as emerging cities because, while their economic strength is low today, their projected economic growth is greater than their projected population growth, indicating projected increases in economic productivity. These cities are more likely to have the capacity to overcome current resource constraints and strengthen their position globally. Most of the cities in this category are in East Asia and the Pacific and South Asia, with some in Europe and Central Asia, and Latin America and the Caribbean as well. 3. Thriving Cities: These cities have a high GDP per capita today, and a high ratio of projected growth in GDP per capita to projected growth in population between 2015 and 2030, as compared to other cities. They are classified as thriving cities because, not only are they economically strong today, their economic growth is projected to outpace their urban population growth in coming years. These cities are growing and thriving. Cities from East Asia, Europe and Central Asia, North America, and Latin America and the Caribbean fall within this category. 4. Stabilizing Cities: These cities have a high GDP per capita today, and a low ratio of projected growth in GDP per capita to projected growth in population between 2015 and 2030, as compared to other cities. They are classified as stabilizing cities because they are economically strong today, but their economic growth is expected to be lower relative to their population growth when compared to emerging or thriving cities. In that sense, these cities are starting to stabilize and in some cases, their economies are starting to shrink. It is primarily cities from North America, Latin America, and the Middle East that fall within this category. In addition, WRI calculated the percent of projected population change for the same cities from the years 2015 to 2030. This data was taken from the same data providers. U.S. Population Projections
description: Climate and land-use change are major components of global environmental change. The first version of the Integrated Climate and Land Use Scenarios (ICLUS) project modeled population, residential development, and impervious surface cover changes by decade to the year 2100. Those modeling choices and assumptions were intended to be consistent with four scenarios from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). ICLUS version 2 is designed to be consistent with a more recent IPCC scenarios framework, drawing from two Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) and two Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). Improvements include the use of updated input data, integration of changing climate variables within the migration model, inclusion transportation network capacity and increase over time, growth in commercial and industrial land uses, and the use of population density-driven demands for residential housing, as well as commercial and industrial development. ICLUS v2.1 consists of population and land use projections produced specifically to support the Fourth National Climate Assessment. The methodology used to produce these population projections differs from ICLUS v2.0. The demographic components of change (i.e., rates of fertility and mortality) for ICLUS v2.1 were taken directly from the Wittgenstein Centre Data Explorer (http://witt.null2.net/shiny/wic/). These projections were produced much more recently than the Census projections used in ICLUS v2.0, and incorporate more recent observations of population change. SSP2 is a “middle-of-the-road” projection, where social, economic and technological trends do not shift markedly from historical patterns, resulting in a U.S. population of 455 million people by 2100. Domestic migration trends remain consistent with the recent past. The SSP5 narrative describes a rapidly growing and flourishing global economy that remains heavily dependent on fossil fuels, and a U.S. population that exceeds 730 million by 2100. ICLUS v2.1 land use projections under SSP5 result in a considerably larger expansion of developed lands relative to SSP2. Note that some versions of ICLUS projections do not include climate change projections to dynamically update location-specific amenities when calculating migration. These projections will include the “nocc” label in the file name to indicate this difference. PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link.

title: Crop Land Area, Yield and Production - India
description: Crop Land Area, Yield and Production - India SOURCE: Directorate of Economics and Statistics, Ministry of Agriculture, Government of India LINK: https://data.desagri.gov.in/website/crops-apy-report-web; https://www.mospi.gov.in/sites/default/files/publication_reports/manual_area_crop_production_23july08_1.pdf Overview The dataset comprises five-year averages of production (in tonnes), productivity/yield (in tonnes per hectare), and area (in hectares) for 55 major crops across India from 1997–98 to 2022–23. The information is provided at the district level, covering major seasonal time periods of each crop within each year. The yearly datasets were derived from crop-wise APY dataset (https://data.desagri.gov.in/website/crops-apy-report-web). Methodology Pre-Processing: The dataset available as excel report was processed and joined with district shapefile (recent by mid of year 2022, containing 755 districts) obtained from Survey of India website. To simplify the presentation, the raw yearly data was averaged into five-year intervals to highlight trends in crop production and acreage across each district. The periods were labelled as follows: 1995-2000 as 2000, 2001-2005 as 2005, 2006-2010 as 2010, 2011-2015 as 2015, 2016-2020 as 2020, and 2021-2023 as 2023. This approach was adopted based on feedback from stakeholder engagements. Layers of interest: Rice Area (in Hectares), Rice Production (in Tonnes), Rice Yield (in Tonnes/Hectare), Cotton Area (in Hectares), Cotton Production (in Tonnes), Cotton Yield (in Tonnes/Hectare) Seasons considered for Rice crop: Kharif, Rabi, Autumn, Summer Seasons considered for Cotton crop: Kharif, Rabi The agricultural crop year in India runs from July to June. The cropping season is divided into two main seasons: (i) Kharif and (ii) Rabi, based on the monsoon. The Kharif season occurs from June/July to September/October during the southwest monsoon. It aligns with the Asian summer monsoon and is mostly rainfed, with limited irrigation arrangements. The Rabi season lasts from October to March and is grown under irrigated conditions. The Summer and Autumn seasons are shorter and found only in a few states. The Summer season runs from February/March to April/May and is mostly grown under irrigated conditions. The Autumn season, from May/June to October, is mainly for long-duration crops like sugarcane and some vegetable crops. For rice crop, the season is followed in particular states of India that do not receive considerable rains from the Asian summer monsoon. Area, Yield, and Production Estimation Methods The methods for estimating area, yield, and production of crops follow standardized processes under India's agricultural statistical framework. 1. Area Estimation Methods 1.1. Temporarily Settled States (Land Record States) Crop area is estimated through field-to-field enumeration by a village accountant (Patwari/Karnam). The data is recorded in the Khasra register (a field-wise crop record). The area statistics are aggregated at village, tehsil, district, and state levels. 1.2. Permanently Settled States (Non-Land Record States) Establishment of Agency for Reporting Agricultural Statistics (EARAS) is used: - A random sample of at least 20% of villages is surveyed annually. - Complete enumeration is conducted within selected villages. - The process ensures coverage of all villages over five years. 1.3. Non-Reporting Areas Area estimates are derived using remote sensing technology and aerial photography. Ground truthing and validation methods are used to improve accuracy. 2. Yield Estimation Methods General Crop Estimation Surveys (GCES) The yield is estimated through scientifically designed crop-cutting experiments (CCE). The methodology is as follows: 2.1. Sampling Design Stratified Multistage Random Sampling: - Strata: Administrative divisions (tehsil/block). - Primary Sampling Units: Villages (selected randomly). - Second-Stage Sampling Units: Fields within selected villages. - Ultimate Sampling Units: Experimental plots of standard size (e.g., 5m x 5m). 2.2. Plot Selection Two fields are randomly selected per village. A random plot (e.g., 5m x 5m) is located within each field using random numbers. For row-planted crops (like cotton), longer plots (e.g., 10m x 5m) are used. 2.3. Harvesting and Recording The experimental plot is harvested before the rest of the field. The produce is: - Weighed immediately for gross yield. - Adjusted if required (e.g., driage experiments for rice). 2.4. Driage Adjustments - Rice: Driage experiments are conducted to adjust for moisture content, ensuring yields are reported as dried grain weight. - Cotton: In the case of cotton, the final produce is expressed in terms of lint after adopting ginning percentage (kapas to lint) as obtained from the ginning factories. 3. Production Estimation Methods Area and yield are multiplied to estimate production at village, district, state, and national levels. 4. Validation of the Area, Production and Yield estimates Final aggregation and validation occur at the national level by the Directorate of Economics and Statistics (DES). Production estimates are validated using: - Remote sensing data, - Historical trends, - Market and trade data, - Reports from local agricultural officers. For the full documentation, please see the source methodology at https://www.mospi.gov.in/sites/default/files/publication_reports/manual_area_crop_production_23july08_1.pdf. Visualizing the Data The data is available as district-level aggregates. By selecting a specific crop, area, production, yield statistic, and preferred season, the relevant layer is displayed with a gradient based on the 2023 crop year, ranging from yellow (for low values) to green (with darker shades representing higher values). The cursor can be dragged over districts and clicked to view the 5-yearly averaged values from 1995 to 2023. The 'No Data' value, represented by black, indicates either that the season was not practiced in the district during that year or that data is unavailable from the source. title: Population Projections
description: The official UN population estimates and projections have been prepared since 1951 by the Population Division of the Department of Economic and Social Affairs of the United Nations Secretariat. The 2017 revision provides a comprehensive set of demographic data and indicators to assess population trends at the global, regional, and national levels and to calculate other key indicators for monitoring progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals. The data are collected from national reported demographic information or major survey programs. The 2017 revision builds on previous revisions by incorporating additional results from the 2010 and 2020 rounds of national population censuses as well as findings from recent specialized sample surveys from around the world. The main results display key demographic indicators for each development group, income group, region, subregion, and country for dates from 1950 to 2100. title: Land Use Harmonization Projected Land Use under RCP 8.5 SSP5 (from REMIND-MAGPIE)
description: As part of the World Climate Research Program Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP6), the international community is developing the next generation of advanced Earth System Models (ESM) able to estimate the combined effects of human activities (e.g. land use and fossil fuel emissions) on the carbon-climate system. In addition, a set of historical data based on HYDE, and multiple alternative scenarios of the future (2015-2100) developed by Integrated Assessment Model (IAM) teams, are being developed as input for these models. The goal of the Land-Use Harmonization (LUH2) project is to prepare a harmonized set of land-use scenarios that smoothly connects the historical reconstructions of land-use with the future projections in the format required for ESMs. The land-use harmonization strategy estimates the global fractional land-use patterns, underlying land-use transitions, and key agricultural management information, annually for the time period 850-2100 at 0.25° x 0.25° resolution, while minimizing the differences at the transition between the historical reconstruction ending conditions and IAM initial conditions, and working to preserve changes depicted by the IAMs in the future. Please see publications for more detail on the development of the Land-Use Harmonization model. In this data set Resource Watch displays the land-use patterns of the projected section of data (2015 – 2100) under RCP 8.5 SSP5 (from REMIND-MAGPIE), and classified pixels as the land use category that had the maximum fractional cover. RCP8.5 is an emissions pathway which reaches a radiative forcing of 8.5 W/m^2 and rising in 2100.

description: The Global Wind Atlas (GWA) mean wind speed dataset was generated by the Department of Wind Energy at the Technical University of Denmark (DTU), World Bank Group and Energy Sector Management Assistance Program (ESMAP). The result of this process is a model of local wind climates over the globe (except the North and South Poles and far offshore ocean areas) at 1 kilometer resolution for three heights: 50 meters, 100 meters and 200 meters. title: Gridded Gross Domestic Product (GDP)
description: Global Gridded Geographically Based Economic Data (G-Econ), Version 4, provides a measure of global cell product (GCP): estimates for the amount of gross domestic product (GDP) produced in each grid cell of a 1-degree grid of the world using 2 metrics: GCP measured in the market exchange rate (MER) from local currencies into US$, and GCP measured in purchasing power parity (PPP), which adjusts country currency GCP according to the equivalent amount of US$ needed to purchase a standardized collection of goods in the country using the country's currency. GCP is defined as the gross value added by activities in a grid cell. Gross value is calculated as the total value of the outputs of local businesses providing goods and services in the grid cell, minus the value of inputs bought by those businesses. The data and methods used to calculate local added value are different for different countries, as the data available are different for different countries. State- and county level gross value data are used whenever possible. PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set. title: Gray Water Footprint and Pollution Levels
description: The Twente Water Centre at the University of Twente (TWC) created a global assessment of nitrogen-related water pollution in river basins, with the option to specify the pollution source by economic sector, and by crop for the agricultural sector. Anthropogenic nitrogen (N) loads to freshwater are estimated to calculate the resultant gray water footprints (GWFs), and relate the GWFs per river basin to runoff to calculate the N-related water pollution level (WPL) per catchment. These calculations were created at a 5-by-5 arc minute spatial resolution over the period 2002-2010. The GWF is calculated by dividing the N load by the difference between the ambient water quality standard for N (the maximum acceptable concentration) and the natural concentration of N in the receiving water body. The water pollution level (WPL), which measures the degree of pollution within a catchment, is estimated as the ratio of the total of GWF in a catchment to the actual runoff from that catchment. The artificial fertilizer application rate data came primarily from the International Fertilizer Industry Association (IFA) and was supplemented with data from the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.

title: Frost Free Season
description: Frost free season represents the annual average longest streak of days above freezing, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](01ae2fd7-b818-429f-a27e-a36c8def971a) as a replacement.**_ The Yield Gap and Potential Yield for Major Crops data set was created by EarthStat, the University of Minnesota's Institute on the Environment and the Land Use (UMN IonE), and the Global Environment Lab at the University of British Columbia (LUGE Lab at UBC) for 16 major crops. Yield gaps are defined as the difference between observed crop yields and the potential yield at the same location. Yield gaps were estimated by comparing observed yields to potential yields determined by identifying high-yielding areas within zones, or bins, of similar climate. To classify climates, 2 parameters, which are known to be fundamental drivers of plant growth, were used to describe a region's climate: growing degree days (GDD) and a crop soil moisture index (the ratio of actual evapotranspiration to potential evapotranspiration). For each climate zone and each crop, a table was generated containing the yield, harvest area, and latitude/longitude position information for each grid cell included in the distribution. The data were sorted from the grid cells by their yield values, ranking them from lowest to highest yield. The grid cells' respective harvest areas were then accumulated until arriving at the statistical information of interest: the mean, median, and 90th percentile yields. The percentage of a crop's harvested area was calculated to define a percentile yield value. The data draw on average of census data between 1997 and 2003 and are shown as 2000 at a 5 minute x 5 minute spatial resolution. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: Hydropolitical Tension and Institutional Vulnerability
description: ### Overview The Transboundary Freshwater Dispute Database (TFDD) catalogs the number and delineation of the world's international river basins and also contains physical, socioeconomic, and political data relating to each of them. In the context of these datasets, an international river basin is defined by its ultimate outlet to an ocean, sea, or inland water body and has year-round flow crossing or drawing a political border. This database includes data at the scale of basins as well as basin country units, which is an area of an international river basin that falls within a particular country. The Relative Risk Category for Hydropolitical Tension estimates the relative level of risk a basin or basin country unit has for political tension over its transboundary rivers. This risk is based on: 1. **water infrastructure development**: the ability to deal with disputes arising from the development of new water infrastructure 2. **institutional vulnerability**: the capacity of a basin country unit to absorb tension, which is expressed by the presence or absence of treaties, treaty provisions, and river basin organizations This data was calculated by TFDD-affiliated researchers as a part of the Governance thematic group within the Transboundary Water Assessment Programme's River Basin Component. ### Methodology The delineation and count of international river basins and basin country units were determined using the [Register of International River Basins](https://transboundarywaters.science.oregonstate.edu/content/register-international-river-basins) and watershed boundaries from the [HydroBASINs](https://www.hydrosheds.org/page/hydrobasins) dataset. HydroBASINS provides global coverage of watershed boundaries with several levels of sub-basin delineations, including watersheds that range in scale from tens to millions of square kilometers (see [Lehner & Gill, 2013](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/hyp.9740)). For full documentation on the spatial boundary data, please see the [methodology](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/07900627.2019.1572497). Institutional Vulnerability is measured by five components of formal transboundary cooperation. The five components are: 1. at least one water treaty 2. at least one treaty with an allocation mechanism 3. at least one treaty with a flow variability management mechanism 4. at least one treaty with a conflict resolution mechanism 5. at least one river basin organization The presence of a component is summed to give the institutional vulnerability score from 0 to 5, with 0 being the most vulnerable and 5 being the least vulnerable. Relative Risk Category for Hydropolitical Tension is calculated based on the basin country unit's institutional vulnerability score and the presence of a large dam or water diversion project in the basin country unit or upstream of it. If a basin country unit has a lower score for its institutional vulnerability and has infrastructure development in the basin country unit or upstream, it is in a higher risk category for Hydropolitical tension. Relative Risk ranges from 1 (very low risk) to 5 (very high risk). For full documentation on the metrics shown in this dataset, please see the [Transboundary River Basins report](https://transboundarywaters.science.oregonstate.edu/sites/transboundarywaters.science.oregonstate.edu/files/Database/ResearchProjects/TWAP/GEF_TWAPRB_FullTechnicalReport_compressed.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: Aqueduct Baseline Water Depletion
description: ### Overview Baseline water depletion measures the ratio of total water consumption to available renewable surface and groundwater supplies. A higher ratio indicates larger impact on the local water supply and decreased water availability for downstream users. These ratios were then converted into risk scores based on the thresholds defined in the methodology. These risk scores range from low water stress (<5%) to extremely high water stress (>75%). Total water consumption includes domestic, industrial, irrigation and livestock consumptive uses. Available renewable water supplies include the impact of upstream water use and large dams on downstream water availability. Water depletion values are available per sub-basin (HydroBASIN level 6). Baseline water depletion is similar to baseline water stress; however, instead of looking at total water withdrawal (i.e. all water removed from source), baseline water depletion is calculated using consumptive withdrawal only (i.e. water withdrawn but not returned to source). ### Methodology Aqueduct used the global hydrological model, PCRaster Global Water Balance (PCR-GLOBWB 2), to calculate five indicators. Baseline water depletion is one of those indicators and was calculated using the gross and net total consumption and available water per sub-basin time series from the default PCR-GLOBWB 2 run. The model was first used to calculate a time series of water depletion per catchment per month. To calculate water depletion, total water consumptions were divided by the available renewable surface and groundwater supplies. Net consumptive water use was subtracted from the total available renewable water supply before the ratio was calculated. This results in 12 monthly time series of water depletion per sub-basin. Water resources in delta sub-basins were pooled. Next, the time series were converted into baseline values using an ordinary least squares (OLS) regression. For example, the regression output for January 2019 represents the chronic, long-term condition of water depletion in January’s from 1979 to 2019. This was repeated for every month, and then averaged into an annual value. All raw values were limited to a maximum of 100% and a minimum of 0%. Sub-basins that were classified “Arid and low water use” were handled separately and were given a raw value for baseline water depletion of -1. Finally, raw baseline water depletion values were converted to risk scores between 0 and 5, based on quantiles. These scores were placed into categories indicating how high the risk for this indicator is. The thresholds for raw baseline water depletion values and the corresponding risk scores that were used in each category are defined below as Risk Category (Risk Scores): Raw Value Thresholds. - Low (0-1): < 5% - Low to medium (1-2): 5 - 25% - Medium to high (2-3): 25 - 50% - High (3-4): 50 - 75% - Extremely high (4-5): > 75% - Arid and low water use: -1 For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/aqueduct-30). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. description: ### Overview This dataset shows the percentage of total final energy consumption(TFEC) that comes from renewable sources in 259 countries from 1990 to present. In this dataset, renewable energy sources are defined as hydropower, solid and liquid biofuels, wind, solar, biogas, geothermal, marine, and waste to energy. The dataset was published as part of the Sustainable Energy for All (SE4ALL) initiative, and the data was compiled by the International Energy Agency (IEA) and the United Nations Statistics Divisions (UNSD). IEA and UNDC are the primary developers of internationally comparable national energy statistics. This dataset tracks the progress of Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) indicator 7.2, to advance the target of increase substantially the share of renewable energy in the global energy mix by 2030. Resource Watch also shows [renewable energy consumption](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene021a-Renewable-Energy-Consumption) and [energy intensity](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene029a-Energy-Intensity) data from the SE4ALL Database. ### Methodology This dataset was compiled using data from IEA and UNSD. Renewable energy consumption was divided by total final energy consumption to calculate the share of renewable energy in the total final energy consumption of each country. Renewable energy consumption was defined as the final consumption of renewables plus the amount of electricity and heat consumption estimated to have come from renewable energy sources. Total final energy consumption was defined as the sum of the final energy consumption in the transport, industry, residential, services, and other sectors. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.seforall.org/sites/default/files/l/2013/09/9-gtf_ch4.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows [renewable energy consumption](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene021a-Renewable-Energy-Consumption) and [energy intensity](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene029a-Energy-Intensity) data from the SE4ALL Database. Actual and Potential Crop Yields
description: Global Yield Gap Atlas Crop Yield Gap (GYGA-Yg) data compare the performance of crop yields in a location to the theoretically potential yields with no water stress (Yp) and potential yields in presence of some water stress (Yw). Yp and Yw are determined by the biophysical characteristics of the location and the needs of each crop type. This information can be used to identify high- and low-performing crop-growing regions, and to motivate technology and expertise transfer to address suboptimal yields. GYGA-Yg data provide a new perspective in the field of crop yield gap analysis, as they move beyond using gridded climate data to incorporate locally observed climate and production data as much as possible. The smallest unit of analysis for the GYGA-Yg is the region around a reference weather station (RWS). Each RWS is surrounded by a 100-km radius circular buffer. These buffers are then intersected with GYGA climate zones (GYGA-CZs), soil types, and cropping system information. These factors are used as inputs to a crop model to estimate Yw and/or Yp for each RWS buffer zone. GYGA-CZs are defined by growing degree days (GDDs), temperature seasonality, and an annual aridity index (AI), all of which are measured on a 5 arc minute grid. GDDs are defined as the number of days that the mean temperature is above 0°C. Temperature seasonality is calculated to be the standard deviation of the 12 mean monthly temperatures. AI is the ratio of mean annual precipitation over mean annual evapotranspiration. Cropping system information includes the amount of harvested area, the cropping intensity of growth, and aspects of management such as use of irrigation, planting date, and development timeline of various crops. Yield gaps are calculated as the difference between Yw/Yp (simulated yield potential with and without water stress, respectively) and on-farm yields (Ya). Ya are taken from recent national crop-specific yield statistics at the finest resolution available. Ideally, this is at a scale smaller than the GYGA-CZ clipped RWS buffer areas. If national statistics are not available, household surveys that ask about crop production may be used, such as are collected by groups like the World Bank and the Consultative Group for International Agricultural Research (CGIAR). If these are not available, then GYGA country agronomist experts' estimates are used. If there are insufficiently detailed estimates available from country experts, the last resort is to use country-level production statistics.

title: Daily Imagery
description: ### Overview The Daily Imagery dataset shows near real-time global satellite imagery from the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) instrument on board the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership (SNPP) satellite. SNPP passes over each pole 14 times per day and crosses the equator at 01:30 local time. VIIRS contains a radiometer that creates imagery by collecting wavelengths of light in the visible bands of the electromagnetic spectrum. The imagery created is at a spatial resolution of 250 meters (m) and has been updated daily since 2015. The Daily Imagery dataset can be used for fire and air quality monitoring, along with flood and sea ice mapping. In addition, long-term records of global daily imagery data can contribute to scientists’ understanding of climate change, earth’s atmosphere, natural disasters and weather predictions. The SNPP satellite is a joint mission from the North American Space Administration (NASA) and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Association (NOAA). It serves as an improvement to the previously launched Earth Observing System (EOS) Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) and is part of the future [Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS)](https://www.jpss.noaa.gov/mission_and_instruments.html). ### Methodology The Daily Imagery dataset was created with data collected by the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) instrument on board the joint NASA/NOAA SNPP satellite. The SNPP satellite passes above or nearly above both poles on each revolution. For this dataset VIIRS collected imagery in the “true color” spectral band, which is a combination of wavelengths similar to what the human eye would see. The bands of light collected were in the VIIRS I and M bands. The I band utilizes a high-resolution 375 m sensor that collects red light, while the M band utilizes a moderate-resolution 750 m sensor that collects blue and green light. After the spectral band data was collected it was compiled to create a 250 m RGB (Red, Green, Blue) composite image of the earth. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows the [Nighttime Imagery] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cli061nrt-Daily-Nighttime-lights) dataset from the VIIRS instrument on board the SNPP satellite. description: ### Overview This dataset includes the most-updated effort to map the global distribution of peatlands. [Peatlands are unique and underappreciated ecosystems, rich in both carbon and biological diversity](https://www.wri.org/blog/2018/01/save-indonesias-carbon-rich-peatlands-start-mapping-them). Peat forms when dead plants partially decay in water-saturated soils and organic matter gradually accumulates, layer upon layer, over hundreds or even thousands of years. Peatlands are important because they store soil carbon and provide water resources and habitats for a range of rare, threatened, or declining species. This dataset estimates the global peatland area to be 4.23 million square kilometers, almost 3% of the world's land area. This dataset was published in 2017 by researchers at the University of Leeds. It may provide a useful reference for policymakers and researchers interested in global ecosystem biodiversity, climate change, carbon cycles, and water resources. It may also help provide support for wetland protection and restoration. ### Methodology The global dataset is put together by compiling the most high quality and freely available data from a wide range of sources that describe peatland distributions at global, regional, and national levels. Data includes information derived from digitized soil maps, wetland databases, and satellite imagery. For areas in Hokkaido (Japan), Mongolia, and North Korea, where peatland-specific datasets were not available, the authors estimated peatland extent based on the distribution of histosols derived from the Harmonized World Soil Database v1.2 (HWSD). For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0341816217303004?via%3Dihub). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/blob/master/for_029_peatlands). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: [Archived] Human Development Index
description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](fc6dea95-37a6-41a0-8c99-38b7a2ea7301) as a replacement.**_ The Human Development Index (HDI), published by the UN Development Programme (UNDP), is a summary measure of average achievement in key dimensions of human development: a long and healthy life, a sufficient education, and a decent standard of living. The HDI is the geometric mean of normalized indices for each of the 3 dimensions. The health dimension is assessed by life expectancy at birth; the education dimension is measured by mean of years of schooling for adults aged 25 years and more and expected years of schooling for children of school-entering age. The standard-of-living dimension is measured by gross national income per capita. The HDI uses the logarithm of income to reflect the diminishing importance of income with increasing gross national income (GNI). The scores for the 3 HDI dimension indices are then aggregated into a composite index using geometric mean. The HDI is calculated for 188 countries annually. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. Urban Expansion Probabilities
description: ### Overview This dataset shows global forecasts of probabilities for urban expansion through 2050. It separates the data into five shared socioeconomic pathways (SSPs), at a 5 kilometer (km) resolution. SSPs represent how different policy and societal choices will affect greenhouse gas emissions. The five scenarios used in this analysis are labeled as: - SSP1: Sustainability – Taking the Green Road (low challenges to mitigation and adaptation) - SSP2: Middle of the Road (medium challenges to mitigation and adaptation) - SSP3: Regional Rivalry – A Rocky Road (high challenges to mitigation and adaptation) - SSP4: Inequality – A Road Divided (low challenges to mitigation, high challenges to adaptation) - SSP5: Fossil-fueled Development – Taking the Highway (high challenges to mitigation, low challenges to adaptation) The dataset was created with information from a combination of five sources based on current urban land extent, population rates, Gross Domestic Product (GDP) information, and SSP scenarios. It is important to understand urban expansion because it can cause implications for warming, water scarcity, land use, and other environmental and social challenges. This dataset can be combined with other socioeconomic data to further examine the impacts of urban expansion. For instance, the dataset authors predicted urban expansion-induced warning in cities and suggested that it will increase extreme heat risks for about half of the future urban population. This will primarily affect communities in the tropical Global South that lack the adaptive capacity to meet environmental change. Policymakers can use this dataset to restrict or redistribute urban expansion and design strategies needed to mitigate Urban Heat Islands (UHIs) to reduce their negative impacts on human health, urban ecosystems, energy systems, and infrastructure. This dataset was published by Seto Lab, based at Yale School of the Environment. ### Methodology Researchers created this dataset using the URBANMOD-ZIPE model. The URBANMOD-ZIPE model was based on a 2012 global urban land change model, URBANMOD, and used to forecast pixels of urban expansion probabilities. The input data sources used for the updated model were: 1. urban land extent from the Global Human Settlement grid 2. urban population from the United Nations 3. Gross Domestic Product from the World Bank 4. future scenarios of the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) from the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis There were two phases to the model. Phase 1 predicted the quantities of urban land by 2050. This was done using a fixed effect panel regression model to relate urban land per capita to GDP per capita. Phase 2 utilized a land change model to allocate new urban lands to map pixels using slope, distance to roads, population density, and land covers as the drivers of land change. The final dataset was produced in raster format at a spatial resolution of 5 km. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1748-9326/ab4b71). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. Resource Watch has previously shown this data for urban expansion probabilities for 2030. This dataset was archived because the methodology has been changed and the global forecasts of probabilities for urban expansion through 2050 is now available. You can still access the archived data [here](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit005-Urban-Expansion-Probabilities_replacement). ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: [Archived] Maritime Boundaries
description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](6af67024-b917-4944-851a-152b566ff1a8) as a replacement.**_ ### Overview The Maritime Boundaries dataset shows boundaries for exclusive economic zones (EEZs), territorial seas (TS) and contiguous zones (CZ) for coastal countries around the world. The [United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS)](http://www.vliz.be/en/imis?module=ref&refid=325469) defined the EEZ, CZ and TS maritime boundaries and coastal baselines. An EEZ is a sea zone over which a country has special rights to explore and use marine resources. Typically, a country’s EEZ extends 200 nautical miles (NM) from its coast (or baseline), unless that distance would overlap with another country’s EEZ. TS are coastal waters that are the sovereign territory of a given country. This zone extends a maximum of 12 NM from a country’s baseline. A CZ is a sea zone that extends an additional 12 NM beyond the outer edge of the TS (up to 24 NM from a country’s baseline). Countries have limited legal rights within the CZ. Data for the Maritime Boundaries dataset was published by the Flanders Marine Institute (VLIZ) in 2018 and is available for download from [Marine Regions](https://marineregions.org/). The Maritime Boundaries dataset is a useful tool for managing and displaying marine data. It provides a standardized map of global maritime boundaries. The Maritime Boundaries dataset is useful for linking marine information, such as species distribution lists or coral reef health, to particular countries. The dataset also shows the various jurisdictional reaches of countries. This is important for understanding marine resource management and the rights that countries have to protect their waters. The Maritime Boundaries dataset was generated by the [Flanders Marine Institute (VLIZ)](https://www.vliz.be/en), a non-profit organization dedicated to scientific research on the ocean, seas, coasts and tidal estuaries. Based in Belgium VLIZ was established in 1999 by the Flemish government and [the Research Foundation - Flanders](https://www.fwo.be/en/). The central focus of VLIZ is to provide knowledge to the research community, educators, the general public, policymakers and marine industries. ### Methodology The boundaries shown in the Maritime Boundaries dataset were generated from a combination of **normal**, **straight** and **archipelagic** baselines. The UNCLOS defines a **normal** baseline as the low-water line along a country’s coast. A **straight** baseline is a straight line representing the baseline where there is a fringe of islands along the coast, or the coast is heavily indented. **Archipelagic** baselines apply to archipelago countries, which are made of a group of islands. These baselines are straight lines that connect the coastlines and contain the main islands of the country. Normal baselines were drawn using a combination of the [Esri Countries 2014 dataset](https://www.arcgis.com/home/item.html?id=ac80670eb213440ea5899bbf92a04998) and the [United Nations Environmental Program (UNEP) Coral Reef Distribution dataset](https://data.unep-wcmc.org/datasets/1), referred to as the World Countries 2014 dataset. Coral reef data was used to draw baselines for countries where reefs were a fundamental part of their maritime boundaries. Straight and archipelagic baselines were drawn based on [definitions from the UN](https://www.un.org/Depts/los/LEGISLATIONANDTREATIES/regionslist.htm) or maritime treaties and agreements. Countries typically define borders at sea in agreements with their neighbors. These borders were used when available. Median lines were drawn between countries where borders at sea were not specified. Median lines connect points at equal distance from neighboring coastal countries. The baselines were used to generate boundaries of EEZ, TS and CZ sea zones. The boundaries are seaward distances of 200 EEZ, 12 TS and 24 CZ NM from a country’s baseline. Polygons representing the EEZ, TS and CZ areas were calculated using a buffer distance measured from the combination of straight, archipelagic and normal baselines. The Maritime Boundaries dataset was created by merging the EEZ, TS and CZ boundaries with the World Countries 2014 dataset using the [Pairwise Dissolve tool](https://pro.arcgis.com/en/pro-app/tool-reference/analysis/pairwise-dissolve.htm) in ESRI ArcGIS Pro 2.5.0. Landlocked countries were removed before merging and added in afterward. Differences between coastlines in the EEZ and World Countries 2014 datasets caused small gaps in the polygons. These gaps were fixed in QGis 3.0 using the [Delete Holes tool](https://docs.qgis.org/3.10/en/docs/user_manual/processing_algs/qgis/vectorgeometry.html#delete-holes) and the [Difference tool](https://docs.qgis.org/3.10/en/docs/user_manual/processing_algs/qgis/vectoroverlay.html#difference). For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.marineregions.org/eezmethodology.php). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. VLIZ also provides boundaries of internal waters, archipelagic waters and high seas. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

[Archived] Ramsar Internationally Important Wetlands
description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](2ac1f43c-30bc-4ed9-846c-8443ce4987a9) as a replacement.**_ Ramsar wetlands refer to "internally important" wetlands as defined by the Convention on Wetlands and are designated by each contracting party. At the time of joining the Convention, each contracting party must designate at least one wetland site within their territory for inclusion in the List of Wetlands of International Importance (the Ramsar List). These Ramsar sites acquire a new national and international status. They are recognized as being of significant value not only for the country or the countries in which they are located but for humanity as a whole. There are currently over 2,200 Ramsar sites around the world. They cover over 2.1 million km2, an area larger than Mexico. Parties continue to designate wetlands for inclusion on the list. They select suitable wetlands for designation by referring to the criteria for identifying wetlands of international importance. The Convention has provided guidance to contracting parties on the management of Ramsar sites, in addition to its guidance on the wise use of all wetlands. The inclusion of a wetland on the list signifies the government’s commitment to take the steps necessary to ensure that the site’s ecological character is maintained. The Convention includes various measures to respond to threats to the ecological character of sites. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set.
