title: Aqueduct Coastal Eutrophication Potential
description: ### Overview Coastal eutrophication potential (CEP) measures the potential for riverine loadings of nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and silica (Si) to stimulate harmful algal blooms in coastal waters. These values were then converted into risk scores based on the thresholds defined in the methodology. Higher values indicate higher levels of excess nutrients with respect to silica, creating more favorable conditions for harmful algal growth and eutrophication in coastal waters downstream. These risk scores range from low (<-5) to extremely high (>5). The CEP indicator is a useful metric to map where anthropogenic activities produce enough point-source and nonpoint-source pollution to potentially degrade the environment. When nitrogen and phosphorus are discharged in excess over silica with respect to diatom, a major type of algae, undesirable algal species often develop. The stimulation of algae leading to large blooms may in turn result in eutrophication and hypoxia (excessive biological growth and decomposition that reduces oxygen available to other organisms). It is therefore possible to assess the potential for coastal eutrophication from a river’s nitrogen, phosphorus, and silica loading. Values are available per sub-basin (HydroBASIN level 6). ### Methodology The calculation described below is based on [Billen and Garnier’s (2007)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.marchem.2006.12.017) Indicator of Coastal Eutrophication Potential (ICEP) methodology. The nutrient data comes from [Bouwman et al. (2015)](https://www.thegef.org/project/global-foundations-reducing-nutrient-enrichment-and-odflb-pollution-support-gnc). In short, the data is based on the Global NEWS 2 model [(Mayorga et al. 2010)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envsoft.2010.01.007) and aligned to Simulated Topological Network basins [(Vörösmarty et al. 2000)](http://dx.doi.org/10.1029/1999GB900092). The NEWS 2 model uses biophysical, natural, and anthropogenic (both point and nonpoint) nutrient sources, along with in-watershed and in-river removal processes, to derive global nutrient yields [(Mayorga et al. 2010)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envsoft.2010.01.007). Total nitrogen and phosphors fluxes were calculated by summing NEWS 2 nutrient yield data for dissolved organic, dissolved inorganic, and particulate nutrients. Silica fluxes are simply the dissolved inorganic silica yields in the basin. The calculation is based on the Redfield molar ratio (C:N:P:Si = 106:16:1:20), which is a representation of the approximate nutrient requirement of marine diatoms [(Billen and Garnier 2007)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.marchem.2006.12.017). A negative value indicated that silica was present in excess over the limiting nutrient and thus suggested the absence of eutrophication. A positive value indicated an excess of nutrients over the potential for diatom growth, suggesting suitable conditions for the growth of harmful algae [(Garnier et al. 2010)](https://doi.org/10.1029/2009GB003583). As a final step, the results were aggregated to HydroBASIN level 6 to align the indicator with the remainder of the framework. Finally, raw coastal eutrophication potential values were converted to risk scores between 0 and 5, based on quantiles. These scores were placed into categories indicating how high the risk for this indicator is. The thresholds for raw coastal eutrophication potential values and the corresponding risk scores that were used in each category are defined below as Risk Category (Risk Scores): Raw Value Thresholds. - Low (0-1): < -5 - Low to medium (1-2): -5 - 0 - Medium to high (2-3): 0 - 1 - High (3-4): 1 - 5 - Extremely high (4-5): >5 For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology]( https://www.wri.org/publication/aqueduct-30). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature U.S. (RCP8.5)
description: The Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average maximum temperature at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average maximum temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the maximum temperature between the years 1985 and 2015. Average maximum temperature projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference. The annual average maximum temperature for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCAdata on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting and averaging all daily maximum temperature data over a given year. The average annual maximum temperatures were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in annual average maximum temperature. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average maximum temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the annual maximum temperatures between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

title: Sustainable Energy for All Progress Tracking
description: The Global Tracking Framework (GTF) provides indicators on progress made toward the SE4ALL goals to ensure universal access to modern energy services, double the global rate of improvement in global energy efficiency, and double the share of renewable energy in the global energy mix. These indicators are assembled by a coalition of partner agencies, led by the World Bank, the International Energy Agency (IEA), and the Energy Sector Management Assistance Program (ESMAP), along with more than 20 other partner agencies. For a full list, see http://gtf.esmap.org/about-us. The 2017 edition of the GTF includes the following indicators on the 3 SE4ALL goals: access to electricity for urban, rural, and total populations; primary energy intensity; and total final energy consumption; the share of renewable energy in total final energy consumption; renewable energy consumption; share of renewable energy in electricity output; total electricity output; and renewable energy electricity output. Each of these indicators has a unique methodology, all of which can be reviewed in the GTF methodology at http://gtf.esmap.org/methodology. Users are encouraged to thoroughly review the methodology for each indicator before using the contained data for planning purposes or other analyses. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

title: Aqueduct Baseline Water Stress
description: ### Overview Baseline water stress measures the ratio of total water withdrawals to available renewable surface and groundwater supplies. A higher ratio indicates more competition among users. These ratios were then converted into risk scores based on the thresholds defined in the methodology. These risk scores range from low water stress (<10%) to extremely high water stress (>80%). Water withdrawals include domestic, industrial, irrigation and livestock consumptive and non-consumptive uses. Available renewable water supplies include surface and groundwater supplies and the impact of upstream consumptive water use and large dams on downstream water availability. Water stress values are available per sub-basin (HydroBASIN level 6). ### Methodology Aqueduct used the global hydrological model, PCRaster Global Water Balance (PCR-GLOBWB 2), to calculate five indicators. Baseline water stress is one of those indicators and was calculated using the gross and net total withdrawal and available water per sub-basin time series from the default model run. The model was first used to calculate a time series of water stress per catchment per month. To calculate water stress, total withdrawals were divided by the available renewable surface and groundwater supplies. Net consumptive water use was subtracted from the total available renewable water supply before the ratio was calculated. The results were output in 12 monthly time series time series of water stress per sub-basin. Water resources in delta sub-basins were pooled. Next, the time series were converted into baseline values using an ordinary least squares (OLS) regression. For example, the regression output for January 2020 represents the chronic, long-term condition of water stress in January’s from 1960 to 2020. This was repeated for every month and then averaged into an annual value. All raw values were limited to a maximum of 100% and a minimum of 0%. Sub-basins that were classified “Arid and low water use” were handled separately and were given a raw value for baseline water stress of -1. Finally, raw baseline water stress values were converted to risk scores between 0 and 5, based on quantiles. These scores were placed into categories indicating how high the risk for this indicator is. The thresholds for raw baseline water stress values and the corresponding risk scores that were used in each category are defined below as Risk Category (Risk Scores): Raw Value Thresholds. - Low (0-1): < 10% - Low to medium (1-2): 10-20% - Medium to high (2-3): 20-40% - High (3-4): 40-80% - Extremely high (4-5): >80% - Arid and low water use (5): -1 For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/aqueduct-30). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: Historical Cyclone Intensity
description: ### Overview The Historical Cyclone Intensity dataset estimates the maximum tropical storm intensity experienced at each point around the globe between 1970 and 2009, as indicated by wind speed. Intensity is described via the Saffir-Simpson hurricane wind scale, meaning each value represents the "strongest" cyclone within each 1 arc minute grid cell during that time. Hurricane‐force winds can destroy buildings and fling dangerous debris. However, storm surge and large waves produced by hurricanes pose the greatest threat to life and property along the coast. A storm surge is an abnormal rise of water generated by a storm's winds.The destructive power of storm surge and large battering waves can result in loss of life, buildings destroyed, beach and dune erosion, and road and bridge damage along the coast. Storm surge can span hundreds of miles of coastland and can travel several miles inland. In estuaries and bayous, salt water intrusion endangers public health and the environment. More powerful storms can lead to stronger winds and larger surges. Tracking historical cyclone events can help in estimating the level of threat posed by storms in a given region. Observations of historical cyclone events are sparse globally, which led researchers to estimate storm characteristics using [a parametric model created by Greg Holland](https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0493(1980)108%3C1212:AAMOTW%3E2.0.CO;2). These modeled results are based primarily on [IBTrACS](https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/ibtracs/) v02r01—the most complete global set of historical tropical cyclones available—but United Nations Environment Programme/Global Resource Information Database-Geneva(UNEP/GRID-Geneva) reconciled a wide range of datasets into a common framework. By applying modeling equations to this unified historical archive, UNEP/GRID-Geneva built a homogeneous structured cyclone database with first level basic meteorological data and spatial data. This global cyclone database makes possible post-analysis of historical cyclone events, such as the dataset presented here. ### Methodology This dataset is derived from a geospatial database of historical tropical storms, which includes estimates of wind speeds and other properties across space and time. This database drew upon [IBTrACS](https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/ibtracs/) v02r01 as well as tropical cyclone data from Regional Specialised Meteorological Centres (RSMCs) and the Tropical Cyclone Warning Centres (TCWCs) of the World Meteorological Organisation. This database was constructed using the [Cyclone Database Manager](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/download?doi=10.1.1.117.6313&rep=rep1&type=pdf) created by UNEP/DEWA/GRID-Geneva. Geospatially complete characterizations of historical tropical storms were extrapolated from historical observations using [a parametric model created by Greg Holland](https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0493(1980)108%3C1212:AAMOTW%3E2.0.CO;2), which was selected on the basis of universal recommendation from all polled tropical cyclone specialists. Data compilation and GIS processing were executed by UNEP/GRID-Europe as part of the production of the [Global Assessment Report on Risk Reduction (GAR)](https://gar.undrr.org/). For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button or see the [source methodology](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/download?doi=10.1.1.117.6313&rep=rep1&type=pdf) for the underlying cyclone database. ### Additional Information Resource Watch displays the [IBTrACS historical tropical cyclone tracks](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/dis015a-Hurricane-Tracks) on which this historical intensity dataset is largely based. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch retrieved the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/ocn_005_historical_cyclone_intensity). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: U.S. Hospitals Per 100,000 People
description: The Heat Vulnerability - Adaptive Capacity: Hospitals per 100,000 people data set was created by the Center for Disease Control and Prevention in order to identify communities at risk and the percentage of possibly vulnerable population in the United States. Hospital location data was provided by the American Hospital Association (AHA) from 2012. The number of hospitals per county were calculated by determining the location of each hospital, as provided by AHA, and which county each hospital resides, as defined by the TIGER boundary data provided by the US Census Bureau. The rate of hospitals per 100,000 people was calculated using the total population per county, as proved by 2010 US Census data. The rate of hospitals per 100 square miles was calculated using US Census TIGER Boundary data for each county. Blanks or missing data within the maps, tables, and charts may be due to one of the following reasons: (1) data were not collected, (2) data were collected but were not provided to CDC, or (3) data were incomplete or did not meet data quality standards.

title: Dynamic World
description: The Dynamic World (Land Cover product) dataset shows globally consistent, high resolution, near real-time (NRT) land use land cover (LULC) classification leveraging deep learning on 10 meters Sentinel-2 imagery. The dataset was created utilizing a highly scalable cloud-based system to apply this approach and provide an open, continuous feed of LULC predictions in parallel with Sentinel-2 acquisitions. The dataset includes the following Land Cover types: water, trees, grass, flooded vegetation, crops, shrub/scrub, built area, bare ground, and snow/ice. You can learn more about the dataset [here](http://dynamicworld.app). Regularly updated global land use land cover (LULC) datasets provide the basis for understanding the status, trends, and pressures of human activity on carbon cycles, biodiversity, and other natural and anthropogenic processes. Annual maps of global LULC have been developed by many groups and while widely used, many important LULC change processes are difficult or impossible to observe at a spatial resolution greater than 100 meters and annual temporal resolution, such as emerging settlements and small-scale agriculture and early stages of deforestation and wetland/grassland conversion. Inability to resolve these processes introduces significant errors in our understanding of ecological dynamics and carbon budgets. Thus, there is a critical need for spatially explicit, moderate resolution (10-30 meters/pixel) LULC products that are updated with greater temporal frequency. The Dynamic World dataset is a first-of-its-kind NRT product, which accommodates a variety of user needs ranging from extremely up-to-date LULC data to custom global composites representing user-specified date ranges. Furthermore, the continuous nature of the product's outputs enables refinement, extension, and even redefinition of the LULC classification. In combination, these attributes enable unprecedented flexibility for a diverse community of users across a variety of disciplines. ### Methodology The classification schema for Dynamic World was determined after a review of global LULC maps. The Dynamic World taxonomy maintains a close semblance to the land use classes presented in the [IPCC Good Practice Guidance](https://www.ipcc-nggip.iges.or.jp/public/gpglulucf/gpglulucf.html) to ensure easier application of the resulting data for estimating carbon stocks and greenhouse gas emissions. The modeling approach relies on semi-supervised deep learning and requires spatially dense annotations. To collect a diverse set of training and evaluation data, the authors divided the world into three regions, then further divided each region by the [14 RESOLVE Ecoregions biomes](https://academic.oup.com/bioscience/article/67/6/534/3102935). At each sample location, an initial selection of Sentinel-2 images from 2019 scenes based on image cloudiness metadata reported in the Sentinel-2 tile’s QA60 band was selected. The authors further filtered scenes to remove images with many masked pixels. Individual tiles of 510x510 pixels centered on the sample sites from random dates in 2019 were finally extracted. Further steps were then taken to obtain an “as balanced as possible” training dataset with respect to the LULC classifications from the respective LULC products. To achieve a large dataset of labeled Sentinel-2 scenes, the authors worked with two groups of annotators: photo-interpretation experts (validating 4,000 tiles) and non-experts (validating 20,000 tiles). A final validation set of 409 image tiles were held back from the modeling effort and used for evaluation as described in the Technical Validation section of the source methodology. To account for an annotation skill differential between the non-expert and expert groups, they one-hot encode the labeled pixels and smooth them according to the confidence in a binary label of the individual annotator (expert/non-expert). For training data collection, the authors used the Sentinel-2 Level-2A (L2A) product, which provides radiometrically calibrated surface reflectance (SR). However, systematically produced Sentinel-2 SR products are currently only available from 2017 onwards. Therefore, for the modeling approach, the authors used the Level-1C (L1C) product, which was generated from 2015 and represents Top-of-Atmosphere (TOA) reflectance measurements. For any L2A image, there is a corresponding L1C image, allowing them to directly map annotations performed using L2A imagery to the L1C imagery used in model training. In addition to their preliminary cloud filtering in training image selection, the authors adopted and applied a novel masking solution that combines several existing products and techniques, including masking cloud shadows. The distribution of Sentinel-2 reflectance values is highly compressed towards the low end of the sensor range, with the remainder mostly occupied by high return phenomena like snow and ice, bare ground, and specular reflection. To combat this imbalance, the authors introduce a normalization scheme that better utilizes the useful range of Sentinel-2 reflectance values for each band. Their broad approach to transferring the supervised label data to a system that could be applied globally was to train a Fully Convolutional Neural Network (FCNN). Conceptually, this approach transforms pre-processed Sentinel-2 optical bands into a discrete probability distribution of the classes in our taxonomy on the basis of spatial context. This is done per image on the hypothesis that sufficient spatial and spectral context is available to recover one of their taxonomic labels at a pixel. The authors introduce a number of novel innovations that achieve state-of-the-art performance on LULC globally with a neural network architecture almost 100x smaller than architectures used for semantic segmentation or regression of ground-level camera imagery. To generate the NRT products, the authors apply the normalization described earlier to the raw Sentinel-2 L1C imagery and pass all normalized bands except B1, B8A, B9, and B10 after bilinear upscaling to ee.Model.predictImage. This output is then masked using the cloud mask derived from the unnormalized L1C image. The creation of these images is triggered automatically when new Sentinel-2 L1C and S2C images are available.The NRT collection is continuously updated with new results. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: Climate - countries available list
Population (Grid, 100m)
description: ### Overview This dataset from WorldPop shows a gridded estimated count of every country’s population. This dataset is shown at a 3 arc second resolution, which is approximately 100 meters at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. This dataset shows constrained population estimates, meaning that population estimates were only generated in areas with built settlements, at an annual timestep from 2000 to 2020. Accurate population counts are an essential part of governance, influencing a range of public services and human rights. In application, this data can feed into land zonation, urban planning and public services, and it can be combined with other datasets to create informed disaster risk reduction plans. Population data is used daily to ensure equitable access to services including those that underlie critical democratic processes like voting. Population data has historically had a poor temporal resolution, being updated on decadal timeframes. Often these data have been of a spatial resolution that is too low to integrate into many essential fields including policy analysis, scientific development, and operational work. WorldPop aims to provide regular, consistent, high resolution population data through methodological innovation. This data aims to support the measurement of local populations, their characteristics and growth across national and regional scales. ### Methodology The most accurate current estimates of population come from housing and population censuses, which are often collected as a country per administrative unit. WorldPop generates a gridded version of the dataset through a top-down [constrained estimation modelling method](https://www.worldpop.org/methods/top_down_constrained_vs_unconstrained). The method uses satellite derived building footprint data in combination with a built settlement growth model to account for the distribution of settlements. Random forest-based modelling is then used to disaggregate the population count estimates to the grid cells identified as containing buildings/built settlements. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.worldpop.org/methods). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Resource Watch visualizes population estimates using the [constrained methodology](https://www.worldpop.org/methods/top_down_constrained_vs_unconstrained); however, the source also offers population estimates under an unconstrained methodology. For additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. Resource Watch previously showed data on Historical Population Density, which included data between 1975 and 2015. This dataset has been archived. You can still access the archived data [here](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/b6ceb159-efd8-42de-9c6a-d658801d8922). ### Visualizing the Data See the documentation on how Resource Watch retrieved the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/soc_107_rw0_population). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

title: [Archived] Current Water Risk
description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](c66d7f3a-d1a8-488f-af8b-302b0f2c3840) as a replacement.**_ In response to growing concerns from private sector actors around water availability, water quality, climate change, and increasing demand, World Resources Institute developed Aqueduct Global Maps to help decision-makers identify areas with higher exposure to water-related risks. Aqueduct employs the composite index approach as a robust communication tool to translate hydrological data into intuitive indicators of water-related risks. 12 indicators were grouped into a framework identifying spatial variation in water risks for 15,006 subcatchments. The 12 global indicators (baseline water stress, interannual variability, seasonal variability, flood occurrence, drought severity, upstream storage, groundwater stress, return flow ratio, upstream protected land, media coverage, access to water, and threatened amphibians) were grouped into 3 categories of risk (physical quantity, quality, and regulatory and reputational risk) and 1 overall score. For 6 of the 12 indicators, an ensemble of time series estimators, spatial regression, and a sparse hydrological model was used to generate novel data sets of water supply and use. The remaining 6 indicators were adapted from existing publications. Aggregation methods were chosen to maximize transparency and communicability, and to allow for dynamic weighting to reflect different users’ sensitivities to water-related risks. Catchments with less than 0.012 m/m²/year of withdrawal and 0.03 m/m²/year of available blue water were masked out as “arid and low water use.” Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. Air Quality: Sulfur Dioxide (SO₂) Modeled Next-day Forecast
description: ### Overview This dataset shows forecasted sulfur dioxide (SO₂) concentrations at Earth's surface, modeled by the Whole Atmosphere Community Climate Model (WACCM). Sulfur dioxide is a colorless, reactive air pollutant with a strong odor. The gas is a respiratory irritant that can harm human health. According to the [Australian Department of Environment and Energy](https://www.environment.gov.au/protection/publications/factsheet-sulfur-dioxide-so2), sulfur dioxide irritates the nose, throat, and airways. It can cause shortness of breath, coughing, wheezing, or a tight feeling around the chest. High concentrations of sulfur dioxide can affect lung function, worsen asthma attacks, and worsen existing heart disease in sensitive groups. Most sulfur dioxide emissions come from the burning of coal, oil or gas for electricity and transportation; these fossil fuels contain sulfur, which is emitted as sulfur dioxide when burned. Sulfur dioxide does not contribute to global warming, but it [reacts easily](https://www.environment.gov.au/protection/publications/factsheet-sulfur-dioxide-so2) with other substances to form harmful compounds such as sulfuric acid and small sulfate particles. When sulfur dioxide reacts with water and oxygen, it [creates acid rain](https://www.epa.gov/acidrain/what-acid-rain). Acid rain has a number of [environmental impacts](https://www.ucsusa.org/clean-energy/coal-and-other-fossil-fuels/hidden-cost-of-fossils), including making lakes, rivers, wetlands and other water bodies more acidic, which can be harmful to fish and other aquatic wildlife. WACCM creates global forecasts for a variety of other air quality indicators, as well. While this dataset shows forecasted sulfur dioxide concentrations, Resource Watch also shows WACCM forecasts for [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-PM-25), [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-Black-Carbon), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-O), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-NO), and [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-CO). WACCM runs the model daily, and on their website you can find forecasted concentrations for each compound up to nine days into the future at three-hour time steps. WACCM was developed by the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) and the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research (UCAR). The data has global coverage at 1.9 x 2.5 degree resolution. ### Methodology WACCM is a comprehensive numerical model, driven by meteorological fields from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration’s (NASA) Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO) Goddard Earth Observing System Model, Version 5 (GEOS-5) model. The development of WACCM is an inter-divisional collaboration that unifies modeling from the High Altitude Observatory ([HAO](http://www2.hao.ucar.edu/)), the Atmospheric Chemistry Observations and Modeling ([ACOM](https://www2.acom.ucar.edu/)) Laboratory, and the Climate and Global Dynamics ([CGD](http://www2.cgd.ucar.edu/)) Laboratory. Upper atmospheric modeling from HAO, middle atmospheric modeling from ACOM, and tropospheric modeling from CGD are combined using the NCAR [Community Earth System Model (CESM)](http://www.cesm.ucar.edu/) as a common numerical framework. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://opensky.ucar.edu/islandora/object/articles%3A12836). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows WACCM forecasts for [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-PM-25), [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-Black-Carbon), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-O), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-NO), and [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-CO). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional forecasted data for other compounds, times, and levels of the atmosphere are also produced by WACCM. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/cit_038_waccm_atmospheric_chemistry_model). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

Emissions Comparison of Electric and Diesel Buses
description: The CO₂ Emissions Comparison for Transit Buses was developed by World Resources Institute (WRI) using emission factors for grid electricity from Ecometrica, fuel combustion emissions data from International Energy Agency 2012 and 2013(IEA), electric power transmission and distribution loss data from the World Bank Group's World Development Indicators, and purchased electricity values from Greenhouse Gas Protocol (GHGP). The climate change impacts of electric vehicles (EV) vary globally depending on the fuel used to power the electric grid. EVs are increasingly becoming a better choice as electric grids improve efficiency and integrate more renewable energy sources. While the efficiency of the vehicle has a large impact on the operational costs, social benefits, and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, it is important to understand the energy mix from your local energy grid – as there is significant variation within countries. The data represents the ratio of CO₂ emissions from electric and diesel buses. The purpose of the data is to compare the GHG emissions of the EV and typical ICE diesel bus for the years 1990-2012 on a national level. Where the interactive Resource Watch global map is green, the emissions from the EV are lower, based on the national average energy grid, compared to the emissions from the typical ICE diesel bus. Where the interactive Resource Watch global map is red, the emissions from the EV are higher, based on the national average energy grid, compared to the emissions from the typical ICE diesel bus.

title: Costa Rica Current Coffee Suitability
description: This data set shows current coffee suitability. It was created using multiple environmental variables as part of a study that attempts to utilize data from four Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPPC) emissions scenarios to determine the impact of climate change on coffee cultivation in coffee growing regions of Costa Rica. The study was done using georeferenced points obtained from Instituto del Café de Costa Rica (ICAFE), and using the MaxEnt model to simulate the adaptability of coffee production. Environmental layers taken into account comprise 19 bioclimatic variables from the Worldclim database. Developed by Hijmans et al. 2005, thousands of data points from meteorological stations around the world were collected for the time period of 1960 to 1990, using an interpolation to create environmental layers (rasters) of average temperature with 24,542 locations, minimum and maximum temperatures with 14,835 locations, and precipitation with 47,554 locations. These were all calculated by month, with a resolution of 1 square km. Bioclimatic variables were derived from monthly temperature and precipitation values with the goal of generating biologically significant variables related to crop development. PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link.

title: [Archived] Terrestrial Ecoregions
description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](d0968f74-f5c1-40a1-b2b5-5bac5de5cb15) as a replacement.**_ The Terrestrial Ecoregions data set released by The Nature Conservancy (TNC), and updated in 2008 from compilations of previous studies, classifies land into 14 major habitat types (MHTs). MHTs reflect groupings of ecoregions with similar biological, chemical, and physical characteristics. The MHTs refer to the dynamics of ecological systems and the broad habitat structures that define them. These groupings can provide a structured framework for examining and comparing the diversity of life in terrestrial systems. MHTs are broadly broken down by latitude, ranging from boreal and tundra, temperature, and tropical regions. Temperate and tropical forests are further broken down into broadleaf and conifers. These regions are also distinguished by moisture level, ranging from desert, xeric, and dry, to moist habitats. Finally, shrublands are distinguished by elevation, from high altitude montane shrublands to flooded lowlands. The ecoregions, originally developed by Olson and Dinerstein (2002), Bailey (1995), and Environment Canada (Wiken 1986), were modified by TNC. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: Land Cover
description: The Climate Change Initiative (CCI) Land Cover (LC) project of the European Space Agency (ESA) delivers consistent global LC maps at 300 m spatial resolution on an annual basis from 1992 to 2015. Each pixel value corresponds to the label of a land cover class defined based on the UN Land Cover Classification System (LCCS). This unique data set was produced thanks to the reprocessing and the interpretation of 5 different satellite missions. Baseline LC maps are generated thanks to the entire MERIS FR and RR archive from 2003 through 2012. Independently from this baseline, LC changes are detected at 1 km based on the AVHRR time series between 1992 to 1999, SPOT-VGT time series between 1999 and 2013, and PROBA-V data for years 2013, 2014, and 2015. When MERIS FR or PROBA-V time series are available, changes detected at 1 km are remapped at 300 m. The last step consists in back- and updating the 10-year baseline LC map to produce the 24 annual LC maps from 1992 to 2015. The resulting data have a total of 22 global land cover classes. For the sake of better visualization, PREPdata shows only a set of simplified classes, based on the IPCC (agriculture, forest, grassland, wetland, settlement, shrubland, sparse vegetation, bare area, water, and permanent ice and snow). PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link.

title: Areas Vulnerable to Coastal Flooding & Sea Level Rise (m)
description: The Areas Vulnerable to Coastal Flooding and Sea-Level Rise data set is prepared by Climate Central. These layers are relative to local high tide lines (mean higher high water, or MHHW). Map areas below the selected water level are displayed in blue, indicating vulnerability to flooding from combined sea-level rise, storm surge, and tides, or to permanent submergence by long-term sea-level rise. Elevation data used for parts of this map within the United States come almost entirely from ~5 m horizontal resolution digital elevation models curated and distributed by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration in its Coastal Lidar collection, derived from high-accuracy laser-rangefinding measurements. Areas outside the United States use elevation data on a roughly 90 m horizontal resolution grid derived from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration’s Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM). Local high tide level is determined using 2 data sources as well: the VDatum tidal model for the contiguous United States and a global tidal model supplied by Mark Merrifield of the University of Hawaii for the rest of the world. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: U.S. Hurricane Strikes
description: NOAA aims to provide tropical cyclone best track data in a centralized location to aid our understanding of the distribution, frequency, and intensity of tropical cyclones worldwide. These data are derived from the NOAA National Weather Service revised Atlantic hurricane database (HURDAT2) data set and the NOAA National Climatic Data Center’s International Best Track Archive for Climate Stewardship (IBTrACS) data set. Storms from 1842 to the present for the United States Atlantic coast are available. Data aquisition tools were developed as part of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Office for Coastal Management's Historical Hurricanes Tool, but contain data and information from a variety of data sources, including non-NOAA data. The strike data includes both direct and indirect hits. When the innermost core regions, or "eye," moved over a county, it was counted as a direct hit. "R" is defined as the radius of maximum winds in a hurricane (the distance in miles from the storm's center to the circle of maximum winds around the center). A county is regarded as receiving a direct hit when all or parts of a county fall within about 2R to the right and R to the left of a storm's landfall. This assumes an observer at sea looking toward shore. On average, this direct hit zone extended about 50 miles along the coastline (Rz15 miles). Of course, some hurricanes were smaller than this and some, particularly in higher latitudes, were much larger. Indirect hits are characterized by the hurricane's strength and size and on the configuration of the individual county coastline. Here, much subjectivity was necessary, often complicated by storm paths and geography. Indirect hits include those areas on either side of the direct hit zone which received hurricane force winds or tides of at least 4 to 5 feet above normal. Cases were judged individually, and many borderline situations had to be resolved. In effect, this data is useful for making general comparisons between counties, but may not represent an exact, objective count.

title: Trees in Mosaic Landscapes
description: ### Overview The trees in mosaic landscapes (TML) data maps tree extent at the ten-meter scale and enables accurate monitoring of trees in urban areas, agricultural lands, and in open canopy and dry forest ecosystems. The data extent covers 1.4 billion hectares of mosaic landscapes in Latin America and Africa. Mosaic landscapes are defined as regions that can support a wide variety of tree distributions, including sparse tree cover, scattered or clustered open canopy forests, and fragmented closed-canopy forests. The data is derived from multi-temporal convolutional neural network models applied to Sentinel optical and radar imagery. Each pixel demarcates the presence of one or more trees with canopy diameters larger than 3 meters and height greater than 5 meters. The value for each pixel represents the sigmoidal probability of detecting a tree , and can be converted to tree cover by averaging the values within a desired window size (e.g. 30 x 30 meter or half-hectare). The data relies on 3 cloud-free observations for 2020 (<97.5% average cloud cover) and less than 1% of the processing area is missing due to the lack of cloud-free observations. ### Methodology Data is generated by analyzing monthly cloud-free mosaics of Sentinel-2 optical imagery and Sentinel-1 radar imagery. We utilize the 10- and 20-meter bottom-of-atmosphere (L2A) bands from Sentinel-2 and the co-polarized vertical transmit/vertical receive (VV) and cross-polarized vertical transmit/horizontal receive (VH) imagery from Sentinel-1. The model used is a modified U-Net convolutional neural network with a temporal gated recurrent unit (GRU) encoder. The methodology is derived from [Brandt and Stolle (2020)](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/01431161.2020.1841324) with additional improvements to be detailed in a forthcoming paper. Code and model specifics can be accessed on the project [GitHub page](https://github.com/wri/sentinel-tree-cover). For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.
update_frequency_raw: The draft TML data will be finalized for the current processing area in early 2022 and will be extended across non-deserted regions in the tropics and subtropics during the latter half of 2022. A yearly or biannual change detection map is planned for 2023.

Urban Built-Up Area
description: ### Overview The Global Human Settlement (GHS) built-up dataset provides a global estimation of built-up area between 1975 and 2014. It is available for four time periods: 1975, 1975-1990, 1990-2000, and 2000-2014. Built-up areas represent any urbanized regions containing man-made structures, like buildings. The dataset is based on Landsat imaging and analyzed using a model. The data is available at 30 m, 250 m and 1 km resolution in the source dataset. The 30 m version of the data is displayed here. GHS built-up dataset was released by the European Commission's Joint Research Centre (EC JRC). This dataset provides an insight into the human presence on Earth. It is important to understand the pattern of cities' growth. It is projected that 68% of the world’s population will live in urban areas by 2050. This information can help governments create more sustainable urbanization policies and have a more long-term plan for urban growth in the future. ### Methodology The data was produced by processing 33,202 satellite images using the Symbolic Machine Learning (SML) method. Each year corresponded to a different source of Landsat data, GLS 1975, GLS 1990, GLS 2000, and ad hoc Landsat 8 collection 2013/2014. The image data records collected by different satellite sensors between 1975 and 2014 were classified and automatically selected if they corresponded to a built-up structure. The information was analyzed using the GHS built-up model. The model utilized algorithms to extract patterns and determine the spatial size of the building surface area. It analyzed knowledge from large amounts of spatial data, and the availability of open and free image data input, to identify areas of the planet with high densities of built-up areas. This dataset was an improved version from the 2015 GHS built-up dataset. It used an improved image processing workflow that allowed for the detection of more built-up areas and reduced the amount of false identifications of built-up areas in the final classification. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://ghsl.jrc.ec.europa.eu/data.php). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for water surface and land with no built-up in any epoch are also available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/cit_033a_urban_builtup_area). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

Erosion Risk
description: This layer shows the risk of erosion around the world, from low to high. Erosion and sedimentation by water involves the process of detachment, transport, and deposition of soil particles, driven by forces from raindrops and water flowing over the land surface. Because soil erosion is difficult to measure at large scales, soil erosion models are crucial estimation tools to extrapolate limited data to other localities and conditions. The Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation (RUSLE), which predicts annual soil loss from rainfall and runoff, is the most common model used at large spatial scales due to its relatively simple structure and empirical basis. The model takes into account rainfall erosivity, topography, soil erodibility, land cover and management, and conservation practices. Because the RUSLE model was developed based on agricultural plot scale and parameterized for environmental conditions in the USA, modifications of the methods and data inputs are necessary to make the equation applicable to the globe. We estimated erosion potential based on the RUSLE model, adjusted to extend its applicability to a global scale. Conservation practices and topography information were not included in this model to calculate global erosion potential, due to data limitation and their relatively minor contribution to the variation in soil erosion at the continental to global scale compared to other factors. The result of the global model was categorized into five quantiles, corresponding to low to high erosion risks. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: Travel Monitoring Analysis System (TMAS) -- U.S.
description: Location referencing information was derived from State Offices of Transportation. The attributes on the point elements of the database are used by FHWA for its Travel Monitoring and Analysis System and by State DOTs. The attributes for these databases have been intentionally limited to location referencing attributes since the core station description attribute data are contained within the Station Description Tables (SDT). There is a separate Station Description Table (SDT) for each of the station types. The attributes in the Station Description Table correspond with the Station Description Record found in Chapter 6 of the 2001 Traffic Monitoring Guide. The SDT contains the most recent stations available for each state and station type. This table was derived from files provided UTCTR by FHWA. The Station Description Table can be linked to the station shapefile via the STNNKEY field.

title: [Archived] Crop Land Area and Production
description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](54af072c-7bb5-4bb1-af84-ea7ba0b4fc22) as a replacement.**_ ### Overview The Crop Land and Production dataset shows global harvested area and production for four major crops: wheat, soybean, rice and maize. The dataset was derived from the 2005 Spatial Production Allocation Model (SPAM). The SPAM model aimed to disaggregate (downscale) national and subnational crop statistics using a variety of inputs, such as cropland surface, location of irrigated areas, crop suitability and potential yields, rural population densities, production systems characteristics and crop prices. Crop data was downscaled to a spatial resolution of 5 arc minutes. This spatial resolution is approximately 10 kilometers x 10 kilometers at the equator, but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. Together, maize, rice, soybean, and wheat account for nearly two-thirds of global agricultural calories. Global demand for these crops is rising as a result of diet shifts, rising population levels and increased biofuel demand. Increased demand for these resources will significantly affect land and resource use, climate change, political agendas and technological developments. A comprehensive understanding of the current spatial distribution of the world’s crops is necessary in order to preemptively address these effects. The Crop Land Area and Production dataset can be used to understand the extent and productivity of key global crops, which will help address food crop demand and its effects. The Crop Land Area and Production dataset was generated by the [Consultative Group on International Agricultural Research Program on Policies, Institutions, and Markets (CGIAR-PIM)](https://pim.cgiar.org/about/). CGIAR-PIM provides support for policies that help farmers improve their lives, produce nutritious and affordable foods, and protect the soil, water and biodiversity in rural landscapes. The program is led by the [International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI)](https://www.ifpri.org/about), a CGIAR-PIM research center. IFPRI provides research-based policy solutions to sustainably reduce poverty and end hunger in developing countries. The Crop Land Area and Production dataset was part of the larger SPAM dataset, which was developed for the HarvestChoice research initiative. Conducted by IFPRI, [HarvestChoice](https://www.ifpri.org/project/harvestchoice) generated knowledge products to help guide strategic investments to improve the well-being of poor people in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia through more productive and profitable farming. ### Methodology The Crop Land Area and Production dataset shows production and harvested area for global wheat, soybean, rice and maize crops. Production and harvested area were derived from crop physical area generated by the SPAM mathematical model. The SPAM model outputs were distinguished by crop production system. This was done to account for differences in resource use (i.e., type and quantity of seeds, water, labor, machinery, fertilizer and pesticides). Industrialized farming is considered to be high input and uses large amounts of outside resources. Low input and subsistence farming typically use resources directly from the farm (i.e., manure and cover crops) for crop management. The four production systems were defined by water and management type: - Irrigated – high input (I) - Rainfed – high input (H) - Rainfed – low input (L) - Rainfed – subsistence (S) The primary inputs for the SPAM were crop harvested area, production and yield statistics. This data was collected at the smallest available administrative level (i.e., region, district). Crop statistics at the national level were provided by the [United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAOSTAT)](http://www.fao.org/faostat/en/#home). Subnational statistics were drawn from these additional FAO datasets: - [the global information system on water and agriculture (AQUASTAT)](http://www.fao.org/aquastat/en/) - [AgroMaps](http://www.fao.org/land-water/land/land-governance/land-resources-planning-toolbox/category/details/en/c/1026341/) - [CountrySTAT](http://www.fao.org/in-action/countrystat/en/) Subnational crop data was also provided by the global dataset of [monthly irrigated and rainfed crop areas around the year 2000 (MIRCA2000)](https://www.uni-frankfurt.de/45218023/MIRCA), country statistics offices, published literature and expert judgments. The national and subnational crop production statistics were then allocated to 5 arc minute pixels via a cross-entropy optimization model. The cross-entropy approach quantifies the difference between two probability models and was used to minimize modeling uncertainty. The output of this model were pre-allocated physical areas for each crop and production system. The SPAM model used additional biological and economic inputs to allocate the statistics within each pixel. Input data included: - Cropland extent: Satellite imagery was used to distinguish cropland from other land types (forest, grassland, waterbodies) and delineate the geographic extent within which crop production could be allocated. Satellite imagery was provided by the [International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA-IFPRI) cropland map](https://iiasa.ac.at/web/home/research/ResearchPartners/IFPRI.en.html). The satellite imagery was upscaled from a spatial resolution of 30 arc seconds to fit the 5 arc minute resolution of the SPAM model. - Crop suitability: Crop suitability measured whether cropland met the specific temperature, moisture and soil requirements of each crop. Areas were categorized as very suitable, suitable, moderately suitable and marginally suitable using data from the [Global Agro-Ecological Zones (GAEZV3.0) dataset](https://webarchive.iiasa.ac.at/Research/LUC/GAEZ/index.htm). - Irrigated areas: Locations of areas equipped for irrigation from the [FAO’s Global Map of Irrigated Areas (GMIA 5.0)](http://www.fao.org/aquastat/en/geospatial-information/global-maps-irrigated-areas) were used to further refine production system and cropland definitions. - Crop prices: Crop prices were used to understand the location and extent of crops, based on the assumption that farmers choose to grow crops that generate the highest revenue. Crop prices were based on FAOSTAT Gross Production Value data from 2004-2006. - Market accessibility: Rural population density was used as a proxy for market accessibility, a factor that affects a farmer’s decision to plant a crop. Population density from the [Global Rural and Urban Mapping Project, Version 1 (GRUMPv1)](https://sedac.ciesin.columbia.edu/data/collection/grump-v1) was used to classify pixels as rural or urban at a spatial resolution of 30 arc seconds. This data was aggregated and reclassified to the 5 arc minute pixel resolution of the SPAM model. - Potential yield: Crop yield is the amount of crop grown per area of land. Potential crop yield information was derived from GAEZ data and used to further direct the allocation optimization process. - Cropping intensity and multiple crops: The cropping intensity parameter accounted for the fact that more than one crop can be grown simultaneously on a plot and that crops can be rotated throughout the year. The SPAM model allocated the crops within each administrative unit with pre-allocated crop statistics within a country using an iterative cross-entropy optimization approach in the [General Algebraic Modeling Software (GAMS)](https://www.gams.com/). The model worked by iteratively minimizing the error between the pre-allocated shares of physical area and the allocated shares of physical area in each pixel. Harvested area and production were calculated from crop physical area in each pixel. Physical area was converted to harvested area using the cropping intensity variable. Total harvested area of each crop in each pixel was calculated by summing estimates across the four production systems. Production was calculated by multiplying harvested area with yield (the amount of production per harvested area in kilograms/hectare). Total production was the sum of production from all of a crop’s production systems and was reported in metric tons. For the full documentation, please see the [SPAM 2005 Technical Documentation](https://dataverse.harvard.edu/dataset.xhtml?persistentId=doi:10.7910/DVN/DHXBJX). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Annual Renewable Energy Capacity
description: ### Overview This dataset shows national-level electricity generation capacity from renewable energy technologies between 2000 and 2019. Renewable energy capacity measures the maximum amount of electricity that could instantaneously be produced by the existing renewable energy sources within a country. Renewable energy is defined as energy that comes from natural resources that are continually restored. In this dataset, renewable energy sources include wind, solar, hydropower, biofuels, municipal waste, biogas, geothermal, and marine energy. Transitioning to renewable energy technologies can be beneficial to the economy and human health, as well as help reduce climate change. Electricity generation is one of the largest [sources of greenhouse gas emissions](https://www.epa.gov/ghgemissions/sources-greenhouse-gas-emissions), directly contributing to climate change. Transitioning to renewable energy technologies can help reduce our greenhouse gas emissions and be part of the solution to addressing climate change. Renewable energy production also produces less air pollution, which is linked to a number of health concerns, than most fossil fuel energy sources. Furthermore, these technologies provide a reliable source of energy and help diversify energy portfolios, reducing the potential of energy scarcity. This dataset was produced by the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) and is updated annually. ### Methodology Data has been obtained from a variety of sources, including an IRENA questionnaire, official national statistics, industry association reports, other reports and news articles. Renewable power generation capacity is measured as the maximum net generating capacity of power plants and other installations that use renewable energy sources to produce electricity. For most countries and technologies, the data reflects the capacity installed and connected at the end of the calendar year. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows IRENA data on [renewable energy generation](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/1ed420e2-9283-4ced-b7b6-d5268be7a324). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional granularity regarding different types of renewable technologies is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. title: Forest Greenhouse Gas Net Flux
description: ### Overview Net forest carbon flux represents the net exchange of carbon between forests and the atmosphere between 2001 and 2020, calculated as the balance between carbon emitted by forests and removed by (or sequestered by) forests during the model period (megagrams CO2e ha-1). Net carbon flux is calculated by subtracting average annual gross removals from average annual gross emissions in each modeled pixel; negative values are where forests were net sinks of carbon and positive values are where forests were net sources of carbon between 2001 and 2020. Net fluxes are calculated following IPCC Guidelines for national greenhouse gas inventories in each pixel where forests existed in 2000 or were established between 2000 and 2012 according to the Global Forest Change tree cover change data of Hansen et al. (2013). This layer reflects the cumulative net flux during the model period (2001-2020) and must be divided by 19 to obtain average annual net flux; net flux values cannot be assigned to individual years of the model. This net flux layer is part of the forest carbon flux model described in Harris et al. (2021). This paper introduces a geospatial monitoring framework for estimating global forest carbon fluxes which can assist governments and non-government actors with tracking greenhouse gas fluxes from forests and decreasing emissions or increasing removals by forests. All input layers were resampled to a common resolution of 0.00025 x 0.00025 degrees each to match Hansen et al. (2013). Net flux is available for download in two different area units over the model duration: 1) megagrams of CO2e ha-1, and 2) megagrams of CO2e pixel-1. The first is appropriate for visualizing (mapping) net flux because it represent the density of carbon fluxes per hectare. The second is appropriate for calculating the net flux in an area of interest (AOI) because the values of the pixels in the AOI can be summed to obtain the total carbon flux for that area. The values in the latter were calculated by adjusting the net flux per hectare by the size of each pixel, which varies by latitude. When estimating net flux occurring over a defined number of years between 2001 and 2020, divide the provided values by the model duration and then multiply by the number of years in the period of interest.

title: Climate Hazard Indicators (Annual maximum temperatures - mean) Historical and SSP scenarios - Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu
description: ### Overview The dataset includes five major climatic indicators viz. annual values for minimum temperature (℃), maximum temperature (℃), mean temperature (℃), total precipitation (mm/year), and the number of rainy days (represented as integers) for two Indian states, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. It features decadal averages from 2020-2100 for Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs), including SSP5-8.5, which reflects a high emissions scenario, and SSP2-4.5, representing moderate challenges to both mitigation and adaptation. Additionally, the dataset provides historical data for all the five indicators averaged over the period from 2005 to 2014. ### Methodology **Pre-Processing**: The decadal time periods were labeled as follows: 2020-2029 as 2020, 2030-2039 as 2030, 2040-2049 as 2040, 2050-2059 as 2050, 2060-2069 as 2060, 2070-2079 as 2070, 2080-2089 as 2080, and 2090-2099 as 2090. **Layers of interest**: Annual averages of minimum temperature (℃), maximum temperature (℃), mean temperature (℃), Annual total precipitation (mm/year), and the annual total number of rainy days (represented as integers). **Data**: The ERA5 reanalysis dataset (ECMWF 2022), a satellite data product of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts with a spatial resolution of 31 kilometers (km), is used as a reference dataset. The ensemble of downscaled daily time series outputs from global climate models (GCMs). These time series include the historical years covered by the observation time series as well as the specified future years of interest. We have used the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 product, which includes outputs from 34 Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) models at approximately 25 km spatial resolution. ### Estimation Methods Out of the 35 models, we select the top 3 climate models that perform best for a specific weather variable in a particular geographic region, and present the ensemble mean of these models. The ERA5 dataset is used as a reference, and the comparison is made for the historical period between 1980 and 2014. After selecting the models, we apply a calibration/bias correction procedure to the future time series of the models. This involves aligning the model's frequency distribution with the historical data by shifting the percentiles of the model's distribution. For instance, if the 20th percentile of the model data corresponds to the 30th percentile of the observations, then the 30th percentile of the calibrated model data will match the 20th percentile of the uncalibrated model data. For the full documentation, please see the source methodology at Wong, T., and P Switzer. 2023. 'Estimating future local climate hazard probabilities.' Technical Note. Washington, DC: World Resources Institute. Available online at: doi.org/10.46830/writn.22.00074.v2. ### Description of the Layers **Annual Maximum Temperature (℃)**: The daily maximum temperature data for each year is extracted and averaged to calculate the yearly average maximum temperature. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years. **Annual Minimum Temperature (℃)**: The daily minimum temperature data for each year is extracted and averaged to calculate the yearly average minimum temperature. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years. **Annual Mean Temperature (℃)**: The daily mean temperature is calculated by averaging the daily minimum and maximum temperatures. The annual mean temperature is obtained by averaging the daily mean temperatures over the course of a year. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years. **Annual Total Precipitation (mm/year)**: The daily precipitation values are summed over the entire year to calculate the annual total precipitation. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years. **Annual Rainy Days (represented as integers)**: A rainy day is defined as a day with precipitation exceeding 2.5 mm (as per the India Meteorological Department). The total number of rainy days in a year is calculated by summing the rainy days throughout the year. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years. ### Visualizing the Data The data is provided at a 25-km resolution and is presented as a raster with a time slider with a separate layer for each variable. The values are visualized using a gradient based on the selected year in the slider, ranging from lighter shade (indicating low values) to darker shade (representing higher values). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source

title: U.S. Drought Monitor
description: The U.S. Drought Monitor, established in 1999, is a weekly map of drought conditions produced jointly by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, the U.S. Department of Agriculture, and the National Drought Mitigation Center at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln. The U.S. Drought Monitor website is hosted and maintained by the drought center. The weekly maps are released at 8:30 a.m. Eastern Standard Time each Thursday and are assessments of past conditions based on data through 7 a.m. Eastern time (8 a.m. Eastern Daylight Time) the preceding Tuesday. The map is based on measurements of climatic, hydrologic and soil conditions as well as reported impacts and observations from more than 350 contributors around the country. Eleven climatologists from the partner organizations take turns serving as the lead author each week. The authors examine all the data and use their best judgment to reconcile any differences among sources. PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set. Seychelles Geologic Events
description: This dataset displays a set of geologic events on the Seychellois island of Mahé from 1862 through 2011. An assessment of area-specific risk for landslides, flooding, and rockfalls was conducted in 2011 as part of the Sustainable Land Management (SLM) project. The SLM report, Compilation of Information in View of Developing a Geological Risk Map of the Islands of Mahé, Praslin, and La Digue, was shared with the researchers by the Seychellois Department of Risk and Disaster Management and provided the underlying data of this map. Historical data including the event type, date, location, and cause of each geologic event was extracted from the report to create these data points. As defined in the source document, landslides are the downslope movement of soil, rock, and organic materials under the effects of gravity. Landslides depicted in this layer represent mass movements in which the material on a zone of weakness is separated from the more stable underlying material. Rockfalls are sudden and rapid processes by which a rock detaches from a slope and descends by falling, bouncing, or rolling. They typically occur along cliffs or steep slopes and result in the displacement of large rocks, sometimes landing on roads or built structures. Rockfalls are strongly influenced by gravity, mechanical weathering, and interstitial weather such as regular intervals of rain. Debris falls are the processes by which a combination of soil, rock, mud, and organic material detaches from a steep slope and descends by falling, bouncing, or rolling as a conglomerate. They typically occur suddenly along cliffs or steep slopes, resulting in displaced materials that can land on roads or built structures. Debris falls are strongly influenced by gravity, mechanical weathering, and interstitial weather such as regular intervals of rain. Debris flow (commonly called a mudslide) is the process by which masses of loose soil, fragmented rocks, mud, organic matter, and water moves down a slope under the influence of gravity. While a debris flow mobilizes as a conglomerate, the components move independently. Source areas of debris flows are typically adorned with steep gullies. Debris flows deposit materials in fan-like shapes at the foot of the slope or accumulate where an obstruction - like a built structure - is encountered. Debris flows are commonly caused by intense surface water flow due to heavy rain that erodes material on a slope. Slope failures are abrupt processes in which a very steep slope collapses due to weakened self-retainability, or the ability to uphold materials. Slope failures typically occur along slopes that are steeper than landslides and are characterized by smaller-scale movement than landslides. Materials displaced as a result of slope failure accumulate at the bottom of the slope. Slope failures are commonly triggered by heavy rain or earthquakes.

description: The World Database on Protected Areas (WDPA) is the most comprehensive global spatial data set on marine and terrestrial protected areas available. Protected area data are provided via Protected Planet, the online interface for the WDPA. The WDPA is a joint initiative of the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) and the UN Environment Programme's World Conservation Monitoring Centre (UNEP-WCMC) to compile spatially referenced information about protected areas. The data are provided as shapefiles and updated monthly. Not all protected areas receive the same degree of protection. While some have strict guidelines designed to preserve intact ecosystems, others allow for sustainable land use, often including limited resource extraction. In addition, not all countries use the same terminology when designating a protected area. Universal management categories are designated by the IUCN that stipulate the level of protection for most protected areas. These categories are defined as follows: (Ia) Strict Nature Reserves: protected areas designed to preserve biodiversity and all geological features. Limited human use (e.g., scientific study, education) is allowed and carefully monitored. Strict nature reserves are often used to understand the impact of indirect human disturbance (e.g., burning fossil fuels) because of the area’s high level of preservation. (Ib) Wilderness Areas: protected areas managed to preserve ecosystem processes with limited human use. Wilderness areas cannot contain modern infrastructure (e.g., a visitor’s center), but they allow for local indigenous groups to maintain subsistence lifestyles. These areas are often established to restore disturbed environments. (II) National Parks: protected areas designed to preserve large-scale ecosystems and support human visitation. With conservation as a priority, these areas allow infrastructure and contribute to the local economy by providing opportunities for environmental educational and recreation. (III) National Monuments or Features: areas established to protect a specific natural feature (e.g., cave, grove) or human-made monument with significant historical, spiritual, or environmental importance and the immediate surroundings. Accordingly, natural monuments or features are typically smaller in area and have high human impact resulting from visitor traffic. (IV) Habitat and Species Management Areas: areas designed to conserve specific wildlife populations and/or habitats. Habitat and species management areas often exist within a larger ecosystem or protected area and are carefully managed (e.g., through hunting abatement or habitat restoration) to conserve a target species or habitat. (V) Protected Landscapes and Seascapes: protected areas with ecological, biological, or cultural importance that have been shaped by human use of the landscape. Protected landscapes and seascapes typically cover entire bodies of land or ocean and allow for a number of for-profit activities (e.g., ecotourism) in accordance with the region’s management plan. (VI) Protected Areas with Sustainable Use of Natural Resources: areas designed to manage natural resources and uphold the livelihoods of surrounding communities. These regions have a low level of human occupation, small-scale developments (i.e., not industrial), and part of the landscape in its natural condition. PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link.
