Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature U.S. (RCP4.5)
description: The Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average minimum temperature at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average minimum temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the minimum temperature between the years 1985 and 2015. Average minimum temperature projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The change in annual average minimum temperature is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.25°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference. The annual average minimum temperature for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by averaging all daily minimum temperature data over a given year. The average annual minimum temperatures were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in annual average minimum temperature. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average minimum temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the annual minimum temperatures between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

title: Food Security and Vulnerability
description: The World Food Programme mobile Vulnerability Analysis and Mapping unit uses phone-based surveys to create a Food Consumption Score for regions at risk of needing food aid or market assistance. Household food consumption is best measured in kilocalories consumed, but these data are difficult to obtain at scale. The WFP mVAM uses the FCS survey to ask households which types of food they have eaten over the past 7 days. These responses are used to create the FCS, which can then be used to prioritize budgets to help high-need populations. The FCS survey is used as a proxy for actual caloric intake and diet quality. It is based on dietary diversity, food frequency, and the relative importance of different food groups. It uses a standardized and transparent methodology to allow for interregional and intertemporal comparability of survey results. The mVAM uses a mobile survey to ask households on how many of the past 7 days they have eaten various food items. Individual food items are grouped into 9 main food groups: cereals, starchy tubers, and roots; legumes and nuts; meat, fish, poultry, and eggs; vegetables (including green leaves); fruit; oils and fats; milk and dairy products; sugar/sweets; and condiments. Food group totals are calculated by summing the answers for the individual food items that comprise the group, each of which range from 0 to 7 days. These food group sums are then multiplied by a factor representing the nutritional importance of the food group. The raw FCS is calculated by summing the weighted food group scores. Standardized thresholds are recommend to classify households into 1 of 3 Food Consumption Groups (FCGs) based on their raw FCS: poor, borderline, or acceptable. Additional classification methods, using clustering techniques such as Principle Component Analysis, can be used which incorporate all of each household's survey responses to group them into 1 of 3 consumption profiles. Expert analysts can then review the 3 resulting groups and determine which represent the poor, borderline, and acceptable FCGs. These classifications can be compared with the raw FCS threshold classification technique to evaluate how well they agree. In most cases they should agree quite well. If they do not, this is motivation for additional investigation to better understand consumption dynamics in the region. The FCS can be calculated for both Comprehensive Food Security and Vulnerability Analyses (CFSVA) and Emergency Food Security Assessments (EFSA). The former are applied in situations where the WFP has a long-term presence and time to conduct detailed analyses; the latter are applied in emergency situations where information is needed immediately to direct life-saving support. A blog about mVAM's work: http://mvam.org A full discussion of the methodology used to construct the FCS is available here: http://documents.wfp.org/stellent/groups/public/documents/manual_guide_proced/wfp197216.pdf Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.

title: [Archived] Projected Cooling Degree Days
description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](6fa000b5-8d91-46c8-8502-07427bc5eafc) as a replacement.**_ A cooling degree day (CDD) is defined as the number of degrees that a day's mean temperature is above 65°F. For example, if a day's average temperature is 80°F, the CDD would be 15. If a second day's average temperature were the same, the combined CDD for those two days would be 30. CDDs are often used as a proxy to estimate heating and cooling needs in buildings. While degree days can be calculated using any reference temperature, this data set uses 65°F (18.3°C), a common threshold for climate indicators, and a temperature at which people are generally comfortable. This indicator is useful in determining energy demands resulting from cooling in different regions and assessing projected climate change impacts. This Cooling Degree Days data set shows projected change in CDDs in 2051-2080, relative to 1971-2000 under RCP 8.5, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5 from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on Resource Watch. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm. Resource Watch shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Learn More link. For access to the processed data set, please contact the PREPdata team at https://www.prepdata.org/. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: Air Quality: Nitrogen Dioxide (NO₂) Modeled 5-day Forecast
description: ### Overview This dataset shows forecasted nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) concentrations at Earth’s surface, modeled by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Goddard Earth Observing System Composition Forecast (GEOS-CF). NO₂ is a highly reactive air pollutant, produced by fossil fuel combustion from power plants and gasoline-burning vehicles. NO₂ is used as the indicator for the larger group of nitrogen oxides (NOx), which includes nitrous acid and nitric acid. NO₂ emissions contribute to the [formation of smog](https://www.environment.gov.au/protection/publications/factsheet-nitrogen-dioxide-no2) and can significantly harm human health. According to the [U.S. Environmental Protection Agency](https://www.epa.gov/no2-pollution/basic-information-about-no2), breathing air with a high concentration of NO₂ can irritate airways in the respiratory system and long-term exposures can contribute to asthma development. Even exposure to elevated NO₂ concentrations over short periods can aggravate respiratory diseases, particularly asthma, leading to respiratory symptoms (such as coughing, wheezing, or difficulty breathing), hospital admissions, and visits to emergency rooms. People with asthma as well as children and the elderly are generally at greater risk for the health effects of NO₂. Resource Watch also shows GEOS-CF forecasts for [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ebc079a1-51d8-4622-ba25-d8f3b4fcf8b3) and [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/645fe192-28db-4949-95b9-79d898f4226b). The GEOS-CF system runs once a day and produces a global, near-real-time forecast up to five days into the future at 15-minute and one-hour time intervals. The data has a global coverage at a resolution of 25 kilometers x 25 kilometers. GEOS-CF also creates global forecasts for a variety of other air quality indicators. GEOS-CF was developed by NASA's Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO). You can find forecasted concentrations for each compound on the GMAO website. ### Methodology The GEOS-CF model provides analysis on the composition of a range of air pollutants including PM2.5, O₃, and NO₂. This model is driven by the GEOS weather forecasting system and the GEOS-Chem atmospheric chemistry model. To produce estimates of aerosol concentrations, the GEOS-CF model runs two aerosol schemes: the GEOS-Chem aerosol mechanism (GCC) and the Goddard Chemistry, Aerosol, Radiation, and Transport (GOCART) module to simulate the effects of aerosols in the atmosphere. The GOCART aerosols are constrained by satellite observed aerosol optical depth, while the GCC aerosols are purely model derived. The PM2.5 data shown on Resource Watch is produced by the GOCART module. All emissions modeling for GEOS-Chem is handled by the [NASA-Harvard emissions component (HEMCO)](https://www.geosci-model-dev.net/7/1409/2014/gmd-7-1409-2014.html), a stand-alone software component for calculating emissions in global atmospheric models. Anthropogenic emissions are acquired as monthly averages from the [HTAPv2.2](https://www.atmos-chem-phys.net/15/11411/2015/) and [RETRO](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdf/10.1029/2007GB003031) emissions inventories. The monthly averages are broken down into hourly values by sector-specific factors. Emissions of CO ([Oda et al., 2017](https://www.earth-syst-sci-data.net/10/87/2018/)) and SO₂ ([Liu et al., 2018](https://www.atmos-chem-phys.net/18/16571/2018/)) are scaled using a factor based on satellite data. Emissions from biomass burning are taken from [Quick Fire Emissions Database (QFEDv2.5)](https://gmao.gsfc.nasa.gov/pubs/docs/Darmenov796.pdf), volcanic emissions of SO₂ are from [CARN (2019)](https://disc.gsfc.nasa.gov/datasets/MSVOLSO2L4_3/summary), and other natural emissions are taken from various sources. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://gmao.gsfc.nasa.gov/pubs/docs/Knowland1159.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows GEOS-CF forecasts for [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ebc079a1-51d8-4622-ba25-d8f3b4fcf8b3) and [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/645fe192-28db-4949-95b9-79d898f4226b). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional forecasted data for other compounds, times, and levels of the atmosphere is also produced by GEOS-CF. description: Ecoregions displayed by biome, created by RESOLVE, show the 14 terrestrial biomes of the world. Seven are forested and seven are not forested. Plant communities in the same biome can appear quite similar in structure but contain very different sets of species. Ecoregions represent geographically distinct assemblages of biodiversity whose boundaries encompass the space required to sustain key ecological processes. Biomes represent major ecological communities of organisms that are adapted to a particular climatic or environmental condition on a large geographic area in which they occur. The temporal coverage of this map is 2017 and the spatial coverage is global. An analysis was conducted across the biomes identifying the ecoregions within them that are protected, and to what extent. This RESOLVE Ecoregions map is an updated version of the Terrestrial Ecoregions of the World from Olson et. al (2001). The map is based upon more than 100 years of biogeographic scholarship, including extensive field investigations. For this reason, ecoregions reflect the on-the-ground distribution of regional biotas differently than do biogeographic units derived from parametric approaches. Please see publication for more detail on the methodology and datasets used for the making of this map. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: Agricultural Exposure to Water Stress
description: This map of baseline water stress in major crop producing areas was created by WRI's Aqueduct program as part of the Water Risk Atlas, an online mapping tool that displays various aspects of water-related risks. The map displays the major crop producing areas for 13 major commodity crops (cocoa, coffee, cotton, maize, oats, oil palm, oranges, canola, rice, rubber, soybeans, sugarcane, and wheat) and 9 crop groups (cereals, fiber crops, fodder crops, fruits, oil crops, legumes, roots and tubers, sugar crops, and tree nuts), and the levels of water stress (low, low to medium, medium to high, high, and extremely high) experienced in these major crop-producing areas. Baseline water stress refers to the annual water withdrawals (municipal, industrial, and agricultural) expressed as a percentage of the total annual available flow. Higher values indicate more competition among users. Arid areas with low water use are shown in gray but scored as high stress when calculating aggregated scores. Baseline water stress is calculated by dividing water withdrawals (2010) by mean available blue water (1950-2008). Areas with available blue water and water withdrawal less than 0.03 and 0.012/m2 respectively are coded as “arid and low water use." Crop production in each category is computed by overlaying gridded crop production data, which was pulled from 2 articles in Global Biogeochemical Cycle (2008), "Farming the Planet: 1. Geographic Distribution of Global Agricultural Lands in the Year 2000" and "Farming the Planet: 2. Geographic Distribution of Crop Areas, Yields, Physiological Types, and Net Primary Production in the Year 2000." The authors of these studies identified croplands and crop production using a high-resolution satellite-derived land cover data set and agricultural inventory data to derive a global map of croplands. description: The International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI) created the 2017 Global Hunger Index (GHI) to highlight successes and failures in hunger reduction and provide insights into the drivers of hunger. By raising awareness and understanding of regional and country differences in hunger, the GHI aims to trigger actions to reduce hunger. Hunger is defined as the distress associated with lack of food. The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) defines food deprivation, or undernourishment, as the consumption of food that is not sufficient to provide the minimum amount of dietary energy that each individual requires to live a healthy and productive life, given his or her sex, age, stature, and physical activity level. The GHI is built on several national-level statistics sourced from the FAO, the World Health Organization (WHO), the World Bank Group, the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF), and when necessary the authors' estimates. The GHI uses 4 indicators: (1) the proportion of undernourished in the population (%); (2) the prevalence of wasting in children under 5 years (%); (3) the prevalence of stunting in children under 5 years (%); and (4) the under-5 mortality rate (%). Once obtained, values for each of these indicators are standardized. A weighted sum of these standardized values equals the GHI score. This calculation results in GHI scores on a 100-point scale where 0 is the best score (no hunger) and 100 the worst. In practice, neither of these extremes is reached. A value of 100 would signify that a country's undernourishment, child wasting, child stunting, and child mortality levels each exactly meet the thresholds set slightly above the highest levels observed worldwide in recent decades. A value of zero would mean that a country had no undernourished people in the population, no children younger than 5 who were wasted or stunted, and no children who died before their 5th birthday. Countries are classified according to their GHI scores as having low, moderate, serious, alarming, or extremely alarming problems related to hunger. description: The National Elevation Dataset (NED) is the primary elevation data product of the USGS. The NED is a seamless data set with the best available raster elevation data of the coterminous United States, Alaska, Hawaii, and territorial islands. The NED is updated on a nominal two month cycle to integrate newly available, improved elevation source data. All NED data are public domain. The NED is derived from diverse source data that are processed to a common coordinate system and unit of vertical measure. NED data are distributed in geographic coordinates in units of decimal degrees, and in conformance with the North American Datum of 1983 (NAD 83). title: Electricity Consumption
description: ### Overview This dataset shows the net electricity consumption in 230 countries from 1980 to 2019. This dataset is published by the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), [which calculates net electricity consumption](https://www.eia.gov/tools/glossary/index.php?id=Net%20electricity%20consumption) as “generation + imports - exports - transmission and distribution losses.” Electricity consumption is a key indicator of the environmental impact and input costs of economic activity. The intensity of electricity consumption and the sources of energy are among the key indicators of sustainable energy, as defined by Sustainable Development Goal 7. ### Methodology EIA collected and analyzed consumption data from multiple external sources. description: The Impervious Surfaces data set was produced by National Aeronautics and Space Administration Socioeconomic Data and Applications Center (NASA SEDAC) and the Columbia University Center for International Earth Science Information Network (CIESIN). title: Uttarakhand Change in Runoff
description: The data represents annual change in the surface runoff for baseline (1981-2010) and mid-century (2021-2050) under RCP 4.5 & 8.5 emission scenarios in millimetre (mm). This data is an output from a hydrologic model, SWAT (Soil and Water Assessment Tool) which has been use to assess the impact of projected climate change on water resources. The SWAT model (Arnold et al., 1981, Neitsch et al., 2022) is a distributed parameter and continuous time simulation model. The SWAT model has been developed to predict the hydrological response of un-gauged catchments to natural inputs as well as the manmade interventions. The model (a) is physically based; (b) uses readily available inputs; (c) is computationally efficient to operate and (d) is continuous time and capable of simulating long periods for computing the effects of management changes. The major advantage of the SWAT model is that unlike the other conventional conceptual simulation models it does not require much calibration and therefore can be used on un-gauged watersheds (in fact the usual situation). The SWAT model is a long-term, continuous model for watershed simulation. It operates on a daily time step and is designed to predict the impact of land management practices on water, sediment, and agricultural chemical yields. The model is physically based, computationally efficient, and capable of simulating a high level of spatial details by allowing the watershed to be divided into a large number of sub-watersheds. Major model components include weather, hydrology, soil temperature, plant growth, nutrients, pesticides, and land management. The model has been validated for several watersheds. Input data used are terrain, landuse, soil, daily weather data (rainfall, maximum and minimum temperature, wind speed,, relative humidity and wind speed), cropping pattern, reservoirs and any man made structure with their characteristics. The outputs provided by the model are very exhaustive covering all the components of water balance spatially and temporally. The sub components of the water balance that are more significant and were used for analyses include: • Precipitation. • Total flow (Water yield) consisting of surface runoff, lateral and base flow. • Actual evapotranspiration (Actual ET). • Base flow. • Ground water recharge. description: These data were created as part of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Office for Coastal Management's efforts to create an online mapping viewer depicting potential lake levels for the United States Great Lakes. The purpose of the mapping viewer is to provide coastal managers and scientists with a preliminary look at potential impacts. The viewer is a screening-level tool that uses nationally consistent data sets and analyses. Data and maps provided can be used at several scales to help gauge trends and prioritize actions for different scenarios. The map illustrates approximate shoreline locations and depths based on a "bathtub" modelling approach and does not account for erosion, subsidence, or future construction. Water levels are shown as they would appear during calm conditions, without wind-driven effects. Water levels are referenced to both the International Great Lakes Datum of 1985 (IGLD85) and the selected lake’s long-term average water level (since 1918).

title: Annual Internal Displacement from Natural Disasters
description: ### Overview This dataset tracks the number of people who have been internally displaced due to natural disasters worldwide each year. “Internal displacement” refers to the forced movement of people within the country that they live in. Millions of people are forced to flee their homes each year due to conflict, violence, development projects, disasters, and climate change and remain displaced within their countries of residence. Internally displaced persons (IDPs) can include both citizens and other habitual residents of the country, such as stateless persons. IDPs from natural disasters may have been displaced by the following types of events: - Geophysical - earthquakes, mass movements, volcanic activity - Meteorological - storms, extreme temperatures - Hydrological - flooding, landslides, wave action - Climatological - wildfires Some of the typical needs and protection risks that arise in internal displacement include family separation, loss of documentation, loss of property, and further exposure to the risk of continued displacement. This dataset is produced by the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre (IDMC) with the aim of informing policy and operational decisions in order to reduce the risk of future displacement and improve the lives of IDPs worldwide. Resource Watch also shows IDMC estimates of the number of people displaced annually due to [conflict](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore?zoom=3&lat=-2.110674954311376&lng=7.456691250000007&basemap=dark&labels=light&layers=%255B%257B%2522dataset%2522%253A%25226974833b-004e-4b24-bdbc-ffbb779c1496%2522%252C%2522opacity%2522%253A1%252C%2522layer%2522%253A%2522cb5daeb3-80ef-4e6e-8ca8-5ed0d6170b3b%2522%257D%255D&page=1&sort=most-viewed&sortDirection=-1) at the national level, as well as [recent internal displacement from conflict, natural disasters, and development](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore?zoom=3&lat=-2.110674954311376&lng=7.456691250000007&basemap=dark&labels=light&layers=%255B%257B%2522dataset%2522%253A%2522d2f6245d-5b9b-4508-874b-d42a2be7d058%2522%252C%2522opacity%2522%253A1%252C%2522layer%2522%253A%25222059a368-b4f1-4c30-b874-b41e49c3c5e4%2522%257D%255D&page=1&sort=relevance&sortDirection=-1&search=soc.062c), which are monitored in near real-time and displayed on an event-by-event basis. ### Methodology lDMC monitors displacements due to natural disasters on an event-by-event basis. At the end of the year, it reports the total number of people who were displaced in each country. For each event, information from a wide variety of different sources is compiled, generating the most comprehensive and reliable displacement estimate. These sources include national and subnational government authorities, UN agencies and other international organizations, related global databases, civil society organizations, news media outlets, and other entities. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://www.internal-displacement.org/database/methodology). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Average Low Temperature
description: Annual average low temperature, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

title: Urban Heat Island Effect
description: The Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect represents the relatively higher temperatures found in urban areas compared to surrounding rural areas owing to higher proportions of impervious surfaces and the release of waste heat from vehicles and heating and cooling systems. Paved surfaces and built structures tend to absorb shortwave radiation from the sun and release long-wave radiation after a lag of a few hours. The Global Urban Heat Island Data Set, 2013, estimates the land surface temperature in urban areas in degrees Celsius (average summer daytime maximum and average summer nighttime minimum) as well as the difference between those temperatures and the temperatures in surrounding rural areas, defined as a 10 km buffer around the urban extent. Urban extents are from SEDAC’s Global Rural-Urban Mapping Project, Version 1 (GRUMPv1), and land surface temperatures are from SEDAC’s Global Summer Land Surface Temperature (LST) Grids, 2013, which are derived from the Aqua Level-3 Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS), Version 5, global daytime and nighttime Land Surface Temperature (LST) 8-day composite data (MYD11A2). For most regions, the UHI data set provides the average daytime maximum (1:30 p.m. overpass) and average nighttime minimum (1:30 a.m. overpass) temperatures in urban and rural areas, and the urban-rural temperature differences, derived from LST data representing a 40-day time span during July-August (Julian days 185-224) in the Northern Hemisphere and January-February (Julian days 001-040) in the Southern Hemisphere. title: Ocean Phosphate Concentration
description: ### Overview This dataset shows global daily and monthly mean phosphate (PO₄) concentrations in seawater from the surface to 5.1 meters in depth. The data are a product of the Global Ocean and Biogeochemistry Analysis system, a global biogeochemical simulation using the [PISCES model](https://www.nemo-ocean.eu/framework/components/engines) and are displayed at a 0.25° by 0.25° resolution. Nutrients, such as nitrogen and phosphorus, are essential for plant and animal growth and nourishment, but the overabundance of these nutrients can be toxic to aquatic organisms. Phosphorous, in the form of phosphate, is naturally abundant in the environment, but high concentrations in water are usually an indicator of pollution.The [main sources of phosphorus pollution](https://www.wri.org/our-work/project/eutrophication-and-hypoxia/sources-eutrophication) are agriculture nutrient sources. Phosphorus, which binds to the soil, is generally lost through soil erosion from agricultural lands, but can also originate from chemical fertilizer run-off, manure from cattle farms, and aquaculture operations. Other sources of phosphorus contamination in seawater include fossil fuel combustion and wastewater. Phosphorus flows from rivers in streams into the ocean, where it disrupts the nutrient balance in marine systems and causes overstimulation of growth of aquatic plants and algae. Excessive growth of these organisms can use up dissolved oxygen as they decompose and block light to deeper waters. This process is known as [eutrophication](https://www.wri.org/our-work/project/eutrophication-and-hypoxia/impacts). If enough oxygen is removed the water can become hypoxic, where there is not enough oxygen to sustain life. This removal of oxygen creates an oxygen “dead zone.” The [Copernicus Marine Service](https://marine.copernicus.eu/) is the marine component of the Copernicus Programme of the European Union. It provides free, regular and systematic authoritative information on the state of the ocean, on a global and regional scale. It is funded by the European Commission (EC) and implemented by [Mercator-Ocean International](https://www.mercator-ocean.fr/). It is designed to serve policy and commitments related to Ocean Governance, to cater for the needs of society at large for global ocean knowledge and to boost the Blue Economy across all maritime sectors by providing free-of-charge state-of-the-art ocean data and information. ### Methodology The data shown are based on the PISCES biogeochemical model available on the [Nucleus for European Modelling of the Ocean (NEMO)](https://www.nemo-ocean.eu/) modelling platform. The model includes 24 predictor variables and simulates biogeochemical cycles of oxygen, carbon, and the main nutrients controlling phytoplankton growth (nitrate, ammonium, phosphate, silicic acid, and iron). Mean nutrient concentrations are interpolated on a standard regular grid in NetCDF format. The output product is validated by comparing systematically the biogeochemical modeled fields with available observations datasets. The data isdisplayed with a 1/4 degree horizontal resolution with regular longitude/latitude equirectangular projection. For the full documentation and additional information about the PISCES model, please see the source [methodology](http://marine.copernicus.eu/documents/QUID/CMEMS-GLO-QUID-001-028.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows daily and monthly nitrate concentration averaged from a depth of 0 to 5.1 meters. CMEMS provides 50 vertical levels covering a depth profile of 0 to 5500 meters from the surface. Resource Watch also shows CMEMS averages for [nitrates](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/92327c78-a473-402b-8edf-409869823216) and [dissolved oxygen](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/877cdf39-5536-409c-bcba-2220e1b72796). Additional biogeochemical fields for chlorophyll concentration, silicate, dissolved iron, primary production, phytoplankton, pH, and surface partial pressure of carbon dioxide are also included in the Global Ocean and Biogeochemistry Analysis and Forecast system. title: Madhya Pradesh Change in Evapotranspiration
description: The data represents projected change in the annual evapotranspiration from baseline (1981-2010) towards mid-century (2021-2050) in percentage. This data is an output from a hydrologic model, SWAT (Soil and Water Assessment Tool) which has been use to assess the impact of projected climate change on water resources.The SWAT model (Arnold et al., 1981, Neitsch et al., 2022) is a distributed parameter and continuous time simulation model. The SWAT model has been developed to predict the hydrological response of un-gauged catchments to natural inputs as well as the manmade interventions. The model (a) is physically based; (b) uses readily available inputs; (c) is computationally efficient to operate and (d) is continuous time and capable of simulating long periods for computing the effects of management changes. The major advantage of the SWAT model is that unlike the other conventional conceptual simulation models it does not require much calibration and therefore can be used on un-gauged watersheds (in fact the usual situation). The SWAT model is a long-term, continuous model for watershed simulation. It operates on a daily time step and is designed to predict the impact of land management practices on water, sediment, and agricultural chemical yields. The model is physically based, computationally efficient, and capable of simulating a high level of spatial details by allowing the watershed to be divided into a large number of sub-watersheds. Major model components include weather, hydrology, soil temperature, plant growth, nutrients, pesticides, and land management. The model has been validated for several watersheds. Input data used are terrain, landuse, soil, daily weather data (rainfall, maximum and minimum temperature, wind speed, relative humidity and wind speed), cropping pattern, reservoirs and any man made structure with their characteristics. The outputs provided by the model are very exhaustive covering all the components of water balance spatially and temporally. The sub components of the water balance that are more significant and were used for analyses include: • Precipitation. • Total flow (Water yield) consisting of surface runoff, lateral and base flow. • Actual evapotranspiration (Actual ET). • Base flow. • Ground water recharge. description: ### Overview The Volcano Eruptions dataset shows the location of currently active and historically active volcanoes since the Holocene Epoch. The Holocene Epoch is a geological time period that began over 10,000 years ago. This dataset was created as a way of better understanding Earth's active volcanoes and their eruptions. Volcanoes were a key component in forming the landscapes we see today and in the present time they can have serious impacts for people living in close proximity to them. Understanding active volcanoes, their trends, and how to predict them serves as a way of protecting people and understanding how the Earth was formed. The data is taken from the Volcanoes of the World database, which is part of the Global Volcanism Program (GVP) run by the Smithsonian Institution. The mission of GVP is to document, understand, and disseminate information about global volcanic activity. ### Methodology The Volcanoes of the World database was created and is continually updated by GVP with information from organizations around the world. During the early stages of an eruption anywhere in the world GVP acts as a clearinghouse of reports, data, and imagery. After GVP staff verifies the information, it is added to the Volcanoes of the World database. The database is made available to the public and updated approximately every 1-3 months. Projected Extreme Heat Days U.S. (RCP8.5)
description: The Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in the average number of days of extreme heat at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. An extreme heat day is a day where the maximum temperature is greater than the 99th percentile maximum temperature during the baseline period. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of extreme heat days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual number of extreme heat days between the years 1985 and 2015. Temperature projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. Positive values indicate that the number of extreme heat days is increasing, while negative values indicate that the number is decreasing. The dataset is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and the resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. In particular, an increased quantity of extreme heat days can lead to human and ecosystem threats caused by more frequent, more intense, and longer heat waves. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference. The average number of extreme heat days for each year, climate model, and scenario were calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting the daily maximum temperature values for a given year and summing the number of days where the maximum temperature was greater than the 99th percentile temperature during the baseline period. The number of extreme heat days were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in extreme heat days. Positive values indicate that the number of extreme heat days is increasing, while negative values indicate that the number is decreasing. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of extreme heat days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual extreme heat days between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.

title: Human Impacts on Oceans
description: The Human Impacts on Oceans data set identifies the areas of the oceans that are most- and least- impacted by human stressors. This 5 km resolution global map was created by Stanford University (Stanford), Imperial College London (Imperial), and University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB). This study considered 20 ocean ecosystem types and 19 stressors. The 19 stressors considered were artisanal fishing, 5 types of commercial fishing (pelagic vs. demersal, high vs. lowbycatch, destructive of habitat vs. nondestructive), commercial shipping, inorganic pollution, organic pollution, nutrient pollution, ocean-based pollution, light pollution, invasive species, 4 climate-change stressors (warming, acidification, sea-level rise, UV changes), direct human use, and oil rigs. Stressor inputs into the model come from data sets for years ranging from 1981 to 2013. The sensitivity of each ecosystem type to each stressor was determined by surveying 135 experts from 19 countries, and these sensitivities were used to weight the impacts of the stressors in different areas of the ocean. Modeling the vulnerability of ecosystems is challenging for many reasons. Ecosystem response to different stressors is often simplified for model development and the combined effects of multiple stressors on an ecosystem are not always well-understood. Additionally, relevant data may be missing or contain errors. Ignoring this uncertainty can lead to poor ocean management decisions. This map identifies regions of the oceans with high and low human impacts that were robust to these uncertainties, meaning that these areas were identified as being highly or minimally impacted by humans in simulations run over a range of plausible ecological conditions. Seven different factors of uncertainty were tested in 3000 simulations, each of which produced a map of the human impact on different parts of the ocean. Within each map, the 25% of ocean areas with the highest and lowest human impacts, respectively, were identified. The number of times each grid cell was categorized as a high-impact area or a low-impact area was counted. This map shows grid cells that were identified in each category in 75-90% of the simulation runs (High/Low Impact Likely) and in over 90% of the simulation runs (High/Low Impact Very Likely). description: ### Overview This dataset shows the change in the global extent of mangroves between 1996 and 2016. Comparable maps of mangrove gain and loss (corresponding to smaller timesteps) were part of the creation of the first global map of mangrove extent produced via an automated, reproducible, and globally consistent methodology, which used a combination of optical and radar satellite data. The data have an effective resolution of approximately 25 meters at the equator. Mangroves are forested intertidal ecosystems that perform critical landscape-level functions related to the regulation of freshwater, nutrients, and sediment inputs into marine areas. They play a key role in helping to control the quality of marine coastal waters. Mangroves are of critical importance as breeding and nursery sites for birds, fish, and crustaceans. Additionally, they constitute important sinks for carbon storage. Once abundant along the world’s tropical and subtropical coastlines, mangroves are in global decline. Significant drivers of change include removal for aquaculture, agriculture, energy exploitation and other industrial development, with an unknown proportion of the remaining mangroves fragmented and degraded. Mangroves are also sensitive to climate change effects such as sea level rise, temperature extremes, and changes in hydrology. The underlying mangrove extent dataset has been generated by the [Global Mangrove Watch (GMW)](https://www.globalmangrovewatch.org) – a collaboration between Aberystwyth University (U.K.), solo Earth Observation (soloEO), Wetlands International, the World Conservation Monitoring Centre (UNEP-WCMC) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). DOB Ecology supported the mapping in Africa through the Mangrove Capital Africa project. ### Methodology The net extent change in global mangrove area from 1996 to 2016 was calculated by comparing the [global mangrove extent maps](https://data.unep-wcmc.org/datasets/45) provided by [Global Mangrove Watch (GMW)](https://www.globalmangrovewatch.org) for the corresponding years. **1996 and 2016 extent maps:** To develop the 1996 and 2016 mangrove extent maps, GMW first created a baseline map of mangroves for 2010 at a global level through a random forests classification of both Landsat sensor spectral composite data (all spectral wavebands) and Advanced Land Observing Satellite (ALOS) Phased Arrayed L-band Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data.The classification was confined using a mangrove habitat mask, which defined regions where mangrove ecosystems can be expected to exist. The mangrove habitat definition was generated based on geographical parameters such as latitude, elevation, and distance from ocean water. Training for the habitat mask and classification of the 2010 mangrove mask was based on randomly sampling 38 million points using historical mangrove maps (for the year 2000) of Giri et al. (2011) and Spalding et al. (2010) and the water occurrence layer defined by Pekel et al. (2017). The maps for 1996 and 2016 were derived by detection and classification of losses (defined as a decrease in radar backscatter) and gains (defined as a backscatter increase) between the 2010 ALOS PALSAR data and JERS-1 SAR (1996) and ALOS-2 PALSAR-2 (2016) data. The change pixels for each year in question were then added or removed from the 2010 baseline raster mask (buffered to allow detection of mangrove gains also immediately outside of the mask) to produce the new extent maps. Classification accuracies of the changes were assessed with over 45,000 points, with an overall accuracy of 75.0%. **1996–2016 mangrove extent change map:** WRI derived the 1996 to 2016 extent change map by directly comparing the corresponding extent layers provided by GMW (rather than combining the change layers calculated by the authors). This comparison was performed by calculating the geometric intersection of the 1996 and 2016 extent layers. The intersection was erased from the 1996 extent to obtain loss polygons and erased from the 2016 extent to obtain gain polygons. description: ### Overview This dataset shows the locations of dams and the areas covered by the reservoirs that they create upstream. The information used to create this dataset is compiled from a variety of sources, creating a global, harmonized account of dams and reservoirs. The current version maps 7,320 dams that were built as recently as 2017, with a combined storage capacity of 6,864 km³. These include reservoirs with a storage capacity of more than 0.1 km³; smaller dams and reservoirs were added if data was available. The production of this dataset was led by a consortium of partners through the Global Water System Project (GWSP) in Bonn, Germany, and is a joint project of the Earth System Science Partnership (ESSP). ### Methodology Datasets were contributed by 11 participating institutions to serve as the foundation for creating the first version of this dataset. The current version of the dataset adds new dams and reservoirs that were mostly derived from data sources available online. These included national repositories, the Clean Development Mechanism project registry of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), some privately maintained databases like Roller Compacted Concrete Dams, and, for validation purposes, information listed by the International Commission on Large Dams (ICOLD). To consolidate the datasets and improve accuracy, the locations of all dams included in the source datasets were verified, updated, and/or newly georeferenced. This process was guided by maps, atlases, and online resources (including Google Earth). Each dam (with a few exceptions, see source [methodology](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1890/100125)) was assigned to a polygon that depicts the reservoir surface. In the first version of the dataset, most polygons used for this procedure were provided by the SRTM Water Body Database (SWBD), a near-global, public mapping product created at 30 m resolution from remote sensing imagery. Additional reservoir outlines were added from various alternative sources or digitized from scratch. In the newest version of the dataset, most of the new reservoir polygons that were added were delineated from the surface water maps produced by the Joint Research Center (JRC) of the European Commission from Landsat imagery at 30 m resolution for the period 1984-2015. Cross-validation of the information provided by different sources was performed, and records with suspicious information were flagged and individually verified. Data gaps were filled by comparing and merging attributes from different databases. If inconsistencies, uncertainties, or data gaps remained, the “Quality” index of the record was lowered accordingly. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1890/100125). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Frost Free Season
description: Frost free season represents the annual average longest streak of days above freezing, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

title: Aqueduct Seasonal Variability
description: ### Overview Seasonal variability measures the average within-year variability of available water supply, including both renewable surface and groundwater supplies. Higher values indicate wider variations of available supply within a year. These values were then converted into risk scores based on the thresholds defined in the methodology. These risk scores range from low variability (coefficient of variation <0.33) to extremely high variability (coefficient of variation >1.33). Seasonal variability values are available per sub-basin (HydroBASIN level 6). ### Methodology Aqueduct used the global hydrological model, PCRaster Global Water Balance (PCR-GLOBWB 2), to calculate five indicators. Seasonal variability is one of those indicators and was calculated using the available water supply time series from the default PCR-GLOBWB 2. Seasonal or within-year variability is defined as the coefficient of variation (CV) of available water between months in a year for each sub-basin. The CV was calculated by dividing the standard deviation (SD) of the available water supply within a year by the year’s mean available water supply. Finally, raw baseline seasonal variability were converted to risk scores between 0 and 5, based on quantiles. These scores were placed into categories indicating how high the risk for this indicator is. The thresholds for raw seasonal variability values and the corresponding risk scores that were used in each category are defined below as Risk Category (Risk Scores): Raw Value Thresholds. - Low (0-1): < 0.33 - Low to medium (1-2): 0.33 - 0.66 - Medium to high (2-3): 0.66 - 1.0 - High (3-4): 1.0 - 1.33 - Extremely high (4-5): > 1.33 For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/aqueduct-30). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Tree Cover Loss
description: This data set, a collaboration between the GLAD (Global Land Analysis & Discovery) lab at the University of Maryland, Google, USGS, and NASA, measures areas of tree cover loss across all global land (except Antarctica and other Arctic islands) at approximately 30 × 30 meter resolution. The data were generated using multispectral satellite imagery from the Landsat 5 thematic mapper (TM), the Landsat 7 thematic mapper plus (ETM+), and the Landsat 8 Operational Land Imager (OLI) sensors. Over 1 million satellite images were processed and analyzed, including over 600,000 Landsat 7 images for the 2000-2012 interval, and more than 400,000 Landsat 5, 7, and 8 images for updates for the 2011-2017 interval. The clear land surface observations in the satellite images were assembled and a supervised learning algorithm was applied to identify per pixel tree cover loss. In this data set, “tree cover” is defined as all vegetation greater than 5 meters in height, and may take the form of natural forests or plantations across a range of canopy densities. Tree cover loss is defined as “stand replacement disturbance,” or the complete removal of tree cover canopy at the Landsat pixel scale. Tree cover loss may be the result of human activities, including forestry practices such as timber harvesting or deforestation (the conversion of natural forest to other land uses), as well as natural causes such as disease or storm damage. Fire is another widespread cause of tree cover loss, and can be either natural or human-induced. This data set has been updated five times since its creation, and now includes loss up to 2017 (Version 1.5). The analysis method has been modified in numerous ways, including new data for the target year, re-processed data for previous years (2011 and 2012 for the Version 1.1 update, 2012 and 2013 for the Version 1.2 update, and 2014 for the Version 1.3 update), and improved modelling and calibration. These modifications improve change detection for 2011-2017, including better detection of boreal loss due to fire, smallholder rotation agriculture in tropical forests, selective losing, and short cycle plantations. Eventually, a future “Version 2.0” will include reprocessing for 2000-2010 data, but in the meantime integrated use of the original data and Version 1.5 should be performed with caution. title: Air Quality: Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) Station Forecasts
description: ### Overview The Air Quality: Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) Station Forecasts dataset provides air quality forecasts for a group of cities taking part in the [CityAQ project](https://airquality.gsfc.nasa.gov/cityaq-pilot-combine-local-monitoring-data-geos-cf-model-outputs-develop-city-scale-operational). Fine particulate matter (PM2.5) concentrations are forecasted at the station level, and are shown in micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³). The dataset is updated daily and shows the forecasted concentration of PM2.5 for the following five days. The forecast is generated by the source at an hourly time step, and Resource Watch aggregates to a 24-hour average. PM2.5 are fine inhalable particles, with diameters that are generally 2.5 micrometers and smaller. These particles come in many sizes and shapes and can be made up of hundreds of different chemicals. Some are emitted directly from a source, such as construction sites or smokestacks, while others are created from complex reactions in the atmosphere. According to the [U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)](https://www.epa.gov/pm-pollution/particulate-matter-pm-basics) the size of these particles allows them to get deep into the lungs, and some may even go into the bloodstream. The CityAQ project aims to help cities around the world to know more about the levels, sources, and impacts of air pollution. Many of the places with the highest level of pollution have the least information to work with to know their air quality and manage it accordingly. Free and publicly-available air quality data from satellites, along with low-cost sensor systems and output from air quality models, have the potential to augment high-quality, regulatory-grade data in countries with in situ monitoring networks and provide much needed air quality information in countries without them. By combining the strengths of these multiple monitoring technologies, an integrated air pollution network has the potential to provide free/low cost and publicly-accessible air quality information to health and air quality managers in cities around the world. These forecasts were modeled by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO) by combining local air quality monitoring information, made available with support from the World Resources Institute (WRI), with the outputs of NASA’s global Goddard Earth Observing System Composition Forecast (GEOS-CF). The CityAQ project objective is to provide participating cities with useful forecasts that they can use to anticipate air quality events, communicate with stakeholders, and manage local interventions more effectively. It looks to test and refine a methodology for combining locally held information with globally consistent analysis to offer new local tools and, in the future, potentially improve global analysis by aggregating fragmented local data into programmatically useful datasets and make the GEOS-CF forecasts usable by all world cities. The organizations involved in the CityAQ project aim to refine a scalable approach for engaging with users to co-create air quality tools that leverage and extend existing scientific analysis. ### Methodology Validated or raw station level measurement data is collected from either government sites or [OpenAQ](https://openaq.org/#/). Validated air quality observations of government sites were obtained from the air quality data portals of [Bogotá](http://rmcab.ambientebogota.gov.co/home/map) and [Sao Paulo](https://servicos.cetesb.sp.gov.br/qa/), or in the case of the Mexican cities of Monterrey, Guadalajara, Salamanca and León were shared directly by state governments. Near-real time, raw observations for the cities of Addis, Jakarta, as well as the following cities in the mexican state of Guanajuato: Guanajuato city, Irapuato, San Miguel de Allende, Silao, Celaya, San Luis de la Paz and Abasolo were retrieved from OpenAQ. For station-level data to be included in OpenAQ’s catalogue, it must meet the minimum data requirements as described by [OpenAQ](https://github.com/openaq/openaq-fetch/blob/master/README.md). Meteorological and atmospheric chemistry information at each of the CityAQ stations is obtained from NASA’s GEOS-CF model. GEOS-CF provides global hourly analyses and forecasts of atmospheric composition at 25-kilometer spatial resolution. To produce estimates of aerosol concentrations, the GEOS-CF model runs two aerosol schemes: the GEOS-Chem aerosol mechanism (GCC) and the Goddard Chemistry, Aerosol, Radiation, and Transport (GOCART) module to simulate the effects of aerosols in the atmosphere. Any correlation between cloud cover and surface PM2.5 should be captured similarly by GCC and GOCART. The PM2.5 dataset shown on Resource Watch is produced by the GCC module. A detailed description of GEOS-CF can be found in [Keller et al. (2021)](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1029/2020MS002413). Since the model output is too coarse to resolve fine-scale air quality features characteristic of urban environments, a bias-correction algorithm is applied to account for the spatial representation error, as well as other potential model biases such as errors in the model representation of transport or chemistry. The bias-correction methodology uses the [XGBoost machine learning algorithm](https://xgboost.readthedocs.io/en/latest/#) to develop a machine learning model that predicts the model bias at each of the observation stations as a function of the current meteorological and chemical environment and time. Once trained, the machine learning model is used on a daily basis to calculate the expected model bias at a given site and this value is added to the ‘raw’ (i.e., uncorrected) GEOS-CF predictions. The machine learning training is based on the 2018–2019 observation–model differences and designed to predict the systematic model bias between hourly PM2.5 observations and the model predictions at that location. These biases can be due to errors in the model, such as emission estimates, sub-grid-scale local influences or meteorology and chemistry. Since model biases are often site-specific, a separate machine learning model is used for each site. The input features to the machine learning algorithm encompass 9 meteorological parameters (as simulated by the GEOS-CF model: surface northward and eastward wind components, surface temperature and skin temperature, surface relative humidity, total cloud coverage, total precipitation, surface pressure, and planetary boundary layer height) and the modeled surface concentrations of 51 chemical species (O3, NOx, carbon monoxide, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and aerosols). In addition, it provides as input features the hour-of-day, day of week, and month of the year; these allow the machine learning model to identify systematic observation-model mismatches related to the diurnal, weekly and seasonal cycle of the pollutants. This bias correction methodology is based on [Keller et al. (2021)](https://acp.copernicus.org/articles/21/3555/2021/). For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows CityAQ datasets for [ozone (O₃)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/403726e5-6852-49f4-9dce-b82b599b09fc) and [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/8ee6a93b-ab7a-41a8-95f5-3d684626d9ea). title: Projected Change in Frost Free Season (RCP4.5)
description: The Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset shows the change in annual average frost free season at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. A frost free season is the largest number of consecutive days in a year where the minimum daily temperatures are above 32 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the frost free season in 2000 is actually an average of the annual frost free seasons between the years 1985 and 2015. Frost free season projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP). RCP 4.5 is a stabilization scenario where total radiative forcing is stabilized around 2050 by employment of a range of technologies and strategies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The change in frost free season is shown as the number of days difference between the frost free season during the projected decade and the baseline time period. The dataset is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.25°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. In particular, it can be used to understand and adapt to changing agricultural growing seasons and productivity in individual regions. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference. The annual average frost free season for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting daily minimum temperature values for a given year and finding the largest number of consecutive days where the minimum temperature exceeded 32°F. The average annual frost free seasons were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then the baseline average was subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in dry spells The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the frost free season in 2000 is actually an average of the annual frost free seasons between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.

title: Availability of Animal Based Foods
description: As nations urbanize and citizens become wealthier, people generally increase the share of resource-intensive foods—such as meats and dairy—in their diets. Although some of this shift reflects health and welfare gains for many people, shifts to high-meat diets will make it harder for the world to achieve several of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, including those on hunger, healthy lives, water management, climate change, and terrestrial ecosystems. The availability of animal based foods data here represent retail-level availability of animal-based foods (meat, dairy, fish, eggs) per capita per day across the world, from 1961-2013, with a "business as usual" projection, RCP 8.5, out to 2050. Data for 1961-2013 are from FAO's Food Balance Sheets. Data for 2050 are from FAO's projection of food demand and production. Because FAO projects that sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia in 2050 will still have insufficient calories to feed everyone adequately, WRI adjusted food amounts upward in those two regions to ensure 3,000 calories are available per person per day in all regions. Data for 2014-2050 are linear interpolations between observed (2013) and projected (2050) data. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: U.S. Billion-Dollar Disasters
description: The National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) is the Nation's Scorekeeper in terms of addressing severe weather and climate events in their historical perspective. As part of its responsibility of monitoring and assessing the climate, NCEI tracks and evaluates climate events in the U.S. and globally that have great economic and societal impacts. NCEI is frequently called upon to provide summaries of global and U.S. temperature and precipitation trends, extremes, and comparisons in their historical perspective. Found here are Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters: the weather and climate events that have had the greatest economic impact from 1980 to 2018. The U.S. has sustained 233 weather and climate disasters since 1980 where overall damages/costs reached or exceeded $1 billion (including Consumer Price Index adjustment to 2018). The total cost of these 233 events exceeds $1.5 trillion. Please note that the map reflects a summation of billion-dollar events for each state affected (i.e., it does not mean that each state shown suffered at least $1 billion in losses for each event).
