description: OpenAQ is an open-source project to surface live, real-time air quality data from around the world. Its “mission is to enable previously impossible science, impact policy and empower the public to fight air pollution.” The data include air pollutant measurements for PM10, PM2.5, sulfur dioxide (SO₂), carbon monoxide (CO), nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), ozone (O₃), and black carbon (BC), from over 5,400 locations in 48 countries as of June 2017. Scientists, researchers, developers, and citizens can use these data to understand how air quality in different locations changes over time. OpenAQ has 5 criteria for including data sources in its platform: 1. Data must represent one of these pollutant types: PM10, PM2.5, SO₂, CO, NO₂, O₃, or BC. 2. Data must be from an official-level stationary, outdoor air quality source, defined as data produced by a government entity or international organization. 3. Data must be "raw" and reported in physical concentrations on their originating site. 4. Data must be at the "station-level," not aggregated into a higher (e.g., city) level. 5. Data must be from measurements averaged between 10 minutes and 24 hours. For more information on OpenAQ, see its article in Medium: https://medium.com/@openaq/where-does-openaq-data-come-from-a5cf9f3a5c85. The most recent OpenAQ data are also available as a public data set on Google BigQuery: https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/public-data/openaq.

title: Air Quality: Carbon Monoxide (CO) Satellite Measurements
description: ### Overview The Air Quality: CO Satellite Measurements dataset provides global monthly averages of carbon monoxide (CO) densities in the total atmospheric column. Each value shown in the dataset represents the density of CO found between Earth’s surface and the top of the atmosphere. The CO density is reported with units of moles of CO per square meter of air (mol/m²). Carbon monoxide (CO) is a colorless, odorless gas that can be harmful when inhaled in large amounts. CO is released during combustion, so the largest outdoor sources of CO are cars, trucks and other vehicles, and machinery that burn fossil fuels. Breathing air with a high concentration of CO reduces the amount of oxygen that can be transported in the bloodstream to critical organs like the heart and brain. At very high levels, which are possible indoors or in other enclosed environments, CO can cause dizziness, confusion, unconsciousness, and death. Very high levels of CO are not likely to occur outdoors. However, when CO levels are elevated outdoors it can be of particular concern to people with preexisting heart disease. These people already have a reduced ability for getting oxygenated blood to their heart. They are especially vulnerable to the effects of CO when exercising or under increased stress. In these situations, short-term exposure to elevated CO may result in reduced oxygen to the heart accompanied by chest pain also known as angina. The dataset is made up of data collected from the Sentinel-5 Precursor (S5p) mission, a low Earth orbit polar satellite system.The S5p mission is part of the Global Monitoring of the Environment and Security (GMES/COPERNICUS) space component program headed by the European Commission (EC) in partnership with the European Space Agency (ESA). Its goal is to provide information and services on air quality, climate, and the ozone layer. The S5p mission includes the TROPOspheric Monitoring Instrument (TROPOMI), which takes daily global observations of key atmospheric components, such as CO, at a 5.5 x 3.5 kilometer (km) resolution. Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-NO), [ozone (O₃)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-O), and [absorbing aerosol index (AAI)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-AER-AI). ### Methodology The TROPOMI CO dataset was created with data collected by the S5P satellite mission. CO data was collected by determining the amount of sunlight reflected by the troposphere in the 2.3 µm spectral range of the solar spectrum. A spectral range is the range of light wavelengths that a specific spectrometer can measure and in this case it refers to the wavelength of light that CO molecules produce in the atmosphere. The CO data collected using this method was then input into the Shortwave Infrared CO Re- trieval (SICOR) algorithm created by the Netherlands Institute for Space Research. Along with CO data, the following information was input into SICOR: - Relative profile of CO and water in the atmosphere for a given region - Solar/viewing geometry and geo-location of the S5P satellite - Temperature, water vapor/pressure profiles, and geo-potential height of the S5P satellite - Estimate of methane (CH₄) abundance as calculated by the TM5-MP global chemistry transport model CH₄ estimates were required as CH₄ is used to help filter out the presence of clouds in the model. The algorithm further takes into consideration cloud cover by changing the column sensitivity (altering the minimal amount of light reflection within the column required to determine CO density) according to the light path created by cloud cover. The final results produced by the algorithm were tropospheric vertical column density of CO and the average CO density for the entire vertical column. The dataset shown on Resource Watch was mapped by the Google Earth Engine team using the [harpconvert] (https://cdn.rawgit.com/stcorp/harp/master/doc/html/harpconvert.html) tool. For more information on this conversion please see the Google Earth Engine documentation. The offline version of this data is displayed on Resource Watch, which is more complete than its near real-time counterpart, but is released on a greater delay due to the additional processing time needed. For the full documentation, please see the [source methodology](https://sentinel.esa.int/web/sentinel/technical-guides/sentinel-5p/products-algorithms) associated with the “Carbon Monoxide (CO) Total Column”. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-NO), [ozone (O₃)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-O), and [absorbing aerosol index (AAI)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-AER-AI). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for formaldehyde (CH₂O), sulphur dioxide (SO₂), methane (CH₄) and clouds are available from the data provider. Both a near real-time and an offline version of each of these compounds are available. Please see the [Google Earth Engine data catalog](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/tags/tropomi) to access this data. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. title: Gini Index
description: ### Overview The Gini index measures economic inequality in a country. Specifically, it is the extent to which the distribution of income (or, in some cases, consumption expenditure) deviates from a perfectly equal distribution among individuals or households within an economy. A Gini index of 0 represents perfect equality, while an index of 100 implies perfect inequality. The Gini index dataset was released by the World Bank. This data is reported at a national level with global coverage. Data is updated annually and is available for the years 1967-present, though most countries only have data for a subset of these years. ### Methodology The Gini Index was calculated from the World Bank’s internationally comparable poverty monitoring database, which draws on income or detailed consumption data from more than 1,000 household surveys across 138 countries in 6 regions and 21 other high-income countries (industrialized economies). To calculate the Gini index, a Lorenz curve plots the cumulative percentages of total income received against the cumulative number of recipients, starting with the poorest individual or household. The Gini index measures the area between the Lorenz curve and a hypothetical (45-degree) line of absolute equality, expressed as a percentage of the maximum area under the line. For full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SI.POV.GINI/). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Agro-Ecological Zones
description: ### Overview The Global Agro-Ecological Zoning version 4 (GAEZ v4) dataset assesses current and future agricultural resources and their potential. It is a standardized framework allowing for the characterization of climate, soil, and terrain conditions that are relevant for agricultural production. Data from the First Theme, Land and Water Resources, is displayed here and allows for the uniform classification of [biophysical](https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english/biophysics) resources that are relevant for agricultural production systems. Outputs are presented at 5 arc minutes resolution, which is approximately 9 km x 9 km at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. ​​Information on the current and future use of land resources is important for agricultural decision-making with implications on food security, sustainability of land and water resources, and agricultural development and policies. The GAEZ v4 dataset brings together multiple data sources to provide information on the biophysical limitations of land, current crop suitability, and information on how different agricultural resources may be impacted by climate change. Understanding what changes may occur in the future will enable different actors the ability to increase resilience, develop techniques or policies to alleviate potential challenges, and maintain food security. The Food and Agricultural Organization of the United Nations (FAO) together with the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) began developing the GAEZ modeling framework in the early 1980s to provide current data on the state of agricultural resources. It has since expanded to support sustainable agricultural development and provide key information on current and future risks to agricultural production, crop development, land productivity, and impacts from climate change. ### Methodology Multiple datasets were used as inputs to the GAEZ v4 modeling framework and provide data on historic and future climate attributes, soil and terrain resources, land cover, protected land, biodiversity areas, water resources, administrative units, population, and livestock. Historical climate data comes from the Climatic Research Unit TS v3.21 datasets which include monthly climate information. Future climate data for AEZ is derived from climate model outputs for four (2.6, 4.5, 6, 8.5) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) from the fifth Assessment Report (AR5) of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. Data processing was broken into several steps and seven main modules summarize the necessary steps within the GAEZ v4 modeling framework. Outputs from each of the modules are categorized into six main themes: 1) Land and Water Resources, 2) Agro-climatic Resources, 3) Agro-climatic Potential Yield, 4) Suitability and Attainable Yield, 5) Actual Yields and Production, and 6) Yield and Production Gaps. The Agro-Ecological Zones (AEZ) sub-theme outputs fall under the first Theme, Land and Water Resources, and provides an inventory of land resources for the assessment of land productivity under specific agro-ecological conditions. Thermal and moisture layers are combined with broad categories of soil and terrain qualities allowing for the identification of land areas with biophysical constraints. A rigorous methodology and set of explicit principles are followed to assemble the AEZ classes and definitions. The following principles ensure that: 1) the map classes align with major climate zones based on the baseline historical period of 1981-2010, 2) map classes reflect broad ranges of the length of growing period boundaries, and 3) AEZ classes have generalized information about the prevailing soil and terrain limitations that are derived from GAEZ v4 terrain and soil resources inventories. The final AEZ layer has 57 different classes that are mapped at a spatial resolution of 5 arc minutes (approximately 9 km at the equator). For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.fao.org/3/cb4744en/cb4744en.pdf). ### Additional Information Our data catalog shows only a subset of the dataset. The Global Agro-Ecological Zoning version 4 Agro-Ecological Zones data has additional data for 2071-2100 and additional RCPs (2.6 and 6). For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on WRI’s data catalog. See the documentation on how we retrieved the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/blob/master/foo_068_rw0_agro_ecological_zones/). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: Average Temperature
description: Annual average temperature, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

title: [Archived] Urban Heat Island Effect
description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](f05fde43-ce5a-4910-83b1-85dafd39bfbb) as a replacement.**_ The Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect represents the relatively higher temperatures found in urban areas compared to surrounding rural areas owing to higher proportions of impervious surfaces and the release of waste heat from vehicles and heating and cooling systems. Paved surfaces and built structures tend to absorb shortwave radiation from the sun and release long-wave radiation after a lag of a few hours. The Global Urban Heat Island Data Set, 2013, estimates the land surface temperature in urban areas in degrees Celsius (average summer daytime maximum and average summer nighttime minimum) as well as the difference between those temperatures and the temperatures in surrounding rural areas, defined as a 10 km buffer around the urban extent. Urban extents are from SEDAC’s Global Rural-Urban Mapping Project, Version 1 (GRUMPv1), and land surface temperatures are from SEDAC’s Global Summer Land Surface Temperature (LST) Grids, 2013, which are derived from the Aqua Level-3 Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS), Version 5, global daytime and nighttime Land Surface Temperature (LST) 8-day composite data (MYD11A2). For most regions, the UHI data set provides the average daytime maximum (1:30 p.m. overpass) and average nighttime minimum (1:30 a.m. overpass) temperatures in urban and rural areas, and the urban-rural temperature differences, derived from LST data representing a 40-day time span during July-August (Julian days 185-224) in the Northern Hemisphere and January-February (Julian days 001-040) in the Southern Hemisphere. title: Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature (RCP8.5)
description: The Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature dataset shows the change in annual average maximum temperature at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average maximum temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the maximum temperature between the years 1985 and 2015. Average maximum temperature projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP). RCP 4.5 is a stabilization scenario where total radiative forcing is stabilized around 2050 by employment of a range of technologies and strategies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.25°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference. The annual average maximum temperature for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting and averaging all daily maximum temperature data over a given year. The average annual maximum temperatures were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in annual average maximum temperature. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average maximum temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the annual maximum temperatures between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](4d2d47c1-fed1-4484-83e3-c91c3f6f7315) as a replacement.**_ The University of Notre Dame Global Adaptation Initiative (ND-GAIN) produces an annual index of climate change adaptation potential annually from 1995 to 2015. A country's ND-GAIN score is composed of a vulnerability score and a readiness score. Vulnerability and readiness are based on compiled indicators. Vulnerability measures a country's exposure, sensitivity, and capacity to adapt to the negative effects of climate change. ND-GAIN measures overall vulnerability by considering 6 life-supporting sectors—food, water, health, ecosystem service, human habitat, and infrastructure—and 36 indicators. Readiness measures a country's ability to leverage investments and convert them to adaptation actions. ND-GAIN measures overall readiness by considering 3 components—economic readiness, governance readiness, and social readiness—and 9 indicators. Each indicator comes from a public data source. title: Environmental Performance Index
description: The Environmental Performance Index (EPI), produced by the Yale Center for Environmental Law and Policy (YCELP) and the Columbia University Earth Institute Center for International Earth Science Information Network (CEISIN), scores countries from 0 to 100 according to each country's relative performance on a set of environmental indicators. High scorers exhibit long-standing policies and programs to protect public health, preserve natural resources, and decrease greenhouse gas emissions. The index is built from 32 national-level indicators relevant to environmental issues, grouped into 11 issues, which are themselves divided into 2 overarching themes: (1) ecosystem vitality and (2) environmental health as it applies to human health. Multiple other data sets were employed to provide context before whittling down to those 32. Each country's value for each indicator is scaled between 0 and 100 to reflect the proximity of its performance in that indicator to best and worst performances. The best performance can either be a statistical measure—such as the 95th percentile of the distribution of all countries' scores—or a scientifically determined target, such as the World Health Organization's designation of safe and dangerous amounts of particulate matter 2.5 (PM2.5) in the air we breathe. Setting the target for worst performance follows a similar logic. 1st or 5th percentile was often used depending on the distribution of the underlying data. The 32 indicators, each scored between 0 and 100, are then weighted and aggregated to produce the overall EPI score for a country. The weights used to calculate EPI scores reflect a mixture of emphases determined by subjective best judgment, data quality, and analysis of global trends. A "materiality threshold" is used to determine whether an indicator should count toward a given country's score. Landlocked countries, for example, are not rated according to their marine protected areas or the health of their fisheries. When these indicators are removed, the remaining indicators receive proportionally higher weights in calculating the country total EPI. The datasets used to calculate EPI come from trusted third-party sources like international governing bodies, nongovernmental organizations, and academic research centers. title: Bathymetry
description: ### Overview The Bathymetry dataset is composed of the GEBCO_2019 Grid, which shows terrain elevation around the world, for both land and the ocean floor. It provides global coverage on a 15 arc-second grid. The data values refer to elevations at the center of grid cells in meters. The GEBCO_2019 Grid is the latest global bathymetric product released by the General Bathymetric Chart of the Oceans (GEBCO) and has been developed through the Nippon Foundation-GEBCO [Seabed 2030 Project](https://seabed2030.gebco.net/). This is a collaborative project between the Nippon Foundation of Japan and GEBCO. The Seabed 2030 Project aims to bring together all available bathymetric data to produce the definitive map of the world ocean floor and make it available to all. ### Methodology The grid used Version 1 of the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) 15+ data set as a ‘base’. This dataset is a fusion of land topography with measured and estimated seafloor topography. It is largely based on version 11 of SRTM30+, augmented with the gridded bathymetric data sets developed by the four Seabed 2030 Regional Centers. The Regional Centers compiled gridded bathymetric data sets for their areas of responsibility. These regional grids were then provided to the Global Center. For areas outside of the polar regions, these data sets are in the form of 'sparse grids,' meaning only grid cells that contain data were populated. For the polar regions, complete grids were provided due to the complexities of incorporating data held in polar coordinates. The majority of the work, for the non-polar regions, was done using the 'remove-restore' procedure. This is a two stage process of computing the difference between the new data sets created by regional centers and the 'base' grid SRTM15+. The difference between the datasets was gridded and then added back to the existing 'base' grid. The aim was to achieve a smooth transition between the 'new' and 'base' data sets with minimum disturbance of the existing base data set. The polar and Red Sea datasets were supplied in the form of complete grids and were created using feather blending techniques from GlobalMapper software version 11.0. The compilation of the GEBCO_2019 Grid from these regional data grids, with some additional source data sets, was carried out at the Global Center, with the aim of producing a seamless global terrain model. The global grid consists of 86,400 rows and 43,200 columns, giving 3,732,480,000 data points. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for the Type Identifier Grid (TID) is available from the data provider. The TID identifies the type of source data that the corresponding grid cells in the GEBCO Grid are based on. title: Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation
description: ### Overview The Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation dataset shows the change in annual average total precipitation at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the total precipitation in 2000 is actually an average of the cumulative precipitation between the years 1985 and 2015. Precipitation projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. Cumulative average precipitation is divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change. Values greater than 1 indicate that cumulative precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. Data is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.25°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation dataset provides projections on how precipitation patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. Precipitation changes are projected to be more varied across the world, generally showing increases in mean precipitation in high-latitude regions and a pole-ward shift of subtropical arid regions. In addition, precipitation is projected to occur in fewer, but more intense events. Except in the few areas that are projected to see substantial drying, historically extreme precipitation events are expected to become more frequent worldwide. Even as precipitation increases, dry periods are projected to increase in length and frequency. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. ### Methodology The Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation dataset was created with precipitation data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference. The cumulative precipitation for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by adding all daily precipitation data over a given year. The cumulative precipitations were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then each of the nine projected decades were divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change in cumulative precipitation. Values greater than 1 indicate that cumulative precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that cumulative precipitation is decreasing. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the cumulative precipitation in 2000 was calculated as an average of the cumulative precipitation between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows projected change NEX-GDDP RCP 8.5 data for [Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/4ca6826c-718d-457d-b4e2-e9277d7ed62c), [Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3d8e2e82-b33a-4898-90e5-6e4a1d007b82), [Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c4b12251-2d61-458f-a2c0-096c37901ade), [Projected Change in Heating Degree Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/1d2f4eae-10e1-4ea6-980c-501b34106de2), [Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6fa000b5-8d91-46c8-8502-07427bc5eafc), [Projected Change in Frost Free Season](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d3f512c0-fbb0-47d5-9ac9-a452574c8e58), [Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3941bbba-181b-434a-84c3-fcdfa5234735), [Projected Change in Dry Spells](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d0f46576-411d-48aa-8df8-d89a3792cdce), [Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/66d28bbc-1e6e-4156-9ba2-875ecab665af). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data. Additional data is available for emissions scenario RCP 4.5. For access to the original NEX-GDDP dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. title: ene.002 Reservoirs in Time
Bonn Challenge Restoration Commitment
description: This data set displays current commitments to the Bonn Challenge by country. Established in 2011, the Bonn Challenge calls for bringing 150 million ha of the world’s deforested and degraded land into restoration by 2020, and 350 million ha by 2030. Underlying the Bonn Challenge is the forest landscape restoration (FLR) approach, which aims to restore ecological integrity at the same time as improving human well-being through multifunctional landscapes. The Bonn Challenge is not a new global commitment but rather a practical means of realizing many existing international commitments, including the CBD Aichi Target 15, the UNFCCC REDD+ goal, and the Rio+20 land degradation neutrality goal. It is an implementation vehicle for national priorities such as water and food security and rural development while contributing to the achievement of international climate change, biodiversity, and land degradation commitments. The Global Partnership on Forest Landscape Restoration (GPFLR) oversees the initiative, with the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) acting as the secretariat. title: Groundwater Environments and Recharge Rates
description: The German Federal Institute for Geosciences and Natural Resources (BGR) partnered with UNESCO's International Hydrological Programme and the International Association of Hydrogeologists to coordinate the World-wide Hydrogeological Mapping and Assessment Programme (WHYMAP). WHYMAP’s goal is to collect, combine and visualize global hydrogeological data to raise awareness of groundwater resources and promote global discussion on water issues. The Groundwater Environments and Recharge Rates Map is a global map of groundwater resources at a scale of 1:25,000,000 and is used to characterize major groundwater environments and recharge rates. The maps used to characterize groundwater environments were selected by evaluating national, regional and continental maps at scales of 1:1,000,000 to 1:15,000,000. Maps at each of these scales were examined to develop continental maps at a scale of 1:10,000,000, which could then be combined into a global map. Differences in each map’s level of detail, philosophy, approach, hydrogeological interpretation and projection had to be considered when combining these maps. These maps were reviewed and redrawn to improve the consistency of methods for each continent. Hydrogeological mapping experts from different parts of the world contributed their regional knowledge to the final revision of these continental maps before they were combined into a final global map. Groundwater recharge rates represent the years 1961-1990. These values are derived from simulations with the global hydrological model WaterGAP, version 2.1f from the University of Frankfurt/Main, Germany. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: Future Precipitation Suitability for Coffee Growth
description: ### Overview These maps show the probability that annual precipitation will be within or outside the range necessary for the growth of coffee (Coffea arabica), as calculated by researchers at World Resources Institute using a combination of historical satellite data and climate simulations of future precipitation. Users can choose to see probabilities of insufficient precipitation, excessive precipitation, or precipitation within coffee’s required range. Because they are probabilities, pixel values range from 0 to 1. Probabilities are available for any location on the globe, for every 10 years from 2020 to 2099. Gridded data is available at a spatial resolution of 0.25 arc degrees, which is approximately 25 kilometers (km) x 25 km at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. Like all agricultural crops, coffee can grow only in locations that meet particular climatic requirements. Coffee requires between 750 mm and 4200 mm of precipitation every year ([FAO ECOCROP]( https://gaez.fao.org/pages/ecocrop)). As global climate patterns change, the locations suitable for growing coffee are likely to shift. It is impossible to predict with certainty where coffee will and will not be able to be grown in the coming decades, but we are able to estimate the probability that any location is suitable. In these maps, we focus on suitability related to precipitation, but similar maps can be generated for coffee’s (and other crops’) temperature ranges, humidity ranges, and combinations of these factors. These maps were generated by the AgriAdapt team at World Resources Institute to support growers, processors, buyers, and investors in making long-term, climate-smart decisions about crops and growing locations. ### Methodology The probabilities are calculated as Bayesian posterior probabilities that yearlong precipitation falls within or outside the range 750 mm – 4200 mm. The prior probability is taken from historical rainfall as reported in the [ERA5](https://confluence.ecmwf.int/display/CKB/ERA5%3A+data+documentation) reanalysis of satellite data. The prior is updated using the [NEX-GDDP](https://esgf.nccs.nasa.gov/esgdoc/NEX-GDDP_Tech_Note_v0.pdf) downscaled simulation ensemble as evidence. NEX-GDDP includes several greenhouse gas emission scenarios. These calculations used the highest-emitting scenario, RCP8.5. The probability rasters have a spatial resolution of 0.25 arc degrees (approximately 25 km at the equator). The full methodology will be published as a WRI Technical Note (Wong and Mackres, forthcoming). ### Additional Information Our data catalog shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on WRI’s data catalog. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: Human Development Index
description: The Human Development Index (HDI), published by the UN Development Programme (UNDP), is a summary measure of average achievement in key dimensions of human development: a long and healthy life, a sufficient education, and a decent standard of living. The HDI is the geometric mean of normalized indices for each of the 3 dimensions. The health dimension is assessed by life expectancy at birth; the education dimension is measured by mean of years of schooling for adults aged 25 years and more and expected years of schooling for children of school-entering age. The standard-of-living dimension is measured by gross national income per capita. The HDI uses the logarithm of income to reflect the diminishing importance of income with increasing gross national income (GNI). The scores for the 3 HDI dimension indices are then aggregated into a composite index using geometric mean. The HDI is calculated for 188 countries annually. title: Forest and Landscape Restoration Opportunities
description: ### Overview The Forest and Landscape Restoration Opportunities dataset is a global dataset that shows where degraded forest lands have the potential to be restored. The dataset was created in 2011 based on current and historic forest extent data at a spatial resolution of 1 kilometer (km). It presents the results as three different forms of forest restoration: wide-scale, mosaic, and remote. Wide-scale restoration aims to restore closed forests (canopy density greater than 45%) in areas where they previously dominated the landscape. Mosaic restoration integrates trees into mixed-use landscapes, such as agricultural lands and settlements, where trees can support people through improved water quality, increased soil fertility, and other ecosystem services. Remote restoration refers to deforested or degraded forest lands that are completely unpopulated and located far away from human settlements, such as northern Canada and Siberia. The restoration of forest lands provides opportunities to reduce poverty, improve food security, mitigate climate change, and protect biodiversity. More than two billion hectares worldwide, an area larger than South America, can be used for either wide-scale or mosaic-type restoration. In particular, mosaic restoration offers the greatest opportunity for restoration efforts, while also increasing economic benefits and protecting the environment. Furthermore, restoration opportunities are not tied to ongoing deforestation. Most of the opportunities described in the dataset are from landscapes that were deforested a long time ago. The dataset was produced by the World Resources Institute (WRI) in collaboration with the University of Maryland (UMD) and the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) as a contribution to the Global Partnership on Forest Landscape Restoration. It was used as a way to quantify the targets of the [Bonn Challenge](https://www.bonnchallenge.org/), an international project to restore 150 million hectares of lost and degraded forests by 2020. ### Methodology The Forest and Landscape Restoration Opportunities dataset was created in two steps. First, the authors mapped how much forest has been lost. Then, the team mapped the opportunities for forests and trees to return. To determine the amount of forest already lost, potential forest coverage was compared to current forest coverage. **Potential forest coverage** shows the forest coverage that would exist, based on today’s climate, if human influences were not present. It was calculated by combining data on soils, climate, elevation, and maps of historical forest extent. The composition and density of these potential forests were then determined using maps of terrestrial ecoregions depicting the extent of different types of forests in the world. **Current forest coverage** shows the global extent of forest coverage and was created by using two datasets from Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) satellite imagery. The first is a global forest map for the year 2000 to 2009, which was used to map the general extent of forests (South Dakota State University, 2011, unpublished dataset). The second is a [tree canopy density map](https://journals.ametsoc.org/doi/abs/10.1175/1087-3562%282003%29007%3C0001%3AGPTCAA%3E2.0.CO%3B2) derived from MODIS vegetation continuous fields (VCF) data. The potential forest coverage and current forest coverage maps were compared to create a map of current forest conditions. The current forest conditions map shows the state of the world’s forests, including areas of historical forest loss and degradation. It shows intact forest areas, fragmented/managed natural forests (fragmented by roads and/or managed for timber production), degraded forest areas, and deforested areas. Finally, data on forest condition and current land use were used to derive a map of forest landscape restoration opportunities. The current land use datasets include population density, urbanized or industrial areas, and cropland distribution. Urban areas, areas with dense rural populations (> 100 person/km²), cultivated areas, and other intensively used areas were considered as having no or low forest restoration potential because they were too far degraded, developed, or integral for human populations. Areas with scattered cropland areas, pastures, agroforestry and all types of forest plantations were considered as providing promising opportunities for restoration ([Pittman, et al., 2010](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/2/7/1844); [LandScan, 2005](https://web.ornl.gov/sci/landscan/); [GLC2000](https://www.glcn.org/index_en.jsp); [Sanderson, et al., 2002](https://www.bioone.org/doi/abs/10.1641/0006-3568(2002)052%5B0891%3ATHFATL%5D2.0.CO%3B2)). Deforested and degraded forest lands were divided into four categories, resulting in a map of restoration opportunity areas and other former forest lands: - Wide-scale restoration: Aims to restore closed forests (canopy density greater than 45%) in areas where they previously dominated the landscape. - Mosaic restoration: Integrates trees into mixed-use landscapes, such as agricultural lands and settlement. - Remote restoration: Deforested or degraded forest lands that are completely unpopulated and located far away from human settlements, such as northern Canada and Siberia. - Agricultural land (non-restoration areas): Croplands used for food production. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology]( https://www.wri.org/our-work/project/global-restoration-initiative/methodology-about-atlas-forest-landscape-restoration). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for forest condition, current forest coverage, potential forest coverage, human pressure, and Bonn Challenge pledges are available from the data provider. title: DRIP Groundwater Use Model Demo Carto
Climate Hazard Indicators (Annual mean temperatures) Historical and SSP scenarios - Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu
description: ### Overview The dataset includes five major climatic indicators viz. annual values for minimum temperature (℃), maximum temperature (℃), mean temperature (℃), total precipitation (mm/year), and the number of rainy days (represented as integers) for two Indian states, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. It features decadal averages from 2020-2100 for Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs), including SSP5-8.5, which reflects a high emissions scenario, and SSP2-4.5, representing moderate challenges to both mitigation and adaptation. Additionally, the dataset provides historical data for all the five indicators averaged over the period from 2005 to 2014. ### Methodology **Pre-Processing**: The decadal time periods were labeled as follows: 2020-2029 as 2020, 2030-2039 as 2030, 2040-2049 as 2040, 2050-2059 as 2050, 2060-2069 as 2060, 2070-2079 as 2070, 2080-2089 as 2080, and 2090-2099 as 2090. **Layers of interest**: Annual averages of minimum temperature (℃), maximum temperature (℃), mean temperature (℃), Annual total precipitation (mm/year), and the annual total number of rainy days (represented as integers). **Data**: The ERA5 reanalysis dataset (ECMWF 2022), a satellite data product of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts with a spatial resolution of 31 kilometers (km), is used as a reference dataset. The ensemble of downscaled daily time series outputs from global climate models (GCMs). These time series include the historical years covered by the observation time series as well as the specified future years of interest. We have used the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 product, which includes outputs from 34 Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) models at approximately 25 km spatial resolution. ### Estimation Methods Out of the 35 models, we select the top 3 climate models that perform best for a specific weather variable in a particular geographic region, and present the ensemble mean of these models. The ERA5 dataset is used as a reference, and the comparison is made for the historical period between 1980 and 2014. After selecting the models, we apply a calibration/bias correction procedure to the future time series of the models. This involves aligning the model's frequency distribution with the historical data by shifting the percentiles of the model's distribution. For instance, if the 20th percentile of the model data corresponds to the 30th percentile of the observations, then the 30th percentile of the calibrated model data will match the 20th percentile of the uncalibrated model data. For the full documentation, please see the source methodology at Wong, T., and P Switzer. 2023. 'Estimating future local climate hazard probabilities.' Technical Note. Washington, DC: World Resources Institute. Available online at: doi.org/10.46830/writn.22.00074.v2. ### Description of the Layers **Annual Maximum Temperature (℃)**: The daily maximum temperature data for each year is extracted and averaged to calculate the yearly average maximum temperature. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years. **Annual Minimum Temperature (℃)**: The daily minimum temperature data for each year is extracted and averaged to calculate the yearly average minimum temperature. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years. **Annual Mean Temperature (℃)**: The daily mean temperature is calculated by averaging the daily minimum and maximum temperatures. The annual mean temperature is obtained by averaging the daily mean temperatures over the course of a year. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years. **Annual Total Precipitation (mm/year)**: The daily precipitation values are summed over the entire year to calculate the annual total precipitation. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years. **Annual Rainy Days (represented as integers)**: A rainy day is defined as a day with precipitation exceeding 2.5 mm (as per the India Meteorological Department). The total number of rainy days in a year is calculated by summing the rainy days throughout the year. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years. ### Visualizing the Data The data is provided at a 25-km resolution and is presented as a raster with a time slider with a separate layer for each variable. The values are visualized using a gradient based on the selected year in the slider, ranging from lighter shade (indicating low values) to darker shade (representing higher values). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source

title: Oil Pipelines
description: The Global Oil Pipelines data set was assembled by Professor Jeff Blossom of Harvard University's Center for Geographic Analysis for a workshop in 2009. It gives a partial view of installed crude oil, natural gas, and petroleum product pipeline infrastructure as of August 2009. It covers the entire globe. The lines may not exactly match up with actual pipeline coordinates in some areas, as there was uncertainty in the source maps. Pipelines are snapped to source cities, and the paths between cities are slightly stylized while maintaining the general trend of each pipeline's path. title: Carbon Footprint by City
description: The Global Gridded Model of Carbon Footprints (GGMCF), created by the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU), shows a gridded estimate of carbon emissions across 189 countries for the year of 2013 with a 250 square meter resolution. The GGMCF was built in four steps: (1) National Carbon Footprints (CFs) of consumption (*CFn*) for 189 countries covering ~100% of global carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions were taken from the Eora multi-region input-output (MRIO) database for the year 2015. (2) For the EU, UK, USA, Japan, and China, existing subnational CF models were used to disaggregate *CFn* into subnational regions *CFr*, where the regions *r* range in size from postcode to province. In steps 3 and 4 these subnational regions are treated the same as countries. The term 'regions' is used to mean the collection of disaggregated subnational regions plus countries which are not disaggregated. (3) Within each region the *CFr* was disaggregated between urban vs rural residents according to the difference in urban vs rural resident expenditure patterns and the total urban vs rural population. For 76 countries (a mixture of developed and developing coutnries, driving 19% of global CO2 emissions) no comparative expenditure data were available. In these countries all households were assumed to have a national average expenditure pattern. (4) CFs of grid cells within a region were calculated by further disaggregating step 3 using gridded population maps and gridded income data. The first step involved in identifying the urban and rural grid cells and subsequently distributing the total urban and rural footprint on the basis of the share of aggregate purchasing power in each cell. Urban cells were identified using the GHS-SMOD layer of urban areas (high and low density population clusters). GHS-SMOD uses a clustering algorithm to identify urban areas as clusters of contiguous cells within a total population and population density above the specified thresholds. Aggregate purchasing power per grid cell was determined by multiplying the population in the cell by the mean purchasing power at that location. Carbon footprints of cities are then defined as the CF of those cells in teh GHS-SMOD layer that are high-density clusters of contiguous grid cells with ≥1500 inhabitants/km2 and within a minimum population of 50,000. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Projected Annual Average Temperature (RCP4.5)
description: The Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature dataset shows the change in annual average temperature at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the temperature between the years 1985 and 2015. Average temperature projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP). RCP 4.5 is a stabilization scenario where total radiative forcing is stabilized around 2050 by employment of a range of technologies and strategies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.25°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Average Annual Temperature dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference. The annual average temperature for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis using the following steps: All daily low temperature data over a given year was extracted and averaged to produce a yearly average low temperature value. All daily high temperature data over a given year was extracted and averaged to produce a yearly average high temperature value. Average annual temperature was calculated by taking the mean of the average daily temperature over a given year. Average daily temperature was calculated by dividing the sum of daily low temperature and daily high temperature by 2. The average annual temperatures were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in annual average temperature. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the annual average temperatures between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

title: Air Quality: Black Carbon Modeled Next-day Forecast
description: ### Overview This dataset shows forecasted black carbon (BC) concentrations at Earth's surface, modeled by the Whole Atmosphere Community Climate Model (WACCM). Black carbon is a particulate emitted from the incomplete combustion of fossil fuels, biofuels and biomass. Major [sources include](https://www.c2es.org/document/what-is-black-carbon/) diesel engines, coal-fired power plants, cook stoves, wood burning and forest fires. According to the [U.S. Environmental Protection Agency](https://www.epa.gov/air-research/black-carbon-research), black carbon is a “global environmental problem that has negative implications for both human health and our climate.” Inhalation of black carbon is associated with [cardiovascular disease, respiratory problems, cancer, and even birth defects](https://www.epa.gov/air-research/black-carbon-research). Black carbon makes up a significant portion of particulate matter pollution. Although black carbon is not a greenhouse gas, it contributes to climate change in a few ways. Its dark color absorbs solar radiation, which warms up the atmosphere. Black carbon also settles on snow and ice, darkening these surfaces that would normally reflect a lot of solar radiation. According to research published in [Nature Geoscience](https://www.nature.com/articles/ngeo473), black carbon may have caused more than 30% of the recent rapid warming in the Arctic. WACCM creates global forecasts for a variety of other air quality indicators, as well. While this dataset shows forecasted black carbon concentrations, Resource Watch also shows WACCM forecasts for [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-SO), [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-PM-25), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-O), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-NO), and [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-CO). WACCM runs the model daily, and on their website you can find forecasted concentrations for each compound up to nine days into the future at three-hour time steps. WACCM was developed by the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) and the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research (UCAR). The data has global coverage at 1.9 x 2.5 degree resolution. ### Methodology WACCM is a comprehensive numerical model, driven by meteorological fields from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration’s (NASA) Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO) Goddard Earth Observing System Model, Version 5 (GEOS-5) model. The development of WACCM is an inter-divisional collaboration that unifies modeling from the High Altitude Observatory ([HAO](http://www2.hao.ucar.edu/)), the Atmospheric Chemistry Observations and Modeling ([ACOM](https://www2.acom.ucar.edu/)) Laboratory, and the Climate and Global Dynamics ([CGD](http://www2.cgd.ucar.edu/)) Laboratory. Upper atmospheric modeling from HAO, middle atmospheric modeling from ACOM, and tropospheric modeling from CGD are combined using the NCAR [Community Earth System Model (CESM)](http://www.cesm.ucar.edu/) as a common numerical framework. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://opensky.ucar.edu/islandora/object/articles%3A12836). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows WACCM forecasts for [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-SO), [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-PM-25), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-O), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-NO), and [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-CO). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional forecasted data for other compounds, times, and levels of the atmosphere are also produced by WACCM. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/cit_038_waccm_atmospheric_chemistry_model). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: [Archived] FDI Regulatory Restrictiveness Index
description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](10b47089-6457-48b4-a955-60f4f964e0f2) as a replacement.**_ The foreign direct investment (FDI) Regulatory Restrictiveness Index, released by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), measures the restrictiveness of a country’s foreign direct investment (FDI) rules by looking at the 4 main types of restrictions: (1) foreign equity limitations; (2) discriminatory screening or approval mechanisms; (3) restrictions on the employment of foreigners as key personnel; and (4) other operational restrictions, for example, restrictions on branching and on capital repatriation or on land ownership by foreign-owned enterprises. Restrictions are evaluated on a 0 (no restrictions) to 1 (full restrictions) scale. Each restriction will be given a score based on an assessment of its importance. The overall restrictiveness index is the weighted average of sectoral scores. The discriminatory nature of measures, such as when they apply to foreign investors only, is the central criterion for scoring a measure. State ownership and state monopolies, to the extent they are not discriminatory toward foreigners, are not scored. This data set contains 62 countries across 22 sectors and is currently available for the following years: 1997, 2003, 2006, and 2010-2016. For OECD and non-OECD countries who are adherents to the OECD Declaration on International Investment and Multinational Enterprises, information is collected based on countries’ lists of exceptions to national treatment. For the non-OECD countries, information is collected through investment policy reviews. Information is updated on a yearly basis following the OECD Freedom of Investment monitoring of investment measures. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days U.S. (RCP4.5)
description: The Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average days of extreme precipitation at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. An extreme precipitation day is defined as a day where precipitation is greater than the 99th percentile precipitation compared to the baseline period. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of extreme precipitation days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual number of extreme precipitation days between the years 1985 and 2015. Precipitation projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. Days of extreme precipitation are divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change. Values greater than 1 indicate that extreme precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. Data is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and the resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation dataset provides projections on how extreme precipitation patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. Generally, extreme precipitation events are expected to become more frequent worldwide. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation dataset was created with precipitation data from LOCA. The LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference. The annual average extreme precipitation days for each year, climate model, and scenario were calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting the daily precipitation values for a given year and summing the number of days where precipitation was greater than the 99th percentile precipitation during the baseline period. The annual average extreme precipitation days were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then each of the nine projected decades were divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change in extreme precipitation. Values greater than 1 indicate that extreme precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the extreme precipitation days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual extreme precipitation days between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.

title: Social and Economic Dependence on Coral Reefs
description: The social and economic vulnerability data set was produced for the Reefs at Risk project by World Resources Institute (WRI) and classifies the Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZs) for 108 coral reef countries and territories according to an index of their reef dependence, adaptive capacity, and social vulnerability. Results are presented as quartiles, with 27 countries/territories classified in each of 4 categories (low, medium, high, and very high for reef dependence and social vulnerability; very low, low, medium, and high for adaptive capacity). The Reef Dependence index is based on the following inputs: reef-associated population, reef fisheries employment, reef-associated exports, nutritional dependence on fish and seafood, reef-associated tourism, and shoreline protection. The Adaptive Capacity index is based on the following inputs: economic resources, education, health (expressed as life expectancy), governance, access to markets, and agricultural resources. The Social Vulnerability index is the result of the combination of the Reef Dependence index, Adaptive Capacity index, and Exposure to Reef Threats (i.e., the Reefs at Risk integrated local threat index). The Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZs) for uninhabited and sparsely inhabited territories with coral reefs are also included in this shapefile, but are not included in the indices. The purpose of this data set is to provide a comparative analysis of coral reef countries and territories according to their reef dependence, adaptive capacity, and social and economic vulnerability to reef loss. Results were compiled at the national level, or in some cases the subnational level where data were available. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: Areas Vulnerable to Coastal Flooding & Sea Level Rise (m)
description: ### Overview The Areas Likely Flooded by Sea Level Rise dataset shows on a global scale which areas can be flooded at different amounts of water rise due to sea level rise, tide, and storm surge. The map presents sea level rise at 30-Meter, 20-Meter, 10 Meter, 5 Meter, 3-Meter, 2.5 Meter, 2-Meter, 1.5-Meter, 1.0- Meter, 0.5-Meter options. Areas that are inundated at each sea level rise value are masked in blue. The data used for surface elevation was collected from multiple sources that range from satellite imagery to flood maps between 1929 and 2015. The resolution of the dataset varies based on region in the world, with the contiguous United states being the highest resolution at 5 m and much of the rest of the world at 90 m. This dataset was created by Climate Central under their project Surging Seas. It has been cited in over 5,000 articles, highlighted on the front page of the White House Climate Initiative website, and accessed by more than 60 federal agencies. It plays an important role in helping world governments understand the effects of climate change, make policies, and develop tools to effectively help communities in the instance of flooding. ### Methodology The dataset was created by first combining multiple digital elevation models to create global coverage. Elevation data was then altered to be expressed relative to local high tide lines. High tide lines used were the average high tide line based on seasonal and monthly fluctuations (Mean Higher High Water). Next, two layers showing standard ocean water coverage and flood control methods for the United States were applied. Lastly, an algorithm was added to show how water coverage would increase based on different amounts of sea level rise, storm surge, and tides. The “bathtub method” algorithm shows water coverage in all areas below a given water height threshold that is input by the user. The final data was projected using raster and tabular data between 60 degrees north and 56 degrees south. Elevation data for the contiguous United States came from National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA) Coastal Lidar collection at 5 m horizontal resolution and information on Alaska came from the United States Geological Survey (USGS) at 60 m resolution. Elevation data for Antigua and Barbuda, Barbados, Corn Island (Nicaragua), Dominica, Dominican Republic, Grenada, Guyana, Haiti, Jamaica, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, San Blas (Panama), Suriname, The Bahamas, and Trinidad and Tobago came from Climate Central’s CoastalDEM database at 10 m resolution. Data for the rest of the world was taken from NASA’s Shuttle Radar Topography Missions (SRTM) at a resolution of 90 m. High tide data was taken from the VDatum tidal model for the contiguous United States and a global tidal model supplied by Mark Merrifield of the University of Hawaii for the rest of the world. title: U.S. Wildfire Hazard Potential
description: Federal wildfire managers often want to know, over large landscapes, where wildfires are likely to occur and how intense they may be. To meet this need we developed a map that we call wildfire hazard potential (WHP) – a raster geospatial product that can help to inform evaluations of wildfire risk or prioritization of fuels management needs across very large spatial scales (millions of acres). Our specific objective with the WHP map was to depict the relative potential for wildfire that would be difficult for suppression resources to contain. To create the 2014 version, we built upon spatial estimates of wildfire likelihood and intensity generated in 2014 with the Large Fire Simulation system (FSim) for the national interagency Fire Program Analysis system (FPA), as well as spatial fuels and vegetation data from LANDFIRE 2010 and point locations of fire occurrence from FPA (ca. 1992 – 2012). With these data sets as inputs, we produced an index of WHP for all of the conterminous United States at 270 m resolution. We present the final WHP map in two forms: 1) continuous integer values, and 2) five WHP classes of very low, low, moderate, high, and very high. On its own, WHP is not an explicit map of wildfire threat or risk, but when paired with spatial data depicting highly valued resources and assets such as structures or powerlines, it can approximate relative wildfire risk to those specific resources and assets. WHP is also not a forecast or wildfire outlook for any particular season, as it does not include any information on current or forecasted weather or fuel moisture conditions. It is instead intended for long-term strategic fuels management. PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set.
